\subsection{A constructive global extension}

\begin{lemma}[Continuous rational extension with an explicit bound]
\label[lemma]{pqc:cb:lem:extension}
The prescriptions \eqref{pqc:cb:eq:terminal}--\eqref{pqc:cb:eq:active} extend to a continuous
rational \PWA{} map $F:[0,1]^3\to[0,1]^3$.  One such extension has global
sup-norm Lipschitz bound
\begin{equation}
 L=9m+6.
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:construction-L}
\end{equation}
The extension can be computed from the finite transition table using rational
arithmetic alone.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For the $\xi$ axis, use all points $0,1$ and
$\alpha_j+k\beta/3$ for $j=0,\ldots,m-1$ and $k=0,1,2,3$, together with the
endpoints of $I_h^+$ and $I_r^+$.  For each of the $v,z$ axes use
$0,1/3,2/3,1$.  Every prescribed box is a union of cells of this rectilinear
grid.

At each grid vertex belonging to a prescribed box, assign the prescribed
rational image.  The disjointness just proved makes the assignment
unambiguous.  Assign $p_r$ to every remaining vertex.  Subdivide each
rectangular cell by the same coordinate-ordered Kuhn triangulation: after
normalizing its coordinates to a unit cube, use the six regions specified by
an ordering of those coordinates.  Interpolate the vertex values affinely on
each simplex.  Adjacent simplices and adjacent rectangular cells agree on
their common faces, so the result is globally continuous.  Convexity of the
cube keeps every interpolated value in the cube.  On any prescribed box,
affine interpolation reproduces its prescribed affine formula.

Every interval in the $\xi$ grid has length at least $\beta/3=1/(9m)$; the
other two axis intervals have length $1/3$.  Along the chain of vertices of a
Kuhn simplex, successive vertices differ in exactly one coordinate.  Hence
each column of its affine linear part is an image difference divided by that
coordinate's interval length.  Each scalar image difference has absolute
value at most one.  Every row-sum norm is therefore at most
$9m+3+3=9m+6$.  The segment-subdivision argument following \eqref{pqc:cb:eq:lip}
makes this a global bound.
\end{proof}

This extension is not claimed to be differentiable, reversible, injective,
volume-preserving, or a polynomial map.  Its continuity on the entire cube,
including off-encoding states and guard boundaries, is part of the proved
statement.  Merely writing a discontinuous guarded update would not be enough
for the robustness argument.

\subsection{Exact simulation and finite input encoding}

If the initial state is $(\alpha_s+\beta u,v,0)$ with a finite encoded tape,
then every active exact iterate satisfies \eqref{pqc:cb:eq:active}, and its third
coordinate remains zero.  The first two coordinates perform exactly the
binary machine computation.  Entering state $h$ places the image in $H$;
entering state $r$ places it in the rejecting band, whose next image is $p_r$.

For a concrete primitive-recursive input coding, let $b_1\cdots b_k$ be the
ordinary binary expansion of $n$ (use $k=1,b_1=0$ for zero), and take the
self-delimiting word
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf{word}(n)=1^k0b_1\cdots b_k1.
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:word}
\end{equation}
These words are prefix-free and end in a one.  Place the word starting under
the head, put blanks elsewhere, and define
\begin{equation}
 \iota(n)=\left(\alpha_s,
       \sum_{i=0}^{\ell(n)-1}\frac{2\,\mathsf{word}(n)_i}{3^{i+1}},0\right).
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:input}
\end{equation}
The encoding is injective and primitive recursive as a rational map.  Its
values lie outside $H$.  No uncomputable real parameter is present.

\section{The universal trichotomy and its quantitative proof}
\label{pqc:cb:sec:universal}

Fix an effective enumeration $(W_a)_{a\in\N}$ of the \cenum{} subsets of $\N$.
Fix also a primitive-recursive pairing bijection on natural numbers, with
primitive-recursive decoding; the usual Cantor pairing suffices.  We use
$\langle a,b,e\rangle=\langle a,\langle b,e\rangle\rangle$.

Choose a \emph{single} deterministic binary universal interpreter that, on
input $\langle a,b,e\rangle$, dovetails the two semideciders for
$e\in W_a$ and $e\in W_b$.  It accepts if the first succeeds first, rejects
if the second succeeds first, and uses a fixed tie convention.  When $W_a$
and $W_b$ are disjoint the tie convention is immaterial.  A binary, one-tape,
two-sided interpreter exists by the usual finite-alphabet and multitape
simulations; those changes only replace one finite table by another.  Its
finite number $m$ of states is fixed from now on.

Apply \cref{pqc:cb:sec:construction} to this table, and fix its map $F$, target $H$,
input encoding $\iota$, and bound $L=9m+6$ once and for all.

\begin{theorem}[Universal three-dimensional trichotomy]
\label{pqc:cb:thm:universal}
For every disjoint \cenum{} pair $(A,B)=(W_a,W_b)$ and every $e\in\N$, put
$x_e=\iota(\langle a,b,e\rangle)$.  Then
\begin{align}
 e\in A&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Hit(x_e),\label{pqc:cb:eq:realize-A}\\
 e\in B&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\rho_F(x_e,H)>0,\label{pqc:cb:eq:realize-B}\\
 e\notin A\cup B&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Frag(x_e).
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:realize-F}
\end{align}
The map and target do not depend on $a,b,e$; only the rational initial point
changes.  Moreover, on every $e\in B$, all sufficiently small perturbed
trajectories enter the enlarged rejecting slab after finitely many steps and
remain there.
\end{theorem}

We prove a quantitative rejection estimate and the emergency mechanism first.

\begin{lemma}[Positive margin for a rejecting computation]
\label[lemma]{pqc:cb:lem:reject-lower}
Suppose the exact interpreter first enters rejecting state $r$ at time
$T\ge1$.  Put $S_T(L)=\sum_{j=0}^{T-1}L^j$.  No pseudo-orbit whose per-step
error is at most
\begin{equation}
 \varepsilon_T=\frac{\beta}{4S_T(L)}
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:epsilon-T}
\end{equation}
can hit $H$.  Every such pseudo-orbit is in the enlarged rejecting slab at
time $T$ and stays there afterward.  In particular, $\rho_F(x,H)\ge\varepsilon_T$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $y_t=F^t(x)$ be the exact orbit and let $x_t$ be a pseudo-orbit from the same
source.  Up to time $T$, global Lipschitz continuity gives
\[
 \norm{x_{t+1}-y_{t+1}}\le\varepsilon_T+L\norm{x_t-y_t}.
\]
Induction yields $\norm{x_t-y_t}\le\varepsilon_T S_t(L)\le\beta/4$ for
$1\le t\le T$.

Before and at rejection, every exact packed coordinate is in a state interval
other than $I_h$.  Its distance from $I_h$ is at least $2\beta$.  Thus no
$x_t$ for $t\le T$ is in $H$.  At time $T$, the exact packed coordinate belongs
to $I_r$, so the perturbed one is in $I_r^+$, because the enlargement has
margin $\beta/2$ and the error is at most $\beta/4$.

On the entire rejecting slab, $F$ is the constant $p_r$.  Since
$\varepsilon_T\le\beta/4$, the next perturbed packed coordinate remains within
$\beta/4$ of the center of $I_r$ and hence within $I_r^+$.  This argument repeats
forever and the slab is disjoint from $H$.  It is important here that the
terminal rule is constant for all values of the other two coordinates.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Arbitrarily small emergency acceptance]
\label[lemma]{pqc:cb:lem:emergency}
If the exact interpreter never enters either terminal state, then
$\rho_F(x,H)=0$.  If it first rejects at time $T\ge2$, then
\begin{equation}
 \rho_F(x,H)\le2\cdot3^{-(T-1)}.
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:reject-upper}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In an infinite active computation, take the first exact step, but change only
the new emergency coordinate from zero to $2\cdot3^{-N}$, where $N\ge1$.
The cost of this single perturbation is $2\cdot3^{-N}$.  Leave every subsequent
step unperturbed.  While $z\le1/3$, the first two coordinates continue the
exact simulation and $z$ is multiplied by three.  At time $N$ the emergency
coordinate is $2/3$; the next step uses \eqref{pqc:cb:eq:emergency} and reaches $p_h$.
Thus arbitrarily small costs suffice.

For a computation first rejecting at time $T\ge2$, use the same construction
with $N=T-1$.  At time $T-1$ the interpreter is still active and $z=2/3$.
At time $T$, the emergency rule accepts instead of taking the rejecting
instruction.  The total path cost is the single initial perturbation
$2\cdot3^{-(T-1)}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{pqc:cb:thm:universal}]
On exact encoded states the interpreter simulation is correct.  If $e\in A$,
the interpreter accepts, so $\Hit(x_e)$ holds and the radius is zero.  If
$e\in B$, it rejects after a finite time, and \cref{pqc:cb:lem:reject-lower} gives
positive radius and robust entry into the rejecting slab.  If $e$ belongs to
neither set, the interpreter remains active forever.  It never exactly
accepts, while \cref{pqc:cb:lem:emergency} gives radius zero.  These mutually exclusive
cases exhaust all inputs and prove all three equivalences.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The time--radius sandwich]
\label[corollary]{pqc:cb:cor:time-radius}
For a first rejection at time $T\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\beta}{4S_T(L)}\le\rho_F(x,H)
 \le\min\{1,2\cdot3^{-(T-1)}\},
 \quad \beta=\frac1{3m},\quad L=9m+6.
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:time-radius}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The lower bound is \cref{pqc:cb:lem:reject-lower}.  For $T\ge2$, combine
\cref{pqc:cb:lem:emergency} with the universal one-step upper bound $\rho\le1$.
For $T=1$, that one-step bound gives the stated right side directly.
\end{proof}

The constants are deliberately conservative.  Their significance is the
explicit dependence on the actual rejection time, not numerical optimality.
A known lower bound $\rho\ge\delta>0$ implies, for $T\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
 T\le1+\log_3(2/\delta).
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:time-from-radius}
\end{equation}
Thus a certified positive margin carries hidden information about how soon
rejection must have occurred.  It is not surprising that no computable inputwise
positive margin can cover every rejecting input.

\section{Arithmetic classification and limits of finite certificates}
\label{pqc:cb:sec:classification}

For the one fixed universal map, define sets of natural codes
\[
 \mathcal H=\{n:\Hit(\iota(n))\},\qquad
 \mathcal S=\{n:\Safe(\iota(n))\},\qquad
 \mathcal F=\{n:\Frag(\iota(n))\}.
\]
These definitions apply to all codes, even those decoding to overlapping
pairs of enumerable sets.  Their trichotomy follows from the dynamics, not
from the disjoint-pair promise used for the universal realization theorem.

\begin{theorem}[Exact computability classification]
\label{pqc:cb:thm:classification}
The sets $\mathcal H$ and $\mathcal S$ are disjoint $\Sigma^0_1$-complete sets.
Their complement $\mathcal F=\N\setminus(\mathcal H\cup\mathcal S)$ is
$\Pi^0_1$-complete.  Completeness holds under primitive-recursive many-one
reductions.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Both positive sets are \cenum{} by \cref{pqc:cb:thm:fixed-poly}.  Let $K_0$ be a standard
\cenum{}-complete halting set, with index $k$, and let $o$ index the empty set.
The map $e\mapsto\langle k,o,e\rangle$ reduces $K_0$ to $\mathcal H$, while
$e\mapsto\langle o,k,e\rangle$ reduces $K_0$ to $\mathcal S$.

The complement of a union of two \cenum{} sets is co-computably enumerable.
On the first slice, $e\notin K_0$ is equivalent to
$\langle k,o,e\rangle\in\mathcal F$, giving $\Pi^0_1$-hardness.  All displayed
coding maps are primitive recursive.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Two existential polynomials and one unavoidable negation}

\begin{corollary}[The Diophantine trichotomy]
\label[corollary]{pqc:cb:cor:dioph-trichotomy}
There are fixed finite integer polynomials $P_{\mathcal H},P_{\mathcal S}$ such
that
\begin{align*}
 n\in\mathcal H&\iff\exists u\in\N^k\ P_{\mathcal H}(n,u)=0,\\
 n\in\mathcal S&\iff\exists v\in\N^\ell\ P_{\mathcal S}(n,v)=0.
\end{align*}
There is no ordinary existential Diophantine representation of $\mathcal F$
over natural witnesses.  It does, however, have the fixed universal
nonvanishing representation
\begin{equation}
 n\in\mathcal F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \forall u\in\N^k\ \forall v\in\N^\ell\quad
 P_{\mathcal H}(n,u)P_{\mathcal S}(n,v)\ne0.
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:frag-universal}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply MRDP to the two \cenum{} sets.  If $\mathcal F$ had an existential
Diophantine representation, enumerating natural witness tuples would make it
\cenum.  Since it is already co-computably enumerable and is $\Pi^0_1$-complete,
this would decide the halting problem.  The product in
\eqref{pqc:cb:eq:frag-universal} is nonzero for every pair of tuples exactly when
neither factor has a zero; the sets of tuples are nonempty, including when a
witness dimension is zero.
\end{proof}

The universal quantifier in \eqref{pqc:cb:eq:frag-universal} cannot be removed by the
methods here.  It expresses a genuine computability obstruction, not simply
a missing clever encoding.  This is a precise boundary for the proposed
Diophantine treatment of unconventional computation: robust rejection has
finite witnesses, but fragile divergence does not.

\subsection{A stronger obstruction: no total separator}

The simultaneous realization of arbitrary disjoint \cenum{} pairs gives more
than separate completeness of the two positive outcomes.

\begin{theorem}[Recursive inseparability]
\label{pqc:cb:thm:inseparable}
There is no total computable Boolean classifier that outputs $1$ on every
$n\in\mathcal H$ and $0$ on every $n\in\mathcal S$, even when either answer is
allowed on $\mathcal F$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We first give the standard diagonal pair explicitly.  Let $(\varphi_e)$ be an
effective enumeration of partial computable functions and set
\[
 A_* =\{e:\varphi_e(e)\downarrow=0\},\qquad
 B_* =\{e:\varphi_e(e)\downarrow=1\}.
\]
These sets are disjoint and \cenum.  Suppose a computable set $C$ contained
$A_*$ and avoided $B_*$.  Let $d$ be an index for its total characteristic
function $\chi_C$.  If $\chi_C(d)=0$, then $d\in A_*\subseteq C$, a
contradiction.  If $\chi_C(d)=1$, then $d\in B_*$ and hence $d\notin C$, again
a contradiction.  Thus no such $C$ exists.

Use \cref{pqc:cb:thm:universal} for $(A_*,B_*)$.  Composing the proposed total
classifier with its primitive-recursive input coding would give exactly such
a separator $C$.  Therefore the classifier cannot exist.
\end{proof}

An algorithm may still run the two semidecision procedures in parallel and
halt on every input promised to be in $\mathcal H\cup\mathcal S$.  The theorem
says that this partial promise procedure has no total computable extension
which remains correct on both positive outcomes.

\subsection{Where decidability returns}

\begin{proposition}[A family without fragile cases]
\label[proposition]{pqc:cb:prop:no-fragile}
For a computable input family of a fixed rational \PWA{} map, suppose every
input is either exactly accepting or robustly avoiding.  Then exact acceptance
on that family is decidable.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Dovetail exact orbit simulation with enumeration of finite safety
certificates.  The two outcomes cannot both occur, and the assumption ensures
that one semidecision halts.  Its identity decides the answer.
\end{proof}

This is a specialized form of the known robustness/decidability phenomenon
\cite{BGH2013}.  The new universal construction shows how the missing third
case can have full co-enumerable complexity, rather than being a negligible
numerical inconvenience.

\section{How the uncomputability hides in the noise scale}
\label{pqc:cb:sec:scale}

Restrict the universal map to the slice $(A,B)=(\varnothing,K_0)$, and write
$\rho(e)=\rho_F(\iota(\langle o,k,e\rangle),H)$.  Then $\rho(e)$ is a uniformly
computable real in $[0,1]$ and
\[
 \rho(e)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad e\in K_0.
\]
For $e\in K_0$, let $T(e)$ be the first rejection time of the fixed
interpreter on that encoded input.  These are interpreter times, not the
step counts of the original machine whose halting is being tested.

\begin{theorem}[No computable positive gap]
\label{pqc:cb:thm:no-gap}
There is no total computable $g:\N\to\N$ such that
\begin{equation}
 e\in K_0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\rho(e)\ge2^{-g(e)}.
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:impossible-gap}
\end{equation}
Indeed, for every total computable $g$, infinitely many $e\in K_0$ violate
\eqref{pqc:cb:eq:impossible-gap}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If such a bound existed, compute an interval for $\rho(e)$ of length less
than $2^{-g(e)}/3$.  Under the dichotomy $\rho(e)=0$ or
$\rho(e)\ge2^{-g(e)}$, the interval distinguishes the two cases and decides
$K_0$.  This contradicts undecidability.

If there were only finitely many violations, hardcode their membership
answers and use the same decision procedure on all other inputs.  A finite
set is computable, irrespective of whether we have effectively found its
list.  This would again contradict undecidability.
\end{proof}
\wtag\ Part~VII's Corollary~\ref{pqc:sc:cor:gap} proves the same absence of a
computable positive gap for the peak value of a strict contraction.

\subsection{A Busy Beaver-type envelope}

For $n\in\N$, define two finite extrema with default values:
\begin{align}
 B(n)&=\max\bigl(\{T(e):e\le n,\ e\in K_0\}\cup\{1\}\bigr),\label{pqc:cb:eq:B}\\
 \mu(n)&=\min\bigl(\{\rho(e):e\le n,\ e\in K_0\}\cup\{1\}\bigr).
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:mu}
\end{align}
Thus $B(n)$ is finite and $\mu(n)>0$ for every $n$, even when no relevant
machine halts.

\begin{proposition}[Quantitative finite-input envelope]
\label[proposition]{pqc:cb:prop:envelope}
For every $n$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\beta}{4S_{B(n)}(L)}\le\mu(n)
 \le\min\{1,2\cdot3^{-(B(n)-1)}\}.
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:envelope}
\end{equation}
The function $B$ has no total computable upper bound.  The positive function
$\mu$ has no total computable strictly positive rational lower bound.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The lower bound follows from \cref{pqc:cb:cor:time-radius}, the monotonicity of
$S_T(L)$ in $T$, and the added default value one.  If $B(n)>1$, an input
attaining that rejection time exists, and its radius gives the upper bound.
If $B(n)=1$, the upper bound is simply $\mu(n)\le1$.

A computable upper bound for $B(e)$ would let us simulate the interpreter
long enough to decide whether input $e$ is in $K_0$.  A positive computable
rational lower bound for $\mu(e)$ would similarly separate $\rho(e)=0$ from
$\rho(e)>0$ using its computable approximation.  Both conclusions are
impossible.
\end{proof}

The phrase ``Busy Beaver-type'' refers to the absence of any computable upper
bound on a finite maximum of halting times.  We do not claim eventual
domination of every computable function for an arbitrary numbering convention.
The precise proved assertion is the one in \cref{pqc:cb:prop:envelope}.

\subsection{Consequences for certificate engineering}

\begin{corollary}[No uniform resolution or witness bound]
\label[corollary]{pqc:cb:cor:witness-bounds}
No total computable function of the input bounds the first mesh index at which
a positive-radius input receives a certificate of \cref{pqc:cb:thm:quartic}.  More
generally, no sound, complete decidable finite-certificate system for
$\mathcal S$ has a total computable inputwise certificate-length bound.
For any fixed Diophantine representation of $\mathcal S$, the height of its
smallest natural witness tuple has no total computable inputwise bound on all
positive instances.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A computable mesh bound would permit checking all meshes up to that bound,
thereby deciding $\mathcal S$.  A computable certificate-length bound would
permit checking all finitely many certificate strings up to that length.
A computable natural-coordinate bound for a fixed polynomial would permit
checking all witness tuples in a finite box.  Each is a decision procedure
for a $\Sigma^0_1$-complete set, which is impossible.
\end{proof}

This result does not say that certificates are usually large, or that useful
subclasses cannot have excellent bounds.  It says that a complete universal
pipeline must expose the possibility of unbounded search rather than promise
a computable worst-case stopping criterion.

\section{Transferring the result to other substrates}
\label{pqc:cb:sec:transfer}

A simulation of exact trajectories need not preserve robustness.  Extra state
coordinates can introduce shortcuts to acceptance which were absent in the
original model.  The following sufficient condition makes the noise issue
explicit rather than hiding it behind the word ``simulation.''

\begin{theorem}[Noise-faithful retract transfer]
\label{pqc:cb:thm:transfer}
Let $f:K\to K$ and $g:M\to M$ be maps of metric state spaces.  Suppose
$E:K\to M$ and $\pi:M\to K$ are Lipschitz maps with positive bounds $A,B$ and
\begin{equation}
 \pi E=\operatorname{id}_K,\qquad gE=Ef,\qquad \pi g=f\pi.
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:retract}
\end{equation}
For $H\subseteq K$, take the target $J=\pi^{-1}(H)$ in $M$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \frac1B\rho_f(x,H)\le\rho_g(E(x),J)\le A\rho_f(x,H).
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:transfer-radius}
\end{equation}
Exact acceptance, positive-radius avoidance, and fragile avoidance coincide
on corresponding encoded inputs.  Thus the three-way arithmetic
classification transfers whenever the input encoding into $M$ is effective.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Lift a path $x_0,\ldots,x_T$ in $K$ by $E$.  Its final point belongs to $J$, and
\[
 d_M(E(x_{t+1}),g(E(x_t)))
 =d_M(E(x_{t+1}),E(f(x_t)))\le A\,d_K(x_{t+1},f(x_t)).
\]
Taking infima gives the upper bound.  Conversely, project any path
$y_0=E(x),\ldots,y_T\in J$ by $\pi$.  Its edge costs are bounded by
\[
 d_K(\pi(y_{t+1}),f(\pi(y_t)))
 =d_K(\pi(y_{t+1}),\pi(g(y_t)))\le B\,d_M(y_{t+1},g(y_t)).
\]
Taking infima gives $\rho_f\le B\rho_g$, proving the lower bound.
The exact conjugacy on the embedded copy and the definition of $J$ give
exact acceptance equivalence.  The two positive constants in
\eqref{pqc:cb:eq:transfer-radius} preserve the sign of the radius, and therefore the
third outcome as well.
\end{proof}

For example, adding auxiliary coordinates by
$g(x,z)=(F(x),q(x,z))$, with $q(x,z_0)=z_0$, the product sup norm, and target
$H\times Z$ preserves the radius \emph{exactly}: use $E(x)=(x,z_0)$ and
$\pi(x,z)=x$, both with bound one.  Invertible affine changes of coordinates
preserve the three outcomes and change the quantitative radius by at most
the associated norm condition factors.  These are concrete transfer results,
not claims about arbitrary physical implementations.

\subsection{A rational recurrent ReLU realization}

There is also a direct neural-circuit interpretation.  Let
$\operatorname{ReLU}(t)=\max\{0,t\}$.  A standard max--min representation theorem
states that a continuous \PWA{} scalar function on a closed convex domain is
a finite maximum of finite minima of its affine components
\cite{Ovchinnikov2002}.  Applying this theorem coordinatewise to $F$ gives
\[
 F_i(x)=\max_{S\in\mathcal A_i}\ \min_{j\in S}\ell_{ij}(x),
 \qquad i=1,2,3,
\]
where all $\ell_{ij}$ are rational affine functions.  This cited representation
theorem is an additional external dependency of the neural corollary, not of
the main dynamical construction.

\begin{corollary}[A fixed rational neural update block]
\label[corollary]{pqc:cb:cor:relu}
There exists a finite feedforward ReLU network with rational weights and
biases and three outputs whose restriction to $[0,1]^3$ is exactly the fixed
map $F$.  Repeatedly applying this one block to its three-dimensional state
register realizes the trichotomy of \cref{pqc:cb:thm:universal}, with exactly the same
critical radius for adversarial perturbations of that state register after
each complete network evaluation.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Replace each maximum and minimum in the displayed representation by the
identities
\[
 \max(a,b)=b+\operatorname{ReLU}(a-b),\qquad
 \min(a,b)=a-\operatorname{ReLU}(a-b).
\]
This produces a finite acyclic circuit of rational affine operations and
ReLU gates.  Signed intermediate wires can be carried through ordinary ReLU
layers by the two nonnegative channels
$\operatorname{ReLU}(t)$ and $\operatorname{ReLU}(-t)$, whose difference is $t$.
Layering the finite circuit and carrying necessary wires forward therefore
gives a standard finite feedforward network with rational parameters and an
affine output layer.  Its update function is $F$ on the cube, so both the exact
and the specified perturbed state trajectories are identical.
\end{proof}

This is a three-dimensional \emph{recurrent state}, not a claim of three
neurons, three layers, or a small hidden network.  The construction gives no
optimized size bound and the network's full weight list is not extracted in
the companion code.  Noise at every hidden neuron, fixed parameter errors,
stochastic noise, finite floating-point hardware, and continuous-time neural
circuits are different models.  Their equivalence would require additional
estimates or a transfer theorem such as \cref{pqc:cb:thm:transfer}.
\wtag\ Part~VII's Proposition~\ref{pqc:sc:prop:gates} gives an explicit ReLU gate
count, $9m+2d_M-3$, for a different map (a strict contraction of $\R^4$); the
weight list of the network above is still not extracted.

\section{A worked example: an unattained critical threshold}
\label{pqc:cb:sec:examples}
\subsection{A contraction with an unattained critical threshold}

\begin{proposition}[An explicit radius]
\label[proposition]{pqc:cb:prop:contraction}
For $f(t)=at$ on $[0,1]$, $0\le a<1$, source zero, and target $[b,1]$ with
$0<b\le1$,
\begin{equation}
 \rho_f(0,[b,1])=(1-a)b.
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:contraction}
\end{equation}
If $0<a<1$, no pseudo-orbit with error at most this exact critical value hits
the target in finite time.  If $a=0$, the critical value is attained in one
step.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Any error-$\varepsilon$ path satisfies
$x_{t+1}\le ax_t+\varepsilon$, so
\[
 x_t\le\varepsilon(1+a+\cdots+a^{t-1})
      =\frac{\varepsilon(1-a^t)}{1-a}.
\]
When $0<a<1$ and $\varepsilon\le(1-a)b$, this is strictly less than $b$ for
finite $t$.  Conversely, when $\varepsilon>(1-a)b$, the positive-error
recursion reaches or passes $b$ after finitely many steps.  One can stop at
$b$ on that step, or clip at one, without exceeding the allowed error.
Thus the infimum is $(1-a)b$ but is not attained.  For $a=0$, every step is
within $\varepsilon$ of zero, and the jump to $b$ has exactly cost $b$.
\end{proof}

For $a=1/2$, $b=3/4$, the exact value is $3/8$.  The reference implementation
gives the following rational enclosures using $L=1/2$.  Every entry was
computed with integer fractions, without floating-point tolerances.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{rrrrr}
\toprule
Mesh $N$ & Vertices & $r_N$ & Certified interval for $\rho$ & Quartic zero found\\
\midrule
4  & 5  & $1/2$    & $[5/16,1/2]$       & yes\\
8  & 9  & $7/16$   & $[11/32,7/16]$     & yes\\
16 & 17 & $13/32$  & $[23/64,13/32]$    & yes\\
32 & 33 & $25/64$  & $[47/128,25/64]$   & yes\\
64 & 65 & $49/128$ & $[95/256,49/128]$  & yes\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{A computable critical radius need not be realized by a critical-cost
finite path.  All intervals contain $3/8$.}
\label{pqc:cb:tab:contraction}
\end{table}

At mesh $N=4$, the vertices are $0,1/4,1/2,3/4,1$, and
$\lambda_N=3/8$.  The cut indicator
\[
 (b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4)=(1,1,0,0,0)
\]
is a zero of \eqref{pqc:cb:eq:quartic}.  Its least outgoing edge has weight $3/8$,
so the cut alone certifies $\rho\ge3/16$.  Optimizing the cut to obtain the
actual bottleneck $r_4=1/2$ gives the stronger lower bound $5/16$ in the table.
The full factored quartic and its witness are supplied as
\code{data/09-continuous-barriers-small_quartic.txt} and \code{data/09-continuous-barriers-small_certificate.json}.

\part{Other substrates, implementation, formalization and questions}
\label{pqc:part:rest}

\section{Other unconventional substrates}\label{pqc:sec:substrates}

The decisive property for the output-law theorem is not a conventional
instruction set. It is an effective, nonovercounting presentation of finite
terminal histories with computable weights. Universality is needed for the
completeness lower bounds, but not for the positive representation theorem.
The following applications state their semantics explicitly.

\paragraph{Randomized combinator reduction.}
A lambda, SK, SKI, or Iota reducer with a specified effective reduction
strategy and a fair-coin branching primitive has finite syntactic
histories and dyadic history weights. Its first-return law therefore has
\eqref{pqc:eq:rootmass}. The random primitive and reduction strategy are part of
the proposed extension; this is not a claim that the inspected repository
already implements that probabilistic language. Adding probabilities does
not excuse ambiguities between deterministic evaluation strategy and
nondeterministic rewrite choice.

\paragraph{Stochastic fractional programs.}
One can give a FRACTRAN-style system an explicit rational random dispatcher
between finite deterministic fractional programs, preserving each program's
ordered divisibility semantics. A transition is then decidable arithmetic,
with a rational branch probability. Finite histories fit our interface.
This construction deliberately avoids saying ``choose an applicable
fraction randomly'' without specifying how conflicts, priorities, and
normalization are resolved. Deterministic FRACTRAN-to-Diophantine reductions
are already present in the literature \cite{larchey-forster}; the additional
object represented here is the probability law and its conditional boundary.

\paragraph{Random local rewriting and cellular systems.}
A finite description of each current active configuration, an effective
finite set of next local choices, and rational transition weights are enough
for an effective first-return presentation. Infinite configurations may
also be admitted when a finite-history simulation and observable can be
computed from their effective descriptions. Merely declaring an arbitrary
infinite initial configuration does not meet that requirement.

\paragraph{Continuous-time jump systems.}
For a countable-state jump process with finitely many outgoing rational
rates $q_{ij}$ at each effectively represented state, the next-jump
probability is $q_{ij}/\sum_kq_{ik}$ when the denominator is positive.
A zero-rate state is treated as absorbing. Events that reach a designated
terminal state after finitely many jumps therefore have an effective
rational-weight history presentation. This application uses the embedded
jump chain. It neither assigns a terminal value to an infinite explosion
history nor claims a result about arbitrary deadline-constrained events.
Those questions require additional semantics and analysis.

\paragraph{Robust observations of computable continuous trajectories.}
Suppose a trajectory is supplied with an algorithm for certified evaluation
at rational times and is continuous. Reaching an effectively open target
at some finite time is semidecidable: enumerate rational times and certified
interior balls, and accept once an evaluation is certified inside one.
Continuity ensures that an actual open-target visit contains an appropriate
rational time, including a one-sided interval at time zero. This yields a
Diophantine reachability predicate by MRDP. It says nothing about exact
zero crossings with no robust margin, or about differential equations whose
solutions are not uniformly computable from the supplied data.

\paragraph{The effective boundary is indispensable.}
An arbitrary real oracle parameter can encode a non-c.e. set, and an
observation that asks for an exact infinite-time limit can move beyond
existential arithmetic. Such a model is not covered merely because it is
called Turing-complete. The theorem concerns effective computational
substrates, not every imaginable extension that contains ordinary Turing
machines as a submodel.

\begin{remark}[\wtag\ Relation to Part~III]
The paragraph on robust observations of computable continuous trajectories
concerns reaching an effectively \emph{open} target in continuous time,
which is semidecidable. Part~III treats the complementary discrete-time
question for \emph{closed} rational targets under adversarial per-step
noise: positive critical radius is semidecidable and has complete quartic
certificates (Theorem~\ref{pqc:cb:thm:quartic}), exact acceptance is
semidecidable, and the remaining noise-fragile outcome is
$\pione$-complete (Theorem~\ref{pqc:cb:thm:classification}).
Theorem~\ref{pqc:cb:thm:transfer} states when such a trichotomy transfers
to another substrate.
\end{remark}
\par\noindent\wtag\ \emph{Batch-64 note (30 September 2026).} Part~VIII (source~18) proves the paragraph's
statement for rational polynomial ODEs with open rational polyhedral targets,
where the trajectory is given by the equation rather than by an evaluation
algorithm: reachability is recursively enumerable, hence Diophantine
(Theorem~\ref{pqc:tu:thm:re}), through an explicit canonical integer checker that
is sound, complete, robust to initial error and bounded forcing, and compiled to
a counted quartic with a unique witness for each unrolling length
(Theorems~\ref{pqc:tu:thm:equivalence} and~\ref{pqc:tu:thm:quartic}). It is
Part~III's open-target, continuous-time counterpart in the sense of this remark
(Section~\ref{pqc:tu:conv:relation}). Infinite-path properties of discrete
systems, such as recurrence and progress deadlines, are classified in the sibling
report \code{liveness-beyond-halting} (see Section~\ref{pqc:conv:qoverlap}).

\section{Implementation and validation}
\label{pqc:conv:impl}\label{pqc:sec:audit}

\subsection{Manuscript 08: what the software actually verifies}
The bundle contains an exact rational budget evaluator, a symbolic
single-fold quartic compiler, a canonical prefix allocator, and an exact
small quantum-circuit evaluator. The script \code{code/08-probabilistic-laws-verify.py} uses a
fixed random seed, $20260930$, for reproducible sampled tests. It also runs
exhaustive tests that do not rely on randomness.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.35\textwidth}p{0.55\textwidth}}
\toprule
Check & Observed result\\
\midrule
Exhaustive binary histories &
780 histories, 3,120 initial-mass cases, and 22,220 forced-pivot candidates;
exactly one valid pivot candidate precisely in each of the 1,330 feasible
cases.\\[3pt]
Multi-outcome and large-integer tests &
192 sampled schedules, including 32 additional rescalings by $10^{100}$;
all exact invariance and feasibility checks pass.\\[3pt]
Symbolic quartic &
$N=2,m=2$: 11 parameters, 33 witnesses, 38 residuals, degree four, 165
expanded monomials. All residuals vanish at the exported witness.\\[3pt]
Mutation checks &
Increasing each of the 33 witness coordinates separately by one is rejected.
This is a finite robustness check, not a search of all wrong tuples.\\[3pt]
Quadratic-field signs &
25,921 small integer pairs cross-checked with high-precision decimal
arithmetic; 200 near-cancelling Pell cases checked by exact identities.\\[3pt]
Quantum circuits &
100 sampled circuits of 30 gates; 3,000 exact norm checks pass, together with
$H^2$, $HTH$, and a Bell-state example.\\[3pt]
Prefix allocation &
12 dyadic approximation stages of the $HTH$ output law; disjoint allocated
mass is $4095/4096$.\\[3pt]
Operator budgets &
Four exact coherent examples and one noncommuting cycle pass symbolic
matrix checks.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The two allocated masses at the twelfth $HTH$ stage are $437/512$ and
$599/4096$. Their sum is $4095/4096$, leaving exactly $1/4096$ unallocated
at that finite stage. No claim is made that twelve stages already represent
the full irrational law. The script also includes floating-point diagnostics
for the sharpness limit in Theorem~\ref{pqc:thm:binary}; those diagnostics are
explicitly labeled illustrative and do not support the exact proof.

The detailed results and software versions are in
\code{data/08-probabilistic-laws-verification.json}. The full finite quartic is supplied
both as a residual specification and as an expanded expression. The code
uses Python integers and \code{Fraction} for exact rational arithmetic;
SymPy is used for symbolic expansion and the matrix checks.

\subsection{Manuscript 07: what the delivered programs do}\label{pqc:qm:sec:implementation}

The package uses only the Python standard library. Matrix entries are \code{fractions.Fraction}; all certificate computations are integer computations. The principal functions in \code{code/07-quantum-mortality-quantum_diophantine.py} are:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{.32\textwidth}p{.60\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Function & Contract \\
\midrule
\code{elementary_gram} & Rational $LDL^{\mathsf T}$ and four-square search; returns a $4d$-row factor and checks its Gram identity. \\
\code{gram_search} & Height-ordered rational search, with an optional cap; succeeds on the included small examples with $d+3$ rows. A cap failure is not an impossibility result. \\
\code{compile_instrument} & Checks the factor, packs its rows, builds all Kraus operators, and verifies normalization exactly. \\
\code{build_certificate} & Constructs the quadratic residuals with free signed-pair matrix inputs and asserts both symbolic counts. \\
\code{canonical_assignment} & Generates the uniquely determined natural assignment associated with a specified word. \\
\code{Certificate.expanded} & Expands the sum of residual squares into a sparse integer polynomial. Expansion is optional and can be large. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The test command, from the root of the delivered package layout (the README explains how to run it on a copy), is
\begin{lstlisting}
python code/run_checks.py
\end{lstlisting}
It writes the example matrices, a canonical zero-word witness, the expanded small quartic, and a machine-readable result report.

\subsection{Manuscript 07: observed test results}

The delivered run passed $32{,}418$ explicit checks. The total is a count of individual assertions, not a count of statistically independent experiments. It includes twelve seeded small random input lists and several deterministic examples. In particular, $3{,}460$ outcome words were checked for the projection formula, exact integer probability formula, and arithmetic gap. The one-step flush implication was checked $12{,}449$ times, using all active final letters when its premise held.

The suite verifies the four-square routine on every integer from $0$ through $300$, exercises the $(d+3)$-row rational search on three small positive forms, and tests the counterexample $7$ to a three-square search within a specified finite height cap. The latter computational cap is only a regression test; the global impossibility is proved in Proposition~\ref{pqc:qm:prop:sharp}.

For the uniform certificate with $(D,K,n)=(2,2,2)$, symbolic expansion yields $647$ monomials and total degree four, with $44$ witnesses and $50$ residuals. For the dimension-four example and word $(2,1,1)$, the generated assignment satisfies all $264$ residuals with $245$ natural witnesses. Increasing any one of those witness coordinates by one makes the certificate nonzero. These mutation tests supplement, but do not replace, the inductive uniqueness proof.

The complete category counts are in \code{data/07-quantum-mortality-check_results.json}. A local run took about five seconds; this is not a benchmark for the general rational Gram search. The reference implementation is intentionally transparent rather than optimized.

The universal interpreter table itself is not supplied or tested, and finite
