\subsection{Abstracts and status statements of the sources}
\label{pqc:conv:b62-V:status}
\paragraph{Abstract of source 13.}
% --- source 13, lines 86-112 ---
\noindent We construct a quantitative, witness-faithful translation from Boolean
circuits to nonnegative integer quartics. A circuit with $k$ input bits and $s$
gates gives a coercive polynomial in at most $k+5s+5$ variables, with coefficient
height at most $4$ and variable-interaction degree at most $3$. Its real zeros
are Boolean and are in bijection with accepting inputs. Every zero is a
nondegenerate minimum with Hessian spectrum in $[2,20]$. Dimension-independent
rounding and convexity estimates identify all sufficiently low sublevel
components with those zeros; the components are contractible and remain
count-faithful under specified smooth perturbations.

Applied to a fair-coin computation stopped at horizon $t$, the construction
makes the probability of halting by $t$ exactly $2^{-t}$ times a finite
Diophantine root count, a low-energy component count, or an Euler
characteristic. The limiting values are precisely the left-computably
enumerable reals in $[0,1]$. Thus noncomputable probabilities occur despite
uniformly bounded coefficients, sparse interactions, separated minima,
well-conditioned Hessians, and a fixed rounding gap. We prove a matching
interaction-degree frontier: degree-two Boolean residual systems can be
counted by path/cycle dynamic programming, whereas degree three already
supports parsimoniously complete counting.

We also give fixed-arity quartic normal forms for strict probability lower
bounds and their quantifier-optimal complements, explain the almost-sure and
finite-mean termination boundaries, and identify exactly what transfers to
coin-augmented unconventional computational substrates. The package contains
a working compiler, a degree-two counter, explicit sparse polynomials, and
6,050 finite exact checks, supplemented by 60 numerical Hessian checks.
\paragraph{Status statement of source 13.}
% --- source 13, lines 116-121 ---
\small\textbf{Status.} This is a self-contained research draft, not a Lean-checked
or independently refereed paper. The simultaneous quantitative construction
and its geometric consequences are developed here; the general MRDP and
probabilistic-termination classifications are classical and are explicitly
credited. Publication priority for the combined construction is not asserted.
No finite-fold or single-fold MRDP conjecture is claimed solved.
\paragraph{Abstract of source 17.}
% --- source 17, lines 59-88 ---
We construct a family of reversible birth--death chains on the nonnegative
integers with transition probabilities in a fixed finite rational alphabet.
Every chain has exponentially decaying stationary tails, a mean return time
to the origin at most two, and the same explicit lower bound
$(3-2\sqrt2)/4$ on its spectral gap. From the origin, total-variation
convergence has a uniform geometric rate. Nevertheless, exact stationary
arithmetic retains the full difficulty of computation.

A single defect placed at a machine's first halting time makes its root
mass a rational number whose equality to $1/2$ is equivalent to nonhalting.
A finite guarded-affine history construction realizes this example as a
random walk along a reversible computational trajectory. More generally,
the root mass is rational exactly when the binary environment is eventually
periodic. Its full range is a Cantor set of dimension
$\log_2((1+\sqrt5)/2)$. Sparse, factorially separated defects give a uniform
rational-versus-Liouville dichotomy: rationality and algebraicity are
$\Sigma^0_2$-complete, while irrationality and transcendence are
$\Pi^0_2$-complete for primitive-recursive environments. A separate
low-complexity criterion, using the theorem of Adamczewski and Bugeaud,
gives an explicit transcendental Thue--Morse equilibrium.

Strict rational comparisons admit complete finite-prefix certificates.
At horizon $N$, the arithmetic layer is a sum-of-squares polynomial of
total degree at most four with $N+1$ natural witnesses and $2N+1$
residuals, with a unique witness tuple whenever the prefix certifies the
comparison. A small-coefficient recurrence presentation is also given. ProveIt's MRDP interface then supplies fixed-polynomial
existence for the unbounded strict cuts, but not for the higher-level
arithmetic predicates. The manuscript includes full proofs of the
construction, reproducible exact-arithmetic checks, a formalization plan,
and twelve further research questions.
\paragraph{Status statement of source 17.}
% --- source 17, lines 91-95 ---
\noindent\textbf{Status.} These are proposed research contributions with ordinary
mathematical proofs and finite computational checks. They have not been
independently refereed or formalized in Lean or Rocq. Historical priority
is not claimed. Classical inputs and exact boundaries of the results are
identified below.

% --- source 13, lines 127-1320 ---
\section{Question, contribution, and relation to \reponame}\label{pqc:ql:sec:intro}
\srcmark{13}

\subsection{Why a probability is not an accepting path}
The usual Diophantine question asks whether an accepting computation exists.
For a probabilistic machine, that is only a small part of the semantics. One
must distinguish existence of a successful random tape, the measure of all
successful tapes, termination with probability one, and finiteness of the
expected running time. The first is existential. The others involve counting,
limits, or additional quantifier alternation.

This distinction matters especially when a compiler introduces auxiliary
witnesses. An equation can represent the right existential relation while
having the wrong number of solutions. A single accepting tape might acquire
many or infinitely many arithmetic witnesses. Dividing that witness count by
$2^t$ would not recover a probability. The construction below avoids this
problem at a fixed horizon: every input tape has exactly one assignment to
all internal wires, including all copy and constant wires.

The stronger question addressed here is geometric. Can a computationally
arbitrary probability be encoded by polynomial landscapes whose accepting
minima are uniformly regular, rather than by a badly conditioned or singular
numerical construction? The answer is yes, with explicit small constants.
The unbounded complexity lives in the increasing family of finite
computations, not in deteriorating local geometry.

\subsection{The theorem package}
The central result combines five properties that should not be conflated:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item a parsimonious finite Boolean-to-quartic compiler;
\item bounded coefficients and a subcubic interaction graph;
\item uniform Hessian, rounding, and low-sublevel topology bounds;
\item exact realization of stochastic halting probabilities as normalized
component counts;
\item a proof of the logical boundary between existential Diophantine
certificates and almost-sure or finite-mean claims.
\end{enumerate}
Here ``parsimonious'' means that the relevant finite sets are in bijection,
not merely equinumerous after an unexplained normalization.

\subsection{Repository boundary and provenance}
The inspected repository revision is
\begin{center}
\texttt{b998f70c6886e6a00339a6f4a02ed8625324d357}.
\end{center}
The relevant foundation is
\texttt{Computability/HilbertTenthProblem}, in particular its public MRDP
interface and guide \cite{b62s13-repoHTP,b62s13-repoMRDP}. The guide states the natural-number
formulation, includes input zero, allows zero witnesses, and emphasizes that
its public theorem is an existence result rather than a practical
polynomial generator. The repository also documents corrected Jones papers
and a universal degree-four construction. We do not re-audit those Lean
builds here.

The finite compiler in this article does not use MRDP. It is a direct,
executable construction. MRDP enters only when an unbounded semidecidable
probability comparison is compressed into one fixed-arity Diophantine
formula. This separation is important: the fixed-arity formulas do not
inherit the finite compiler's Boolean witnesses or its solution-count
bijection.

Boolean arithmetization and parsimonious counting reductions are classical;
Valiant's work supplies the standard counting-complexity background
\cite{b62s13-valiant}. The arithmetical classifications of probabilistic termination
are due to earlier work, notably Kaminski and Katoen \cite{kaminski-katoen}. We give
self-contained reductions suited to the present representation and do not
present those classifications as newly discovered.


Quartic sum-of-squares reductions of satisfiability are also established;
Duda gives an explicit such reformulation \cite{b62s13-duda}. Ahmadi and Zhang
study degree-sensitive complexity questions for critical points and local
minima \cite{b62s13-ahmadi}. Our claim is not the first quartic encoding of SAT.
Nor is our decision problem the existence of an arbitrary local minimum:
every coercive polynomial here already has a global minimum. The problem
is whether its \emph{zero level} is attained, and the quantitative result
combines counting-faithful witnesses, coefficient height four, subcubic
interactions, and explicit uniform low-energy geometry. The cited
literature provides context, not an exhaustive priority audit.

\section{Conventions and probabilistic semantics}
\srcmark{13}

\subsection{Numbers, circuits, and graph conventions}
We use $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. The coefficient height of an integer polynomial
is the maximum absolute value of an expanded coefficient, including the
constant coefficient. A circuit has $k$ designated free Boolean input wires,
$s$ further gates, and one output wire. Gates belong to
\[
\mathsf{AND},\quad\mathsf{NOT},\quad\mathsf{COPY},\quad
\mathsf{ZERO},\quad\mathsf{ONE}.
\]
The gate graph is acyclic. Repeated operands are allowed initially; the
compiler separates occurrences before producing polynomial residuals.
Circuit parameters such as program text or an ordinary data input are fixed
by the compiler, not counted as extra random input bits.

For a family of residuals $r_j$, its \emph{interaction graph} has one vertex
per variable and joins two distinct variables when they occur together in a
residual. In our construction this is also the expanded polynomial's
monomial-interaction graph: no pair occurs in two residuals, so cancellation
cannot remove the relevant edge. In the degree-two counting theorem, the
residual presentation is part of the input.

\subsection{One fair bit per clock tick}
Fix an effective deterministic machine model with an additional instruction
that branches on a fair bit. There is no scheduler or demonic
nondeterminism. The accepting/halting state is absorbing. We may supply an
independent fair bit at every clock tick, even if a deterministic instruction
ignores that bit. This convention does not change the distribution of the
bits that the program actually uses.

For a program $e$, ordinary input $x$, and infinite coin stream $\omega$, let
$\tau_{e,x}(\omega)\in\N\cup\{\infty\}$ be its first halting time. Put
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:pt}
 p_{e,x,t}=\Prob(\tau_{e,x}\le t),\qquad
 p_{e,x}=\Prob(\tau_{e,x}<\infty).
\end{equation}
Exactly $t$ bits determine the event $\tau\le t$. Thus, for a decidable
Boolean predicate $A_{e,x,t}$ on $\Bit^t$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:at}
 a_{e,x,t}=\#\{b\in\Bit^t:A_{e,x,t}(b)=1\},\qquad
 p_{e,x,t}=\frac{a_{e,x,t}}{2^t}.
\end{equation}
A stream that has already halted stays successful under either next bit,
so $a_{t+1}\ge 2a_t$ and $p_t\uparrow p$.

All finite-horizon predicates can be compiled to finite circuits. For a
fixed local tape-machine model, an ordinary space-time simulation yields
$O((t+1)(|x|+t+1))$ Boolean gates, with a model-dependent constant; the same
statement holds for a fixed universal interpreter with its program text
included in the input length. No assumption that an arbitrary mathematical
function is a unit-cost machine instruction is made.

\subsection{Three different representation levels}
A finite circuit gives a finite polynomial whose dimension depends on the
horizon. A probability is a limit of normalized finite counts. A fixed-arity
Diophantine predicate is a single polynomial whose witness dimension is
independent of the horizon and whose natural witnesses can be unbounded.
The word ``uniform'' below always specifies which of these levels is meant.

\section{A sparse, witness-faithful quartic compiler}\label{pqc:ql:sec:compiler}
\srcmark{13}

\subsection{Distributed constants and fresh occurrences}
Introduce one new unit wire $u_*$, with residual $u_*-1$. Every occurrence of
a Boolean constant one is supplied by a copy of this unit wire. A NOT gate
uses a local unit occurrence, rather than a new literal constant. The
unrouted residual templates are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Operation & Residual & Defining interpretation\\
\midrule
AND & $z-xy$ & $z=xy$\\
NOT & $z+x-u$ & $z=u-x$, with $u=1$\\
COPY or ONE & $z-x$ & $z=x$\\
ZERO & $z$ & $z=0$\\
Root unit & $u_*-1$ & $u_*=1$\\
Final acceptance & $o-u$ & require output one\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The final acceptance comparison is not a definition. All other residuals
define exactly one noninput wire.

We now route \emph{every operand occurrence}, including the two operands of
final acceptance and all unit occurrences. Suppose an original wire has
$d>0$ uses. Add one fresh copy wire as a trunk. If $d=1$, the trunk itself is
the occurrence wire. If $d\ge2$, grow a binary copy tree below that trunk,
with $d$ fresh leaves, one per use. Every tree edge $v\to w$ has residual
$w-v$. The root original wire therefore has only one outgoing copy edge,
and the leaves used in a gate are all distinct.

The tree has $2d-1$ new wires for every $d\ge1$. This follows from the usual
$2d-2$ edges of a full binary tree with $d$ leaves, plus the trunk edge;
for $d=1$ it gives the single trunk wire. Balanced splitting is convenient
for the implementation but is not required for the proof.

\begin{lemma}[Routing invariants]\label[lemma]{pqc:ql:lem:routing}
The routed system has the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Every noninput variable has exactly one defining residual, and all
definitions are acyclic.
\item Each non-Boolean residual involves at most three distinct variables.
\item Each variable occurs in at most three non-Boolean residuals.
\item Each pair of distinct variables occurs together in at most one
non-Boolean residual.
\item The interaction graph has maximum degree at most three.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Acyclicity follows by replacing each use edge of an acyclic circuit by a
copy tree directed toward the use. The root unit has its own definition.
A fresh occurrence leaf is consumed only at its assigned use; even two
occurrences of the same original operand become different leaves. This
proves the first two assertions.

An original gate output occurs in its defining residual and, if used, in
one trunk-copy residual. A free input occurs only in its trunk-copy
residual. An internal tree variable occurs in one incoming and at most two
outgoing copy residuals. An occurrence leaf occurs in its incoming copy
residual and one consuming residual. The root unit obeys the same count,
with its pinning residual counted as its definition. Thus incidence is at
most three.

A copy edge uses a unique child. An original gate's operands are private
leaves, and its output is not one of those leaves. Two private leaves are
never consumed together again. This proves pair uniqueness. For graph
degree, an original gate output has at most two neighbors in its defining
gate and one trunk neighbor; an internal copy vertex has at most three tree
neighbors; a leaf has one parent and at most two consuming-gate neighbors.
The remaining vertices have smaller degree.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The polynomial and exact size}
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be all routed variables, including the $k$ original
inputs. If $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ are the non-Boolean residuals, define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:energy}
 \cE_C(X)=\sum_{i=1}^n \bigl(X_i(X_i-1)\bigr)^2
              +\sum_{j=1}^m r_j(X)^2.
\end{equation}
Each summand has degree at most four, and the univariate Boolean penalties
ensure that the degree is exactly four.

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative compiler]\label{pqc:ql:thm:compiler}
From a circuit $C$ with $k$ Boolean inputs and $s$ gates one can effectively
construct \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:energy} with
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:sizes}
 n\le k+5s+5,\qquad m=n-k+1.
\end{equation}
It has $2n-k+1$ displayed squared residuals, coefficient height at most $4$,
constant coefficient exactly $1$, and interaction degree at most $3$.
Projection to the $k$ input coordinates is a bijection
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:bijection}
 \{X\in\R^n:\cE_C(X)=0\}
 \;\longrightarrow\; \{b\in\Bit^k:C(b)=1\}.
\end{equation}
The same zero set is obtained over $\N^n$ or $\Z^n$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
There are $k+s+1$ original variables after the root unit is added. Let $L$ be
the number of unrouted operand occurrences. AND and NOT have two each;
COPY and ONE have one; ZERO and the root unit have none; final acceptance
has two. Therefore $L\le2s+2$. Routing uses at most $2L$ new wires, giving
$n\le k+s+1+4s+4$. Every noninput variable has one definition, and final
acceptance contributes one more residual, so $m=n-k+1$.

Over $\R$, a sum of squares is zero exactly when every summand is zero.
The Boolean residuals force $X\in\Bit^n$. The root pin and copy trees
force every local unit to be one. Induction along the acyclic definitions
then forces every gate and copy wire to be the unique circuit evaluation
on the given input. The last residual vanishes exactly for output one.
Conversely that evaluation makes every residual zero. This proves the
bijection and the assertion about number domains.

It remains to check coefficients after expansion, rather than merely the
small coefficients of the unexpanded residuals. The Boolean term is
$X_i^4-2X_i^3+X_i^2$. No non-Boolean square has a pure cubic or pure quartic
term, since its distinct-variable templates are $z-xy$, $z+x-u$, $z-x$,
$z$, and $u_*-1$. Each contributes at most one to a pure quadratic
coefficient, and at most three such residuals involve any variable.
Consequently a pure quadratic coefficient is at most four. A mixed
monomial can occur in at most one residual square by pair uniqueness, and
its coefficient there has absolute value at most two. The only nonzero
linear coefficient is $-2u_*$, and the only constant term is the one from
$(u_*-1)^2$. Thus the height is at most four. Graph degree is
\cref{pqc:ql:lem:routing}(e).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the trunk matters]
Merely limiting fan-out to two gives a possible degree-four graph vertex:
a gate output can have two gate neighbors and two outgoing copies. The
single trunk edge reduces this to three without changing the conservative
linear variable bound. Distributing the unit similarly prevents a
high-degree global constant vertex and a growing constant coefficient.
\end{remark}

\section{Real geometry: rounding, conditioning, and topology}\label{pqc:ql:sec:geometry}
\srcmark{13}

\subsection{Coercivity and conditioning at zeros}
\begin{theorem}[Uniform minimum geometry]\label{pqc:ql:thm:hessian}
The polynomial $\cE_C$ is nonnegative and coercive on $\R^n$. At every real
zero $b$, its Hessian satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:hesszero}
 2I\preceq \nabla^2\cE_C(b)\preceq20I.
\end{equation}
In particular each zero is an isolated nondegenerate minimum, with Hessian
condition number at most ten. Distinct zeros have Euclidean distance at
least one.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Nonnegativity is immediate. The lower bound
$\cE_C(X)\ge\sum_iX_i^2(X_i-1)^2$ tends to infinity when
$\|X\|_\infty$ tends to infinity, proving coercivity in each finite dimension.

Let $J$ be the Jacobian of the non-Boolean residuals at a Boolean zero.
All residuals vanish there. The derivative of $X_i(X_i-1)$ is
$2b_i-1\in\{-1,1\}$. Differentiating the sum of squares gives
\[
 \nabla^2\cE_C(b)=2I+2J^{\mathsf T}J.
\]
Each row of $J$ has at most three entries of absolute value at most one;
each column has at most three such entries by incidence. Hence
$\|J\|_\infty\le3$, $\|J\|_1\le3$, and
$\|J\|_2^2\le\|J\|_1\|J\|_\infty\le9$. The claimed spectral interval
follows. Distinct zeros are distinct Boolean vectors.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Nondegenerate minimum versus smooth hypersurface]
The nondegeneracy in \cref{pqc:ql:thm:hessian} is Morse nondegeneracy of the
\emph{energy minimum}. Necessarily $\nabla\cE_C(b)=0$. We do not claim that
the hypersurface defined by the single equation $\cE_C=0$ is nonsingular
at $b$ in the algebraic-geometric gradient sense. Nor do we claim that its
complex zero set is Boolean; sum-of-squares positivity was used over $\R$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A dimension-independent rounding gap}
\begin{lemma}[Scalar Boolean rounding]\label[lemma]{pqc:ql:lem:roundscalar}
For every $x\in\R$, let $d(x)=\min(|x|,|x-1|)$. Then
\[
 d(x)\le2|x(x-1)|.
\]
Consequently, if $b$ is obtained by nearest-Boolean rounding of $X$, then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:rounddistance}
 \|X-b\|_2^2\le4\sum_i\bigl(X_i(X_i-1)\bigr)^2\le4\cE_C(X).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Inside $[0,1]$, $|x(x-1)|=d(x)(1-d(x))\ge d(x)/2$. Outside that interval it
is $d(x)(1+d(x))\ge d(x)$. Squaring the scalar bound and summing proves
\eqref{pqc:ql:eq:rounddistance}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Robust witness extraction]\label{pqc:ql:thm:rounding}
If $\cE_C(X)\le1/64$, nearest-Boolean rounding is unambiguous and yields a
zero $b$ of $\cE_C$. In particular, if $C$ has no accepting input, then
\[
 \min_{X\in\R^n}\cE_C(X)>\frac1{64}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $\epsilon=\sqrt{\cE_C(X)}\le1/8$. Each coordinate is within
$\eta=2\epsilon\le1/4$ of its rounded bit. Every non-Boolean residual has
$|r_j(X)|\le\epsilon$. A linear template changes by at most $3\eta$ under
rounding. For an AND template, with $|x-b_x|,|y-b_y|,|z-b_z|\le\eta$,
\begin{align*}
 |(z-xy)-(b_z-b_xb_y)|
 &\le |z-b_z|+|x|\,|y-b_y|+|b_y|\,|x-b_x|\\
 &\le (3+\eta)\eta.
\end{align*}
The same bound dominates all templates. Therefore
\[
 |r_j(b)|\le\epsilon+(3+2\epsilon)2\epsilon
 \le\frac18+\frac{13}{4}\frac14=\frac{15}{16}<1.
\]
But $r_j(b)$ is an integer. Thus all those residuals vanish; the Boolean
ones vanish by construction. Coercivity ensures that the global minimum
is attained, and the contrapositive proves the strict gap when no zero
exists.
\end{proof}

The gap is an extraction theorem, not a polynomial-time optimization
algorithm. Finding a point below the gap can still encode a hard search
problem. The useful guarantee is that a sufficiently good approximate
solution cannot be a numerically convincing false positive.

\subsection{Uniform convex neighborhoods}
For a Boolean zero $b$, set
\[
 Q_b=\{X:\|X-b\|_\infty\le1/32\}.
\]
\begin{lemma}[Convex well boxes]\label[lemma]{pqc:ql:lem:boxes}
Throughout $Q_b$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:boxhessian}
 I\preceq\nabla^2\cE_C(X)\preceq24I.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
More generally let $\|X-b\|_\infty\le\rho\le1/32$. For the Boolean
Jacobian contribution, $|2X_i-1|\ge1-2\rho$ and
$|2X_i-1|\le1+2\rho$. Its residual-Hessian correction has absolute diagonal
entries at most $4\rho(1+\rho)$.

For non-Boolean residuals, a Jacobian row has absolute sum at most
$3+2\rho$, and a column has absolute sum at most $3(1+\rho)$. Thus their
positive semidefinite Jacobian contribution is bounded above by
$6(1+\rho)(3+2\rho)I$.

Only an AND residual has a nonzero second derivative: an off-diagonal
$-1$ at its two operands. Since $r_j(b)=0$, the preceding Lipschitz
estimate gives $|r_j(X)|\le(3+\rho)\rho$. The absolute row sum of all
non-Boolean residual-Hessian corrections is at most
$6(3+\rho)\rho$, using the incidence bound three. Therefore the full
Hessian has lower spectral bound
\begin{align*}
 2(1-2\rho)^2-4\rho(1+\rho)-6(3+\rho)\rho
 =2-30\rho-2\rho^2
 \ge\frac{543}{512}>1.
\end{align*}
Its upper spectral bound is at most
\[
 2(1+2\rho)^2+6(1+\rho)(3+2\rho)
       +4\rho(1+\rho)+6(3+\rho)\rho
 \le\frac{11215}{512}<24.
\]
These deliberately conservative estimates suffice uniformly in $n$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Components and Euler characteristic}
Put $\etastar=1/4096$, and for $0<\delta\le\etastar$ define
\[
 \cK_C(\delta)=\{X\in\R^n:\cE_C(X)\le\delta\}.
\]
\begin{theorem}[Low-energy topology]\label{pqc:ql:thm:topology}
Every connected component of $\cK_C(\delta)$ is a compact convex set
containing exactly one zero of $\cE_C$. The components are in bijection
with the accepting inputs of $C$. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:betti}
 b_0\bigl(\cK_C(\delta)\bigr)
 =\#\cZ_C=\#\{b:C(b)=1\},\qquad
 b_i\bigl(\cK_C(\delta)\bigr)=0\quad(i>0),
\end{equation}
where homology may be taken with rational coefficients. The Euler
characteristic is the same finite count. If the count is zero, the
sublevel set is empty.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{pqc:ql:thm:rounding}, a point in the sublevel set rounds to a zero $b$;
by \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:rounddistance}, its sup-norm distance from $b$ is at most
$2\sqrt\delta\le1/32$. Thus the sublevel set is contained in the union of
the pairwise disjoint boxes $Q_b$. Its intersection with each box is a
convex sublevel set of a strongly convex function, by \cref{pqc:ql:lem:boxes}, and
contains $b$. It is compact by coercivity. Distinct boxes are a positive
distance apart, so these nonempty intersections are exactly the connected
components. They are contractible by straight-line contraction to $b$.
The homology and Euler-characteristic assertions follow.
\end{proof}

There are no additional positive-energy local minima inside this low
sublevel set: within its box, strict convexity leaves $b$ as the only
critical minimum. No corresponding assertion is made about the landscape
at larger energies.

\begin{theorem}[A specified perturbation stability]\label{pqc:ql:thm:perturb}
Let $h:\R^n\to\R$ be $C^2$, with
\[
 \sup_{\R^n}|h|\le\etastar/4,
 \qquad \|\nabla^2h(X)\|_2\le\tfrac12
 \quad\text{on every zero box }Q_b.
\]
Then $\{X:\cE_C(X)+h(X)\le\etastar/2\}$ has exactly one compact convex
component for every zero of $\cE_C$, and none else. Each component has a
unique interior minimum.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A point in this perturbed sublevel satisfies
$\cE_C(X)\le3\etastar/4<\etastar$, and hence lies in a zero box. Each
zero $b$ itself belongs to the perturbed sublevel, since
$h(b)\le\etastar/4$. On a box the perturbed Hessian is at least $I/2$,
so each intersection is convex. The original energy on the boundary of
a zero box is at least $\tfrac12(1/32)^2=2\etastar$, by integrating the
Hessian lower bound from its zero. The perturbed boundary energy is
therefore greater than the chosen level. Compactness and strict convexity
now give the unique interior minimum. Disjointness of the boxes finishes
the component argument.
\end{proof}

This theorem concerns the stated bounded smooth perturbations. It does not
assert stability under arbitrary changes of expanded polynomial
coefficients, which need not stay uniformly small on $\R^n$.

\section{Two sharp finite-computation frontiers}\label{pqc:ql:sec:frontier}
\srcmark{13}

\subsection{Degree four is necessary for a nonnegative multiwell model}
\begin{proposition}\label[proposition]{pqc:ql:prop:degree}
A globally nonnegative real polynomial of degree at most three cannot have
two isolated zeros. If it is also coercive, it has at most one zero.
Consequently degree four is minimal for globally nonnegative coercive
polynomial encodings capable of having two accepting minima.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A nonzero odd-degree leading homogeneous part takes opposite signs on
opposite rays, so a globally nonnegative polynomial of degree at most
three actually has degree at most two. If such a quadratic vanishes at
$b$, its gradient vanishes there, and it has the form
$(X-b)^{\mathsf T}A(X-b)$ with $A$ positive semidefinite. Its zero set is
$b+\ker A$, an affine subspace. Coercivity makes $A$ positive definite.
\end{proof}
This is a statement about globally nonnegative real landscapes, not a
claim that degree-three Diophantine existence has been classified.

\subsection{Degree-two interactions can be counted exactly}
\begin{theorem}[Tractable interaction boundary]\label{pqc:ql:thm:degree2}
Consider a presented system
\[
 F(X)=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(X_i-1)\bigr)^2+\sum_j r_j(X)^2,
\]
with integer residuals, and suppose its residual-interaction graph has
maximum degree at most two. The number of real, integer, or natural zeros
can be computed in polynomial time from this presentation. After the
local Boolean predicates have been tabulated, only linearly many
arithmetic transfer operations are required.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Zeros are Boolean, so each residual defines a local allowed-assignment
predicate. Its variable support forms a clique in the interaction graph.
A degree-two graph has components that are isolated vertices, paths,
cycles, or triangles. Any residual with three distinct variables fills
a triangle, and that triangle is an entire connected component. No
residual can have four distinct variables. Triangle components can
therefore be enumerated on their eight assignments.

Every larger path or cycle has only unary and binary constraints. Combine
all constraints on a vertex into $U_v(b)\in\Bit$, and all on an edge
$uv$ into $T_{uv}(a,b)\in\Bit$. Along a path $v_1,\ldots,v_\ell$, let
\[
 D_1(b)=U_{v_1}(b),\qquad
 D_{i+1}(b)=U_{v_{i+1}}(b)\sum_{a\in\Bit}
 D_i(a)T_{v_iv_{i+1}}(a,b).
\]
Its count is $D_\ell(0)+D_\ell(1)$. For a cycle, fix the first bit to zero
and then to one, run the same recurrence, and impose the closing edge
before summing. Multiply the component counts. Intermediate counts have
at most $n+1$ bits. Local truth tables require evaluation only at Boolean
assignments on at most three variables, so their construction also has
polynomial bit complexity.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Subcubic counting completeness]\label[corollary]{pqc:ql:cor:counting}
Counting zeros, or the components in \cref{pqc:ql:thm:topology}, of compiler-output
quartics is $\#\mathsf P$-complete under parsimonious polynomial-time
reductions. This remains true with coefficient height at most four,
interaction degree at most three, and all the geometric guarantees above.
Deciding whether a zero exists is $\mathsf{NP}$-complete on this class.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Any polynomial-time Boolean witness verifier can be unrolled into a
polynomial-size Boolean circuit, with one input assignment per witness.
The compiler preserves that count exactly. This gives the usual
$\#\mathsf P$ and $\mathsf{NP}$ hardness, in the counting framework of
\cite{b62s13-valiant}. Membership holds because a Boolean zero is a
polynomial-length certificate and can be checked by evaluating the
presented residuals. Alternatively, on compiler outputs one may count
only the $k$ free input bits and reconstruct the unique remaining wires.
\end{proof}

Together, \cref{pqc:ql:thm:degree2,pqc:ql:cor:counting} give a sharp interaction-degree
frontier for these presented Boolean residual systems: degree two has an
exact polynomial-time count; degree three already realizes all Boolean
witness-counting problems. The statement is a reduction theorem, not an
unconditional separation of $\mathsf{FP}$ from $\#\mathsf P$.

\section{Stochastic computation as a count of minima}\label{pqc:ql:sec:stochastic}
\srcmark{13}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-horizon stochastic compiler]\label{pqc:ql:thm:stochastic}
For every fair-coin program $e$, ordinary input $x$, and horizon $t$, there
is an effectively constructed polynomial $\cE_{e,x,t}$ satisfying all
properties of \cref{pqc:ql:thm:compiler,pqc:ql:thm:hessian,pqc:ql:thm:rounding,pqc:ql:thm:topology}, with
$k=t$ free Boolean inputs, such that
\begin{align}
 p_{e,x,t}
 &=2^{-t}\#\{X\in\N^{n_{e,x,t}}:\cE_{e,x,t}(X)=0\}\label{pqc:ql:eq:probroot}\\
 &=2^{-t}b_0\bigl(\{X\in\R^{n_{e,x,t}}:
               \cE_{e,x,t}(X)\le\etastar\}\bigr)\label{pqc:ql:eq:probbetti}\\
 &=2^{-t}\chi\bigl(\{X:\cE_{e,x,t}(X)\le\etastar\}\bigr).
 \label{pqc:ql:eq:probchi}
\end{align}
For a fixed local machine model, the dimension is polynomial in the
horizon and the finite input length.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Construct the bounded-simulation circuit for $A_{e,x,t}$ and apply
\cref{pqc:ql:thm:compiler}. Its input bits are the $t$ tick-indexed fair bits.
The root bijection gives \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:probroot}; the topology theorem gives
the other equalities. Circuit size and \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:sizes} give the dimension
bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Padding is necessary, not an arbitrary multiplicity}
Suppose a run halts after $h<t$ ticks. It has $2^{t-h}$ extensions to a
length-$t$ coin tape. Those extensions are separate circuit inputs and
must contribute separate roots. Their total normalized weight is
$2^{t-h}/2^t=2^{-h}$, the probability of the corresponding cylinder.

By contrast, duplicate auxiliary witnesses for the \emph{same} tape would
be an error. The copy trees and the common unit introduce no such
duplicates. The distinction between padding multiplicity and arithmetic
witness multiplicity is the reason that the exact bijection was proved
before discussing probability.

\subsection{Compatible injections across horizons}
For an accepted $t$-bit tape $b$ and a bit $c$, append $c$ and reconstruct
the unique root at horizon $t+1$. This defines an effective injection
\[
 \cZ_{e,x,t}\times\Bit\hookrightarrow\cZ_{e,x,t+1}.
\]
It is not a literal coordinate inclusion: the internal circuits and their
copy-wire names can change with $t$. It is the canonical map induced by
input-tape projection followed by unique extension. Hence the normalized
root and component counts are monotone even though the ambient dimensions
change.

\subsection{What is being normalized}
The denominator in \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:probroot} is $2^t$, not $2^{n_{e,x,t}}$.
Internal coordinates encode deterministic consequences and are not
independently sampled. Nor is the formula a claim about the volume of
attraction basins under gradient descent, or about a Gibbs distribution on
$\R^n$. Equal counting weight on the free coin tapes is the precise
probability model. Different well curvatures do not change that counting
measure.

\section{A geometric realization theorem for noncomputable reals}\label{pqc:ql:sec:leftce}
\srcmark{13}

\begin{definition}
A real $\alpha$ is \emph{left-computably enumerable}, or left-c.e., if it is
the limit of a computable nondecreasing sequence of rational numbers.
Equivalently, its strict rational lower cut is computably enumerable.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Uniformly regular quartic realization]\label{pqc:ql:thm:realization}
The limits in \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:probroot}--\eqref{pqc:ql:eq:probchi}, as $e,x$ vary over
fair-coin computations, are exactly the left-c.e. reals in $[0,1]$. In
particular every such real is a limit of normalized component counts of
coercive integer quartics having, simultaneously:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item coefficient height at most $4$ and interaction degree at most $3$;
\item only Boolean real zeros, separated by distance at least $1$;
\item Hessian spectrum in $[2,20]$ at every zero;
\item the fixed rounding threshold $1/64$ and low-energy level $1/4096$;
\item compact convex low-energy components with no higher homology.
\end{enumerate}
The construction is effective from an index for a computable increasing
rational approximation to $\alpha$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For any program, \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:at} is a computable nondecreasing rational
sequence converging to its halting probability. This gives one inclusion.

Conversely, let $a_s\uparrow\alpha\in[0,1]$ be a computable rational
approximation, clipped into $[0,1]$ if necessary. A fair-coin program
constructs an infinite uniform binary real $U\in[0,1]$, one bit at a time.
After $s$ bits, write the current binary cylinder as
\[
 [u_s,u_s+2^{-s}],\qquad u_s=\frac{j_s}{2^s}.
\]
The program computes $a_s$ and halts when
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:sampler}
 u_s+2^{-s}<a_s.
\end{equation}
All comparisons are rational and all stage computations are finite. If
it halts, then $U<\alpha$. If $U<\alpha$, choose a positive gap smaller
than $\alpha-U$; eventually $a_s$ is sufficiently close to $\alpha$ and
$2^{-s}$ is sufficiently small that \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:sampler} holds. Thus the
halting event agrees, up to the measure-zero endpoint convention, with
$\{U<\alpha\}$ and has probability $\alpha$. Unrolling this ordinary
fair-coin program and applying \cref{pqc:ql:thm:stochastic} gives every geometric
property claimed.
\end{proof}

Halting probabilities and left-c.e. reals have an extensive established
theory; universal prefix-free halting probabilities provide the familiar
algorithmically random examples \cite{b62s13-barmpalias}. The point here is not a
new characterization of left-c.e. reals by computation. It is their
simultaneous realization by the explicitly regular sparse quartics just
constructed. \wtag\ The characterization half of the theorem (the limits are exactly the left-c.e.\ reals in $[0,1]$) is the one-output case of Theorem~\ref{pqc:thm:semimeasure} and Lemma~\ref{pqc:lem:leftce} of Part~I; what is new here is the simultaneous realization with the uniform geometric constants (i)--(v).

\subsection{An explicit noncomputable target without randomness theory}
Let $K$ be a fixed noncomputable c.e. halting set, and define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:cantorhalting}
 \alpha_K=\sum_{j\in K}\frac{2}{3^{j+1}}.
\end{equation}
Finite stages of an enumeration give a computable increasing rational
approximation, so \cref{pqc:ql:thm:realization} applies.

To see directly that $\alpha_K$ is noncomputable, suppose the digits below
$j$ have already been recovered. Subtract their contribution. If $j\notin
K$, the remaining tail is at most $3^{-(j+1)}$; if $j\in K$, it is at least
$2\cdot3^{-(j+1)}$. An approximation with error smaller than one quarter
of $3^{-(j+1)}$ distinguishes the cases. Induction would decide $K$ from
a computable real name for $\alpha_K$, a contradiction.

\begin{corollary}[Regular geometry does not give a convergence modulus]
There is a single computable family of the above quartics for which the
normalized component counts have no computable modulus of convergence.
Consequently no general modulus can be inferred solely from the displayed
coefficient, interaction, gap, separation, or Hessian bounds.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Choose the family realizing \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:cantorhalting}. A computable modulus,
together with the computable finite counts, would compute its limit.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A useful obstruction to over-compression}
\begin{proposition}[Finite Boolean witnesses cannot be universally MRDP]
Suppose a fixed polynomial family $P(e,x,w)$ has a fixed number $n$ of
witness coordinates, and every natural witness satisfying $P=0$ lies in
$\Bit^n$. Then its existential input relation is decidable.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Evaluate $P$ on all $2^n$ Boolean witness tuples. More generally, any known
computable finite witness bound gives a finite decision procedure.
\end{proof}
Thus the increasing horizon or an unbounded witness domain is essential.
Our regular Boolean quartics are not a counterexample to this elementary
obstruction, and their dimensions are not fixed as $t\to\infty$.

\section{Fixed-arity quartic probability predicates}\label{pqc:ql:sec:normalforms}
\srcmark{13}

\subsection{A standard quartic reduction, stated precisely}
We use MRDP in the form that every c.e. relation on a finite tuple of
natural inputs is the existential projection of an integer polynomial
zero set \cite{b62-matiyasevich1970,b62s13-repoMRDP}. The multi-input form follows from
the one-input form by polynomial tuple coding. For example,
$J(a,b)=(a+b)^2+a$ is an injective natural-number pairing map: the intervals
$[s^2,s^2+s]$ for successive $s=a+b$ are disjoint. Iterating this pairing
and substituting it into a representing polynomial suffices.

\begin{lemma}[Quartic normalization]\label[lemma]{pqc:ql:lem:quarticMRDP}
Every c.e. relation has an existential natural-number representation by a
single nonnegative integer polynomial of degree at most four, with a fixed
finite number of witnesses.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Start with an MRDP polynomial $P$. Write $P=P_+-P_-$, where $P_+$ and $P_-$
have nonnegative integer coefficients. Evaluate them by addition and
multiplication circuits on natural inputs and witnesses. Introduce one
natural wire value per arithmetic gate. Equations $z=x+y$ and $z=xy$ have
degree at most two; equate the two final outputs. The sum of the squares
of all residuals is a nonnegative integer polynomial of degree at most
four. Its natural zeros are exactly the valid arithmetic evaluations of
zeros of $P$.
\end{proof}
This lemma preserves the multiplicity of the \emph{pre-existing} MRDP
witnesses, but does not make those witnesses unique. It also does not
supply the small coefficients, Booleanity, coercivity, or sparse graph of
\cref{pqc:ql:thm:compiler}. \wtag\ The lemma is Lemma~\ref{pqc:lem:quarticlower} of Part~I; the proof above is a second route to it.

\subsection{Strict lower cuts are Diophantine}
Write rational thresholds as $q=a/b$, with $a\in\N$ and $b\ge1$.
Denominator validity can be built into the c.e. relation; alternatively
use $b=d+1$ as a parameterization by all naturals.

\begin{theorem}[Probability lower-cut polynomial]\label{pqc:ql:thm:lowercut}
There is one fixed nonnegative integer quartic $D$ with a fixed witness
tuple $w$ such that, for every program, input, and valid rational threshold,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:D}
 p_{e,x}>a/b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists w\in\N^r\ D(e,x,a,b,w)=0.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By monotone convergence,
\[
 p_{e,x}>a/b\iff\exists t\; b\,a_{e,x,t}>a\,2^t.
\]
The finite count $a_{e,x,t}$ is computable by enumeration of all $t$-bit
tapes, regardless of efficiency. The displayed relation is c.e. Apply
\cref{pqc:ql:lem:quarticMRDP} to the tuple $(e,x,a,b)$.
\end{proof}
The program index is an input to a single universal c.e. predicate here;
we are not silently choosing a different polynomial after learning a
halting outcome. The present package outputs the finite-horizon quartics,
not an expanded coefficient list for this much larger universal $D$. \wtag\ For effective output laws this is Corollary~\ref{pqc:cor:strict} of Part~I, proved by the same monotone-approximation argument.

\subsection{One additional universal block is unavoidable}
Apply the same construction to the c.e. relation
\[
 p_{e,x}>\frac ab-\frac1{k+1}.
\]
It has a fixed quartic representation $Q(e,x,a,b,k,z)=0$. Thresholds below
zero cause no difficulty: the finite integer comparison remains
computable and is automatically true when appropriate.

\begin{theorem}[Exact quantifier normal forms]\label{pqc:ql:thm:quantifiers}
For valid $a,b$ the following equivalences hold:
\begin{align}
 p_{e,x}>a/b &\iff\exists w\;D(e,x,a,b,w)=0,\label{pqc:ql:eq:nf1}\\
 p_{e,x}\le a/b &\iff\forall w\;D(e,x,a,b,w)\ne0,\label{pqc:ql:eq:nf2}\\
 p_{e,x}\ge a/b &\iff\forall k\,\exists z\;Q(e,x,a,b,k,z)=0,\label{pqc:ql:eq:nf3}\\
 p_{e,x}<a/b &\iff\exists k\,\forall z\;Q(e,x,a,b,k,z)\ne0.\label{pqc:ql:eq:nf4}
\end{align}
Equality is the conjunction of \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:nf2} and \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:nf3}.
Almost-sure termination is the special case
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:ASTquartic}
 p_{e,x}=1\iff\forall k\,\exists z\;Q(e,x,1,1,k,z)=0.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first two statements are \cref{pqc:ql:thm:lowercut} and its complement.
For any real $p$, the assertion $p\ge q$ is equivalent to
$p>q-1/(k+1)$ for every $k$. Its complement says that for some $k$,
$p\le q-1/(k+1)$. This gives the next two statements. Finally $p\le1$
is automatic for a probability.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Completeness and nonexistence of existential substitutes}
The classical hierarchy results \cite{kaminski-katoen} can be recovered directly in
this setting. We record the reductions because they determine which
requested Diophantine representations are possible. \wtag\ For a fixed interior threshold $0<q<1$ these are the classifications of Theorem~\ref{pqc:thm:unconditionaltable} in Part~I; the reductions below are second routes to it.

Sample $N\in\N$ with $\Prob(N=n)=2^{-(n+1)}$, and then run an ordinary
program $M$ on $N$. Every finite $n$ has positive probability, so this
probabilistic program halts almost surely exactly when $M$ halts on every
input. The latter property is $\pitwo$-complete: any predicate
$\forall n\exists t\,R(e,n,t)$ with decidable $R$ is represented by the
program that searches for a suitable $t$ on input $n$. Thus \AST\ is
$\pitwo$-complete. \wtag\ The sampler is the totality sampler \eqref{pqc:eq:te} of Part~I.

For any fixed rational $0<q<1$, a fair-coin program can enter that
probabilistic computation with probability exactly $q$ and otherwise loop
forever. Its halting probability is $q p$. A rational gate can be
implemented by finite-block rejection sampling, which terminates almost
surely. Consequently $p\ge q$ and $p=q$ are $\pitwo$-hard, and $p<q$ is
$\sigtwo$-hard. The normal forms give the matching upper bounds. To obtain
$\sigone$-hardness of $p>q$, choose a dyadic $r>q$, enter a simulation of a
fixed ordinary halting instance with probability $r$, and otherwise loop.
The resulting probability is either zero or $r$. Complementation gives
$\pione$-completeness of $p\le q$.

\wtag\ Source 13's summary table also listed the five classifications for a fixed
interior threshold $0<q<1$: $p>q$ is $\sigone$-complete, $p\le q$ is
$\pione$-complete, $p\ge q$ and $p=q$ are $\pitwo$-complete, and $p<q$ is
$\sigtwo$-complete, with the normal forms \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:nf1}--\eqref{pqc:ql:eq:nf4}.
Those classes are exactly the ones of Theorem~\ref{pqc:thm:unconditionaltable}
in Part~I, which is not reprinted. The rows that Part~I does not print are
kept:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Property & Exact class & Normal form\\
\midrule
$p=1$ (\AST) & $\pitwo$-complete & \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:ASTquartic}\\
$p=0$ & $\pione$-complete & \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:nf2} with $a/b=0/1$\\
$\E\tau<\infty$ (scheduler-free) & $\sigtwo$-complete & \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:meanquartic}; Theorem~\ref{pqc:ql:thm:geometricmean}\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Endpoint thresholds have exceptions: for example $p=0$ is
$\pione$-complete, not $\pitwo$-complete, and $p>1$ is empty.

Since existential polynomial relations are c.e., hierarchy strictness
rules out an exact existential Diophantine representation of \AST\ on
program indices. This is a proved obstruction, not a failure of a chosen
coding technique. Bounded unique witnesses do not remove the extra
universal quantifier.

\section{Finite expected runtime and the danger of simulation slowdown}\label{pqc:ql:sec:mean}
\srcmark{13}

\subsection{A root-count formula for the mean}
For a nonnegative integer-valued stopping time, allowing infinity,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:mean}
 \E\tau=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\Prob(\tau>t)
 =\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\left(1-2^{-t}\#\cZ_{e,x,t}\right).
\end{equation}
Indeed $\tau(\omega)=\sum_{t\ge0}\mathbf1_{\{\tau(\omega)>t\}}$ pointwise,
and monotone convergence permits expectation to pass through the sum.
Every finite partial sum is an exactly computable rational.

Finiteness is therefore
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:meanquantifier}
 \E\tau<\infty\iff
 \exists M\in\N\ \forall N\in\N\quad
 \sum_{t<N}(1-p_t)\le M.
\end{equation}
The violation predicate ``some partial sum exceeds $M$'' is c.e. By
quartic normalization, there is a fixed quartic $V$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ql:eq:meanquartic}
 \E\tau<\infty\iff\exists M\,\forall w\;V(e,x,M,w)\ne0.
\end{equation}
This is the $\sigtwo$ form of positive almost-sure termination in the
scheduler-free model, consistent with \cite{kaminski-katoen}.

\subsection{Hardness even after a single random-sampling phase}
The following proof makes the source of the second quantifier block
particularly transparent.

\begin{theorem}[Geometric-input finite-mean hardness]\label{pqc:ql:thm:geometricmean}
There is an effective family of fair-coin programs with the form
``sample one geometric natural number; then execute a total deterministic
body'' for which almost-sure termination always holds, but finite expected
runtime is $\sigtwo$-complete.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use a standard effective enumeration $W_e$ of c.e. sets, arranged to emit
at most one previously unseen element at a stage. Let $I_e(s)\in\Bit$
indicate whether stage $s$ emits a new element. Its computation is a
bounded simulation with polynomial overhead in $s$ for each fixed $e$.

Sample $S$ with $\Prob(S=s)=2^{-(s+1)}$. Compute $I_e(s)$. If it is one,
perform a delay of $\Theta(2^s)$ elementary machine steps; then halt.
Otherwise halt immediately. The body is total for every finite $s$.
The sampling loop's infinite path has probability zero, so every program
in the family is almost-surely terminating.

The expected bounded-simulation and sampling overheads are finite, since
$\sum_s2^{-s}s^d<\infty$ for every fixed $d$. The expected delay is finite
exactly when
\[
 \sum_s2^{-(s+1)}2^s I_e(s)=\frac12\sum_s I_e(s)
\]
is finite. The constant-factor delay estimates suffice: each positive
stage contributes an amount bounded above and below by positive constants.
The last sum is finite exactly when $W_e$ is finite.

For completeness, $\FIN=\{e:W_e\text{ is finite}\}$ is $\sigtwo$-complete.
Membership follows by asserting that after some stage no new element is
emitted. For hardness, given $\exists n\forall t\,R(e,n,t)$ with decidable
$R$, let $n_s$ be the least $n\le s$ satisfying every test $R(e,n,t)$ for
$t\le s$, or $s+1$ if none exists. Emit the distinct values that occur in
this sequence. If a least genuine witness $n$ exists, every smaller
candidate is eventually refuted and $n_s$ eventually stabilizes at $n$.
Only finitely many values are emitted. If none exists, every fixed
candidate is eventually refuted, so $n_s\to\infty$ and infinitely many
values are emitted. This is an effective reduction to $\FIN$.
Together with \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:meanquantifier}, it proves the claim.
\end{proof}

A delay of $\Theta(2^s)$ can be implemented without a hidden huge-integer
unit-cost instruction: traverse the full binary recursion tree of depth
$s$, using a stack. Its number of nodes is $2^{s+1}-1$, and a fixed local
stack machine has constant work per node. Other standard models may add
a polynomial factor; choosing a sampling law adapted to a documented
time bound gives the same hardness, but the above explicit stack model
avoids that detour.

\subsection{Probability preservation is weaker than mean preservation}
\begin{proposition}[Polynomial slowdown can destroy finite mean]
A path-faithful simulation with polynomial time overhead need not
preserve finite expected running time.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Sample $N$ by continuing with probability $1/4$ at each iteration. Then
$\Prob(N=n)=3/4^{n+1}$. A computation with delay $T=2^N$ has
\[
 \E T=\frac34\sum_{n\ge0}2^{-n}=\frac32<\infty,
 \qquad
 \E(T^2)=\frac34\sum_{n\ge0}1=\infty.
\]
The sampling overhead also has finite expectation. A simulation that
slows the delay quadratically has infinite mean, while preserving exactly
which coin streams eventually halt.
\end{proof}

An affine pathwise bound $\tau'\le A\tau+B$ is sufficient to preserve
finite mean in the forward direction. Two-sided suitable bounds are
needed for equivalence. It would be incorrect to transfer the finite-mean
classification to every Turing-complete substrate merely from an
unspecified effective simulation.

\section{Transfer to unconventional computational substrates}\label{pqc:ql:sec:substrates}
\srcmark{13}

\subsection{The precise transferable hypothesis}
\begin{definition}
A \emph{coin-faithful simulation} of a stochastic machine into a substrate
is an effective translation with a deterministic evaluation strategy,
finite simulation of each completed source step, and the following
property: on the same stream of requested fair bits, the target eventually
halts exactly when the source does. Extra target operations do not make
independent probabilistic choices.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Stochastic substrate transfer]\label{pqc:ql:thm:transfer}
A substrate admitting a coin-faithful simulation of fair-coin Turing
computation inherits the full class of halting probabilities and the
almost-sure termination hardness. If its bounded operational semantics is
effective, it also has the finite-horizon quartic representations of
\cref{pqc:ql:thm:stochastic}, using its own step convention. Finite-mean properties
transfer only under additional time-overhead hypotheses.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Coin faithfulness identifies the two halting events on the product
probability space, so their measures agree. This also preserves the
predicate that the measure is one. Effective bounded operational
semantics gives a computable finite coin-tape predicate, which can be
compiled into a Boolean circuit; the explicit circuit compiler then
applies. The final qualification is the preceding slowdown proposition.
\end{proof}

The bounded circuit may be much larger than a source-machine circuit.
Effectiveness suffices for representability; a polynomial circuit-size
bound requires a separate efficient-simulation argument.

\subsection{A minimal randomized combinator example}
Start with a deterministic evaluation strategy for a universal combinator
calculus. Add a primitive $\mathsf{coin}(A,B)$ that returns $A$ or $B$ with
probability $1/2$, and insist that it reduces only when demanded by that
strategy. An ordinary universal simulation can translate a source coin
instruction to exactly one occurrence of this primitive and perform all
other source instructions deterministically. That gives a coin-faithful
simulation.

The demand restriction matters. Unrestricted reduction could duplicate a
random expression before it is sampled, or sample it before duplication;
those operations have different joint distributions. For example,
copying one sampled Boolean value gives perfectly correlated copies,
whereas reducing two independent coin expressions does not. The theorem
requires operational semantics that fixes this distinction, not merely
Turing completeness of the underlying rewrite rules.

\subsection{Other legitimate targets and exclusions}
The same interface can be attached to effective stack machines, pointer
heap machines, finite-string rewriting evaluators, or cellular
computational models with a specified random-bit input channel, provided
a deterministic universal simulation and its coin discipline are supplied.
These are applications of the transfer theorem, not claims that every
chemical, physical, or biological system automatically has those
properties.

In particular, a finite-state Markov chain has decidable rational linear
algebra for its absorption probabilities; an unbounded effective state
space is the source of the general computability phenomena here.
State-dependent irrational transition laws need effective presentations
and are outside the fair-coin assumptions as stated. Adding adversarial
nondeterministic schedulers changes the problem substantially: work on
positive almost-sure termination with such schedulers reaches
$\Pi^1_1$-completeness \cite{b62s13-majumdar2023}. The scheduler-free
$\sigtwo$ classification must not be carried over to that different model.

\wtag\ \emph{Batch-76 note (2 October 2026).} Part~IX makes the first sentence
of the paragraph above explicit and quantum: for a rational,
finite-dimensional, time-homogeneous quantum loop, exit probabilities, stopped
output states and all finite-path moments are rational, given by four quadratic
matrix identities and a finite recurrence, and certified by a quartic with a
unique natural witness (Sections~\ref{pqc:iq:sec:group}--\ref{pqc:iq:sec:compiler}).
Its Proposition~\ref{pqc:iq:prop:scheduled} adds that a computable schedule, even
in dimension one, already brings back the general computability phenomena.

\section{Worked examples and exact artifacts}\label{pqc:ql:sec:examples}
\srcmark{13}

\subsection{A four-variable one-bit polynomial}
For the circuit $C(x)=x$, let $u$ be the root unit, $a$ the output occurrence,
and $b$ the unit occurrence. The compiler gives
\begin{align}\label{pqc:ql:eq:onebit}
 F(x,u,a,b)={}&\sum_{v\in\{x,u,a,b\}}v^2(v-1)^2\\
 &+(u-1)^2+(a-x)^2+(b-u)^2+(a-b)^2.\notag
\end{align}
Its only real zero is $(1,1,1,1)$. There is one accepted input out of two,
so the corresponding probability is $1/2$.

The expanded polynomial is
\begin{align*}
 F={}&x^4+u^4+a^4+b^4-2(x^3+u^3+a^3+b^3)\\
 &+2x^2+3u^2+3a^2+3b^2-2u-2ax-2bu-2ab+1.
\end{align*}
Its coefficient height is three. At its zero, in coordinate order
$(x,u,a,b)$, the Hessian is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}
 4&0&-2&0\\
 0&6&0&-2\\
 -2&0&6&-2\\
 0&-2&-2&6
 \end{pmatrix},
\]
which is $2I+2J^{\mathsf T}J$ for the four displayed linear residuals.

\subsection{Geometric waiting time}
Consider a program that halts at the first tick with bit one. Its
horizon-$t$ predicate is the OR of its $t$ input bits. Thus
\[
 a_t=2^t-1,\qquad p_t=1-2^{-t},\qquad p=1.
\]
For $t\ge1$, the demonstration circuit uses $4(t-1)$ gates by iterating
$x\lor y=\neg(\neg x\land\neg y)$. The implementation produces:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrrl}
\toprule
$t$ & Gates & Variables & Non-Boolean residuals & Zeros & Probability\\
\midrule
0&1&4&5&0&$0$\\
1&0&4&4&1&$1/2$\\
2&4&20&19&3&$3/4$\\
3&8&36&34&7&$7/8$\\
4&12&52&49&15&$15/16$\\
5&16&68&64&31&$31/32$\\
6&20&84&79&63&$63/64$\\
7&24&100&94&127&$127/128$\\
8&28&116&109&255&$255/256$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Here the $t=0$ predicate is constant zero. Sparse expanded polynomials and
residual lists for horizons $0,1,2,3$ are included in the package.

\subsection{A constant noncomputable limit with increasing finite objects}
For the sampler of \eqref{pqc:ql:eq:cantorhalting}, every horizon still gives a
finite exactly computable polynomial and a finite exactly computable
count. What cannot be uniformly completed is the limiting probability.
There is no contradiction between a finite exact artifact at each stage
and a noncomputable limit. The present geometric theorem makes that
separation explicit without appealing to fragile numerical encodings.

\texttt{verify.py} executes deterministic checks using seed

The structural audits check expanded degree, coefficient height, constant

A further 60 floating-point Hessian tests examined 30 exact zeros and 30
points in their prescribed boxes. At the sampled zeros, the smallest

sanity checks, not a proof of the spectral inequalities. The exact

$543/512>1$ and $11215/512<24$.

The source does not implement a general Turing-machine-to-circuit frontend,

this article. Its executable boundary is the explicit Boolean circuit
compiler and the degree-two counter. The machine simulation and
fixed-arity representations are established by the mathematical arguments
