\section{A formalization plan for \reponame}\label{pqc:ql:sec:formalization}
\srcmark{13}

\subsection{An appropriate module boundary}
A natural new project is a stochastic compilation layer adjacent to the
existing Hilbert-tenth development, rather than a modification of the
MRDP core. Its first formal object should be an acyclic circuit with
explicit input wires, gate definitions, and a distinguished output. A
routed certificate should carry its defining equations and occurrence
ownership, making incidence and graph bounds structural invariants.

The proof obligations separate into four layers. The finite algebraic
layer proves unique evaluation, the sum-of-squares zero equivalence, and
the expanded coefficient bound. The finite graph layer proves the trunk
routing invariant and the degree-two count. The analytic layer proves
rounding, Hessian bounds, and low-sublevel components. The measure layer
relates cylinder probabilities to finite counts and then to the limit.

For the fixed-arity comparison predicates, the existing
\texttt{Diophantine.mrdp} interface is the correct foundation
\cite{b62s13-repoMRDP}. One first proves that finite-horizon acceptance counts are
computable, then that a strict threshold crossing is c.e., and only then
invokes MRDP. This avoids attempting to formalize probability itself as
an existential arithmetic witness.

\subsection{Suggested first formal milestones}
The shortest valuable milestone is the finite bijection, entirely over
Boolean vectors and integer residuals. It already certifies every sparse
JSON polynomial produced by a proved version of the compiler. Next comes
the coefficient-height and subcubic graph theorem, followed by the
real-valued rounding lemma. These are more local than the homology theorem
and can be audited independently.

The low-energy topology proof can initially be stated without homology:
a finite disjoint union of nonempty compact convex sets indexed by
accepted inputs. Betti numbers and Euler characteristic are then derived
consequences rather than prerequisites. Likewise, a first probability
formalization can prove the rational finite-horizon identity before any
infinite product-space construction is introduced.

A verified general-purpose frontend need not be the first deliverable.
The elementary OR family, a bounded register-machine interpreter, or a
fixed universal local machine would provide progressively stronger
integration tests. The ordinary data input must remain distinguished
from free random bits throughout.

\subsection{Trust boundary}
No new Lean file is presented as checked in this package. A downstream
formalization should not import the mathematical theorems as axioms and
then describe the compiler as verified. The repository's published MRDP
interface, the present paper's informal proofs, executable finite tests,
and any future proof-assistant certificates are four different evidence
levels and should remain separately labeled.

% --- source 17, lines 104-1340 ---
\section{The question: what does fast mixing fail to decide?}
\label{pqc:rv:sec:intro}
\srcmark{17}
A quantitative convergence theorem answers an approximation question.
It need not answer an exact equality question, and it gives even less
reason to expect a decision procedure for rationality or algebraicity.
This distinction becomes especially sharp when a system simultaneously
has rational local rules, reversibility, strong drift, and a spectral gap
bounded away from zero. The purpose of this article is to exhibit that
distinction in one elementary model, with explicit reductions and
arithmetic certificates rather than a bare appeal to universality.

Our starting point is the following binary choice of birth probabilities:
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:kernel-intro}
 P_b(n,n+1)=\frac{2-b_n}{8},\qquad
 P_b(n,n-1)=\frac12\quad(n\geq1),\qquad b_n\in\{0,1\}.
\end{equation}
The remaining probability is assigned to staying put; there is no death
move at zero. A flag $b_n=1$ is called a \emph{defect}. It reduces an
already inward-biased birth probability. Defects can therefore record
information without destroying confinement.

The results answer four concrete questions about this model. Can exact
stationary equality still encode halting under a uniform mixing estimate?
Yes, even when every stationary coordinate is rational. Can one characterize
exactly which environments have rational root mass? Yes: precisely the
eventually periodic ones. Can rationality or algebraicity be certified by
one existential polynomial for all effectively specified environments?
No: both properties already have second-level arithmetical complexity.
Which equilibrium assertions do admit finite Diophantine certificates?
Strict rational comparisons do, and their finite arithmetic layer has a
small canonical quartic presentation.

\subsection{Main results at a glance}
The same stationary family underlies the following statements. The input
model is part of each assertion; a statement about a known rational input
is not a statement about a program producing an approximation to a real.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{0.28\textwidth}X@{}}
\toprule
Property or task & Result proved here \\
\midrule
Uniform analytic control & Reversibility, exponential tails, root return
mean $\leq2$, sharp common gap $\delta=(3-2\sqrt2)/4$, root-start
mixing $\leq\tfrac12(1-\delta)^t$. \\
Symbolic arithmetic & Rational root mass if and only if the environment
is eventually periodic; the attainable-mass set has dimension
$\log_2((1+\sqrt5)/2)$. \\
One-defect computation & All masses are rational, but exact equality to
$1/2$ is $\Pi^0_1$-complete. No computable description-length bound
on reduced denominators exists. \\
Primitive-recursive environments & Rationality and algebraicity are
$\Sigma^0_2$-complete; irrationality and transcendence are
$\Pi^0_2$-complete. \\
Finite certificates & Sharp prefix bounds; a unique arithmetic witness
with $N+1$ coordinates and $2N+1$ squared residuals in the compact presentation. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\subsection{Relation to ProveIt and to earlier work}
This manuscript is based on the repository snapshot \pin. The relevant
formal foundation is ProveIt's natural-number MRDP interface,
\code{Diophantine.mrdp}, together with its converse
\code{Diophantine.mrdp_iff} \cite{b62s17-proveit-mrdp}. It says that a
computably enumerable subset of $\N$ is the projection of the natural
zero set of one integer polynomial. It is an existence interface, not a
stated practical compiler with numerical degree and witness bounds.
We use it only with that scope.

The repository also contains a substantial informal report on
probabilistic output laws, quantum mortality, and continuous-computation
barriers (\wtag\ Parts~\ref{pqc:part:prob}--\ref{pqc:part:continuous} of the present report; the source cites that report's README at the pin). The present construction concerns stationary
measures of countably infinite reversible chains, their arithmetic type,
and a binary-environment coding. It does not reproduce that report's
normalization-budget or quantum-mortality constructions. This is a
comparison with the inspected relevant material, not a claim that every
file in the repository has been exhaustively audited.

Undecidability of exact stationary distributions is not new. Gamarnik
proved it for constrained homogeneous random walks, even with an input
linear Lyapunov function witnessing positive recurrence
\cite{b62s17-gamarnik}. Our contribution is an explicit combination of
reversibility, a sharp common spectral gap, a uniform root-start mixing
estimate, rational-valued hard instances, and a complete symbolic
rationality criterion. A programmable one-dimensional environment and a
constrained homogeneous random walk in a fixed-dimensional orthant are
different input models. The result here is not asserted to strengthen
all restrictions in Gamarnik's theorem.

History recording is a classical route to logically reversible
computation \cite{b62s17-bennett}. We give the actual local history map needed
here, rather than invoking reversibility as a black box. Counter-machine
instruction sets must be specified carefully: reversibility can change
halting decidability differently for different instruction sets
\cite{b62s17-morita,b62s17-dudenhefner}. The lift below uses a history counter with
multiplication by a fixed base, and does not claim a new theorem about a
minimal reversible two-counter instruction set.

The self-similar-set dimension calculation is a specialization of
classical separated-iterated-function-system theory \cite{b62s17-hutchinson}.
The sparse-defect transcendence proof uses the elementary Liouville
principle \cite{b62s17-liouville}, which is proved in the needed form here.
The low-complexity transcendence corollary uses the deeper theorem of
Adamczewski and Bugeaud \cite{b62s17-ab}; that theorem is explicitly imported,
not reproved or presented as a new result.

\subsection{Conventions and levels of effectivity}
We write $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. An environment is an infinite binary
word $b$. At first it need not be computable. A \emph{primitive-recursive
environment code} is a finite syntactic expression for a
primitive-recursive function of one natural variable, followed by
reduction modulo two. All such expressions can be enumerated and
uniformly evaluated by a total computable interpreter; no universal
primitive-recursive evaluator is assumed.

A real is \emph{computable} when a program supplies rational intervals
of arbitrarily small prescribed width containing it. This is not the
same as producing its reduced numerator and denominator when it happens
to be rational. A set is \emph{Diophantine} here if it has a fixed
existential integer-polynomial representation with natural witnesses.
By MRDP this is equivalent to being computably enumerable
\cite{b62s17-proveit-mrdp}. Arithmetic hierarchy statements concern computable
many-one reductions and the usual finite coding of tuples.

\section{The chain and its exact stationary law}
\label{pqc:rv:sec:stationary}
\srcmark{17}
Fix $b\in\{0,1\}^{\N}$, and define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:weights}
 r_n=\frac{2-b_n}{4},\qquad D_n=\sum_{k<n}b_k,\qquad
 w_n=\prod_{k<n}r_k=2^{-n-D_n},\qquad Z_b=\sum_{n\geq0}w_n.
\end{equation}
Empty products are one. The kernel is given by
\cref{pqc:rv:eq:kernel-intro} and its holding probability. Write
$\alpha_b=\pi_b(0)$ for the stationary root mass.

\begin{theorem}[Stationarity and uniform confinement]\label{pqc:rv:thm:stationary}
For every environment $b$, the chain is irreducible, aperiodic and
positive recurrent, with unique stationary distribution
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:stationary}
 \pi_b(n)=\frac{w_n}{Z_b},\qquad
 \frac43\leq Z_b\leq2,\qquad \frac12\leq\alpha_b\leq\frac34.
\end{equation}
It is reversible. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:tail}
 \pi_b(n)\leq\frac34\,2^{-n},\qquad
 \sum_{n\geq M}\pi_b(n)\leq\frac32\,2^{-M},\qquad
 \mathbb E_{\pi_b}[a^X]\leq\frac{3}{4(1-a/2)}\quad(1\leq a<2).
\end{equation}
The expected positive return time to zero is $Z_b\leq2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every birth and every available death move has positive probability;
every state has a positive holding probability. Also
$4^{-n}\leq w_n\leq2^{-n}$, so summing the two geometric series gives
$4/3\leq Z_b\leq2$. The identity
\[
 \pi_b(n)P_b(n,n+1)=\frac{w_n}{Z_b}\frac{2-b_n}{8}
 =\frac{w_{n+1}}{2Z_b}
 =\pi_b(n+1)P_b(n+1,n)
\]
proves detailed balance and hence stationarity. An irreducible chain
with a stationary probability distribution is positive recurrent and
has that distribution uniquely. The displayed tail and moment bounds
follow by geometric summation. The return identity
$\mathbb E_0\tau_0^+=1/\pi_b(0)$ is the usual cycle formula for a
positive recurrent chain: successive visits to zero divide a path into
identically distributed regenerative cycles, each with one initial
visit to zero. Dividing the occupation count at zero by mean cycle
length gives its stationary frequency. Thus the mean is $Z_b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
There is no conflict between this mean return bound and a very late
computational event. Most returns occur without visiting a remote defect.
The stationary mass of a state carrying a long computation is
exponentially small in its trajectory index.
\end{remark}

The kernel is specified by a single bit at each state. All its nonzero
entries belong to
\[
 \left\{\frac18,\frac14,\frac38,\frac12,\frac34,\frac78\right\}.
\]
No undecidable information has been put into an individual real-valued
transition coefficient. When $b$ is computable, every row is exactly
computable with rational arithmetic.

\section{A sharp common spectral gap and a uniform mixing estimate}
\label{pqc:rv:sec:gap}
\srcmark{17}
Let $L^2(\pi_b)$ have norm $\|f\|_{2,\pi_b}$, and let
\[
 \mathcal E_b(f,f)=\langle f,(I-P_b)f\rangle_{\pi_b}
 =\frac12\sum_{k\geq0}\pi_b(k+1)(f(k+1)-f(k))^2.
\]
The last expression counts each edge once after using detailed balance.
For reversible chains, standard operator and Dirichlet-form background
can be found in Aldous and Fill \cite{b62s17-aldous-fill}; the estimate needed
here has a short direct proof.

\begin{lemma}[A weighted half-line Poincare estimate]\label[lemma]{pqc:rv:lem:poincare}
Suppose a birth--death chain has a strictly positive stationary
distribution $\pi$, constant death probability $q>0$, and ratios $\pi(n+1)/\pi(n)\leq r<1$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:poincare}
 \Var_\pi(f)\leq\frac{1}{q(1-\sqrt r)^2}\,\mathcal E(f,f)
 \qquad(f\in L^2(\pi)).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $g_k=\sqrt{\pi(k+1)}(f(k+1)-f(k))$. Since the mean minimizes
squared distance to constants,
\[
 \Var_\pi(f)\leq\sum_{n\geq1}\pi(n)(f(n)-f(0))^2.
\]
The anchored differences obey
\begin{align*}
 \sqrt{\pi(n)}\,|f(n)-f(0)|
 &\leq\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\sqrt{\frac{\pi(n)}{\pi(k+1)}}\,|g_k|\\
 &\leq\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}r^{(n-k-1)/2}|g_k|.
\end{align*}
The final expression is a convolution with the summable sequence
$1,\sqrt r,r,\ldots$. The triangle inequality for its shifted
$\ell^2$ vectors gives
\[
 \left(\sum_{n\geq1}\pi(n)(f(n)-f(0))^2\right)^{1/2}
 \leq\sum_{j\geq0}r^{j/2}\|g\|_2
 =\frac{\|g\|_2}{1-\sqrt r}.
\]
As $\mathcal E(f,f)=q\|g\|_2^2$, squaring proves the claim. The same
argument applies to infinite sequences by convergence of the shift sum
in $\ell^2$; alternatively truncate the convolution and pass to the
limit. The Dirichlet form is finite for $f\in L^2(\pi)$ since a
stationary Markov operator is a contraction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform mixing, with the optimal common gap]\label{pqc:rv:thm:mixing}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:delta}
 \delta=\frac{3-2\sqrt2}{4},\qquad
 \rho=1-\delta=\frac{1+2\sqrt2}{4}.
\end{equation}
Every $P_b$ has spectral gap at least $\delta$, and this common lower
bound cannot be increased. For every integer $t\geq0$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:mixing}
 \|\delta_0P_b^t-\pi_b\|_{\TV}
 \leq\frac12\sqrt{Z_b-1}\,\rho^t
 \leq\frac12\rho^t
 \leq\frac12\left(\frac{23}{24}\right)^t.
\end{equation}
The estimate is uniform in the entire environment.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{pqc:rv:lem:poincare} with $q=r=1/2$ to obtain the gap.
Each holding probability is at least $1/4$, so
$P_b=\tfrac14 I+\tfrac34 K$ for a reversible stochastic kernel $K$.
Consequently the spectrum of $P_b$ is bounded below by $-1/2$.
On the orthogonal complement of the constants it is bounded above by
$1-\delta$, and its absolute value is at most $\rho$.

The density of $\delta_0$ with respect to $\pi_b$, minus one, has
squared $L^2(\pi_b)$ norm $1/\pi_b(0)-1=Z_b-1$. By reversibility,
the density after $t$ steps is obtained by applying $P_b^t$.
Cauchy--Schwarz bounds half its $L^1$ distance by half its $L^2$
distance, proving the first two inequalities. Finally,
$\delta>1/24$: equivalently $17>12\sqrt2$, whose square is $289>288$.
The optimality of $\delta$ is established in \cref{pqc:rv:app:sharp} by test
vectors for the defect-free chain.
\end{proof}

The same constant appears in a drift computation. For
$V(n)=(\sqrt2)^n$ and $n\geq1$,
\[
 \frac{P_bV(n)}{V(n)}
 =1+p_n(\sqrt2-1)+\tfrac12(1/\sqrt2-1)\leq\rho,
 \qquad p_n=\frac{2-b_n}{8}.
\]
Thus confinement is visible directly in the local rules as well as in
the stationary formula. The root is a single exceptional small set.

\begin{remark}[What uniformity means]\label[remark]{pqc:rv:rem:uniformity}
The bound is uniform over environments when the initial state is zero.
It is not uniform over all starting states. A walk begun at $m$ cannot
reach zero in fewer than $m$ nearest-neighbor steps. In particular,
no assertion of uniform ergodicity in the all-starting-states sense is
being made. Also, a Markov step is not automatically a constant-time
operation on the bit representation of a large computational state.
\end{remark}

\section{The equilibrium as a uniquely decodable binary object}
\label{pqc:rv:sec:coding}
\srcmark{17}
The stationary formula has more structure than mere computability.
It records the defect positions in a constrained binary expansion.

\begin{theorem}[The defect expansion]\label{pqc:rv:thm:defects}
List the defect positions in increasing order as $d_1<d_2<\cdots$,
with a finite or empty list allowed. Then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:defect-series}
 Z_b=2-\sum_j2^{-(d_j+j)}.
\end{equation}
The binary expansion of $L_b=2-Z_b$ is the infinite word
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:morphism}
 c=h(b),\qquad h(0)=0,\quad h(1)=10.
\end{equation}
In particular, this expansion contains no two consecutive ones.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Since $2w_{n+1}=(1-b_n/2)w_n$,
\[
 w_n-2w_{n+1}=\frac12 b_nw_n.
\]
Summing over $n\geq0$ gives $2-Z_b=\tfrac12\sum_n b_nw_n$.
At the $j$th defect, $D_{d_j}=j-1$, so its contribution is exactly
$2^{-d_j-j}$. The $j$th one in the morphic word appears at binary
position $d_j+j$, where binary positions start at one. This proves
both descriptions. Successive positions differ by at least two, so
there is no ambiguity from a tail of all ones. In the finite-defect
case the chosen expansion terminates in zeros.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The self-similar range}
Let $\mathcal K=\{Z_b:b\in\{0,1\}^{\N}\}$ and
$\mathcal C=\{\alpha_b:b\in\{0,1\}^{\N}\}$. Removing the first
flag gives
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:ifs}
 Z_b=F_{b_0}(Z_{\sg b}),\qquad
 F_0(z)=1+\frac z2,\qquad F_1(z)=1+\frac z4,
\end{equation}
where $\sg$ is the left shift. The two first-level intervals are
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:interval-gap}
 F_1([4/3,2])=[4/3,3/2],\qquad
 F_0([4/3,2])=[5/3,2].
\end{equation}
They are disjoint, separated by a gap of length $1/6$.

\begin{theorem}[Geometry and faithful coding]\label{pqc:rv:thm:cantor}
The map $b\mapsto Z_b$ is a homeomorphism from binary Cantor space
onto $\mathcal K$. The latter is the compact invariant set
$F_0(\mathcal K)\cup F_1(\mathcal K)$, and
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:dimension}
 \dim_H\mathcal K=\dim_H\mathcal C
 =\log_2\left(\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\right).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Agreement on $N$ initial flags gives agreement on the first $N$ maps
in \cref{pqc:rv:eq:ifs}; their product contraction is at most $2^{-N}$.
This proves continuity. The disjoint first-level intervals, applied
again after any common prefix, prove injectivity. Compactness of the
domain and the Hausdorff property of $\R$ give the homeomorphism.
The invariance equation follows by prepending either bit.

For completeness, the dimension argument can be given directly. Put
$D=\diam[4/3,2]=2/3$, and let $s>0$ solve
$2^{-s}+4^{-s}=1$. At depth $k$, the cylinder intervals have lengths
$D R_u$, where $R_u$ is the product of the contractions in the word
$u$. Their $s$-powers sum to $D^s$. Their maximum length tends to
zero, proving $\dim_H\mathcal K\leq s$.

Assign a cylinder the probability $R_u^s$. These assignments are
consistent because $2^{-s}+4^{-s}=1$, and so define a probability
measure on $\mathcal K$. For a small $\eps>0$, stop each branch when
its cylinder interval first has length at most $\eps$. Every stopped
interval has length greater than $\eps/4$. They are pairwise
disjoint, and any interval of length $2\eps$ can meet at most ten
of them: except possibly the two end intervals, the others lie
inside it and have disjoint interiors of length greater than
$\eps/4$. Each has mass at most $(\eps/D)^s$. Hence every ball of
radius $\eps$ has mass at most $10(\eps/D)^s$. Covering the support
and summing this inequality yields positive $s$-dimensional Hausdorff
content up to a fixed normalization, and thus dimension at least $s$.

Writing $x=2^{-s}$ gives $x+x^2=1$, which yields the displayed
value. Finally $z\mapsto1/z$ is bi-Lipschitz on $[4/3,2]$:
\[
 \frac14|z-z'|\leq|z^{-1}-{z'}^{-1}|\leq\frac9{16}|z-z'|.
\]
It therefore preserves Hausdorff dimension.
\end{proof}

This dimension calculation is an elementary instance of the separated
self-similar-set theorem \cite{b62s17-hutchinson}, not a new general fractal
dimension theorem. Its significance here is that the same set carries
a faithful arithmetic representation of all binary environments.

\subsection{Rationality is exactly eventual periodicity}
\begin{theorem}[Exact rationality criterion]\label{pqc:rv:thm:rationality}
For every binary environment $b$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:rational-iff}
 \alpha_b\in\Q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 Z_b\in\Q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 b\text{ is eventually periodic}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Reciprocation proves the first equivalence. If $b$ consists of a finite
prefix followed by repetitions of a finite nonempty word, the repeated
word defines an affine map $z\mapsto A+Rz$ with rational $A,R$ and
$0<R<1$. Its fixed point is $A/(1-R)$; applying the prefix map gives
a rational $Z_b$.

Conversely suppose $Z_b=p/q$. Starting at $z_0=Z_b$, repeatedly use
the disjoint intervals in \cref{pqc:rv:eq:interval-gap} to recover the bit
and the next tail:
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:rational-decoder}
 z_{n+1}=\begin{cases}
  4(z_n-1),&z_n\in[4/3,3/2],\quad b_n=1,\\
  2(z_n-1),&z_n\in[5/3,2],\quad b_n=0.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Every $z_n=Z_{\sg^n b}$ lies in $[4/3,2]$ and in $q^{-1}\Z$.
Only finitely many such rational values exist. The deterministic
iteration must repeat a value, and from then on it repeats the same
bits. Thus $b$ is eventually periodic.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Decidable membership for a supplied rational]\label[corollary]{pqc:rv:cor:rational-membership}
Given an exact rational $a$, it is decidable whether $a\in\mathcal C$.
When the answer is yes, an eventually periodic environment can be
computed.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Reject $a\notin[1/2,3/4]$. Starting with $z=1/a$, iterate
\cref{pqc:rv:eq:rational-decoder}. Reject on leaving the union of the two
closed intervals, and accept on a repeated value. The fixed rational
grid in the bounded interval makes one of these events inevitable.
In the acceptance case the cycle gives a periodic tail; contraction
proves that this itinerary has exactly the original value.
\end{proof}

The number of visited rational grid points is at most $q+1$ when
$q$ is the denominator of the initial $z$, so this is a numerical
bound, not a claim of polynomial complexity in the bit length of $q$.
For example, $a=5/8$ is immediately rejected: $1/a=8/5$ lies in the
first gap. Later we show that determining whether the limit supplied
by a program is rational is $\Sigma^0_2$-complete. There is no
contradiction: the exact rational is input in this corollary, rather
than an unknown arithmetic property of a computable limit.

\section{Halting hidden in a single rational defect}
\label{pqc:rv:sec:halting}
\srcmark{17}
Fix a deterministic universal machine $U$ with a chosen convention for
its first halting time $T(e)\in\N\cup\{\infty\}$. The input $e$
includes its program and data. Define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:halt-bit}
 b^e_n=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T(e)=n.
\end{equation}
This is a uniformly primitive-recursive predicate: simulate only $n$
steps and check whether the first halt is at that step. The rule does
not ask an unbounded halting oracle whether to place a defect.

\begin{theorem}[Hard exact arithmetic with rational equilibria]\label{pqc:rv:thm:halting}
For the family \cref{pqc:rv:eq:halt-bit},
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:halt-mass}
 \alpha_e=\begin{cases}
  \dfrac12,&T(e)=\infty,\\[4pt]
  \dfrac{2^{T(e)+1}}{2^{T(e)+2}-1},&T(e)<\infty.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Every stationary coordinate is rational. Nevertheless, the set
$\{e:\alpha_e>1/2\}$ is $\Sigma^0_1$-complete and Diophantine,
whereas $\{e:\alpha_e=1/2\}$ is $\Pi^0_1$-complete and is not
Diophantine. There is no uniform algorithm returning the exact reduced
rational $\alpha_e$ for every input $e$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
There are either no defects or exactly one at $T$. By
\cref{pqc:rv:thm:defects}, $Z_e=2$ or $Z_e=2-2^{-T-1}$, respectively.
Taking reciprocals gives \cref{pqc:rv:eq:halt-mass}. Every $w_n$ is rational,
so every $\pi_e(n)=w_n/Z_e$ is rational as well.

The strict inequality $\alpha_e>1/2$ is equivalent to halting, and
the equality is equivalent to nonhalting. The halting set is
computably enumerable and complete at the first existential level;
its complement is not computably enumerable. MRDP gives the claimed
positive polynomial representation and rules out the negative one
\cite{b62s17-proveit-mrdp}. An exact rational-output algorithm would decide
equality to $1/2$ by ordinary integer arithmetic, deciding halting.
\end{proof}
\wtag\ Cf.\ \cref{pqc:prop:totalcuts} of Part~I, which classifies strict comparisons and equality under the probability-one promise with the same halting-time device ($x_e=2^{-t}$ at the halting time $t$); here the device places one defect in an exactly stationary, reversible and uniformly mixing chain.

For a halting computation the separation is explicitly
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:separation}
 \alpha_e-\frac12=\frac{1}{2(2^{T(e)+2}-1)}.
\end{equation}
A late halt leaves a correspondingly tiny equilibrium signature. This
is not a slow-mixing phenomenon: the estimate \cref{pqc:rv:eq:mixing} has
no dependence on $T(e)$. It is an exact-symbolic phenomenon, because
no prescribed finite precision distinguishes equality from every
possible positive separation.

\begin{corollary}[No computable symbolic-height bound]\label[corollary]{pqc:rv:cor:height}
For any ordinary finite description of machine inputs, there is no
total computable function of description length that bounds the
reduced denominator of $\alpha_e$ for all inputs of that length.
There is also no such bound on the bit length of the denominator.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For a halting input the numerator in \cref{pqc:rv:eq:halt-mass} is a power
of two and its denominator is odd, so the fraction is reduced.
A computable denominator bound $B(\ell)$ would bound
$2^{T(e)+2}-1$ whenever a length-$\ell$ input halts. Computing an
integer $M$ with $2^{M+2}-1>B(\ell)$ and simulating for $M$ steps
would decide halting. A bit-length bound likewise bounds $T(e)+2$.
\end{proof}

This is a Busy-Beaver-type obstruction in symbolic output size, not
in the mixing time. It also applies to the exact mean return time
$Z_e$ and, by restriction to the value $1/2$, shows that the graph of
the exact rational-output function is not computably enumerable.
The fraction $1/\alpha_e$ is easy to approximate but not uniformly
easy to recognize as the correct finite fraction.

\subsection{A transfer principle for other computational substrates}
The machine model in this section is incidental. Suppose a substrate
has finite encodings of initial states, deterministic effective steps,
and a decidable halting flag. Suppose also that its halting problem
is computably enumerable complete. Replacing $U$ by its bounded
simulation gives exactly the same reduction. When the bounded
simulation is primitive recursive, the environment family above is
jointly primitive recursive in its code and position. A more general
computable bounded simulation still suffices for the equality
undecidability and numerical approximation results.

Thus a proved simulation from lambda terms, register programs, tag
systems, or another effective universal model is enough to transfer
halting into \cref{pqc:rv:eq:halt-mass}. This statement is a general compiler
principle, not a claim that each such front end was implemented in
the accompanying code. The next section supplies a concrete local
front end, so the interpretation is not limited to a row generator
that reruns an entire computation from scratch.

\section{A finite-rule reversible counter substrate}
\label{pqc:rv:sec:counter}
\srcmark{17}
There are two different meanings of reversibility in this article.
A \emph{logically reversible} transition has at most one predecessor.
A \emph{reversible Markov chain} satisfies detailed balance with its
stationary law. The following construction connects the two.

Consider a deterministic counter program with a finite control state
$q$ and counters $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\N^m$. Instructions are
increments, decrement/zero-test branches with explicitly named
successors, and halt. Such unrestricted finite-control counter
programs are a universal model; care concerning more restrictive
instruction sets is documented in \cite{b62s17-dudenhefner}.

Split each decrement instruction into two guarded branches. Assign a
different positive tag $j$ to every primitive branch, and choose a
fixed base $B$ larger than all tags. Add a natural history counter
$H$. A branch with counter change $v$ becomes
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:history-rule}
 (q,x,H)\longmapsto(q',x+v,BH+j).
\end{equation}
Its guard is either always true, $x_i=0$, or $x_i>0$; in the last
case a decrement is permitted. Add a fresh state \code{done}; a halt
instruction takes one step into \code{done}, and \code{done} keeps
appending its own tag forever. The original halting control states,
not \code{done}, are the defect states.

\begin{theorem}[Local reversible realization]\label{pqc:rv:thm:counter}
The finite guarded-affine rules \cref{pqc:rv:eq:history-rule} have a
computable partial inverse and a unique forward successor from every
well-formed state. From any initialized state with $H=0$, the forward
trajectory is an infinite ray with no repetitions. It contains one
defect exactly when the original program halts.

On this rooted trajectory, assign probability $(2-b)/8$ to the
forward successor, probability $1/2$ to the predecessor when present,
and the remaining probability to holding. The resulting chain is
isomorphic to the one-defect family of \cref{pqc:rv:thm:halting}, with all
the bounds of \cref{pqc:rv:thm:stationary,pqc:rv:thm:mixing}. A fixed universal
counter program yields a fixed finite rule set with varying initial
counter data.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For an alleged successor with history $H'$, compute its quotient and
remainder on division by $B$. The remainder must be one of the
positive branch tags. It identifies the branch uniquely. Subtract
its counter change, verify the source guard and target control, and
use the quotient as the preceding history. If any check fails there
is no predecessor; if all pass there is exactly one. Equivalently,
the inverse edge is the integer relation $H'=BH+j$ together with the
corresponding finite guards. No unbounded search is required.

The original program selects exactly one enabled branch. The halt
and \code{done} rules make the forward transition total. Since
$BH+j>H$, the history increases strictly. An initialized $H=0$
state has no predecessor, and its forward trajectory is therefore
an infinite ray. Original execution before halting is preserved.
On first reaching a halt control, the defect is present; the next
step enters \code{done}, and no further defect is possible.

Number the successive states on the ray by $0,1,2,\ldots$. The
assigned probabilities then agree exactly with \cref{pqc:rv:eq:kernel-intro}.
The stationary law and the analytic estimates transfer through this
bijection. Universality of a fixed ordinary counter interpreter,
followed by this fixed history construction, gives the last assertion.
\end{proof}

The probabilistic process need not advance monotonically through its
computation; it repeatedly undoes and redoes history. Its equilibrium
remembers whether a halting configuration exists arbitrarily far
along the ray. Finite computation and random reversible motion have
been separated without discarding either.

\begin{remark}[Domain of the irreducibility claim]
The full set of counter-history configurations contains many different
components. Irreducibility is asserted on the component generated by
the specified initialized state, not on their disjoint union. There
is no hidden reachability test in the local inverse: tag, quotient,
control and guard checks suffice. An arbitrary malformed-history
state may simply have no predecessor. The globally defined local
system is not claimed to be one irreducible chain.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[The implemented countdown]\label[example]{pqc:rv:ex:countdown}
Use control $0$ to decrement counter $x$ when positive and return to
$0$; when it is zero go to halt control $1$. Let control $2$ be
\code{done}. With tags $1,2,3,4$ and base $5$, an input $x=3$ starts
\[
 (0,3,0)\to(0,2,1)\to(0,1,6)\to(0,0,31)
 \to(1,0,157)\to(2,0,788)\to(2,0,3944)\to\cdots.
\]
There is one defect at trajectory index $4$. Its root mass is
$2^5/(2^6-1)=32/63$. Each step is reversible using the last base-five
tag. The code verifies this example and a nonhalting increment loop;
it does not implement a full universal counter interpreter.
\end{example}

The history multiplication in \cref{pqc:rv:eq:history-rule} is a primitive
operation of the stated guarded-affine substrate. Replacing it by
unit-counter microsteps changes the trajectory clock and requires
its own compiler analysis. Nothing here asserts universality of a
homogeneous nearest-neighbor walk on $\N$, a finite-state Markov
chain, or an unguarded one-species chemical reaction network.

\section{Sparse defects and the rational--Liouville dichotomy}
\label{pqc:rv:sec:liouville}
\srcmark{17}
The one-defect example is enough for an equality obstruction. To make
the arithmetic type itself encode a harder property, allow defects
at widely separated computable positions.

\begin{lemma}[Sparse defects force Liouville approximation]\label[lemma]{pqc:rv:lem:sparse}
Suppose infinitely many defects occur, and put $m_j=d_j+j$.
If
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:lacunary}
 \frac{m_{j+1}}{m_j}\longrightarrow\infty,
\end{equation}
then $\alpha_b$ is a Liouville number, in particular transcendental.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $L_j=\sum_{i\leq j}2^{-m_i}=A_j/2^{m_j}$ and
$L=2-Z_b$. The remaining terms satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:sparse-tail}
 0<L-L_j<2^{1-m_{j+1}}.
\end{equation}
The rational approximants
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:liouville-approximant}
 \alpha_j=\frac1{2-L_j}
 =\frac{2^{m_j}}{2^{m_j+1}-A_j}
\end{equation}
have denominators at most $2^{m_j+1}$ even after reduction. Also
\[
 0<\alpha_b-\alpha_j
 =\frac{L-L_j}{(2-L)(2-L_j)}<2^{1-m_{j+1}}.
\]
For any fixed positive integer $k$, condition \cref{pqc:rv:eq:lacunary}
eventually gives $m_{j+1}>k(m_j+1)+2$. Thus the error is smaller
than the $k$th inverse power of the displayed denominator, and hence
of the reduced denominator.

To check irrationality independently of these estimates, note that
the defect gaps tend to infinity. An eventually periodic word with
infinitely many ones has bounded gaps between ones. Hence $b$ is
not eventually periodic, and \cref{pqc:rv:thm:rationality} makes
$\alpha_b$ irrational. Its distinct rational approximants consequently
have unbounded reduced denominators. The estimates just proved
are the Liouville property. The elementary algebraic lower bound in
\cref{pqc:rv:app:liouville} excludes algebraicity.
\end{proof}

Fix a standard enumeration $W_e$ of computably enumerable sets, with
finite nested primitive-recursively decidable stages $W_{e,s}$ and
$W_{e,-1}=\varnothing$. Let $E(e,s)$ hold when at least one new
\emph{distinct} element enters at stage $s$. Set
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:factorial-env}
 b^e_n=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists s\leq n\;\bigl(n=(s+2)!\ \text{and}\ E(e,s)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Both the factorial calculation and the finite-stage event test are
bounded primitive-recursive computations. Consequently this is a
jointly primitive-recursive family of environments.

\begin{theorem}[The arithmetic-type dichotomy]\label{pqc:rv:thm:dichotomy}
For the chains defined by \cref{pqc:rv:eq:factorial-env},
\begin{align}
 W_e\text{ finite}
 &\Longleftrightarrow\alpha_e\text{ rational}
 \Longleftrightarrow\alpha_e\text{ algebraic},\label{pqc:rv:eq:finite-rat}\\
 W_e\text{ infinite}
 &\Longleftrightarrow\alpha_e\text{ irrational}
 \Longleftrightarrow\alpha_e\text{ transcendental}.
 \label{pqc:rv:eq:infinite-trans}
\end{align}
In the infinite case the mass is in fact Liouville. Every chain still
satisfies the same confinement and mixing bounds.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A finite set has only finitely many stages at which a new distinct
element appears. Hence there are finitely many defects, so
\cref{pqc:rv:thm:defects} gives a rational mass.

If $W_e$ is infinite, list its event stages as
$s_1<s_2<\cdots$. Then
$d_j=(s_j+2)!$ and $m_j=(s_j+2)!+j$. Since $j\leq s_j+1$,
\[
 \frac{m_{j+1}}{m_j}
 \geq\frac{(s_j+3)!}{(s_j+2)!+s_j+1}
 \longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Apply \cref{pqc:rv:lem:sparse}. The analytic bounds hold for every binary
environment, so they are unchanged.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact arithmetical-hierarchy classification}
For clarity we include the elementary completeness fact used by the
reduction. Write
$\mathrm{FIN}=\{e:W_e\text{ is finite}\}$ and
$\mathrm{INF}=\N\setminus\mathrm{FIN}$.

\begin{lemma}\label[lemma]{pqc:rv:lem:fin}
The set $\mathrm{FIN}$ is $\Sigma^0_2$-complete and
$\mathrm{INF}$ is $\Pi^0_2$-complete.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Finiteness has the form
$\exists M\,\forall s\; W_{e,s}\subseteq\{0,\ldots,M\}$,
which is $\Sigma^0_2$.
For hardness consider any predicate
$A(e)\Longleftrightarrow\exists u\,\forall v\,R(e,u,v)$
with decidable $R$. At stage $s$ let $a_s$ be the least $u\leq s$
satisfying all the finitely many tests $R(e,u,v)$ for $v\leq s$,
and put $a_s=s+1$ when none does. Enumerate the successive values
$a_s$. The sequence is nondecreasing: a failed small candidate
never becomes valid later. If there is a genuine witness $u$, the
least genuine witness eventually becomes the permanently least
candidate, and the enumerated range is finite. If there is none,
every candidate is eventually rejected and the range is infinite.
This gives a computable reduction to $\mathrm{FIN}$; taking
complements proves the other statement.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Complete classification for primitive-recursive codes]
\label{pqc:rv:thm:hierarchy}
Among all primitive-recursive binary-environment codes, rationality
and algebraicity of $\alpha_b$ are $\Sigma^0_2$-complete.
Irrationality and transcendence are $\Pi^0_2$-complete.
Neither rationality, algebraicity, irrationality nor transcendence
has a uniform existential Diophantine representation on these codes.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{pqc:rv:thm:rationality}, rationality can be written
\[
 \exists N\,\exists p\geq1\,\forall n\quad
 b(N+n)=b(N+n+p),
\]
a $\Sigma^0_2$ formula under a total computable evaluation of
primitive-recursive syntax.

For algebraicity, first note that $\alpha_b$ is uniformly computable
from its code. For example, geometric tail bounds in
\cref{pqc:rv:eq:weights} give arbitrarily narrow rational enclosures;
\cref{pqc:rv:sec:certificates} will give sharp ones. For a nonzero
$P\in\Z[X]$, evaluation of $P(\alpha_b)$ is therefore uniformly
computable. Its equality to zero is $\Pi^0_1$: compute an
approximation $r_k$ with error at most $2^{-k}$ and require
$|r_k|\leq2^{-k}$ for every $k$. Existence of a nonzero integer
polynomial satisfying this condition is a $\Sigma^0_2$ definition
of algebraicity.

The map $e\mapsto b^e$ in \cref{pqc:rv:eq:factorial-env} is a computable
map to primitive-recursive syntax. By \cref{pqc:rv:thm:dichotomy,pqc:rv:lem:fin},
it reduces $\mathrm{FIN}$ to each of rationality and algebraicity,
proving completeness. Complementation proves the two $\Pi^0_2$
classifications. Strictness of the arithmetical hierarchy implies
that none of these complete sets is computably enumerable; MRDP
therefore precludes the stated existential representations.
\end{proof}

Only the standard hierarchy separation is used in the last sentence;
no assertion that the four predicates are equivalent on arbitrary
environments is intended. Their pairwise coincidence in
\cref{pqc:rv:eq:finite-rat,pqc:rv:eq:infinite-trans} is a special feature of the
sparse reduction family. In particular, this proof does not settle
whether an algebraic irrational root mass occurs somewhere in the
full Cantor set $\mathcal C$.

\section{Low-complexity environments and an explicit transcendental mass}
\label{pqc:rv:sec:complexity}
\srcmark{17}
Sparse coding gives powerful uniform reductions, but one can also
write a short, familiar formula for an individual environment whose
root mass is transcendental. Let $p_b(n)$ denote the number of distinct
length-$n$ contiguous blocks occurring in $b$.

\begin{lemma}[Complexity of the equilibrium digit code]\label[lemma]{pqc:rv:lem:complexity}
For $c=h(b)$ with $h(0)=0$, $h(1)=10$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:complexity}
 p_c(n)\leq2p_b(n+1)\qquad(n\geq1).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Any length-$n$ block of $c$ starts either at the beginning of an image
word or at the second symbol of an image of $1$. It is determined by
that offset and the next $n+1$ input symbols: every image has length
at least one, so this many symbols always suffice. There are at most
two offsets per input block.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A low-complexity transcendence criterion]\label{pqc:rv:thm:low-complexity}
Suppose $b$ is not eventually periodic and
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:lowcomplex}
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{p_b(n)}n<\infty.
\end{equation}
Then $Z_b$ and $\alpha_b$ are transcendental.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~1 of Adamczewski and Bugeaud \cite{b62s17-ab} says that the
base-$B$ digit complexity of every algebraic irrational satisfies
$\liminf p(n)/n=\infty$, for each integer $B\geq2$.
By \cref{pqc:rv:thm:rationality}, $L_b=2-Z_b$ is irrational.
Its binary expansion is $c=h(b)$ by \cref{pqc:rv:thm:defects}, and
\cref{pqc:rv:lem:complexity,pqc:rv:eq:lowcomplex} give finite liminf complexity
ratio for that expansion. Thus $L_b$ cannot be algebraic.
Subtracting from two and taking a nonzero reciprocal preserve
algebraicity in both directions, so $Z_b$ and $\alpha_b$ are
transcendental too.
\end{proof}

This proof imports a deep digit-complexity theorem. The contribution
here is the explicit equilibrium coding that makes it applicable;
there is no new proof of the general transcendence theorem.

\begin{corollary}[Thue--Morse equilibrium]\label[corollary]{pqc:rv:cor:tm}
Let $b_n$ be the parity of the number of ones in the binary expansion
of $n$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:tm}
 \alpha_{\mathrm{TM}}
 =\left(\sum_{n\geq0}2^{-n-\sum_{k<n}b_k}\right)^{-1}
\end{equation}
is transcendental, and it is the root mass of a chain satisfying
\cref{pqc:rv:thm:mixing}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The Thue--Morse word satisfies the length-two substitution
$0\mapsto01$, $1\mapsto10$. Its block complexity is $O(n)$ by a
direct covering argument: choose $k$ with $2^{k-1}<n\leq2^k$.
A length-$n$ block lies in the images, under the $k$fold substitution,
of at most two consecutive letters. It is determined by one of at
most four letter pairs and an offset smaller than $2^k$.
Thus $p_b(n)\leq4\cdot2^k<8n$, with the small case adjusted trivially.

It is not eventually periodic. If a positive eventual period $p$
existed, for all sufficiently large $k$ one would have
$b_{2^k-p}=b_{2^k}=1$. But $2^k-p=(2^k-1)-(p-1)$ is the
$k$-digit binary complement of $p-1$, so
\[
 b_{2^k-p}\equiv k-s_2(p-1)\pmod2,
\]
which alternates as $k$ increases. This is a contradiction.
Apply \cref{pqc:rv:thm:low-complexity} and then \cref{pqc:rv:thm:mixing}.
\end{proof}

Unlike the sparse construction, this argument does not show that
$\alpha_{\mathrm{TM}}$ is Liouville. It establishes transcendence
without claiming an irrationality exponent. The supplied code gives
an exact rational enclosure from its first eighty environment bits.

\section{Sharp finite-prefix bounds and canonical quartic certificates}
\label{pqc:rv:sec:certificates}
\srcmark{17}
The preceding obstructions concern exact arithmetic type. Strict rational
inequalities have a different status: a finite prefix eventually certifies
every true strict comparison. This section makes that statement completely
explicit and separates its arithmetic layer from the computation of the
prefix itself.

\subsection{Exact enclosing intervals}
For a given prefix $b_0,\ldots,b_{N-1}$, introduce integer sequences
\begin{align}
 W_0=S_0=Q_0&=1,\label{pqc:rv:eq:prefix-init}\\
 W_{i+1}&=(2-b_i)W_i,\nonumber\\
 S_{i+1}&=4S_i+W_{i+1},\label{pqc:rv:eq:prefix-rec}\\
 Q_{i+1}&=4Q_i.\nonumber
\end{align}
By induction,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:prefix-values}
 W_i=4^iw_i,
 \qquad S_i=4^i\sum_{k=0}^iw_k,
 \qquad Q_i=4^i.
\end{equation}
All quantities here are computed from only $i$ flags.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp prefix enclosure]\label{pqc:rv:thm:prefix}
Every continuation of the prefix satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:bounds}
 L_N:=\frac{Q_N}{S_N+W_N}\leq\alpha_b\leq
 U_N:=\frac{3Q_N}{3S_N+W_N}.
\end{equation}
Both endpoints are attained by continuations: all zeros attain $L_N$,
and all ones attain $U_N$. The enclosing intervals are nested as
$N$ increases, and
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:width}
 0\leq U_N-L_N\leq\frac23\,2^{-N}.
\end{equation}
They therefore converge to the single value $\alpha_b$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $s_N=\sum_{k=0}^Nw_k$ and $w=w_N$. Ratios after the prefix
lie between $1/4$ and $1/2$, so
\[
 \frac w3\leq\sum_{k>N}w_k\leq w.
\]
The lower and upper bounds are attained by constant-one and
constant-zero suffixes, respectively. Reciprocation reverses the
inequalities, yielding \cref{pqc:rv:eq:bounds}. Appending a flag restricts
the set of possible continuations, which proves nesting because
the two extrema were attained. Finally,
\[
 U_N-L_N
 =\frac{(2/3)w}{(s_N+w/3)(s_N+w)}
 \leq\frac23 w\leq\frac23\,2^{-N}.
\]
Here $s_N\geq1$ and $w\leq2^{-N}$. The bound proves convergence.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The interval is the smallest closed interval enclosing the attainable
masses of the prefix cylinder. It is not asserted that every number
between its endpoints is attainable: the actual set is a reciprocal
affine image of the Cantor set from \cref{pqc:rv:sec:coding}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A small-coefficient recurrence presentation}
Let $a\in\N$, $v\geq1$ represent the rational threshold $a/v$.
A lower certificate asserts that the whole prefix cylinder satisfies
$\alpha_b>a/v$; an upper certificate asserts $\alpha_b<a/v$.
The necessary and sufficient integer tests are
\begin{align}
 vQ_N-a(S_N+W_N)&=1+\eta \quad\text{(lower)},\label{pqc:rv:eq:lower-res}\\
 a(3S_N+W_N)-3vQ_N&=1+\eta \quad\text{(upper)},\label{pqc:rv:eq:upper-res}
\end{align}
with a natural slack $\eta$. These are strict inequalities because
the left-hand sides are integers.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical recurrence certificates]\label{pqc:rv:thm:quartic-full}
Fix $N$. Take the residuals of \cref{pqc:rv:eq:prefix-init,pqc:rv:eq:prefix-rec},
the $N$ Boolean residuals $b_i(b_i-1)$, and one threshold residual
from \cref{pqc:rv:eq:lower-res,pqc:rv:eq:upper-res}. The sum of their squares is
an integer polynomial of total degree at most four. Its free
parameters are the flags and $a,v$, and its natural witnesses are
\[
 (W_0,\ldots,W_N,S_0,\ldots,S_N,Q_0,\ldots,Q_N,\eta).
\]
There are $3N+4$ witnesses and $4N+4$ residuals. For valid binary
flags and $v\geq1$, it has exactly one natural witness tuple if the
selected prefix bound strictly certifies the comparison, and none
otherwise.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Each residual has degree at most two in all its variables, including
parameters. Squaring and summing gives degree at most four. A sum of
integer squares vanishes exactly when every residual vanishes.
The three initial values and the deterministic recurrences force
all $W,S,Q$ coordinates uniquely. The final residual then forces
$\eta$ uniquely; it is natural exactly when the appropriate integer
gap is positive. There are three initial residuals, four per flag,
and one threshold residual. Counting coordinates gives $3(N+1)+1$.
\end{proof}

For fixed numerical flags and threshold the degree in the auxiliary
coordinates alone can be lower. The quartic claim refers to the
polynomial with all input parameters left as variables. No optimality
claim is made for this presentation.

\subsection{Eliminating the redundant witnesses}
When $N$ is an external compiler parameter, the $Q_i$ are constants
and the $S_i$ can be eliminated by a linear expression. Define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:AN}
 W_0:=1,\qquad
 A_N(W)=4^N+\sum_{i=1}^N4^{N-i}W_i.
\end{equation}
This equals $S_N$ whenever the weight recurrences hold.

\begin{theorem}[Compact unique quartic certificates]\label{pqc:rv:thm:compact}
For every fixed horizon $N$, define
\begin{align}
 C_i&=b_i(b_i-1),\nonumber\\
 R_i&=W_{i+1}-(2-b_i)W_i\quad(0\leq i<N),\label{pqc:rv:eq:compact-res}\\
 G_-&=v4^N-a\bigl(A_N(W)+W_N\bigr)-1-\eta,\nonumber\\
 G_+&=a\bigl(3A_N(W)+W_N\bigr)-3v4^N-1-\eta.\nonumber
\end{align}
Use $G_-$ for a lower certificate and $G_+$ for an upper certificate.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rv:eq:compact-poly}
 \mathcal P_N^{\pm}=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}(C_i^2+R_i^2)+G_{\pm}^2
\end{equation}
is a polynomial of degree at most four with exactly $N+1$ natural
witnesses $W_1,\ldots,W_N,\eta$ and $2N+1$ squared residuals.
For every valid prefix and threshold it has the same existence and
unique-witness property as \cref{pqc:rv:thm:quartic-full}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The residuals are obtained by substituting $W_0=1$, $Q_N=4^N$ and
$S_N=A_N(W)$ into the full presentation. Each remains of degree at
most two. The weight recurrence forces $W_1,\ldots,W_N$ uniquely;
the threshold forces $\eta$ uniquely. Their forced values satisfy
all residuals exactly when the corresponding strict prefix bound
holds. The count is immediate, including $N=0$, when the only
witness is $\eta$ and the only residual is the threshold residual.
\end{proof}

This compression trades recurrence variables for coefficients as large
as $4^N$. Each coefficient has $O(N)$ bits. The unexpanded residual list has
$O(N)$ terms and $O(N^2)$ coefficient bits with explicit binary storage;
the geometric coefficient sequence can also be generated from $N$.
The full presentation has uniformly small recurrence coefficients and
is useful when composing with other arithmetic circuits. Neither
presentation claims an optimal variable count.

\begin{example}[An explicit four-witness quartic]\label[example]{pqc:rv:ex:quartic}
For $N=3$, a lower certificate uses witnesses $W_1,W_2,W_3,\eta$.
The polynomial is
\begin{align*}
 &\sum_{i=0}^2b_i^2(b_i-1)^2
 +(W_1-2+b_0)^2
 +(W_2-(2-b_1)W_1)^2\\
 &\quad +(W_3-(2-b_2)W_2)^2\\
 &\quad +\bigl(64v-a(64+16W_1+4W_2+2W_3)-1-\eta\bigr)^2.
\end{align*}
It has seven squared residuals and, when expanded with all parameters
free, 51 monomials. For the prefix $(0,1,0)$ and threshold $1/2$, its
unique natural witness is
\[
 (W_1,W_2,W_3,\eta)=(2,2,4,15).
\]
The sharp enclosure is $[4/7,24/41]$, whose lower endpoint exceeds
$1/2$. The archive includes the expanded polynomial and its residual
specification, not merely a schematic existence assertion.
\end{example}

\subsection{From bounded certificates to fixed-polynomial cuts}
\begin{theorem}[Diophantine strict cuts, and a boundary at equality]
\label{pqc:rv:thm:cuts}
For primitive-recursive environment codes $e$, the two relations
\[
 \alpha_e>a/v\qquad\text{and}\qquad\alpha_e<a/v
 \quad(a\in\N,\ v\geq1)
\]
are computably enumerable and hence Diophantine after tuple coding.
Both are $\Sigma^0_1$-complete as relations with a rational threshold
parameter. Exact equality to a rational threshold is
$\Pi^0_1$-complete and is not in general Diophantine.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Compute successive prefixes from the actual code $e$ and their sharp
bounds. If $\alpha_e>a/v$, eventually $L_N>a/v$, and if
$\alpha_e<a/v$, eventually $U_N<a/v$. These tests never certify a
false statement. They provide the two semidecision procedures and,
by ProveIt's MRDP interface, fixed-polynomial representations.

The lower relation is complete by the one-defect family with threshold
$1/2$. For the upper relation, set $b^e_n=1$ exactly when the machine
has not halted by time $n$. A nonhalting machine gives the all-one
environment and mass $3/4$. A halting machine produces a zero suffix,
strictly increases $Z$ from $4/3$, and makes its mass strictly less
than $3/4$. This is a reduction of halting to the upper relation.

For equality, the condition that $a/v$ belongs to every computable
interval $[L_N,U_N]$ is $\Pi^0_1$ and is equivalent to equality.
The one-defect construction with threshold $1/2$ gives
$\Pi^0_1$-hardness and failure of computable enumerability.
\end{proof}
\wtag\ Cf.\ \cref{pqc:prop:totalcuts} of Part~I (same halting-time device).

Two boundaries are essential. First, the flags in
\cref{pqc:rv:thm:compact} are input parameters. They must be tied to the
actual environment program by a verified prefix computation; allowing
arbitrary flag witnesses would certify statements about some different
chain. A complete front end can use finite evaluator traces for the
prefix predicate, followed by MRDP or a separate bounded trace compiler.
The supplied implementation checks concrete supplied prefixes and does
not implement this entire universal arithmetic front end.

Second, $N$ is an external compiler parameter in
\cref{pqc:rv:thm:compact}. Passing from its horizon-indexed family to one
fixed-arity polynomial is an MRDP step. The unique-witness assertion
for a fixed prefix is not a single-fold representation of arbitrary
unbounded computation. The existence theorem supplies no such
multiplicity control, and nothing in this article settles the
single-fold or finite-fold representability frontier discussed in
ProveIt's related reports (\wtag\ Section~\ref{pqc:conv:qoverlap} of this report, and the sibling report \code{canonical-diophantine-certificates}).

\section{Worked equilibria and reproducible verification}
\label{pqc:rv:sec:verification}
\srcmark{17}
\subsection{Exact examples}
The defect-free environment has $Z=2$ and $\alpha=1/2$. The all-one
environment has $Z=4/3$ and $\alpha=3/4$. For the periodic word
$(01)^\omega$, its two-letter affine map is
$z\mapsto3/2+z/8$, so $Z=12/7$ and $\alpha=7/12$.
For a single defect the first few values are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Defect time $T$ & $0$ & $1$ & $2$ & $5$ & $10$\\
\midrule
Root mass & $2/3$ & $4/7$ & $8/15$ & $64/127$ & $2048/4095$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
No finite truncation distinguishes the zero-defect case from a case
whose one defect lies beyond the truncation, although their exact
stationary masses differ.

For the Thue--Morse chain, eighty flags give the exact enclosure
\begin{align*}
 \alpha_{\mathrm{TM}}&\geq
 \frac{664613997892457936451903530140172288}
 {1115932292267376191302758860221799791},\\
 \alpha_{\mathrm{TM}}&\leq
 \frac{498460498419343452338927647605129216}
 {836949219200532143477069145166349843}.
\end{align*}
The approximate display is $0.5955683893169543$; the fractions,
not the decimal display, are the certified numerical data. Their
width is recorded exactly in \code{results/examples.json}.

\subsection{What the programs do}
The core module \code{code/equilibria.py} uses Python's standard
library and exact rational arithmetic. It implements transition
rows, scaled prefix recurrences, sharp intervals, periodic-tail
normalizers, the finite-defect formula, rational membership decoding,
both certificate presentations, and the local counter-history lift.
Invalid bit values, negative natural witnesses and nonpositive
rational denominators are rejected explicitly. The rational decoder
raises an exception on an imposed operational step limit rather than
mistaking that limit for nonmembership; setting the limit to
\code{None} runs the terminating mathematical procedure without a cap.

The verification driver \code{code/verify.py} uses SymPy only for
symbolic expansion of the two horizon-three polynomials. Its random
choices, limited to additional finite Poincare checks, use the fixed
seed \code{20260930}. The recorded run used Python 3.13.5 and
SymPy 1.14.0 and passed \textbf{113,686 explicit checks}. Checks are
performed by a custom assertion function, so Python's optimization
flag does not silently disable them.

The suite exhausts all 511 binary prefixes of lengths zero through
eight for defect identities, endpoint bounds, interval nesting and
several threshold tests. It also checks rational-decoder round trips
for 930 supplied eventually periodic codes, halting formulas through
$T=100$, forward/backward counter histories, and coordinate mutations
of valid certificates. There are 320 exact rational Poincare checks
on finite reflecting chains. The full horizon-three polynomial has
63 monomials; the compact one has 51. All counts are emitted by the
run rather than manually inferred from the output files.

These checks are finite regression tests, not proofs of the
infinite-state spectral theorem, transcendence, hierarchy completeness,
or universality. Those conclusions rest on the mathematical arguments
and explicitly cited theorems. No Lean build was performed, no universal
MRDP polynomial was expanded, and no proof-checker certification is
claimed for the new results.

\subsection{Reproduction}
From the unpacked archive directory, run
\begin{lstlisting}
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python code/verify.py
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{lstlisting}
The verification run rewrites only files in \code{results/} and its
JSON report in \code{verification/}. The TeX source includes its
bibliography and requires no external figures or data downloads.
The README identifies the core-only and symbolic-check dependencies
and the exact scope of every artifact.

\section{A formalization route for ProveIt}
\label{pqc:rv:sec:formalization}
\srcmark{17}
The natural integration point is the existing Hilbert-tenth/MRDP
project, but the new analysis should be kept separate from the old
formal theorem boundary. A useful dependency order is the following.

\paragraph{Finite arithmetic first.}
Define the $W,S,Q$ recurrences over naturals and prove
\cref{pqc:rv:eq:prefix-values} by induction. Formalize polynomial evaluation
for the residual lists and prove that a sum of integer squares
vanishes if and only if every residual does. The canonical-witness
and elimination proofs in \cref{pqc:rv:thm:quartic-full,pqc:rv:thm:compact} are
finite algebra and induction, with no probability infrastructure.
The exact horizon-three artifact can then be checked as an instance.

\paragraph{Infinite sums and interval semantics.}
Define the positive weights and prove the summability sandwich
$4^{-n}\leq w_n\leq2^{-n}$. Establish $Z$, its reciprocal, and
\cref{pqc:rv:thm:prefix,pqc:rv:thm:defects}. At this point a finite arithmetic
certificate already has a theorem connecting it to the actual real
root mass; that is a more important trust milestone than simply
being able to evaluate a polynomial.

\paragraph{Computability and reductions.}
Specify a bounded machine evaluator and its first-halt flag.
Prove the single-defect formula and the sparse-event compiler's
correctness. Show that the strict-cut semideciders use the correct
prefixes, then apply \code{Diophantine.mrdp}. Rationality's eventual
periodicity characterization can be formalized without using
transcendence. The sparse transcendence proof needs only a small
algebraic-approximation lemma, whereas the low-complexity corollary
requires a much larger external theorem.

\paragraph{Analysis as an independent layer.}
Construct the Markov kernel, verify detailed balance, and establish
the weighted $\ell^2$ convolution estimate. The elementary inequality
in \cref{pqc:rv:lem:poincare} is the critical reusable lemma. The spectral
and total-variation consequences can then be derived using the chosen
operator and probability libraries. Their formalization should not
be made an unnecessary dependency of the finite polynomial checker.

\paragraph{Local reversible semantics.}
For the counter lift, prove the quotient/remainder tag decoder is a
left inverse of each forward rule, prove strict history growth, and
identify the rooted orbit with $\N$. Only after those statements are
proved should the chain on local configurations inherit the analytic
results. This keeps logical reversibility, Markov reversibility and
reachability-domain restrictions distinct.

All of these are proposed integration tasks, not existing source
modules or completed Lean proofs. ProveIt's own MRDP guide explicitly
separates its existential polynomial theorem from numerical degree,
witness and compiler guarantees \cite{b62s17-proveit-mrdp}; the same
separation is preserved here.

\section{Source 13 appendix: reproducibility and machine-readable data}
The JSON polynomial format stores each monomial as a sorted list of
variable indices. Repetition denotes exponentiation: the list
\texttt{[2,2,5]} denotes $X_2^2X_5$. Each entry records its integer
coefficient. Residual lists, source circuit gates, and structural
statistics accompany the expanded polynomial, allowing an independent
reader to re-evaluate both representations.

The verification program reruns deterministically and rewrites
\texttt{results/verification\_report.json}. The optional NumPy check can
produce insignificant last-bit differences across linear-algebra
implementations; exact counts, exact polynomial coefficients, and rational
bounds do not depend on NumPy. The supplied PDF was built from this
\LaTeX\ source. The archive excludes TeX auxiliary files and Python cache
files.

\section{Source 17 appendix: why the common spectral-gap bound is sharp}
\label{pqc:rv:app:sharp}
For the defect-free environment, $\pi(n)=2^{-n-1}$. Under the unitary
map $f\mapsto g$ with $g_n=\sqrt{\pi(n)}f(n)$ from $L^2(\pi)$
to $\ell^2(\N)$, the Markov operator becomes a symmetric Jacobi
operator $A$. Away from zero its diagonal entry is $1/4$ and its
off-diagonal entries are
\[
 \sqrt{P(n,n+1)P(n+1,n)}=\frac1{2\sqrt2}.
\]
At zero the diagonal is $3/4$. Its stationary unit vector is
$\psi_n=\sqrt{\pi(n)}$, with $A\psi=\psi$.

Take a vector supported on $L$ consecutive sites beginning at
$M\geq1$, with values proportional to
$\sin(\pi j/(L+1))$, $j=1,\ldots,L$, and normalize it to unit
$\ell^2$ norm. The constant-coefficient tridiagonal calculation gives
\[
 \langle g,(I-A)g\rangle
 =\frac34-\frac1{\sqrt2}\cos\left(\frac\pi{L+1}\right).
\]
Subtract its projection onto $\psi$:
$\widetilde g=g-\langle g,\psi\rangle\psi$.
The energy is unchanged because $(I-A)\psi=0$, while
\[
 \|\widetilde g\|_2^2
 =1-|\langle g,\psi\rangle|^2\longrightarrow1
 \quad(M\to\infty),
\]
since the $\ell^2$ tail of $\psi$ tends to zero. Thus the mean-zero
Rayleigh quotient can be made arbitrarily close to the displayed
value. Letting first $M$ and then $L$ tend to infinity yields
\[
 \gap(P_0)\leq\frac34-\frac1{\sqrt2}
 =\frac{3-2\sqrt2}{4}.
\]
The reverse inequality is \cref{pqc:rv:thm:mixing}. Therefore the all-zero
environment itself attains the asserted gap, and no larger common
lower bound is possible. This argument does not require the spectral
edge to be an eigenvalue.

\section{Source 17 appendix: the elementary algebraic approximation bound}
\label{pqc:rv:app:liouville}
Suppose $\xi$ is algebraic irrational of degree $d\geq2$, and let
$P\in\Z[X]$ be its irreducible polynomial. For a rational $p/q$ in
lowest terms, $P(p/q)\ne0$ and $q^dP(p/q)$ is a nonzero integer.
Hence $|P(p/q)|\geq q^{-d}$. If $|p/q-\xi|\leq1$, the mean value
estimate on $[\xi-1,\xi+1]$ gives
\[
 |P(p/q)-P(\xi)|\leq M|p/q-\xi|,
 \qquad M=\max_{|x-\xi|\leq1}|P'(x)|>0.
\]
Consequently
\[
 |p/q-\xi|\geq M^{-1}q^{-d}.
\]
A Liouville number has rational approximations with arbitrarily large
denominators and error smaller than their $(d+1)$st inverse powers,
contradicting this inequality for large denominators. This elementary
argument is the only transcendence input needed for the factorially
sparse family; the historical source is Liouville \cite{b62s17-liouville}.

\section{Conclusions of Part V}
\label{pqc:conv:b62-V:conclusions}
% --- source 13, lines 1400-1419 ---
\subsection{Source 13}
A finite probabilistic computation can be translated not just into an
existential polynomial relation, but into a sparse quartic landscape with
one explicitly controlled accepting minimum per successful coin tape.
Fresh occurrence wires eliminate auxiliary multiplicity; a single trunk
per used wire makes the interaction graph subcubic; one distributed unit
keeps all expanded coefficients bounded. Boolean penalties give coercivity,
separation, and a uniform Hessian contribution. These elementary pieces
combine to yield fixed rounding, convexity, topology, and perturbation
bounds.

The resulting normalized component counts realize every left-c.e.
probability, including noncomputable ones. Their difficulty does not
require poorly conditioned accepting minima. It arises from unbounded
computation and from the distinction between finite evidence and a
limiting measure. MRDP captures strict lower-cut evidence in fixed arity;
almost-sure and finite-mean claims retain their required universal
quantifiers. This is both a constructive extension of the repository's
Diophantine program and a boundary that prevents misleading generalizations.

% --- source 17, lines 1456-1477 ---
\subsection{Source 17}
Reversibility, a fixed rational transition alphabet, strong confinement
and a uniform spectral gap do not remove computational complexity from
exact equilibrium arithmetic. The mechanism is explicit: defects carry
a binary message in the normalizing constant, while their inward bias
preserves the analytic estimates. A first-halting defect produces only
rational equilibria but destroys uniform symbolic extraction. Sparse
defects raise arithmetic-type recognition to the second level of the
arithmetical hierarchy, with a rational--Liouville dichotomy. Low symbolic
complexity gives another route to individual transcendental examples.

At the same time, the model has an effective positive theory. Numerical
enclosures are sharp, the root-mass range has a faithful self-similar
coding, supplied rational membership is decidable, and strict inequalities
have canonical finite quartic certificates. The useful Diophantine
boundary is therefore not between conventional and unconventional
computation. It is between properties witnessed by finite information
and properties that quantify over an unbounded tail. ProveIt's MRDP
interface is well suited to formalizing that boundary, provided the
finite certificate, the environment semantics and the fixed-polynomial
existence theorem remain explicitly distinguished.


\section{Further research questions of Part V}
\label{pqc:conv:b62-V:questions}
\wtag\ Source~13 posed ten numbered questions and source~17 twelve question
environments; both sets are printed in full. A \wtag\ note after a question
names the question of Parts~I--IV it duplicates or bears on. Which of Part~I's
questions these sources partly answer is recorded after those questions and in
Section~\ref{pqc:conv:qoverlap}.

% --- source 13, lines 1321-1399 ---
\subsection{Source 13: probabilities from well-conditioned quartics}\label{pqc:ql:sec:future}

\paragraph{1. Planar subcubic realization.}
Can the entire quantitative package be realized with a planar interaction
graph, while preserving a unique extension for each input tape and linear
or near-linear overhead? An ordinary Boolean crossover gadget is not
enough: its witness multiplicity, unit distribution, and Hessian constants
must all be audited. A positive answer would bring the construction closer
to spatially local two-dimensional substrates.

\paragraph{2. Coefficient height three or two.}
The present height-four term occurs at a Boolean copy-tree vertex incident
to three linear constraints. Can a different parsimonious fan-out gadget
reduce the expanded height without losing subcubic interactions and
uniform conditioning? Establish either a compiler with a better constant
or a lower bound for a clearly specified local-gadget class.

\paragraph{3. Geometry-preserving composition.}
Our compiler rebuilds a circuit at each horizon. Can one construct a
local extension rule for the energy itself, so that the injection
$\cZ_t\times\Bit\hookrightarrow\cZ_{t+1}$ becomes an explicit embedding
of well neighborhoods? This could give a more intrinsic topology of the
increasing computation rather than merely a sequence of component counts.

\paragraph{4. Effective convergence from semantic restrictions.}
Which program classes yield computable upper as well as lower bounds for
the normalized counts? Finite-state models, effective tail bounds, and
suitable supermartingale certificates are plausible starting points.
The target is an explicit modulus extracted from extra semantics, not
from the universal geometric constants alone. Existing probabilistic
termination proof systems provide relevant background \cite{b62s13-majumdar2024}. \wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:histories}.

\paragraph{5. Probability-preserving quantum analogues.}
For finite quantum computations, amplitudes of different paths interfere;
one cannot replace amplitude addition by a count of successful classical
tapes. An exact analogue should handle an explicitly presented algebraic
gate field, interference, and Born probabilities without smuggling a
counting oracle into an existential witness. The classical positivity
argument identifies precisely which step needs replacement. \wtag\ Partly answered for finite circuits by source~10 in Part~VI: its cyclotomic contraction certificates (Theorems~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:cyclotensor} and~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:quantum}) keep interference and the Born rule, with one witness per correct output; unbounded quantum controllers are reached there only through MRDP (Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:positivehalting}).

\paragraph{6. Resource-sensitive substrate transfers.}
For a chosen randomized combinator, tag, or heap machine, determine sharp
pathwise simulation bounds. Probability and almost-sure termination need
only coin faithfulness, but finite moments require quantitative overhead
control. Establishing preservation of the $r$th moment under a specified
simulation would be more informative than an undifferentiated claim of
probabilistic universality. \wtag\ Compare the question on cost-preserving compilation between substrates in the sibling report \code{canonical-diophantine-certificates}.

\paragraph{7. Fixed-arity versus finite counting interfaces.}
Can useful subclasses of threshold predicates admit explicit small
fixed-arity quartics whose witnesses have a controlled, computable
multiplicity? Such a result must state its subclass and must not infer a
general finite-fold theorem from the bounded Boolean compiler. A good
first target is a bounded-state process with an effective absorption-tail
certificate. \wtag\ Compare Questions~\ref{pqc:q:counting} and~\ref{pqc:qm:q:frontier}.

\paragraph{8. Robustness under local coefficient perturbations.}
\Cref{pqc:ql:thm:perturb} assumes a globally bounded smooth perturbation. Physical
or numerical models often perturb local coefficients instead. Find
size-independent hypotheses under which such local perturbations preserve
the low-energy component count, possibly after shifting the reference
energy separately in each well. Large ambient domains and accumulated
constant shifts are real obstacles, not cosmetic technicalities.

\paragraph{9. Certified optimization-to-witness extraction.}
The rounding theorem can turn an approximate real point into an exact
Boolean certificate. Develop a verified interval-arithmetic interface
that checks the energy upper bound without trusting floating-point
residual cancellation, then extracts and rechecks the discrete witness.
This would exploit the proven gap without asserting that global
optimization is easy.

\paragraph{10. Minimal structural obstructions at degree two.}
The degree-two counter works because residual scopes lie on paths,
cycles, and isolated triangles. Study analogous exact frontiers for
bounded treewidth, bounded feedback-vertex number, or constrained
fan-out. The aim is a classification of which structural promises make
well counting tractable while retaining the same local geometric bounds. \wtag\ Compare the width-parameterized contraction certificates of source~10 (Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:integer-tensor}).
