\section{The problem, the contribution, and the repository boundary}
\label{pqc:cc:sec:introduction}
\srcmark{10}

\subsection{Why coherent computation is a different substrate}

The question motivating this article is not merely whether quantum computation
can be simulated by an ordinary effective machine. Once a finite gate alphabet
and an effective observation semantics are fixed, such a simulation often gives
a route to MRDP. The more informative question is whether arithmetic certificates
can retain the actual algebraic semantics of coherence: addition of amplitudes,
complex conjugation, destructive interference, and exact comparison of the
resulting probabilities.

For a classical nondeterministic computation, exhibiting an accepting path is
an adequate existential certificate of reachability. For a coherent computation,
an accepting-looking path can have a nonzero amplitude while the total amplitude
of its endpoint is zero. Conversely, a probability is a sum of squared
\emph{total} amplitudes, not a sum of the squared weights of its fine-grained
paths. The order of summation and squaring is essential.

Dawson et al. already express amplitudes of Hadamard--Toffoli circuits through a
difference of solution counts over $\mathbb F_2$ \cite{b62s10-Dawson}. In the customary
notation, an amplitude with $h$ Hadamards has the form
\begin{equation}
2^{-h/2}(N_0-N_1).
\label{pqc:cc:eq:pathgap}
\end{equation}
That connection is a starting point, not a novelty claim here. Our certificate
records a complete arithmetic evaluation, including both signs, with exactly one
natural witness for fixed data. It does not existentially choose one of the
paths counted by $N_0$ or $N_1$.

\subsection{What was actually inspected in ProveIt}

The repository was inspected at commit
\begin{center}\small\SHA.\end{center}
The relevant direct reads were the Hilbert-tenth-problem README and the Lean
file \texttt{Diophantine/MRDP.lean} under
\texttt{Computability/HilbertTenthProblem/Lean/} \cite{b62s10-ProveItReadme,b62s10-ProveItMRDP}.
The README describes corrected Jones articles, universal Diophantine systems,
and a Lean development of both directions of MRDP. The inspected theorem file
states a finite-polynomial equivalence, including input zero: every recursively
enumerable subset of $\N$ is the projection of the natural zero set of one
integer polynomial with finitely many witnesses, and conversely.

The repository's theorem is used only in Section~\ref{pqc:cc:sec:unbounded}. The finite
compilers in Sections~\ref{pqc:cc:sec:wires}--\ref{pqc:cc:sec:mbqc} are proved directly and do
not invoke MRDP. Repository assertions about axiom audits were not independently
rechecked by a Lean build in this work. Code-search results included an older
indexed revision; mathematical dependencies were taken from the pinned direct
reads rather than silently equating that index with the inspected commit.

This is a selective extension of the repository, not an audit of its many other
claims. In particular, no numerical universal-polynomial optimization from the
repository is needed for any theorem below.

\subsection{The main representation theorem in preview}

Let a closed tensor network have $m$ leaves, each edge taking $D$ values. At a
binary merge, let $A,B$ be the sets of boundary edge labels of its children. Set
\begin{equation}
 \Lleaf=\sum_{\text{leaves }v}D^{\deg(v)},\qquad
 \Tmul=\sum_{\text{merges}}D^{|A\cup B|},\qquad
 O=\sum_{\text{merges}}D^{|A\triangle B|}.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:profile-preview}
\end{equation}
These quantities describe a \emph{supplied} contraction tree. The merge-union
width is $w=\max |A\cup B|$. It is a deliberately explicit resource measure; it
is not being identified without proof with another author's treewidth or
contraction-complexity convention.

For integer entries, the compiler uses exactly $2(\Lleaf+2\Tmul-O)$ natural variables
before constant sharing. For entries in $\calR=\Z[e^{i\pi/4}]$, it uses exactly
$2(4\Lleaf+32\Tmul-4O)$ before constant sharing, and therefore at most $8\Lleaf+64\Tmul$.
All constraints are quadratic. Their sum of squares is a single quartic
Diophantine equation. Fixed output assertions preserve the property that the
witness set is either empty or a singleton.

For the doubled tensor network of an exact quantum circuit, a strict rational
probability query requires at most 39 additional variables and 50 additional
quadratic equations. The witness coordinates have polynomial bit length in the
network and threshold description, even when their \emph{number} is exponential
in width. This last distinction is forced by the conditional obstruction in
Section~\ref{pqc:cc:sec:complexity}.

\subsection{Novelty and scope}

Tensor contraction as a simulation method, and its dependence on graph width,
are established results; Markov and Shi are a central reference \cite{b62s10-MarkovShi}.
Clifford+T exact arithmetic and measurement-based universality are likewise
established \cite{giles-selinger,b62s10-RaussendorfBriegel}. The proposed contribution
here is the assembled, fully specified \emph{natural-witness} compiler: canonical
signed coordinates, exact resource constants, a height proof that uses the
contraction tree, a single-valued algebraic comparison gadget, and a sharp
separation between exact finite descriptions and approximation-name inputs.

Theorems are proved below rather than asserted on the basis of tests. The
implementation provides additional finite checks, not a formal proof of the
compiler. The construction resolves the concrete representation problem posed
here. It should not be advertised as a verified historically new solution to an
established major conjecture.

\section{Canonical arithmetic wires and a quartic normal form}
\label{pqc:cc:sec:wires}
\srcmark{10}

Throughout, $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. Integer coefficients are allowed in all
polynomials, but existential variables range over $\N$. For a pair of natural
variables $z^+,z^-$ write $\Delta z=z^+-z^-$. A \emph{canonical signed wire}
is such a pair together with the constraint
\begin{equation}
 z^+z^-=0.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:canonical}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Unique signed representation]
\label[lemma]{pqc:cc:lem:canonical}
For every $z\in\Z$, there is exactly one pair in $\N^2$ satisfying
$\Delta z=z$ and \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:canonical}. It is
$(\max(z,0),\max(-z,0))$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The product condition says that at least one coordinate is zero. If the first
coordinate is zero, the difference is nonpositive and determines the second;
if the second is zero, the difference is nonnegative and determines the first.
At zero both coordinates are zero. These alternatives also prove existence.
\end{proof}

The product condition is indispensable for multiplicity control. The equation
$x-y=2$ alone has the infinitely many solutions $(2+k,k)$, $k\in\N$.
Introducing unrestricted positive and negative parts is therefore not a
single-witness encoding.

\begin{definition}[Arithmetic evaluation network]
An arithmetic evaluation network is a finite directed acyclic graph with $q$
source wires and $s$ gates. Source values are fixed integers, or fixed integer
parameters. Every gate is a binary addition, subtraction, or multiplication.
Its output is a new wire; earlier wires may be reused. Let $N=q+s$.
\end{definition}

For every wire impose \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:canonical}. A source of value $c$ has residual
$\Delta z-c$. For a gate output $z$ with inputs $x,y$, use respectively
\begin{equation}
 \Delta z-\Delta x-\Delta y,\qquad
 \Delta z-\Delta x+\Delta y,\qquad
 \Delta z-(\Delta x)(\Delta y).
\label{pqc:cc:eq:gate-residuals}
\end{equation}
If natural input codes are required for signed parameters, write the latter as
the difference of their supplied natural coordinates. The theorem is then
understood separately for every fixed parameter tuple.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical quartic compilation]
\label{pqc:cc:thm:wires}
An arithmetic evaluation network with $N$ wires has a system of $2N$ equations
of degree at most two in $2N$ natural variables whose unique solution is its
canonical evaluation. If the residuals are $F_1,\ldots,F_{2N}$, then
\begin{equation}
 P=\sum_{j=1}^{2N}F_j^2
\label{pqc:cc:eq:sumsquares}
\end{equation}
has degree at most four and exactly the same natural solutions. Adding fixed
linear output assertions gives either that unique solution or no solution.
Before collection of monomials, a crude bound for the base polynomial is $37N$
monomial contributions.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Assign each wire the canonical pair of its actual integer value. All source,
gate, and canonical residuals vanish, proving existence. Conversely, take any
natural solution. The source equations and Lemma~\ref{pqc:cc:lem:canonical} uniquely
fix every source. In a topological order, a gate equation uniquely fixes the
integer difference of its output from already fixed input differences; the
canonical equation fixes the two output coordinates. Induction proves
uniqueness and correct evaluation at every wire.

Each residual is quadratic or linear. Over integers, a sum of squares is zero
if and only if every summand is zero. This proves the quartic assertion and
also shows that $P$ is nonnegative on all real substitutions, although the
uniqueness statement is specifically about natural substitutions. An output
assertion only removes the unique solution when the asserted value is false.

A source or gate residual has at most six monomials before like terms are
collected. Its square has at most 36 contributions. Each canonical residual
has one monomial, and its square also has one. There are $N$ residuals of each
type, giving $37N$. This is a bound on a particular sparse expansion, not on
the minimum number of terms in an equivalent equation.
\end{proof}

The construction is syntactic: the residuals can be emitted without first
knowing the final output. Evaluating the network supplies the witness but is
not needed to justify the equations. Constants have their ordinary binary
encoding; a large constant is not a unit-cost object in a bit-complexity claim.
When desired, a constant of bit length $b$ can instead be constructed from
$0,1$ with $O(b)$ doubling and addition gates. The latter preserves quadratic
constraints and canonicality. It does not establish a new optimum for the
number of variables or coefficients.

\wtag\ \emph{Batch-76 note (2 October 2026).} Part~IX's
Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:quartic} (source~19, printed as ``Canonical rational
quartic compilation'') extends Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:wires} to rational wires:
seven natural coordinates per wire, with a bounded B\'ezout coefficient, keep
one natural encoding of each rational number and so a unique witness.

\begin{remark}[Why a general DAG has no small height bound]
A chain $z_0=2$, $z_{i+1}=z_i^2$ has $z_i=2^{2^i}$. The bit length is exponential
in the number of gates. The polynomial height bound proved next is not a
property of every arithmetic DAG: it comes from the disjoint-leaf structure
of a tensor contraction tree.
\end{remark}

\section{Tensor contractions with exact size and height accounting}
\label{pqc:cc:sec:tensors}
\srcmark{10}

\subsection{Networks and supplied contraction trees}

A closed tensor network is a finite undirected multigraph without self-loops.
Each edge has its own label and domain $[D]=\{0,\ldots,D-1\}$. At vertex $v$,
a tensor $t_v$ assigns an integer to every assignment of values to its incident
edge labels. Parallel edges are distinct labels. The network value is
\begin{equation}
 Z_{\mathcal T}=\sum_{\sigma:E\to[D]}\prod_{v}t_v(\sigma|_{E(v)}).
\label{pqc:cc:eq:network-value}
\end{equation}
Disconnected networks are allowed. Their values multiply.

For a subset $S$ of vertices, let $\partial S$ be the edge labels with exactly
one endpoint in $S$, and let $e(S)$ count edges with both endpoints in $S$.
The partial tensor on $S$ sums over internal edges while keeping the values on
$\partial S$ fixed. A binary contraction tree has the vertices as its leaves.
At a merge of disjoint subsets, put $A=\partial S_1$, $B=\partial S_2$.
The shared labels $C=A\cap B$ are precisely the edges joining the two subsets.
Their union has boundary $A\triangle B$, and
\begin{equation}
 t_{S_1\cup S_2}(z)=\sum_{c\in[D]^{C}}
       t_{S_1}(z|_{A\setminus B},c)
       t_{S_2}(z|_{B\setminus A},c).
\label{pqc:cc:eq:merge}
\end{equation}
All sums are finite; the formula follows directly by partitioning assignments
in \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:network-value}. When $C$ is empty, the sum has one term, so no
special empty-sum convention is needed.

Choose a fixed lexicographic order on assignments in every sum. Use one
multiplication for each summand and a left-associated chain of additions to
sum them. This convention makes the full witness, not only its output,
well-defined relative to the tree.

\begin{theorem}[Integer contraction compiler]
\label{pqc:cc:thm:integer-tensor}
Let $\mathcal T$ have $m\ge2$ tensors, $E$ edges, edge dimension $D\ge2$, and
integer entries of absolute value at most $M\ge1$. Fix a binary contraction
tree and its profile $(\Lleaf,\Tmul,O)$ from \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:profile-preview}. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The prescribed evaluation has $\Lleaf$ source wires and $2\Tmul-O$ arithmetic
gates. Its canonical quadratic system has exactly $2(\Lleaf+2\Tmul-O)$ natural
variables and as many equations before sharing identical constants.
\item Every fixed output-value query is represented by a single polynomial
of degree at most four with at most one natural witness.
\item Every coordinate of the base witness is at most
$H=D^E M^m$. In particular, its bit length is at most
$1+\lceil E\log_2D+m\log_2M\rceil$.
\item For merge-union width $w$, the number of base variables is at most
$(6m-4)D^w$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At a merge there are $D^{|A\triangle B|}$ output entries. Each has
$D^{|A\cap B|}$ summands, so the total number of products is
$D^{|A\triangle B|+|A\cap B|}=D^{|A\cup B|}$. The addition count is that
number minus the number of output entries. Summing gives $\Tmul$ products and
$\Tmul-O$ additions. Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:wires} proves (i) and (ii).

A partial tensor entry for $S$ is a sum of $D^{e(S)}$ products of $|S|$ leaf
entries. Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 |t_S(z)|\le D^{e(S)}M^{|S|}.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:partialheight}
\end{equation}
For two children, an individual product before summing shared labels has
absolute value at most
$D^{e(S_1)+e(S_2)}M^{|S_1|+|S_2|}$. A partial sum over any initial segment
of shared assignments is bounded by the full sum of these absolute-value
bounds, hence by \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:partialheight} for the union. Thus every
intermediate arithmetic wire, not only each completed tensor entry, has
absolute value at most $D^E M^m$. Canonical coordinates have the same or smaller
magnitude. This proves (iii).

At the first merge involving a given leaf, its entire incident edge set is
contained in the merge union. Therefore every leaf degree is at most $w$.
There are $m-1$ merges, whence $\Lleaf\le mD^w$ and $\Tmul\le(m-1)D^w$. Dropping the
nonpositive term $-2O$ gives
$2(\Lleaf+2\Tmul-O)\le 2mD^w+4(m-1)D^w$, proving (iv).
\end{proof}

The case of a single scalar tensor is handled by a source wire without any
merge. Non-scalar one-vertex closed networks would require self-loops, which
were excluded; such loops may instead be contracted as an explicit preliminary
finite sum.

\subsection{What the height proof does and does not say}

The important structural fact is that the two children of every merge depend
on disjoint sets of leaf tensors. Their products expand into products in which
each leaf is used exactly once. Reuse of a \emph{table entry} in several output
entries is harmless: it does not make a single output monomial reuse an entire
subcomputation as a factor. This is why the repeated-squaring counterexample
from Section~\ref{pqc:cc:sec:wires} does not apply.

The theorem bounds the coordinates of the unique witness, not the computational
effort needed to discover a favorable contraction tree. For a supplied tree,
emitting the system takes time polynomial in its explicit arithmetic expansion
and in the bit lengths of the leaf entries. In particular, for fixed $D$ and
$w=O(\log m)$ with polynomial-bit input entries, the certificate description,
its witness, and its direct verification are polynomial in the original network
size. This follows by the displayed counts and height bound; it is consistent
with established low-width tensor simulation \cite{b62s10-MarkovShi}.

\begin{proposition}[Independence of the chosen order]
\label[proposition]{pqc:cc:prop:orders}
Any two complete contraction trees for the same closed network produce the
same output integer. The corresponding canonical witness sets for a fixed
output query are either both empty or both singletons. A witness in one order
can be replaced effectively by the canonical witness in the other order.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Each order evaluates \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:network-value}, by repeated use of
\eqref{pqc:cc:eq:merge}. Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:integer-tensor} gives the assertion about
witness sets. Re-evaluating the other finite tree gives the stated effective
replacement. There is no assertion that the replacement is local, or that the
two witness spaces have the same dimension.
\end{proof}

\section{Cyclotomic arithmetic without noncanonical auxiliary choices}
\label{pqc:cc:sec:cyclotomic}
\srcmark{10}

\subsection{A four-coordinate integer algebra}

Put $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$ and $\calR=\Z[\omega]$. Every element has a unique form
\begin{equation}
 A=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3,\qquad a_j\in\Z,
\label{pqc:cc:eq:cyclonormal}
\end{equation}
with $\omega^4=-1$. For completeness, $X^4+1$ is irreducible over $\Q$:
substituting $X+1$ gives $X^4+4X^3+6X^2+4X+2$, to which Eisenstein's criterion
at 2 applies. This proves uniqueness of the four-coordinate form.

Addition uses four integer additions. Multiplication has coordinates
\begin{equation}
 c_k=\sum_{\substack{0\le i,j<4\\i+j=k}}a_i b_j
       -\sum_{\substack{0\le i,j<4\\i+j=k+4}}a_i b_j,
 \qquad 0\le k<4.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:cyclomul}
\end{equation}
Across the four output coordinates there are 16 products, four per coordinate,
and 12 additions or subtractions. The first term for coordinate $k$ may be
chosen as the positive product $a_0b_k$. Thus a direct scalar evaluation uses
28 arithmetic gates per ring multiplication, without a separate initial
negation or accumulator.

For $A$ as in \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:cyclonormal}, define
$\|A\|_1=\sum_j|a_j|$. Reduction modulo $X^4+1$ can only combine signed
coefficients, so
\begin{equation}
 \|AB\|_1\le\|A\|_1\|B\|_1.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:l1submult}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Cyclotomic contraction compiler]
\label{pqc:cc:thm:cyclotensor}
For a closed $\calR$-valued tensor network and a supplied contraction tree, the
base canonical quadratic system has, before constant sharing,
\begin{equation}
 V_R=2(4\Lleaf+32\Tmul-4O)
\label{pqc:cc:eq:ringexactcount}
\end{equation}
natural variables and $V_R$ equations. In particular,
\begin{equation}
 V_R\le 8\Lleaf+64\Tmul\le (72m-64)D^w.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:ringbound}
\end{equation}
It has exactly one solution, encoding the entire contraction in the basis
\eqref{pqc:cc:eq:cyclonormal}. Let
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_v=\max\bigl(1,\max_{\text{entries }a\text{ of }t_v}\|a\|_1\bigr).
\end{equation}
Every natural coordinate is bounded by
\begin{equation}
 H_R=D^E\prod_v\lambda_v.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:ringheight}
\end{equation}
If every scalar coefficient in a leaf entry has absolute value at most
$M\ge1$, then also $H_R\le D^E(4M)^m$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
There are $4\Lleaf$ integer source wires. Each of the $\Tmul$ ring products uses 28
scalar gates; each of the $\Tmul-O$ ring additions uses four. Thus the scalar gate
count is $28\Tmul+4(\Tmul-O)=32\Tmul-4O$. Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:wires} proves
\eqref{pqc:cc:eq:ringexactcount}, uniqueness, and the quartic conversion.
The width bound follows as in Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:integer-tensor}.

For a subset $S$, the $\ell^1$ norm of a partial entry is at most
$D^{e(S)}\prod_{v\in S}\lambda_v$, by \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:l1submult}. Each scalar
product in \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:cyclomul} is bounded by the product of the input norms;
the absolute value of any partial signed sum of its terms is bounded by the
sum of the absolute values of all those products. This is at most that same
product of norms. Subsequent partial sums over shared edge assignments are
bounded exactly as in \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:partialheight}. Because every $\lambda_v\ge1$,
the bound for any subset or intermediate is at most \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:ringheight}.
The lower bound 1 in the definition also avoids a zero leaf incorrectly
forcing the height bound for unrelated intermediates to be zero.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Conjugation, real values, and exact norms}

Conjugation is the signed coordinate permutation
\begin{equation}
 \overline{(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3)}=(a_0,-a_3,-a_2,-a_1).
\label{pqc:cc:eq:conjugation}
\end{equation}
An element is real precisely when $a_2=0$ and $a_3=-a_1$. Since
$\omega-\omega^3=\sqrt2$, such an element is $a_0+a_1\sqrt2$. These assertions
follow by comparing coefficients in \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:conjugation}; the positive square
root identity follows either from the chosen embedding or from squaring
$\omega-\omega^3$ and checking its sign.

In particular, for an amplitude $A$,
\begin{align}
 A\overline A&=a+b\sqrt2,\label{pqc:cc:eq:normcoords}\\
 a&=a_0^2+a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2,\notag\\
 b&=a_0a_1-a_0a_3+a_1a_2+a_2a_3.\notag
\end{align}
This identity is obtained by multiplying \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:cyclonormal} by
\eqref{pqc:cc:eq:conjugation} and reducing $\omega^4=-1$. It also illustrates why
ordinary integer signs of the two output coordinates do not determine the
sign of the represented real number.

\subsection{A unique quadratic nonnegativity gadget}

An unrestricted difference of naturals is not canonical, and neither is an
unrestricted four-square witness for nonnegativity. For this application we
can avoid both sources of multiplicity.

\begin{lemma}[Integer comparison with a unique witness]
\label[lemma]{pqc:cc:lem:intsign}
Given a canonical signed wire $z$, introduce $b,s\in\N$ and impose
\begin{equation}
 b(b-1)=0,\quad b z^-=0,\quad
 z^--(1-b)(s+1)=0,\quad bs=0.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:intsign}
\end{equation}
There is exactly one solution in $(b,s)$. It has $b=1$ if and only if
$\Delta z\ge0$; its slack is $s=\max(z^--1,0)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first equation forces $b\in\{0,1\}$. If $b=1$, the second forces $z^-=0$
and the fourth forces $s=0$, while the third is satisfied. If $b=0$, the third
forces $z^-=s+1>0$, uniquely determining $s=z^--1$; the other equations hold.
Canonicality of $z$ makes $z^-=0$ equivalent to $\Delta z\ge0$.
\end{proof}

Write $\NN(z)$ for this uniquely computed Boolean, remembering that its two
auxiliary variables and four equations are part of the system.

\begin{theorem}[Single-valued comparison in $\Q(\sqrt2)$]
\label{pqc:cc:thm:sqrt2sign}
Given canonical integer wires $p,q$, nonnegativity of $p+q\sqrt2$ has a
quadratic Boolean-output circuit with a unique auxiliary assignment. With
constant wires $0$ and $2$ already available, the circuit introduces 21 natural
variables and 29 equations. A strict positivity assertion is obtained by
applying it to $-p,-q$ and requiring its output to be zero.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Compute $d=p^2-2q^2$ and $-d$. Let
\[
 \alpha=\NN(p),\qquad \beta=\NN(q),\qquad
 \gamma=\NN(d),\qquad \delta=\NN(-d).
\]
Introduce natural variables $e,f,B$ with
\begin{equation}
 e=\alpha(1-\beta),\qquad f=(1-\alpha)\beta,\qquad
 B=\alpha\beta+e\gamma+f\delta.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:quadraticsign}
\end{equation}
All three equations have degree at most two. The four sign cases prove the
claimed interpretation. If $p,q\ge0$, then $B=1$. If $p,q<0$, then $B=0$.
If $p\ge0>q$, the inequality is $p\ge |q|\sqrt2$, equivalent to $d\ge0$;
thus $B=\gamma$. If $p<0\le q$, the inequality is $q\sqrt2\ge|p|$,
equivalent to $d\le0$, and $B=\delta$. These arguments include zero
coordinates and equality. The case $p=q=0$ gives $B=1$.

Every preceding scalar wire is unique by Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:wires}, the four
comparators are unique by Lemma~\ref{pqc:cc:lem:intsign}, and \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:quadraticsign}
then fixes $e,f,B$. The output is automatically Boolean, without another
Boolean constraint.

The scalar operations $p^2,q^2,2q^2,d,-d$ contribute ten natural variables and
ten equations. Four instances of \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:intsign} contribute eight variables
and sixteen equations. Finally $e,f,B$ contribute three variables and three
equations. This gives 21 and 29. For any real $x$, $x>0$ is equivalent to the
failure of $-x\ge0$, proving the strict comparison claim.
\end{proof}

This construction deliberately computes all integer sign tests
\emph{unconditionally}. Multiplying a quadratic residual by a Boolean branch
guard would raise its degree to three; squaring that guarded residual would
no longer give the promised quartic bound. Equations
\eqref{pqc:cc:eq:intsign}--\eqref{pqc:cc:eq:quadraticsign} avoid that mistake.
The same proof works for $p+q\sqrt d$ with any fixed positive nonsquare integer
$d$, replacing the constant 2 by $d$. No general number-field comparison
compiler is asserted by this observation.

\section{Exact quantum probabilities as single-witness Diophantine queries}
\label{pqc:cc:sec:quantum}
\srcmark{10}

\subsection{The gate model and denominator discipline}

Use a finite gate alphabet containing
\[
 H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},
\]
and the computational-basis permutations $X$, CNOT, and Toffoli. The gates
$T^\dagger,S,Z$, and controlled-$Z$ may also be included. These choices retain
an exact cyclotomic arithmetic interface. The relationship between exact
Clifford+T synthesis and $\Z[1/\sqrt2,i]$ is established in
\cite{giles-selinger}; the compiler here only needs the displayed local matrices,
not the converse synthesis theorem. Hadamard--Toffoli universality in the
appropriate real-computation setting is discussed in \cite{b62s10-Shi}.

Let $C$ be a circuit with $n\ge1$ qubits, $g$ gates, and $h$ Hadamards.
Replace each $H$ by its numerator matrix $H_0=\sqrt2 H$. Leave all other gates
unchanged, obtaining a matrix $\widetilde U_C$ over $\calR$. Then
\begin{equation}
 U_C=2^{-h/2}\widetilde U_C.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:denominator}
\end{equation}
For a computational-basis input $x$, write
$A_y=\bra y\widetilde U_C\ket x$. An output cylinder event $B$ specifies fixed
values on some subset of the output qubits and leaves the rest unobserved.
Its probability is
\begin{equation}
 p_C(B)=2^{-h}U_B,\qquad
 U_B=\sum_{y\in B}A_y\overline{A_y}\in\Z[\sqrt2].
\label{pqc:cc:eq:probability}
\end{equation}
The physical normalization gives $0\le U_B\le2^h$ in the chosen real embedding.
The symbol $2^h$ is a known integer determined by the finite circuit. It is not
an exponentiation relation with an unconstrained existential exponent.
Its binary description has $h+1$ bits.

\subsection{A doubled closed network}

Construct one copy of the circuit numerator network and one entrywise-conjugate
copy. Give their wire segments independent edge labels. Attach basis-input
vectors on both copies. At each output qubit attach the two-index tensor
\begin{equation}
 D_j(a,b)=
 \begin{cases}
  1,&a=b\text{ and the equality agrees with the event, if specified},\\
  0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\label{pqc:cc:eq:outputtensor}
\end{equation}
For an unspecified output qubit, this is just $\delta_{ab}$. The resulting
network is closed and has value $U_B$. Expanding all edge assignments first
sums the ket amplitude and bra amplitude independently; the output tensors
then identify their final basis labels and enforce the event.

If gate $j$ has arity $k_j$, this particular dense-table construction has
\begin{equation}
 m=2g+3n,\qquad E=2n+2\sum_{j=1}^g k_j,\qquad
 \Lleaf=8n+2\sum_{j=1}^g4^{k_j}.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:quantum-network-counts}
\end{equation}
There are $2n$ input vectors, $2g$ gate tensors, and $n$ output tensors.
Each side starts with $n$ edge labels and creates $k_j$ new labels at gate $j$,
proving the edge count. The input and output tables together contribute $8n$
entries, while each of the two copies of an arity-$k_j$ gate has $2^{2k_j}$
entries. This proves the last count. No sparsity optimization is hidden in it.

Every nonzero entry of these tensors is a signed power of $\omega$ with a
single nonzero coefficient in the basis \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:cyclonormal}. Thus every
$\lambda_v$ in Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:cyclotensor} equals 1, and every base witness
coordinate is at most $2^E$.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical exact-probability certificates]
\label{pqc:cc:thm:quantum}
Fix a circuit $C$, basis input, cylinder event $B$, and contraction tree for the
doubled network. Write its output in real coordinates as $U_B=a+b\sqrt2$.
Then the following constructions are effective.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The graph of the exact output pair $(a,b)$ has a natural-witness quartic
representation with at most $8\Lleaf+64\Tmul$ base witness variables. A fixed correct
output pair has exactly one witness, and an incorrect pair has none.
\item For fixed integers $u\ge0$, $v>0$, the assertion $p_C(B)>u/v$ has a
quartic representation with at most $8\Lleaf+64\Tmul+39$ natural witness variables.
The base system gains at most 50 quadratic equations. The witness set has
cardinality one if the assertion is true, and zero otherwise.
\item Let $H_*=2^E$ and $K=vH_*+u2^h$. All witness coordinates, including the
comparison auxiliaries in (ii), are at most $2K^2$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:cyclotensor} gives a unique full contraction witness with output
coordinates $(a,b,0,-b)$. Appending linear assertions equating $a,b$ to the
supplied target differences proves (i). If targets are supplied by signed
natural pairs, their interpreted values are those differences. The uniqueness
is for each fixed target code; the output's own canonical pairs remain fixed.

For (ii), compute the signed integer wires
\begin{equation}
 p=va-u2^h,\qquad q=vb.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:thresholdcoords}
\end{equation}
Because $v2^h>0$,
\[
 p_C(B)>u/v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p+q\sqrt2>0.
\]
Compute the nonnegativity Boolean for $-p,-q$ from
Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:sqrt2sign} and require it to be zero. Also impose the two
linear reality checks on the full ring output, $c_2=0$ and $c_3+c_1=0$.
They are redundant for a correct doubled network but make the query interface
explicit. All operations and sign choices are unique. Hence a true query has
one witness and a false one has none. Squaring and summing all residuals gives
the asserted polynomial of degree at most four.

Here is the full overhead audit. Constructing $p,q,-p,-q$ uses five scalar
gates, hence ten variables and ten equations. The comparison circuit adds 21
variables and 29 equations. At most four new integer constants are needed:
$0,2,v,u2^h$, costing at most eight variables and eight equations. The two
reality checks and the final Boolean assertion add three equations and no
variables. The totals are 39 variables and 50 equations. Constant sharing can
only lower these bounds.

For (iii), the base contraction coordinates are bounded by $H_*$, so
$|p|,|q|\le K$. During the comparison, the scalar squares and the twice-square
are bounded by $2K^2$. Their difference satisfies
$|p^2-2q^2|\le2K^2$, and the same bound holds after sign reversal. The integer
comparison slacks are smaller than the corresponding negative parts. The
remaining variables are Boolean or constants of size at most $\max(K,2)$.
As $K\ge1$, all are bounded by $2K^2$.
\end{proof}
\wtag\ This is the explicit, counted form of the direct bounded evaluator sketched at the end of the proof of Proposition~\ref{pqc:prop:finitequantum} in Part~II, which states no witness count; it also supplies per-coordinate heights and a single-valued comparator in place of Part~II's case analysis of $A^2$ against $2B^2$.

For fixed gate arity, the description lengths of $C,u,v$ bound $E,h$ and
$\log_2K$ polynomially. Therefore the height statement in (iii) is a
\emph{polynomial per-coordinate bit bound}. The number of coordinates still
has its width-dependent factor. No general polynomial-time classical simulation
of quantum computation follows.

Exact equality with $u/v$ can be encoded more simply by
$va-u2^h=0$ and $vb=0$. The equivalence uses the irrationality of $\sqrt2$.
Non-strict inequalities use the nonnegativity output directly. For a general
Boolean predicate of the output bits, its cost must be included: for example,
compute its flag reversibly and then use a cylinder event on that flag. A
large predicate table is not supplied for free by the cylinder theorem.

\subsection{Two examples that expose the semantic issue}

First take $C=HH$ and input $\ket0$. The unnormalized output amplitudes are
$A_0=1+1=2$ and $A_1=1-1=0$, while $h=2$. There are two nonzero fine-grained
paths to output 1, but they cancel. Therefore
\[
 p_C(1)=0,\qquad p_C(0)=1.
\]
A Diophantine certificate for the existence of one path to 1 would answer the
wrong question. The contraction certificate answers the right one, and an
explicit eight-variable quartic for this calculation is given in
Appendix~\ref{pqc:cc:app:quartic}.

Next take $C=HTH$, meaning that $H$, then $T$, then $H$ is applied. Here
\[
 A_0=1+\omega,\qquad A_1=1-\omega,\qquad h=2,
\]
and \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:normcoords} gives
\begin{equation}
 p_C(0)=\frac{2+\sqrt2}{4},\qquad
 p_C(1)=\frac{2-\sqrt2}{4}.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:hth}
\end{equation}
Thus $p_C(0)>1/2$ and $p_C(1)<1/2$ are certified without a numerical
approximation to $\sqrt2$. The example demonstrates both coherent addition
and a genuinely nonrational probability. For the integer-entry
Hadamard--Toffoli subcase, the numerator $U_B$ is an ordinary integer and the
quadratic-field comparator can be replaced by integer comparison. \wtag\ Both examples are Part~II's Example~\ref{pqc:ex:hhhth}, computed there in the coordinates $a+b\sqrt2+i(c+d\sqrt2)$ over $2^L$ with $L$ the number of gates; here they are computed in the four coordinates of $\Z[\omega]$ over $2^{h/2}$ with $h$ the number of Hadamards. What source~10 adds is the explicit eight-variable quartic of Appendix~\ref{pqc:cc:app:quartic} and the certificate sizes of Section~\ref{pqc:cc:sec:implementation}.

\section{An unconventional realization: adaptive graph-state measurements}
\label{pqc:cc:sec:mbqc}
\srcmark{10}

\subsection{Exact branch semantics}

Measurement-based computation replaces a sequence of coherent gates on a moving
register by measurements of an entangled resource, with later measurement
choices depending on earlier outcomes. Its universality on suitable resource
families is due to Raussendorf and Briegel \cite{b62s10-RaussendorfBriegel}. We now
provide a direct arithmetic interface for individual branches; no claim is
made that every graph is a universal resource.

Let $G=(V,F)$ be a simple graph with $n$ vertices and $r$ edges. Its graph state is
\begin{equation}
 \ket G=\prod_{\{i,j\}\in F}CZ_{ij}\ket+^{\otimes n}
 =2^{-n/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}
       (-1)^{\sum_{\{i,j\}\in F}x_i x_j}\ket x.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:graphstate}
\end{equation}
Measure each vertex once, in the order $1,\ldots,n$, in the equatorial basis
whose outcome-$s_i$ bra is
\begin{equation}
 2^{-1/2}\bigl(\bra0+(-1)^{s_i}\omega^{-k_i}\bra1\bigr).
\label{pqc:cc:eq:equatorialbra}
\end{equation}
For a fixed transcript $s\in\{0,1\}^n$, the angle index is
$k_i=k_i(s_1,\ldots,s_{i-1})\pmod8$. We assume these causal rules are explicitly
given finite tables or Boolean circuits. This makes their evaluation effective
with accounted-for finite input size, rather than hiding a possibly
nonterminating classical subroutine in the word ``adaptive.''

\begin{theorem}[Canonical branch certificates]
\label{pqc:cc:thm:graphstate}
For the complete measurement transcript $s$, define
\begin{equation}
 A_{G,s}=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}
  (-1)^{\sum_{\{i,j\}\in F}x_i x_j+\sum_i s_i x_i}
  \omega^{-\sum_i k_i(s_{<i})x_i}.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:graphbranch}
\end{equation}
Then its probability is
\begin{equation}
 \Prob(s)=4^{-n}A_{G,s}\overline{A_{G,s}}.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:graphprobability}
\end{equation}
This numerator has a closed $\calR$-valued binary-edge network realization
using only tensors of arity at most three, with at most $4n+6r$ tensors and
$2n+8r$ edges. For every supplied contraction tree, it has the canonical
quartic certificate of Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:cyclotensor}. Every base coordinate is
at most $2^{2n+8r}$. Exact rational threshold assertions use the comparator
construction, with denominator $4^n$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Expand \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:graphstate} and apply the product of the bras
\eqref{pqc:cc:eq:equatorialbra}, evaluating the adaptive choices on the fixed
transcript. The graph-state normalization contributes $2^{-n/2}$ and the $n$
bras contribute another $2^{-n/2}$. Hence the branch amplitude is
$2^{-n}A_{G,s}$, proving \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:graphprobability}. This unnormalized branch
calculation includes the product of all conditional measurement probabilities;
one must not separately normalize intermediate branches and then forget the
normalizing factors.

For the amplitude numerator, use one binary factor
$(-1)^{x_i x_j}$ per graph edge and one unary factor
$(-1)^{s_i x_i}\omega^{-k_i x_i}$ per vertex. A variable occurring in several
factors is represented by a copy tensor: its value is 1 when all incident
binary labels agree, and 0 otherwise. Summing the common value implements the
sum over that variable. A rank-$k$ copy tensor can be split into a tree of
ternary copy tensors for $k\ge3$, with rank-one and rank-two cases treated
separately. Each satisfying external assignment extends uniquely to the
internal labels, so this introduces neither a weight nor a multiplicity.
These are equality constraints on tensor indices, not a physical operation
that clones an arbitrary quantum state.

At vertex $i$ the copy rank is $\deg(i)+1$. It needs at most
$\max(1,\deg(i)-1)$ copy tensors and $\max(\deg(i)-2,0)$ internal edges.
Consequently the amplitude network has at most $2n+3r$ tensors: $n$ unary
factors, $r$ edge factors, and at most $n+2r$ copy tensors. Its external
factor-to-copy connections number $n+2r$, and its additional internal copy
edges number at most $2r$. It therefore has at most $n+4r$ edges.

Take an independent conjugate copy and multiply the two scalar contractions.
This doubles both bounds and gives the claimed numerator network, allowing
disconnected components as in Section~\ref{pqc:cc:sec:tensors}. Each nonzero tensor
entry is a signed power of $\omega$, so every $\lambda_v=1$.
Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:cyclotensor} gives the height bound and canonical quartic
representation. Replacing $2^h$ by $4^n$ in
\eqref{pqc:cc:eq:thresholdcoords} proves the threshold statement.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Adaptivity, coarse events, and honest size accounting}

For one fixed transcript, the angle rules can be evaluated first, so the
coherent tensor construction has exactly the branch semantics above. A
collection of accepted transcripts has probability equal to the sum of their
individual probabilities. Explicitly enumerating those transcripts and adding
the corresponding numerator networks is always valid, but can be exponential.
One cannot claim a polynomial-size compilation of a coarse adaptive event
merely because each local angle rule is small. A better construction must
include the classical control factors and account for their induced width.

This gives a useful separation of responsibilities. The quantum part is
certified by the ring-valued contraction. The classical causal rule is either
evaluated on the fixed transcript or represented by its own deterministic
arithmetic circuit. The final event predicate has its own counted cost. None
of these components is replaced by an unexplained assertion that a chosen
measurement branch is ``legal.''

The graph-state result supplies a non-gate-level example of the same
Diophantine interface. Together with an effective unbounded classical
controller and an unbounded family of finite resources, such models fit the
Turing-complete setting of Section~\ref{pqc:cc:sec:unbounded}. An individual finite
graph, like an individual finite circuit, is only a bounded computation.

\section{A certificate-size obstruction from Boolean unsatisfiability}
\label{pqc:cc:sec:complexity}
\srcmark{10}

The preceding construction has small witness \emph{heights} but can have many
witness \emph{coordinates}. The distinction cannot simply be optimized away
without a substantial complexity-theoretic consequence.

\begin{theorem}[Zero-probability certificate obstruction]
\label{pqc:cc:thm:npconp}
Suppose a polynomial-time algorithm takes any finite circuit over
$H,X,\mathrm{CNOT},\mathrm{Toffoli}$ with a specified output event and produces a
sparse integer polynomial $P_C$ of some fixed bounded degree, such that
\[
 p_C(B)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists z\in\N^{k_C}\;P_C(z)=0.
\]
Suppose further that the polynomial description has polynomial binary length,
and that every true instance has a witness whose total binary length is
polynomial in the circuit description. Then $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}$.
Uniqueness of the witness is not required.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $\varphi$ be a Boolean formula on $n$ bits. Its Boolean evaluation has a
reversible circuit of polynomial size over $X$, CNOT, and Toffoli, using clean
ancillas. To see this directly, compute Boolean subexpressions into fresh
work bits: Toffoli computes an AND into a zero target; CNOT copies a bit into
a zero target; and NOT and a constant-one bit are supplied by $X$. OR can be
expressed through AND and NOT. Copy the result into a flag and reverse the
computation to clean the work bits. This implements
\[
 \ket x\ket{0}_{\mathrm{work}}\ket0_{\mathrm{flag}}
 \longmapsto
 \ket x\ket{0}_{\mathrm{work}}\ket{\varphi(x)}_{\mathrm{flag}}.
\]
Start the input register in $H^{\otimes n}\ket{0^n}$. Distinct inputs $x$
remain orthogonal, so the flag-1 probability is
\begin{equation}
 p_\varphi(1)=\frac{\#\{x:\varphi(x)=1\}}{2^n}.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:satprob}
\end{equation}
It is zero exactly when $\varphi$ is unsatisfiable.

Apply the hypothesized compiler to this polynomial-size circuit. On an
unsatisfiable formula, guess a witness of the promised polynomial binary
length and check the resulting sparse polynomial equation. This verification
is polynomial-time: the degree is fixed, the coefficients and variable values
have polynomial bit length, and there are polynomially many terms. On a
satisfiable formula no witness passes. Therefore UNSAT belongs to NP.
Since UNSAT is coNP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions
(the complement of the SAT completeness theorem~\cite{b62s10-Cook}),
$\mathrm{coNP}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}$, and complementation gives equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The obstruction also applies to strict thresholds]
\label[corollary]{pqc:cc:cor:threshold-obstruction}
A universal polynomial-size, polynomial-bit certificate compiler for the
queries $p_C(B)>u/v$, with binary rational thresholds as part of the input and
fixed bounded polynomial degree, would also imply
$\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use the complementary flag event in \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:satprob} and the threshold
\[
 r_n=1-2^{-(n+1)}.
\]
Its binary numerator and denominator have $O(n)$ bits. The probability
$1-\#\mathrm{SAT}(\varphi)/2^n$ exceeds $r_n$ exactly when the integer
$\#\mathrm{SAT}(\varphi)$ is zero. The same NP-verification argument applies.
\end{proof}

The proof already uses nonnegative classical counting inside a quantum circuit.
Thus interference is not the only reason that exact probability certification
can be expensive. Coherent cancellation explains why a path witness is
semantically inadequate; exact counting explains why a globally cheap
replacement is implausible under standard complexity expectations.

These statements are conditional consequences, not proofs that
$\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}$. They do not exclude small certificates on
restricted families, certificates with exponentially many variables, or
fixed-arity MRDP representations whose least witnesses have no polynomial bit
bound. They also require a genuinely polynomially checkable polynomial
encoding; a succinct circuit that repeatedly squares gigantic integers is not
a substitute for the sparse bounded-degree condition without another
verification argument.

\section{Exact descriptions versus approximation names}
\label{pqc:cc:sec:names}
\srcmark{10}

\subsection{The representation of a parameter is part of the theorem}

For an explicitly supplied rational number $a/b$, equality to zero is decided
by its numerator. For an explicitly supplied element of $\calR$, equality is
decided by four integer coefficients. A \emph{fast Cauchy name}, in contrast,
is an algorithm producing a rational $q_k$ with a guaranteed error
$|q_k-x|\le2^{-k}$. Effective approximation does not by itself provide a test
for exact equality. This is a basic distinction in computable analysis
\cite{b62s10-Weihrauch}; the following reduction shows exactly how it obstructs a
Diophantine interpretation of a quantum observation.

\begin{theorem}[A one-gate exact-zero obstruction]
\label{pqc:cc:thm:cauchy}
There is a uniform computable family of fast Cauchy names for single-qubit
unitary matrices $R_e$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item every actual matrix $R_e$ has rational entries;
\item the probability of observing 1 after applying $R_e$ to $\ket0$ is zero
if and only if Turing machine $e$ never halts on blank input;
\item this zero-probability index set is not computably enumerable, hence
has no existential Diophantine representation over $\N$;
\item there is no total computable procedure that, from $e$, produces an
integer polynomial whose natural solvability is equivalent to this zero event.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Number machine steps starting at 1 and define
\begin{equation}
 a_e=\begin{cases}
 2^{-t},&\text{if machine $e$ first halts at step }t,\\
 0,&\text{if it never halts}.
 \end{cases}
\label{pqc:cc:eq:haltingreal}
\end{equation}
To approximate $a_e$ to error $2^{-k}$, simulate $e$ for $k$ steps. If a halt
is seen at step $t$, output $2^{-t}$; otherwise output zero. A later halt
would give a value smaller than $2^{-k}$, so this is a uniform total fast
Cauchy-name algorithm. Every $a_e$ is individually rational and lies in
$[0,1/2]$.

Now use the rational parametrization of a planar rotation,
\begin{equation}
 R(a)=\frac1{1+a^2}
 \begin{pmatrix}1-a^2&-2a\\2a&1-a^2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad R_e=R(a_e).
\label{pqc:cc:eq:cayley}
\end{equation}
The identity $(1-a^2)^2+(2a)^2=(1+a^2)^2$ proves that $R(a)$ is orthogonal,
hence unitary. Its entries are rational whenever $a$ is rational. On the
interval $[0,1/2]$, the derivatives of both scalar entry functions are bounded
in absolute value by 2. Thus approximating $a_e$ at precision $k+3$ and
substituting the rational approximation into \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:cayley} gives a rational
approximation to each matrix entry with error less than $2^{-k}$. This proves
uniform validity of the gate names, not merely a promise on an unknown subset
of names.

The required output probability is
\begin{equation}
 p_e=\frac{4a_e^2}{(1+a_e^2)^2}.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:cayleyprob}
\end{equation}
Its denominator is positive, so $p_e=0$ exactly when $a_e=0$, which is exactly
nonhalting. The nonhalting set is not computably enumerable: if it and the
halting set both were, dovetailing their enumerations would decide halting,
contradicting the diagonal halting argument. On the other hand, the projection
of the natural zero set of an integer polynomial is computably enumerable,
by exhaustive search of natural tuples. This proves (iii).

Finally, suppose the procedure in (iv) existed. On input $e$, compute its
polynomial and enumerate all natural tuples of the returned finite dimension,
evaluating the polynomial exactly. The search halts exactly on the zero-event
instances, making the nonhalting set computably enumerable. This contradiction
proves (iv).
\end{proof}

The strength of the example is that \emph{rational-valuedness alone does not
repair the problem}. Each member has a finite exact rational description, but
no uniform exact numerator/denominator extraction is available from these
approximation names. The obstruction lies in the effective input interface,
not in the existence of transcendental numbers.

Nothing in the theorem assumes a physical device that can manufacture these
rotations exactly from arbitrary machine indices. It is a theorem about
mathematical specifications and exact predicates, not an experimentally
available halting oracle. Finite noisy observations cannot certify the
difference between probability zero and an arbitrarily small positive value
with a uniform finite guarantee. \wtag\ Source~16 in this Part sits on the other side of the same boundary; see Section~\ref{pqc:conv:b62-VI:boundary}.

\subsection{What remains effectively observable}

\begin{proposition}[Strict inequalities survive approximation names]
\label[proposition]{pqc:cc:prop:strictsemidecision}
For a uniformly computable family of finite circuits with computable entries,
and a fixed finite measurement event whose probability has a computable error
bound, $p>r$ is computably enumerable for rational $r$. Under these valid-name
assumptions, equality $p=r$ is co-computably enumerable. Exact zero is
$\Pi^0_1$-complete already on the family in Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:cauchy}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Compute rational intervals $[l_k,u_k]$ containing $p$, of widths tending
effectively to zero. For $p>r$, search for $l_k>r$. The search succeeds
exactly for the strict inequality. The analogous search for $u_k<r$ decides
strict inequality on the other side semidecidably. Dovetailing these searches
semidecides $p\ne r$, proving the equality assertion. For finite circuits,
finite additions and multiplications of certified entry approximations give
such intervals; a coarse uniform entry bound is available from unitarity.
The reduction in Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:cauchy}, and nonhalting's form
$\forall t\,[e\text{ has not halted by }t]$, give completeness on that family.
\end{proof}

MRDP may therefore supply an existential arithmetic representation of a strict
observable for a uniformly valid approximation-name family. It need not supply
one for exact equality. A proposed ``universal substrate compiler'' must state
both its parameter representation and the logical form of the observation;
Turing completeness by itself settles neither issue.

\section{Unbounded algebraic controllers and the quantifier boundary}
\label{pqc:cc:sec:unbounded}
\srcmark{10}

\subsection{A genuinely unbounded computational substrate}

Consider finite programs with an ordinary Turing-complete classical controller,
a finite quantum register at each finite time, allocation of qubits in
$\ket0$, gates from the exact alphabet of Section~\ref{pqc:cc:sec:quantum}, and
computational-basis measurements whose outcomes may affect the controller.
There is an absorbing classical halting flag. One controller step performs a
bounded number of these elementary actions. Arbitrarily long computations and
arbitrarily large finite registers are permitted; an individual program still
has a finite effective description.

This is Turing-complete even without using its coherent operations, because the
classical controller can simulate an ordinary Turing machine. Its finite quantum
prefixes also cover the coherent and measurement-based constructions above.
No claim of super-Turing computational power is involved.

For a coded program/input pair $z$, let $H_t(z)$ be the probability that the
halting flag has been set by step $t$. A finite prefix has finitely many
measurement transcripts and a finite quantum register on each branch. Simulate
unnormalized branch vectors instead of repeatedly normalizing conditional
states. Their entries use exact cyclotomic arithmetic, and their squared norms
have effectively known powers-of-two denominators. Summing halted branches
therefore computes $H_t(z)$ exactly as an element of $\Q(\sqrt2)$. In
particular, rational comparisons with $H_t$ are decidable. Also
\begin{equation}
 0\le H_t(z)\le H_{t+1}(z)\le1,\qquad
 H_\infty(z)=\sup_t H_t(z).
\label{pqc:cc:eq:haltlimit}
\end{equation}
The exact computation may be very expensive; only its effectiveness is used.

\wtag\ The next two theorems are the quantum-controller cases of the endpoint thresholds $p>0$ and $p=1$ that Part~I records after Theorem~\ref{pqc:thm:unconditionaltable}; the arguments are second routes, and the totality sampler~\eqref{pqc:cc:eq:totalityreduction} is~\eqref{pqc:eq:te}.

\begin{theorem}[Positive-probability halting is uniformly Diophantine]
\label{pqc:cc:thm:positivehalting}
The set of program/input codes $z$ with $H_\infty(z)>0$ is
$\Sigma^0_1$-complete. Consequently there are a fixed integer $k$ and a fixed
integer polynomial $P(z,w_1,\ldots,w_k)$ such that
\begin{equation}
 H_\infty(z)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists w\in\N^k\;P(z,w)=0.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:unboundedmrdp}
\end{equation}
The polynomial can also be replaced by a fixed degree-at-most-four polynomial
with finitely many additional witnesses. No single-witness assertion follows
for this uniform unbounded representation.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By monotonicity and the definition of supremum,
$H_\infty(z)>0$ is equivalent to $\exists t\,[H_t(z)>0]$. The bracketed predicate
is decidable by exact finite-prefix evaluation, proving membership in
$\Sigma^0_1$. Ordinary deterministic halting reduces to this problem by using
only the classical controller: its eventual halting probability is 1 if it
halts and 0 otherwise. Deterministic halting is $\Sigma^0_1$-complete, as any
predicate $\exists s\,R(z,s)$ with decidable $R$ is implemented by searching
for such an $s$.

Apply MRDP to this computably enumerable set of natural codes
\cite{b62-matiyasevich1970}. This is exactly
the finite-polynomial interface stated in the inspected ProveIt theorem
\cite{b62s10-ProveItMRDP}, and yields \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:unboundedmrdp}. To obtain degree at most
four, express evaluation of the fixed polynomial $P$ by a finite arithmetic
DAG, introduce the signed-wire constraints of Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:wires}, require
its output to be zero, and sum the squared residuals. The old witnesses $w$
remain quantified, and the additional wire variables evaluate $P$ canonically.
For every fixed old tuple there is exactly one auxiliary evaluation, but MRDP
may supply many different old witness tuples. Thus canonical evaluation does
not turn a many-witness MRDP representation into a single-witness one.
\end{proof}

The quantifier order in \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:unboundedmrdp} matters: $k$ and $P$ are chosen
before $z$, not separately after a finite running time is known. A family of
finite trace polynomials with more variables for larger $t$ is not, by itself,
a fixed-arity Diophantine representation. MRDP supplies precisely that missing
uniform compression; it does not supply the finite-circuit height or
multiplicity bounds.

\subsection{Almost-sure halting has a different logical form}

\begin{theorem}[Almost-sure halting]
\label{pqc:cc:thm:ast}
For the algebraic quantum controllers above, the property
$H_\infty(z)=1$ is $\Pi^0_2$-complete. It is not computably enumerable and thus
cannot be the projection of the natural zero set of an integer polynomial.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Using \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:haltlimit}, almost-sure halting is equivalent to
\begin{equation}
 \forall k\ge1\;\exists t\quad H_t(z)>1-2^{-k}.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:astquantifiers}
\end{equation}
The finite-prefix comparison is decidable, giving the upper bound.

For hardness, take an index $e$ for an ordinary partial computable function.
Sample $n\in\N$ with probability $2^{-(n+1)}$, by tossing fair coins until the
first zero and counting preceding ones. Fair coins are implemented by preparing
$\ket0$, applying $H$, and measuring. The probability of sampling forever is
zero. After choosing $n$, simulate machine $e$ on input $n$ and halt exactly
when that simulation halts. The eventual halting probability is
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{n\ge0}2^{-(n+1)}
       \mathbf1_{\{e(n)\text{ halts}\}}.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:totalityreduction}
\end{equation}
It equals 1 if and only if $e$ is total: every omitted input has a strictly
positive weight. Totality is $\Pi^0_2$-complete. Indeed, for a predicate
$\forall n\exists s\,R(x,n,s)$ with decidable $R$, the machine that on input
$n$ searches for an $s$ satisfying $R(x,n,s)$ is total exactly for the desired
$x$. This proves the lower bound.

For a direct non-enumerability argument, nonhalting reduces to totality. Given
a blank-input machine $e$, construct a machine which, on input $n$, simulates
$e$ for $n$ steps, halts if no halt was seen, and otherwise loops forever.
This machine is total exactly when $e$ never halts. Combining this reduction
with \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:totalityreduction} shows that almost-sure halting cannot be
computably enumerable. Polynomial solvability is computably enumerable, so
no existential Diophantine representation of this index set is possible.
\end{proof}

The classical probabilistic almost-sure-termination classification is already
established by Kaminski and Katoen \cite{kaminski-katoen}. The theorem above gives
its explicit embedding into the present algebraic quantum-controller model,
together with an exact finite-prefix upper bound. It is not a claim to have
newly discovered the classical $\Pi^0_2$ result.

\subsection{Three interfaces that must not be conflated}

The finite exact-circuit interface admits direct canonical quartic witnesses,
with dimensions dependent on a contraction schedule. The unbounded
positive-halting interface admits a fixed polynomial by MRDP, but loses the
proved unique-witness and height guarantees. The almost-sure interface contains
an essential universal quantifier and admits no such existential polynomial.
The approximation-name exact-zero interface already fails enumerable
observability with one gate. These are differences in predicates and effective
representations, not contradictions between models of computation.

\section{Implementation, exact experiments, and reproducibility}
\label{pqc:cc:sec:implementation}
\srcmark{10}

\subsection{The delivered prototype}

The package includes a standard-library-only Python implementation for
Python 3.10 or later. The file \texttt{code/coherent.py} implements four-integer
cyclotomic arithmetic, canonical signed wires, sparse quadratic residuals,
exact quantum state evaluation, doubled probability networks, ternary-copy
measurement networks, and the $\sqrt2$ comparison gadget. The tensor prototype
uses binary edges ($D=2$); the mathematical theorem permits general finite $D$.

Two deterministic contraction schedules are provided. The \texttt{greedy}
policy chooses a pair minimizing the current merge-union size, breaking ties
by output rank and current indices. The \texttt{queue} policy merges the first
two current tensors and appends their result. Neither is an optimization
certificate for the best contraction tree. In particular, ``greedy'' is a
heuristic, not a theorem about the globally smallest width.

The prototype constructs witnesses while emitting their constraints, allowing
an immediate exact evaluation check. Its scalar ring multiplication always uses
the explicit 16-product, 12-addition/subtraction formula, even when many entries
are zero. This makes it an auditable implementation of the proved count, not
an optimized state-of-the-art simulator. Equal scalar constants are shared.
If $c$ distinct scalar constants occur in the leaf tables, the observed base
count is
\begin{equation}
 V_{\mathrm{shared}}=2c+64\Tmul-8O,
\label{pqc:cc:eq:sharedcount}
\end{equation}
which is bounded by \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:ringexactcount} because $c\le4\Lleaf$.

\subsection{The finite verification suite}

All arithmetic checks use integers or rational numbers; no floating-point
tolerance is used to decide an identity or a sign. The run recorded in
\texttt{data/verification.json} passed the following tests:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{4.9in}r@{}}
\toprule
Check & Count\\
\midrule
Exact circuit states, each with a normalization check & 926\\
Doubled circuit-network values against direct state evaluation & 3,966\\
Adaptive graph-state amplitudes against independent gate realization & 296\\
Complete adaptive branch-distribution normalizations & 44\\
Native graph-factor amplitude/probability network equalities & 592\\
High-degree tests of ternary copy-tensor decomposition & 2\\
Cyclotomic norm identities on coefficient tuples in $\{-2,\ldots,2\}^4$ & 625\\
Exact $\sqrt2$ sign-circuit checks on $[-24,24]^2$ & 2,401\\
Integer-sign gadgets exhaustively checked in covering boxes & 13\\
Quadratic-certificate instances, including false-query rejection & 43\\
Single-coordinate witness mutations rejected & 240\\
Contraction/comparison witness-height checks & 42\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The circuit states include every word of length at most four in the one-qubit
alphabet $H,T,X$, for both basis inputs; every word of length at most three in
a specified two-qubit alphabet, for all four basis inputs; and 60 seeded
three-qubit circuits. The random seed is \texttt{20260930}. The graph-state tests
use all simple graphs on one through three vertices, all output transcripts,
and four causal angle-rule families. Higher-degree copy decompositions are
also exercised on a six-vertex star and a five-vertex complete graph.

For the sign tests, an independent rational enclosure of $\sqrt2$ is built by
integer square root at denominator $10^{30}$. This enclosure separates every
nonzero tested expression, so the comparison test does not merely call the
same sign routine twice. For norm checks, the integer formula
\eqref{pqc:cc:eq:normcoords} is compared to multiplication by the conjugate in the
four-coordinate algebra.

A separate program, \texttt{code/check\_certificate.py}, imports no generator
code. It checks natural coordinates and the vanishing of all exported
quadratic residuals. For the small expanded quartic, it also independently
multiplies and collects the residual squares and verifies the polynomial
identity, not just its value at the supplied point. This checker validates
algebraic witnesses, while correspondence to the stated circuit remains the
semantic compiler theorem and the cross-checks above.

\subsection{Representative certificate sizes}

The following are actual base counts from the delivered run. ``Bits'' is the
largest coordinate bit length in that base witness. The two exported full
circuit examples additionally include four linear output-value assertions;
those four equations do not add variables and are not included in this table.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Circuit / observed event & Schedule & $w$ & $\Tmul$ & Variables & Bits\\
\midrule
$HH$, output 1 & greedy & 2 & 22 & 1,326 & 2\\
$HH$, output 1 & queue  & 4 & 52 & 3,086 & 2\\
$HTH$, output 0 & greedy & 2 & 30 & 1,806 & 2\\
$HTH$, output 0 & queue  & 4 & 64 & 3,806 & 2\\
$HTH$, output 1 & greedy & 2 & 30 & 1,806 & 2\\
$HTH$, output 1 & queue  & 4 & 64 & 3,806 & 2\\
Bell preparation, qubit 0 equals 0 & greedy & 6 & 192 & 11,678 & 1\\
Bell preparation, qubit 0 equals 0 & queue  & 5 & 140 & 8,414 & 1\\
Two Hadamards, Toffoli flag equals 1 & greedy & 8 & 860 & 53,342 & 1\\
Two Hadamards, Toffoli flag equals 1 & queue  & 8 & 848 & 51,838 & 1\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

All examples start in the all-zero basis state. Bell preparation means $H$ on
qubit 0 followed by CNOT from 0 to 1. The Toffoli example applies $H$ to each
control, then Toffoli to a zero target; its flag-1 probability is $1/4$.
The Bell event has probability $1/2$. The $HTH$ values are
\eqref{pqc:cc:eq:hth}. The queue schedule beating the greedy heuristic on the Bell
example is a useful warning against reading an optimization guarantee into
local pair selection.

These counts are intentionally not advertised as competitive minimal
Diophantine representations. Applying generic ring multiplication to every
zero entry is wasteful. The value of the prototype is that the unoptimized
construction, exact counts, output semantics, and height checks are all visible
and reproducible. The much smaller hand-specialized quartic in
Appendix~\ref{pqc:cc:app:quartic} illustrates how large the optimization margin is.

\subsection{Commands and trust boundary}

From the package directory, run:
\begin{lstlisting}
python code/verify.py
python code/check_certificate.py data/HH_expanded_quartic.json \
  data/HH_zero_certificate.json data/HTH_zero_certificate.json
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{lstlisting}
The first command recreates the JSON examples and test record. Its elapsed-time
field is naturally machine-dependent. The tests use Python assertions and
should not be run with the \texttt{-O} optimization flag. The PDF uses standard
LaTeX packages and an embedded bibliography, so no external bibliography
processor is needed.

No Lean files are supplied as supposedly completed proofs. A sensible
formalization would separate canonical arithmetic evaluation, finite tensor
semantics, the four-coordinate algebra, real comparison, and the operational
controller model. The small independent checker is useful for auditing an
individual witness, but it does not replace a proof that every emitted system
has the intended meaning. General uniqueness follows from the topological
induction, not from the 240 mutation tests.

its delivered layout; the README gives the rerun recipe on a copy.
