\section{A fixed complete specialization}
\label{pqc:dr:sec:universal}
\srcmark{16}

Undecidable word problem alone would not justify the stronger phrase
``c.e.-complete.'' We give a construction that obtains many-one
completeness explicitly.

\subsection{Coding the halting set into an amalgam}
Let $\mathcal K\subseteq\N$ be a fixed c.e.-complete halting set.
In two free groups $F(a,b)$ and $F(c,d)$ put
\[
 u_n=a^n b a^{-n},\qquad v_n=c^n d c^{-n},\qquad n\geq0.
\]
The $u_n$ freely generate the subgroup they span, and the same holds
for the $v_n$. The block-expansion proof of Lemma~\ref{pqc:dr:lem:rankfree}
works without change for every finite collection of distinct indices,
including zero.

Let $U$ be generated by the $u_n$ with $n\in\mathcal K$, and $V$ by
the corresponding $v_n$. The basis correspondence $u_n\mapsto v_n$
defines an isomorphism $U\simeq V$. Form the amalgamated free product
\begin{equation}
 Q_{\mathcal K}=F(a,b)*_{U=V}F(c,d)
 =\pres{a,b,c,d}{u_n=v_n\ (n\in\mathcal K)}.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:amalgam}
\end{equation}
The presentation is recursively enumerable and has four generators.

\begin{lemma}
\label[lemma]{pqc:dr:lem:haltingamalgam}
For every $n\in\N$,
\[
 n\in\mathcal K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 u_nv_n^{-1}=1\text{ in }Q_{\mathcal K}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $n\in\mathcal K$ the equality is a defining relation. If
$n\notin\mathcal K$, freeness of the indicated bases shows $u_n\notin U$
and $v_n\notin V$. The word $u_nv_n^{-1}$ is then a reduced alternating
word with two syllables outside the amalgamated subgroup. It is nontrivial
by the normal-form theorem for free products with amalgamation.

To specify the normal-form input: choose coset transversals for the common
subgroup in each factor. Successively absorb subgroup elements and combine
adjacent syllables from the same factor. The resulting alternating
transversal form represents the identity only when no nontrivial
transversal syllable remains. In particular, a two-factor word whose
syllables are outside the common subgroup cannot be the identity. No
algorithm for deciding membership in $U$ is used in this existence argument.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Passing to a finite presentation}
Higman's embedding theorem states that every finitely generated recursively
presented group embeds in a finitely presented group \cite{b62-higman}.
Apply it to $Q_{\mathcal K}$, obtaining a finite presentation of a group
$G_0$ and an embedding $\jmath:Q_{\mathcal K}\hookrightarrow G_0$.
Fix once and for all finite words representing the images of $a,b,c,d$.
Substitution in $u_nv_n^{-1}$ gives a total computable map $n\mapsto w_n$
such that
\begin{equation}
 n\in\mathcal K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w_n=_{G_0}1.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:higmanreduction}
\end{equation}
The word problem of a finitely presented group is c.e.: enumerate finite
products of conjugates of defining relators and their inverses, freely
reduce, and compare with the input word. Therefore $\WP(G_0)$ is
c.e.-complete under many-one reductions.

For the local theorem in the next section, fix instead
\begin{equation}
 G=G_0*\langle t\rangle.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:freeextra}
\end{equation}
It is finitely presented, its word problem is still c.e.-complete, and its
presentation kernel is nontrivial. A free group has decidable word problem,
so a presentation of a group with complete word problem cannot have
trivial kernel. Take at least two generators, adding a redundant
generator with a defining relation if necessary.

\begin{corollary}[Fixed gates, varying target]
\label[corollary]{pqc:dr:cor:fixedcomplete}
The finite alphabet $\mathcal S_G$ for \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:freeextra} is fixed,
dense, rational, and symmetric. Its rational-matrix membership problem
is c.e.-complete.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{pqc:dr:thm:compiler} gives the reduction from $\WP(G)$ and density.
Membership is c.e. by enumeration of all finite gate words with exact
rational multiplication. Matrix validity and equality are decidable.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{What is and is not explicit.}
The compiler \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:rankembedding}, \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:gates},
\eqref{pqc:dr:eq:alphabet} is an explicit algorithm on a supplied finite
presentation. Its implementation is included. The preceding existence
argument fixes a universal finite presentation and fixed embedding words,
but this article does not print those potentially long constants.
Thus it proves existence of a fixed universal alphabet without claiming
a numerical universal gate count. The numerical example in
Section~\ref{pqc:dr:sec:verification} uses a different, decidable presentation
and is labeled accordingly.

\section{Completeness in every open neighborhood}
\label{pqc:dr:sec:local}
\srcmark{16}

The free generator $t$ supplies a way to localize hard instances without
changing their yes/no answer. Throughout this section $G=G_0*\langle t\rangle$
and $\Gamma=\Gamma_G$ are fixed as above.

\begin{lemma}[Commutator test]
\label[lemma]{pqc:dr:lem:commtest}
For $w\in G_0$ and an integer $k\geq1$,
\[
 [w,t^k]=1\text{ in }G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=1\text{ in }G_0,
\]
where $[u,v]=uvu^{-1}v^{-1}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The forward implication fails for no nontrivial $w$: if $w\ne1$, the
four syllables $w,t^k,w^{-1},t^{-k}$ are all nontrivial and alternate
between the two free factors. Their free-product normal form is nonempty.
The reverse implication is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform small commutators]
\label[lemma]{pqc:dr:lem:smallcomm}
For unit quaternions $p,q$,
\[
 |pqp^{-1}q^{-1}-1|\leq2|q-1|,
 \qquad \Frob{L(pqp^{-1}q^{-1})-I_4}\leq4|q-1|.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Right multiplication by $q$ preserves the Euclidean quaternion norm, so
\[
 |pqp^{-1}q^{-1}-1|=|pqp^{-1}-q|
 \leq|p(q-1)p^{-1}|+|q-1|=2|q-1|.
\]
From \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:leftmatrix}, each coordinate of a quaternion appears four
times up to sign, and hence $\Frob{L(z)}=2|z|$. Apply this to
$z=pqp^{-1}q^{-1}-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Local c.e.-completeness]
\label{pqc:dr:thm:local}
For every positive rational $\varepsilon$, there is a computable reduction
from $\WP(G_0)$ to exact membership in $\Gamma$ all of whose output
matrices satisfy $\Frob{M-I_4}<\varepsilon$. More generally, the same
holds with any rational center $C\in\SO(4)$ and any positive rational
radius $r$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The quaternion $q_t=\rho_d(t)$ has infinite order. Its powers are dense
in their circle, so there exists $k\geq1$ with
$|q_t^k-1|<\varepsilon/4$. This $k$ is computable by enumerating positive
integers and comparing the exact rational squared norm with
$(\varepsilon/4)^2$.
For an input word $w$ in the generators of $G_0$, output
\begin{equation}
 M_{w,\varepsilon}=L\bigl(\rho_d([w,t^k])\bigr).
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:localtarget}
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{pqc:dr:lem:smallcomm} gives the required bound uniformly in $w$.
Theorem~\ref{pqc:dr:thm:compiler} and Lemma~\ref{pqc:dr:lem:commtest} show
\[
 M_{w,\varepsilon}\in\Gamma
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad [w,t^k]=_G1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=_{G_0}1.
\]
Thus hardness survives inside any ball about the identity.

For a rational center $C$ and radius $r$, enumerate gate words until
finding $g\in\Gamma$ with $\Frob{g-C}<r/2$; density guarantees
termination. Use the preceding construction with $\varepsilon=r/2$
and output $gM_{w,r/2}$. Orthogonal invariance of the Frobenius norm gives
\[
 \Frob{gM_{w,r/2}-C}
 \leq\Frob{M_{w,r/2}-I_4}+\Frob{g-C}<r.
\]
Since $g\in\Gamma$, multiplication by $g$ preserves the membership
answer. The restricted language is c.e., because rational ball membership
is decidable and gate membership is c.e. Therefore it is c.e.-complete.
\end{proof}

For each fixed ball, the power $k$ and the translating word $g$ are fixed
constants independent of the hard input. The theorem asserts much more
than that yes-instances and no-instances are both dense: a full complete
family of instances can be placed inside the prescribed neighborhood.
It still makes no claim that physically indistinguishable targets can
be distinguished by finite-precision measurements.

\section{Approximation, exact separation, and the precision boundary}
\label{pqc:dr:sec:approx}
\srcmark{16}
\wtag\ The first subsection of source~16's section, on ordinary approximation,
is printed in the shared core (Section~\ref{pqc:gates:sec:density}).
% --- source 16, lines 906-1018 ---
\subsection{Exact rational separation}
\begin{theorem}[Length-height gap]
\label{pqc:dr:thm:gap}
Let $S_0,\ldots,S_{s-1}\in\Q^{4\times4}$ have a common positive
integer denominator $D$, with $S_0=I_4$. Let $M=T/q$, where $q>0$ is
an integer and $T$ is an integer matrix. For every word value $W$ of
length at most $n$,
\begin{equation}
 W\ne M\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \max_{i,j}|W_{ij}-M_{ij}|\geq\frac1{qD^n}.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:gap}
\end{equation}
The same lower bound holds for its Frobenius distance.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Pad the word with identity gates to length $n$. Since each $DS_j$
is integral, $W=A/D^n$ for an integer matrix $A$. If $W\ne M$,
some entry of $qA-D^nT$ is a nonzero integer. That entry has absolute
value at least one. Dividing by $qD^n$ proves the maximum-entry bound,
and the Frobenius norm is no smaller than that maximum.
\end{proof}

In particular, for the \emph{actual output length} $\len(W)$,
\begin{equation}
 \Frob{W-M}<\bigl(qD^{\len(W)}\bigr)^{-1}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad W=M.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:selfcert}
\end{equation}
This gives an exact boundary between two different specifications.
A requested tolerance $\varepsilon$ fixed \emph{before} searching is
always attainable. A tolerance required to shrink with the length of
the word \emph{that is returned}, at the rate in \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:selfcert},
is attainable exactly for synthesizable targets. Density says nothing
that removes this self-consistency requirement.

The strict inequality is essential to the statement as proved. The
bound is a rational-lattice separation estimate; no optimality for a
particular gate alphabet is asserted. Likewise the denominator $q$ need
not be minimal: a larger valid $q$ yields a smaller, still valid threshold.

\subsection{A simple exact length lower bound}
For the gates with $D=5^K$, the special target
$L(\rho_d(w))$ has denominator $5^{\ell_d(w)}$. Any exact synthesis
of length $n$ therefore obeys
\begin{equation}
 n\geq\left\lceil\frac{\ell_d(w)}K\right\rceil.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:elementarylower}
\end{equation}
This linear lower bound is elementary. The next section shows why no
computable upper bound in the same height parameter can work in the
complete example.

\section{A geometric synthesis-depth function of halting degree}
\label{pqc:dr:sec:depth}
\srcmark{16}

For the fixed complete group $\Gamma$ define $\lambda(M)$ to be the
least length of a gate word equal to $M$, for $M\in\Gamma$. Set
\begin{equation}
 E(h)=\max\{\lambda(M):M\in\Gamma,\ 5^hM\in\Z^{4\times4}\},
 \qquad h\in\N.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:E}
\end{equation}
The set is nonempty because it contains $I_4$. It is finite because
each entry of an orthogonal matrix has absolute value at most one;
there are at most $(2\cdot5^h+1)^{16}$ possible integer numerator arrays.
Thus $E(h)$ is a well-defined total nondecreasing function.

\begin{theorem}[Noncomputable exact depth]
\label{pqc:dr:thm:depth}
The function $E$ is lower semicomputable, has Turing degree
$\mathbf0'$, and has no total computable majorant. For every total
computable $f:\N\to\N$, the inequality $E(h)>f(h)$ holds for
infinitely many $h$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Enumerate all labeled gate words in increasing length. For each new
matrix of denominator dividing $5^h$, its first occurrence gives its
minimal length. The running maximum of these first-occurrence lengths
increases to $E(h)$, since there are only finitely many eligible matrices.
This proves lower semicomputability.

With a halting oracle, enumerate all integer numerator arrays bounded
by $5^h$, test orthogonality and determinant, and decide for each candidate
whether it belongs to $\Gamma$. The latter is a c.e. question, hence
decidable by that oracle. For the affirmative candidates, ordinary word
enumeration computes their minimal lengths. Taking the finite maximum
computes $E(h)$, so $E\leq_T\mathbf0'$.

Conversely, an oracle for $E$ decides $\WP(G)$. Given a source word $w$,
compute its target $L(\rho_d(w))$ and $h=\ell_d(w)$. Search all gate
words of length at most $E(h)$ for exact equality with that target.
If the target belongs to $\Gamma$, its minimal length is at most $E(h)$;
if it does not, no searched word equals it. By \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:reduction}
this decides the complete word problem, so $\mathbf0'\leq_T E$.

The same decision argument works with any computable majorant in place
of $E$, contradicting completeness. Finally, if some computable $f$
exceeded or equaled $E$ at all but finitely many arguments, those finitely
many exceptions could be absorbed in one fixed integer constant, producing
a total computable majorant. Therefore violations occur infinitely often.
\end{proof}

This is a precise bounded-geometry analogue of a busy-beaver phenomenon.
Every state lies on a fixed compact manifold, and every height-bounded
family of rational targets is finite; nevertheless the maximal minimum
exact description length cannot be bounded computably. The theorem does
\emph{not} prove that $E$ eventually dominates every computable function.
That stronger assertion is not needed and is not being claimed.

Together with Theorem~\ref{pqc:dr:thm:net}, it separates two tasks on the same
alphabet: a computable bound on the length required for any prescribed
approximation scale, and no computable bound on the length required for
exact synthesis at a prescribed rational height.

\section{Why this commuting-factor construction needs dimension four}
\label{pqc:dr:sec:dimension}
\srcmark{16}

\begin{theorem}[A mechanism-specific dimension obstruction]
\label{pqc:dr:thm:dimension}
There is no injective group homomorphism
$F_2\times F_2\to\OO(3)$. Hence the faithful real orthogonal
commuting-free-factor mechanism of this article has minimum dimension
four.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First suppose the target is $\SO(3)$. Let $a,b$ be free generators in
the first factor. Their images have infinite order, since an injective
map preserves the absence of nontrivial torsion. An infinite-order
rotation in $\SO(3)$ has an axis and an angle different from zero and
$\pi$. Its centralizer consists exactly of the rotations around that
same axis: a commuting orthogonal map must preserve its real fixed
axis and act compatibly with its nonreal conjugate eigenvalues on the
perpendicular plane.

The images of $a,b$ do not commute, so their axes differ. The intersection
of their two axial rotation groups is the identity. Every element of
the second factor must commute with both, and hence has trivial image.
This contradicts injectivity.

For an embedding into $\OO(3)$, take in each factor the subgroup generated
by the squares of its two free generators. Each such subgroup is free
of rank two, and the determinant of each of its image elements is
positive. Restricting the proposed embedding would therefore give an
embedding of $F_2\times F_2$ into $\SO(3)$, already excluded. Lower
orthogonal dimensions embed into $\OO(3)$ by adjoining identity blocks.
Lemma~\ref{pqc:dr:lem:spin} supplies an embedding in dimension four.
\end{proof}

This theorem does not decide arbitrary rational $\SO(3)$ subgroup or
semigroup membership. It also does not rule out an entirely different
computational encoding in dimension three. The lower bound is for a
faithful copy of two commuting nonabelian free factors. Broader
embedding classifications, such as the Lie-group study in
\cite{b62s16-CampagnoloKammeyer}, should be consulted before treating it as
a new general classification result.

\section{Explicit quartic certificates for finite executions}
\label{pqc:rr:sec:certificates}
\srcmark{11}

We now turn the substrate into Diophantine equations without hiding the
finite-execution construction inside MRDP. The construction applies to
\emph{any} fixed finite list of rational $4\times4$ gates, not just the
hard family. Orthogonality is needed only for the subsequent height bound.

Let the gates be $G_1,\ldots,G_k$, choose $D\geq1$ with
$A_j=DG_j\in M_4(\Z)$, and write the source and target as
\[
 x=u/d,\qquad y=v/e,\qquad u,v\in\Z^4,\quad d,e\in\Z_{>0}.
\]
Fix an external length $T\in\N$. Introduce integer variables
\[
 b_{tj}\ (0\leq t<T,\ 1\leq j\leq k),\qquad
 z_t\in\Z^4,\ h_t\in\Z\ (0\leq t\leq T).
\]
The scale variables avoid inserting the exponentially large coefficient
$D^T$ directly into an endpoint equation.

Define the following residuals:
\begin{align}
 h_0-d&=0,&z_{0,a}-u_a&=0 &&(1\leq a\leq4),\label{pqc:rr:eq:certinit}\\
 b_{tj}(b_{tj}-1)&=0,&\sum_{j=1}^k b_{tj}-1&=0,
     &&\label{pqc:rr:eq:certselector}\\
 h_{t+1}-Dh_t&=0,
 &&&&\label{pqc:rr:eq:certscale}\\
 z_{t+1,a}-\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{c=1}^4
       b_{tj}(A_j)_{ac}z_{t,c}&=0
 &&&&(1\leq a\leq4),\label{pqc:rr:eq:certstep}\\
 e z_{T,a}-h_T v_a&=0
 &&&&(1\leq a\leq4).\label{pqc:rr:eq:certend}
\end{align}
The step-indexed equations hold for $0\leq t<T$; the Boolean equations
hold for every selector in that range. Let $\mathcal C_T$ be the sum of
the squares of all left-hand sides.

\begin{theorem}[Exact finite-word quartic]\label{pqc:rr:thm:quartic}
The polynomial $\mathcal C_T$ has integer coefficients and total degree
at most four. Its integer zeros are in bijection with labelled gate
words of length exactly $T$ sending $x$ to $y$. It uses
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rr:eq:certcounts}
 (k+5)T+5\text{ variables},\qquad (k+6)T+9\text{ squared residuals}.
\end{equation}
For a fixed gate list its sum-of-squares description and its expanded
polynomial have size linear in $T$. With $k$ variable, the unexpanded
quadratic system has size $O(kT)$ and a direct expanded sum has
$O(k^2T)$ terms before collecting cancellations.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
All residuals have degree at most two. A sum of squares of integers is
zero precisely when every residual is zero, so the degree and exact
conjunction claims follow.

An integer root of $b(b-1)=0$ is $0$ or $1$. Together with the sum
constraint, this selects exactly one gate at each time. The initial and
scale equations uniquely force $h_t=dD^t$. The state equations uniquely
force the integer recurrence $z_{t+1}=A_{j_t}z_t$ and $z_0=u$.
Therefore
\[
 \frac{z_{t+1}}{h_{t+1}}
   =G_{j_t}\frac{z_t}{h_t}.
\]
The endpoint equations say exactly $z_T/h_T=v/e$. Conversely, any
labelled gate word that makes the transfer supplies these uniquely
specified selectors, scales and states. This proves the bijection,
including the case $T=0$.

There are $kT$ selectors, $4(T+1)$ state coordinates and $T+1$ scales.
The residual counts are five initially, $k+6$ per step and four at the
endpoint. Each quadratic step has $O(k)$ terms in the fixed dimension;
squaring it gives $O(k^2)$ terms. The remaining claims follow.
\end{proof}

The bijection is with \emph{labelled words}, not with distinct matrices
or distinct state trajectories. Different labels can represent identical
gates, and different control words can have the same product. No
canonicality of unbounded proofs is being inferred.

\begin{corollary}[Natural witnesses and height]\label[corollary]{pqc:rr:cor:natcert}
The fixed-length certificate can be converted to natural witnesses
without increasing its degree above four. For orthogonal gates and unit
source, every genuine integer trace satisfies
\[
 h_t=dD^t,\qquad \sum_{a=1}^4z_{t,a}^2=h_t^2,
 \qquad \abs{z_{t,a}}\leq dD^t.
\]
Consequently its witness coordinates have bit length
$O(\log d+T\log D)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Replace each signed state coordinate $z$ by $z^+-z^-$ with
$z^+,z^-\in\N$ and add the quadratic equation $z^+z^-=0$. This is the
unique disjoint-support decomposition of an integer. The selectors and
scales may themselves be taken natural: the equations already force
selectors to be Boolean and $h_t$ to be positive. Substitution preserves
the degree-two residual bound and hence the quartic sum-of-squares bound.
The displayed norm identity follows from orthogonality and
$z_t/h_t$ being the true unit state.
\end{proof}

This finite-length height estimate does not conflict with the
nonrecursive exact-transfer barrier: the missing quantity is a recursive
bound on \emph{which length $T$ must be tried}.

\section{The unbounded Diophantine representation}
\label{pqc:rr:sec:mrdp}
\srcmark{11}

Let $\mathcal O_\xi\subseteq\N$ be the set of canonical codes of rational
unit vectors in $\Gamma\xi$, rejecting invalid codes. Exact evaluation
of a finite rational gate word is computable, and enumerating words
semidecides this set. Thus $\mathcal O_\xi$ is computably enumerable.

\begin{theorem}[Fixed polynomial, and fixed quartic after lifting]
\label{pqc:rr:thm:MRDP}
There are a fixed integer $m$ and a fixed polynomial
$P\in\Z[n,w_1,\ldots,w_m]$ such that
\[
 n\in\mathcal O_\xi
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists w\in\N^m\ P(n,w)=0.
\]
With more fixed auxiliary variables, $P$ can be replaced by a polynomial
of total degree at most four. The same statements hold for the positive
indices in the hard recurrence family, with the convention at index zero
specified in Section~\ref{pqc:rr:sec:recurrence}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion is MRDP, applied to the described semidecider. It has
exactly the finite-natural-witness shape of the public ProveIt endpoint
\cite{b62s11-ProveItMRDP}.

For the quartic assertion, evaluate $P$ by a fixed arithmetic circuit.
Introduce an integer variable for each intermediate result. Each
addition gate gives a linear residual and each multiplication gate a
quadratic residual; require the output to be zero. Replace signed
intermediate variables by disjoint-support differences of natural
variables, as in Corollary~\ref{pqc:rr:cor:natcert}, and square and sum every
residual. The circuit is fixed independently of $n$, so the number of
new witnesses is fixed, and the resulting degree is at most four.
Finally, the recurrence-index language is computably enumerable by
generating $y_n$ exactly and using the same reachability semidecider.
\end{proof}

\subsection{What the two certificate levels do and do not say}

The quartic $\mathcal C_T$ is an explicit sparse family whose number of
variables grows with the externally fixed length $T$. The polynomial
in Theorem~\ref{pqc:rr:thm:MRDP} has a fixed number of variables and handles
unbounded lengths, but its coefficients are not expanded here. The
existence of universal quartic representations is classical; this
argument does not improve the variable or operation counts of the Jones
constructions documented in ProveIt \cite{b62s11-ProveItGuide}.

The unique trace attached to a \emph{chosen} bounded word does not imply
single-fold or finite-fold representation of the unbounded orbit set.
There can be many accepted words and arbitrarily many lengths. The
MRDP witnesses themselves are not asserted to be unique or finite in
number. Hence no finite-fold conjecture is settled by this construction.

Nonreachability from $\xi$ cannot have a natural Diophantine representation,
because such a representation would make it computably enumerable,
contrary to Section~\ref{pqc:rr:sec:bounds}. For the easy orbit of $e$, both
membership and nonmembership are decidable, so both are Diophantine by
MRDP after coding. This provides an arithmetic form of the two-orbit
separation.

All the Diophantine statements here quantify over integers or naturals.
Rational coordinates are supplied by finite integer encodings. Nothing
in the construction assumes a solution to Hilbert's tenth problem over
$\Q$ with unrestricted rational witnesses.

\section{Explicit parsimonious quartic certificates}
\label{pqc:dr:sec:certificates}
\srcmark{16}

\subsection{Natural variables without ambiguous signed encodings}
Fix any finite rational rotation alphabet
$\mathcal S=(S_0,\ldots,S_{s-1})$, with a common positive integer
denominator $D$, and let
\[
 B_j=DS_j\in\Z^{4\times4}.
\]
Write the target matrix as
\begin{equation}
 M=\frac{T}{q},\qquad q=Q+1,\qquad T=U-V,
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:targetparameters}
\end{equation}
where $Q$ and all entries of $U,V$ are natural-number \emph{input
parameters}. They need not be witnesses, and no uniqueness of the
input encoding is assumed. A canonical external encoding may choose
$U_{ik}=\max(T_{ik},0)$ and $V_{ik}=\max(-T_{ik},0)$.

For a horizon $n$, introduce the natural witnesses
\[
 e_{tj}\ (0\leq t<n,\ 0\leq j<s),\qquad
 d_t\ (1\leq t\leq n),\qquad
 Y_{t,ik}\ (1\leq t\leq n,\ 0\leq i,k<4).
\]
The initial quantities are constants, not witnesses:
\begin{equation}
 d_0=1,\qquad Y_{0,ik}=\delta_{ik}+1.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:initial}
\end{equation}
The intended meaning for a chosen word $j_0\cdots j_{n-1}$ is
\begin{equation}
 d_t=D^t,\quad W_t=S_{j_0}\cdots S_{j_{t-1}},\quad
 A_t=d_tW_t,\quad Y_{t,ik}=A_{t,ik}+d_t.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:meaning}
\end{equation}
Since $W_t$ is orthogonal, $-d_t\leq A_{t,ik}\leq d_t$, so all
$Y_{t,ik}$ are natural and at most $2d_t$. This shift avoids introducing
two unconstrained natural numbers for every signed entry.

\subsection{The full equations}
The selector equations are
\begin{align}
 e_{tj}(e_{tj}-1)&=0 &&(0\leq t<n,\ 0\leq j<s),\label{pqc:dr:eq:boolean}\\
 \sum_{j=0}^{s-1}e_{tj}-1&=0 &&(0\leq t<n).\label{pqc:dr:eq:onehot}
\end{align}
The scale and matrix recurrences are
\begin{align}
 d_{t+1}-Dd_t&=0,\label{pqc:dr:eq:scale}\\
 F_{t,ik}:=Y_{t+1,ik}-d_{t+1}
 -\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}e_{tj}\sum_{l=0}^3
 (Y_{t,il}-d_t)(B_j)_{lk}&=0.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:matrixrec}
\end{align}
Finally impose
\begin{equation}
 H_{ik}:=(Q+1)(Y_{n,ik}-d_n)-d_n(U_{ik}-V_{ik})=0.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:terminal}
\end{equation}
The factor $d_n$ multiplying the target numerator is indispensable:
$Y_n-d_n\mathbf1$ represents $D^nW_n$, not $W_n$ itself; here $\mathbf1$ is the all-ones matrix.
Equation~\eqref{pqc:dr:eq:terminal} is the cross-multiplied equality
$qA_n=d_nT$.

Define one polynomial by summing the squares:
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
 P_n(Q,U,V;e,d,Y)={}&
 \sum_{t=0}^{n-1}\left[
   \sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\bigl(e_{tj}(e_{tj}-1)\bigr)^2
   +\left(\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}e_{tj}-1\right)^2\right.\\[-2pt]
 &\hspace{5.5em}\left. +(d_{t+1}-Dd_t)^2
   +\sum_{i,k=0}^3F_{t,ik}^{\,2}\right]
   +\sum_{i,k=0}^3H_{ik}^{\,2}.
\end{split}
\label{pqc:dr:eq:quartic}
\end{equation}
All coefficients are integers. Every unsquared expression has total
degree at most two, including the input parameters. Thus
$\deg P_n\leq4$.

\begin{theorem}[Bijection with gate words]
\label{pqc:dr:thm:certificate}
For fixed input parameters $Q,U,V$, the natural zero set of $P_n$ is
in bijection with labeled words of length $n$ whose value is the target
matrix in \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:targetparameters}. For every labeled word there
is exactly one assignment to its selector, scale, and shifted-matrix
variables that can be a zero.

The number of witness variables is $n(s+17)$, and the number of
squared equations in \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:quartic} is $n(s+18)+16$.
In particular, each fixed input has at most $s^n$ natural zero tuples.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose first that a labeled word realizes $M$. Set its selectors to
one at the chosen label and zero elsewhere, and use \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:meaning}
for $d,Y$. These are natural witnesses by orthogonality. The one-hot
and scale equations hold by construction. The identity
\[
 A_{t+1}=A_tB_{j_t}
\]
gives \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:matrixrec}. The endpoint $W_n=T/q$ gives
$qA_n=d_nT$, proving \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:terminal}. Hence every squared summand
vanishes and $P_n=0$.

Conversely, a sum of squares of integers is zero only when each square
is zero. Equations~\eqref{pqc:dr:eq:boolean}--\eqref{pqc:dr:eq:onehot} specify
exactly one label $j_t$ at each time. The scale recurrence forces
$d_t=D^t$. Starting from \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:initial}, the matrix recurrence
then uniquely forces
\[
 Y_{t,ik}-d_t=(D^tW_t)_{ik}
\]
by induction on $t$. The terminal equations say $qD^nW_n=D^nT$.
Since $q>0$ and $D^n>0$, this is exactly $W_n=T/q$.
There are no unassigned slack variables, so the witnesses determined
by a label sequence are unique.

There are $ns$ selectors, $n$ scales, and $16n$ shifted entries.
At each of the $n$ steps there are $s$ Boolean equations, one one-hot
equation, one scale equation, and $16$ matrix equations. The $16$
terminal equations complete the count.
\end{proof}

The endpoint is not assumed in advance to be orthogonal. If the
parameters encode a nonrotation, the soundness argument proves that
no zero tuple exists. For $n=0$, there are no witnesses and
$P_0$ is the sum of the $16$ squares of
$(Q+1)\delta_{ik}-(U_{ik}-V_{ik})$; it vanishes exactly at $I_4$.
Identity padding makes existence at horizon $n$ equivalent to synthesis
in at most $n$ steps, but the bijection counts length-$n$ labeled words,
not equivalence classes under padding or cancellation.

\subsection{Size, multiplicity, and computational use}
At any zero, the maximum scale is $D^n$ and the maximum shifted entry
is at most $2D^n$. Thus the largest witness coordinate uses
$O(1+n\log D)$ bits. Summing over all times gives total witness bit
length
\[
 O\bigl(ns+n^2(1+\log D)\bigr).
\]
The recurrence equations have $O(ns)$ terms before squaring, in fixed
dimension. The displayed sum-of-squares circuit has linear size in $n$
for fixed alphabet; fully expanding each square still has linear size
in $n$ with a constant depending on $s$. This does not imply that
searching for a successful word is efficient.

The bijection is \emph{parsimonious}: the number of natural zeros equals
the number of successful labeled executions at the specified horizon.
It is not a unique-witness theorem for the target. Different words can
realize the same rotation, and repeated gate labels or cancellation
loops can increase the count. This distinction matters in comparisons
with single-fold and finite-fold Diophantine representations.

\section{Unbounded Diophantine representation and its limits}
\label{pqc:dr:sec:mrdp}
\srcmark{16}

\subsection{The repository interface}
Fix an effective natural-number code for rational $4\times4$ matrices,
with malformed codes rejected. Let
\[
 \mathcal E=\{z\in\N:z\text{ codes a member of }\Gamma\}.
\]
The set $\mathcal E$ is c.e. by exact word enumeration. ProveIt's public
interface has the mathematical shape
\begin{equation}
 S\text{ c.e.}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \exists k\in\N\ \exists P\in\Z[X,Z_1,\ldots,Z_k]\
 \forall x\in\N:\quad
 x\in S\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists z\in\N^k\ P(x,z)=0.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:mrdp}
\end{equation}
The guide identifies \code{Diophantine.mrdp} as a public endpoint,
together with \code{mrdp_iff} and \code{mrdp_dioph_iff}
in the same namespace
\cite{b62s16-ProveItMRDP}. Applying the mathematical theorem to $\mathcal E$
gives one fixed polynomial with a fixed number of witnesses.
This is an existence application, not an extraction of that polynomial
from a Lean term in the present work.

\subsection{A fixed quartic exists}
\begin{proposition}[Circuit degree reduction]
\label[proposition]{pqc:dr:prop:quadraticcircuit}
Every natural-witness integer-polynomial representation can be replaced
by one of total degree at most four, with additional natural witnesses.
For each original witness tuple, the extra circuit witnesses can be
chosen uniquely.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Evaluate the original polynomial by a fixed arithmetic circuit using
integer constants, additions, subtractions, and multiplications.
For every signed intermediate integer $v$, introduce two natural
variables $v^+,v^-$ with
\[
 v=v^+-v^-,\qquad v^+v^-=0.
\]
The second equation makes this representation canonical: exactly one
pair represents any specified integer. Express each circuit gate as
an equation on these differences. Addition and subtraction give linear
equations, and multiplication gives equations of degree at most two.
Require the final difference to be zero and sum the squares of all
gate, complementarity, and output equations.

The resulting polynomial has degree at most four. Circuit induction
shows that every satisfying assignment computes the original polynomial,
and that every original zero has exactly one extension by canonical
signed intermediate values. Thus the projection and the claimed
uniqueness of the extension are correct.
\end{proof}

Consequently $\mathcal E$ has a fixed quartic Diophantine representation.
No bound on its number of witnesses follows from this argument without
first specifying the MRDP polynomial and the chosen circuit. The direct
family $P_n$ and the unbounded polynomial are different objects:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
 &\text{Horizon-specific }P_n&\text{Unbounded MRDP polynomial}\\\hline
\text{Arity}&\text{grows linearly with }n&\text{fixed}\\
\text{Equations}&\text{printed in full as a scheme}&\text{not expanded here}\\
\text{Witness meaning}&\text{individual gate word and its trace}&\text{MRDP-dependent}\\
\text{Fiber size}&\text{at most }s^n&\text{not controlled here}
\end{array}
\]

\subsection{Why bounded canonicity does not settle finite-fold questions}
The trace at a specified horizon is canonical once the labels are fixed.
It does not follow that unbounded synthesis has one arithmetic witness,
or finitely many arithmetic witnesses, per target. Identity padding and
inverse pairs already produce infinitely many raw successful executions
for every synthesizable target. Replacing arbitrary executions by a
shortest execution still requires a separate arithmetic construction;
an MRDP representation of that selection process need not have controlled
auxiliary multiplicity.

There is a second logical pitfall. A computable many-one reduction
between c.e. sets preserves ordinary Diophantine representability through
MRDP. It does \emph{not}, by itself, supply a finite-fold representation
of the reduction's graph. Therefore c.e.-completeness of $\mathcal E$
should not be used here to claim equivalence with a general finite-fold
conjecture. Any such transfer requires an additional finite-multiplicity
argument. Proposition~\ref{pqc:dr:prop:quadraticcircuit} preserves multiplicity
\emph{after} an original representation is given; it does not create
finite-foldness that was absent or unproved before.

Finally, no fixed polynomial representing $\mathcal E$ can have a total
computable bound $f(x)$ guaranteeing that every affirmative input $x$
has some witness tuple with all coordinates at most $f(x)$. Such a
bound would allow finite exhaustive search and decide the complete set.
This is a witness-size obstruction, not a denial of the existence of
individual finite certificates.

\section{Executable examples, checks, and trust boundaries}
\label{pqc:rr:sec:implementation}
\srcmark{11}

The package contains \code{code/rotations.py} and \code{code/verify.py}.
They use only Python's standard library, exact integers and
\code{fractions.Fraction}. No floating-point approximation enters an
acceptance decision. The implementation includes the binary and
finite-rank quaternion decoders, the tensor lift reconstruction, the
presentation compiler, Miller normal forms, full rational-matrix
membership using that word algorithm, and finite quartic residual
construction and evaluation.

\subsection{A completely explicit small example}

For a reproducible example rather than an unprinted universal
presentation, take $Q=\pair{x\mid x^2}$. The padded Miller presentation is
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:rr:eq:toy}
\begin{split}
G=\langle z,q,x,t,u\mid {}&z,\;txt^{-1}x^{-1},\;uxu^{-1}x^{-1},\\
 &tqt^{-1}x^{-1}q^{-1}x,\;
 uqu^{-1}x^{-2}q^{-1}\rangle.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
The compiler produces twenty labelled gates. Let
$R=uqu^{-1}x^{-2}q^{-1}$ be the last relator. Starting from $\phi(q)$,
apply $C_u$ and then left multiplication by $\phi(R^{-1})$. The free
word identity
\[
 R^{-1}(uqu^{-1})=qx^2
\]
shows that the endpoint is exactly $\phi(qx^2)$. The checked coordinates
are
\begin{align*}
 \phi(q)&=\left(\frac35,0,-\frac{28}{125},\frac{96}{125}\right),\\
 \phi(qx^2)&=\left(\frac{147}{3125},\frac{2304}{3125},
                   -\frac{33044}{78125},-\frac{40992}{78125}\right).
\end{align*}
The actual least common denominator of this twenty-gate list, as
computed by the program, is $5^{20}=95367431640625$. The two-step
integer quartic uses 55 variables and 61 squared residuals. Its value
on the constructed witness is exactly zero. This example illustrates the
compiler and certificate; it is not itself the universal hard instance.

\end{lstlisting}

\section{Concrete implementation and finite verification}
\label{pqc:dr:sec:verification}
\srcmark{16}

\subsection{A fully instantiated, decidable example}
The supplied program \code{verify.py} uses only Python's standard
library, integer arithmetic, and \code{fractions.Fraction}. Its finite
presentation example is
\begin{equation}
 G_{\mathrm{ex}}=\pres{x,y,t}{xyx^{-1}y^{-1}}
 \simeq\Z^2*\Z.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:example}
\end{equation}
This example has decidable word problem. It is \emph{not} the universal
specialization of Section~\ref{pqc:dr:sec:universal}. Its purpose is to test the
same compiler and certificates on concrete matrices whose sizes remain
manageable.

The rank-three embedding gives the nine labels
\[
 I_4,\ A_x,A_y,A_t,R,\ A_x^{-1},A_y^{-1},A_t^{-1},R^{-1},
 \qquad R=L(\rho_3([x,y])).
\]
The least common denominator of these matrices is
\begin{equation}
 D=5^{14}=6\,103\,515\,625.
 \label{pqc:dr:eq:exampleD}
\end{equation}
The three positive diagonal gates have denominators $5^6,5^{10},5^{14}$,
and the relator gate has denominator $5^{10}$. Their transposes have
identical denominators. All numerator matrices are printed in the
machine-readable file \code{example_gates.json}.

For horizon two, the certificate has $52$ natural witnesses and $70$
squared equations. The word consisting of the relator gate followed by
the identity is a direct successful two-step example for target $R$.
The recurrence tests include every label sequence through horizon three,
not only this particular sequence.

\subsection{What was checked}
The accompanying run record \code{verification_results.json} reports:
\begin{center}

\toprule
Exact finite check & Cases\\
\midrule
All reduced $a,A,b,B$ words through length eight, including empty & $13\,121$\\
Norm, exact denominator, and full decoder on each such word & $13\,121$\\
Explicit quaternion nonmembers rejected by the decoder & $4$\\
Seeded Spin$(4)$ homomorphism, orthogonality, determinant tests & $100$\\
Valid example traces at horizons zero through three & $820$\\
Deliberately corrupted traces or targets rejected & $3\,277$\\

The $820$ successful trace checks equal $1+9+9^2+9^3$.
For each nonempty trace, the tests perturb a shifted matrix entry,
a scale, and a selected Boolean value separately; for every trace,
they perturb a target numerator. The sum-of-squares residual must become
positive. These tests catch, among other errors, a missing scale factor
in the terminal equation.

A locality illustration chooses $\varepsilon=1/5$. Enumerating powers
of $\rho_3(t)$ finds $k=61$ with
$|\rho_3(t)^{61}-1|<1/20$. The script verifies using exact squared norms
that the commutator target associated with $x$ lies within Frobenius
distance $1/5$ of the identity. This is a check of the quantitative
inequality, not a numerical proof of undecidability.

Finite tests cannot establish freeness for all lengths, density,

\section{A formalization route for ProveIt}
\label{pqc:dr:sec:lean}
\srcmark{16}

The proposed integration should expose small independent interfaces rather
than a single theorem whose computational and algebraic assumptions are
hard to audit. The repository already supplies the final MRDP endpoint;
the new work lies principally before that endpoint.

\paragraph{Layer 1: exact arithmetic.}
Formalize the quaternion multiplication table over $\Z$, $\Q$, and
$\mathrm{ZMod}\,5$, the map \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:sigma}, and the sixteen pairings
in \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:pairings}. A finite checked table plus an induction on
reduced words proves that the numerator residue never vanishes. This
is a compact starting target: it yields freeness, denominator growth,
and decoder correctness without computability theory.

\paragraph{Layer 2: group compiler.}
Formalize $\iota_d$, its reduced-block argument, the $\Phi$ action and
its kernel, and the generator characterization of $M_G$. The main
interface should state \eqref{pqc:dr:eq:reduction} for an arbitrary finite
presentation. Density is logically independent of the membership
reduction and should be in a separate module. That separation permits
the arithmetic application to proceed even before the Lie-theoretic
closure argument is available.

\paragraph{Layer 3: bounded polynomials.}
Define the one-hot selectors and the shifted integer recurrence. Prove
Theorem~\ref{pqc:dr:thm:certificate} first as a system of equations, then as a
single sum of squares. The exact endpoint must be
$qA_n=d_nT$, not $qA_n=T$. Record the witness count as part of the
interface, and use a datatype of labeled words so that duplicate gate
values cannot silently invalidate the counting theorem.

\paragraph{Layer 4: unbounded semantics.}
Give rational-matrix coding and the exact finite-word evaluator an
explicit computability proof. Its c.e. range may then be passed to
\code{Diophantine.mrdp}. The repository's guide describes a one-natural-input
interface, so multicoordinate matrices should be encoded before invoking
it; simply writing many free matrix variables does not automatically
match the existing theorem \cite{b62s16-ProveItMRDP}.

\paragraph{Layer 5: universality and local hardness.}
Treat the finitely presented complete group as an explicit imported
mathematical dependency until a concrete presentation and reduction have
been formalized. The local theorem needs only the free-product normal
form and a computable small-power search on a unit quaternion. State
that dependency plainly instead of inserting an untracked assumption
that ``the word problem is universal.''

These are proposed interfaces and proof tasks, not claims about code
already present in the pinned repository. In particular, the source
report of its MRDP audits should not be read as an audit of this article.

\section{Source 10 appendix: a complete eight-variable quartic for destructive interference}
\label{pqc:cc:app:quartic}

This appendix gives a small explicit equation, not just a compiler existence
statement. Let $u^+,u^-,v^+,v^-,\allowbreak w^+,w^-,z^+,z^-\in\N$ and write
$\Delta u=u^+-u^-$, with analogous notation for the other pairs. Define
\begin{align}
 P={}&(u^+u^-)^2+(\Delta u-1)^2
       +(v^+v^-)^2+(\Delta v-2\Delta u)^2\notag\\
    &+(w^+w^-)^2+(\Delta w)^2
       +(z^+z^-)^2+
          \bigl(\Delta z-(\Delta w)^2\bigr)^2+(\Delta z)^2.
\label{pqc:cc:eq:explicitquartic}
\end{align}
This polynomial has integer coefficients and degree four. Its nine squared
residuals describe
\[
 u=1,\qquad v=u+u=2,\qquad w=u-u=0,\qquad z=w^2=0,
\]
together with the assertion $z=0$. Here $v$ and $w$ are the two numerator
amplitudes of $HH\ket0$; $z/4$ is the output-1 probability.

Because every summand is a square of an integer, $P=0$ forces all nine
residuals to vanish. Successively applying the canonical-pair lemma gives the
unique solution
\begin{equation}
 (u^+,u^-,v^+,v^-,w^+,w^-,z^+,z^-)
   =(1,0,2,0,0,0,0,0).
\end{equation}
This is a fully explicit single-witness Diophantine certificate of the zero
probability, although it is intentionally specialized to a very small example.
It is not a universal polynomial or a claim about minimal variable count.

The delivered file \texttt{data/HH\_expanded\_quartic.json} contains the complete
33-monomial sparse expansion, all nine quadratic residuals, variable names,
and the witness. In that format a term is an integer coefficient and a list
of variable indices; repeated indices represent powers. The empty list is a
constant term. The independent checker verifies that the 33-term polynomial
is identically the sum of the nine residual squares.

\section{Source 10 appendix: proof-audit checklist and dependency ledger}
\label{pqc:cc:app:audit}

The following checks delimit the claims proved in this manuscript.

\begin{longtable}{@{}p{1.6in}p{4.6in}@{}}
\toprule
Potential gap & Resolution or explicit limitation\\
\midrule
\endhead
Unrestricted signed pairs & The equation $z^+z^-=0$ is imposed on every
integer wire; Lemma~\ref{pqc:cc:lem:canonical} proves uniqueness over $\N$.\\[0.5em]
Discarding interference & Both signed amplitude sums are retained inside a
complete contraction before taking a squared norm.\\[0.5em]
Wrong scalar domain & All existential coordinates are natural numbers;
negative integers occur only through differences and polynomial coefficients.\\[0.5em]
Hidden denominators & Hadamard factors are removed globally. The known
integer $2^h$, or $4^n$ for complete graph-state measurements, is retained
explicitly and counted in binary length.\\[0.5em]
A cubic guarded residual & Sign tests are unconditional; the branch-combining
equations themselves are quadratic. No Boolean is multiplied by a quadratic
equality as an extra guard.\\[0.5em]
Arithmetic-DAG height & The small-height theorem uses disjoint leaf subsets.
It is not asserted for unrestricted repeated squaring.\\[0.5em]
Tensor-width convention & The parameter is precisely $\max|A\cup B|$ of the
supplied merge tree. No equality with a different treewidth convention is
assumed.\\[0.5em]
A probability from one path & The $HH$ example explicitly rejects that
interpretation. The polynomial certifies the total numerator, including zero.\\[0.5em]
Uncounted adaptive logic & Branch rules are explicit finite descriptions.
Aggregating many transcripts may cost exponentially many terms unless a
separate causal compilation and width analysis is supplied.\\[0.5em]
Parameter representation & The one-gate obstruction uses Cauchy names,
not explicit rational numerators and denominators. Every name in the reduction
is uniformly valid.\\[0.5em]
Unbounded variable count & The direct finite compiler is not itself a
fixed-arity unbounded polynomial. MRDP is invoked separately for enumerable
positive-halting observations.\\[0.5em]
Single-fold MRDP claim & Canonical circuit evaluation supplies unique
auxiliaries only after the original MRDP witnesses are fixed. It does not
prove uniqueness of those witnesses.\\[0.5em]
Almost-sure versus possible & $\exists t\,[H_t>0]$ and
$\forall k\exists t\,[H_t>1-2^{-k}]$ are distinguished and separately analyzed.\\[0.5em]
Finite tests as proof & Tests check examples and implementation invariants.
General soundness, completeness, uniqueness, and height bounds are established
by the proofs in the text. No Lean build was performed.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

The only deep representation theorem used as a dependency is MRDP, and only
in Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:positivehalting}. The finite arithmetic compiler, tensor
counts, cyclotomic comparison, graph-state factorization, and explicit
reductions are proved directly. Universality, path-count representations,
low-width simulation, and the classical almost-sure-termination result are
cited as established context, not claimed as discoveries of this work.

\section{Source 11 appendix: a compact specification of the full compiler}
\label{pqc:rr:app:compiler}

Given a finite presentation $Q=\pair{Y\mid\mathcal R}$, the following
specifies the complete construction without an informal choice of
coordinates.

Order the padded Miller generators as
\[
 z,\ q,\ Y,\ \{\theta_y:y\in Y\},\
 \{\theta_R:R\in\mathcal R\}.
\]
Number them $x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1}$. Its relators are $z$ together with the
left side times the inverse of the right side of
\eqref{pqc:rr:eq:millerrels1}--\eqref{pqc:rr:eq:millerrels3}. Evaluate each $x_j$ as
$a^jba^{-j}$, taking the quaternions $a,b$ from
\eqref{pqc:rr:eq:alphabeta}. For every generator emit conjugation by its
quaternion. For every relator emit left multiplication by its evaluated
quaternion. Append the transposes of all emitted matrices. This order
agrees with \code{MillerMachine.presentation()} and
\code{Presentation.gates()} in the code, except that Python uses
one-based signed letters for group words and zero-based gate labels.

For $p=(p_0,p_1,p_2,p_3)$, left multiplication is
\[
 L(p)=\begin{pmatrix}
 p_0&-p_1&-p_2&-p_3\\
 p_1&p_0&-p_3&p_2\\
 p_2&p_3&p_0&-p_1\\
 p_3&-p_2&p_1&p_0
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The matrix of $v\mapsto v\bar q$ is
\[
 R(\bar q)=\begin{pmatrix}
 q_0&q_1&q_2&q_3\\
 -q_1&q_0&-q_3&q_2\\
 -q_2&q_3&q_0&-q_1\\
 -q_3&-q_2&q_1&q_0
 \end{pmatrix},
\]
so $\Phi(p,q)=L(p)R(\bar q)$. These formulas also make the integer
coefficient and denominator claims directly checkable.

The membership routine first recovers rational unit lifts, then decodes
both to free words, then applies the Miller word algorithm to their
quotient. The orbit-of-$e$ routine omits the lift step. A semidecider for
the orbit of $\xi$ simply enumerates chronological gate lists and tests
the resulting endpoint exactly. The finite certificate evaluator uses
the same chronological convention:
\[
 x_{t+1}=G_{j_t}x_t,
 \qquad x_T=G_{j_{T-1}}\cdots G_{j_0}x_0.
\]

\section{Conclusions of Part VI}
\label{pqc:conv:b62-VI:conclusions}
% --- source 10, lines 1500-1515 ---
\subsection{Source 10}

A legal path is the wrong witness for coherent acceptance. A canonical
arithmetic evaluation of the complete tensor contraction is the right one,
and it can be expressed using natural variables and a single polynomial of
degree at most four. The ring lift, exact comparison gadget, and resource
counts make this statement constructive for gate circuits and adaptive
graph-state branches.

The limits are equally informative. Width can force many coordinates even
when every coordinate is short; approximation names can make exact zero
non-enumerable even for individually rational gates; and almost-sure eventual
behavior requires a different quantifier pattern from positive-probability
halting. A Diophantine theory of unconventional computation should therefore
organize itself around \emph{effective observation semantics}, not merely
around a list of Turing-complete substrates.
% --- source 11, lines 1450-1468 ---
\subsection{Source 11}

The construction separates three notions that are easily conflated:
recognizing an entire rational transformation, finding one transformation
that satisfies a state constraint, and achieving a positive numerical
tolerance. A fixed family of reversible rational isometries can make the
first polynomial-time decidable, the second computably enumerable
complete, and the third uniformly attainable. Two small rational starting
states already distinguish an easy dense orbit from a hard dense orbit.
The hard queries can lie in a fixed fifth-order rational recurrence
family, and exact transfer requires no recursively bounded precision
budget even though candidate matrices are easy to recognize.

For the Diophantine program in ProveIt, this gives a concrete substrate
with an explicit finite-trace quartic compiler and a clearly delimited
MRDP endpoint. Its value is the proved separation and the inspectable
interfaces between group theory, rational dynamics, and arithmetic, not
a claim to have rediscovered rotation undecidability or solved an
unbounded witness-multiplicity conjecture.
% --- source 16, lines 1552-1573 ---
\subsection{Source 16}
The finite-presentation compiler gives a precise sense in which a compact,
norm-preserving, reversible system can carry full c.e. computational
complexity. The geometry does not expand; exact rational descriptions and
algebraic relations carry the complexity instead. The generated group
can be dense, and the hard instances can be localized arbitrarily close
to any rational rotation, while ordinary approximation remains a
terminating computational task.

The most concrete arithmetic results are the exact denominator theorem,
its residue decoder, and the explicit bounded quartic polynomial.
They expose information that an undifferentiated appeal to MRDP would
conceal: which word is represented, how its rational height grows,
where precision forces equality, and how many natural witnesses encode
a bounded execution. The classical foundations and the uninstantiated
universal constants are kept separate from those explicit constructions.

This provides a research and formalization path for ProveIt with clear
interfaces and testable claims. It also identifies the genuinely
unfinished parts: an optimized numerical universal alphabet, a certified
end-to-end implementation, historical novelty assessment, and stronger
unbounded witness control.

\subsection{Source 10: coherent computation}
\label{pqc:cc:sec:research}

The following are proposed projects rather than additional claimed results.
They are ordered roughly from immediately implementable proof infrastructure
to more substantial representation questions.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.},itemsep=0.7em]
\item \textbf{A verified canonical-wire backend.}
Formalize Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:wires} with an explicit evaluator, a polynomial
compiler, and a theorem giving the unique extension of every fixed input.
Prove the variable, degree, and sparse-size bounds as statements about the
compiler output. This is a small foundation reusable outside quantum
computation and does not depend on a formal theory of Hilbert spaces. \wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:kernel}.

\item \textbf{A formal finite-contraction interface.}
Represent boundary labels, disjoint leaf subsets, and supplied binary trees
so that \eqref{pqc:cc:eq:merge} and the identity of the two full semantics are proved
by finite-sum reindexing. The target is a machine-checked version of the height
argument for \emph{every scalar intermediate}, not only the final tensor.
A separately verified tree checker should reject missing or repeated leaves.

\item \textbf{Reduce the ring arithmetic constants.}
Search for lower-cost four-coordinate multiplication circuits, allowing a
tradeoff between integer products and additions. An improvement must be
measured after canonical wires are introduced; reducing multiplications alone
need not reduce the total number of natural variables. Preserve an explicit
bound on intermediate coefficient growth and prove every optimized circuit
identity exactly.

\item \textbf{Certified zero and sparsity elimination.}
The present implementation expends 28 scalar gates even on products involving
zero entries. A compiler could propagate known zero patterns, permutation
tensors, and shared phases before emitting residuals. Can one produce
schedule-sensitive sparse profile bounds while keeping a deterministic,
unique-witness evaluation trace? The optimization must be justified
syntactically, rather than using an unverified approximate zero test.

\item \textbf{Structure other than contraction width.}
Develop analogous certificate theorems for circuits decomposed into a small
number of tractable components, or with a small number of non-Clifford gates.
The objective is a transparent bound in the decomposition size, coefficient
heights, and verification cost. Such a theorem should explain explicitly how
it avoids the universal obstruction of Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:npconp}. \wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:frontend}, which Theorems~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:integer-tensor} and~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:npconp} partly answer.

\item \textbf{Coarse adaptive events without transcript enumeration.}
Build one network for an entire adaptive success predicate, including Boolean
angle circuits, outcome wires, and final acceptance logic. Determine the
additional width forced by causal dependencies. This would strengthen
Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:graphstate}, which certifies a fixed branch and deliberately
does not hide the cost of aggregating exponentially many branches.

\item \textbf{Canonical comparisons in larger fixed number fields.}
For a fixed ordered algebraic number field, can exact sign testing be compiled
with comparably explicit quadratic degree and single-witness bounds? A
candidate uses a proved root-isolation algorithm with a canonical choice of
interval and trace. Arbitrary existential isolating intervals would generally
reintroduce multiple witnesses; this is the issue to solve, not just the
existence of an order test. \wtag\ Compare Questions~\ref{pqc:q:operator} and~\ref{pqc:q:fields}.

\item \textbf{Exact channels and mixed-state programs.}
Extend the backend to explicitly described Kraus operators or superoperators,
with denominators cleared and conjugation handled algebraically. Separate the
certificate for a probability from the certificate that a supplied operation
is completely positive and trace preserving. Trusted finite gate alphabets
avoid that second obligation; arbitrary user-specified channels do not. \wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:fields}.

\item \textbf{Quantitative robustness under a supplied gap.}
For promised instances satisfying $|p-r|\ge\varepsilon$ with an explicit
rational $\varepsilon>0$, compare exact cyclotomic certificates with certified
interval evaluation. Determine which certificate dimensions and bit lengths
can be bounded in terms of $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ and network structure.
The promise must be supplied or separately certified; it cannot be inferred
uniformly from an arbitrary Cauchy name. \wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:promise}.

\item \textbf{Restricted unbounded canonical compression.}
Identify useful controller classes for which a fixed-arity Diophantine
representation retains a finite or unique witness property. Any proof must
control the witnesses introduced when coding an unbounded computation and
eliminating its time quantifier. Canonical finite traces alone are not such a
proof. This project should be stated with restrictions rather than assuming
the general finite-fold or single-fold MRDP conjectures. \wtag\ Compare Questions~\ref{pqc:qm:q:frontier} and~\ref{pqc:q:counting}.

\item \textbf{Representation-aware observational types.}
A substrate interface could distinguish exact algebraic descriptions,
computable approximation names, strict inequalities, exact equalities, and
limit assertions. Prove a classification theorem for a chosen program
language showing which interfaces yield enumerable observations and which
require alternating arithmetic quantifiers. Theorems~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:cauchy} and
\ref{pqc:cc:thm:ast} supply mandatory counterexamples to an overbroad design. \wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:algebra}.

\item \textbf{Proof-carrying compilation into the repository.}
Integrate the small backend with ProveIt's MRDP interface without confusing
the direct finite theorem with the unbounded existential consequence.
A useful deliverable would carry the source circuit, a checked contraction
tree, polynomial residuals, and a theorem connecting their evaluation.
Separate tests and axiom audits should record exactly which layers have been
verified and which remain mathematical specifications. \wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:direct}.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Sources 11 and 16: exact rational rotations}
\label{pqc:rr:sec:research}\label{pqc:dr:sec:future}
\emph{Source 11.}
% --- source 11, lines 1355-1358 ---
The following are concrete next questions arising from the construction.
They are not all asserted to be previously published open problems; in
particular, dimensional minimality and optimization would require a
broader literature audit before any priority claim.
\emph{Source 16.}
% --- source 16, lines 1456-1460 ---
The following are research directions arising from the construction.
They are not all claims of independently established open problems in
the literature. Where a status classification matters, it must be
checked for the exact formulation before a publication makes an
``open problem'' assertion.

\begin{question}[Minimal dimension; lower dimensions]
\label{pqc:rr:q:dimension}\label{pqc:dr:q:dimension}
\emph{Source 11 (``Minimal dimension under the full separation requirements'').}
% --- source 11, lines 1362-1370 ---
Can a fixed symmetric family in $\SO(3,\Q)$ have polynomial-time
rational-matrix membership but a computably enumerable complete rational
state orbit? The four-dimensional proof uses independent left and right
quaternion factors, so it does not descend automatically. The relevant
question is not merely an unrestricted rotation-semigroup problem: the
simultaneous membership, reversibility and fixed-source constraints are
part of the target statement. The historical three-dimensional problem
noted in the rotation literature should not be presumed to have remained
unchanged through 2026 without a dedicated survey.
\emph{Source 16 (``Explore lower dimensions without misusing the obstruction'').}
% --- source 16, lines 1510-1515 ---
Theorem~\ref{pqc:dr:thm:dimension} rules out the present product embedding in
$\OO(3)$. It leaves other mechanisms untouched. A targeted study should
separate fixed-subgroup membership, variable-generator semigroup
membership, point reachability, and matrix reachability in rational
three-dimensional rotations. These are different decision problems;
an answer for one cannot be transferred to another by terminology alone.
\wtag\ Compare Part~II's Question~\ref{pqc:q:instruments} (smaller rational
instruments), which concerns a different predicate.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[An expanded universal numerical example]
\label{pqc:rr:q:example}
% --- source 11, lines 1374-1381 ---
Choose a concrete finite presentation with an explicit halting reduction,
then run the Miller and rotation compilers to print every rational gate.
The present theorem specifies a terminating finite compiler and proves
existence of a suitable fixed input, but does not optimize or expand that
input. A useful artifact would include the source machine model, exact
presentation, reduction words, gate matrices, common denominator, and
independent proofs that all links commute. Equation~\eqref{pqc:rr:eq:gatecount}
provides a baseline against which smaller constructions can be measured.
\wtag\ Compare Questions~\ref{pqc:dr:q:instantiate} and~\ref{pqc:qm:q:compiler}.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[How low can the hard recurrence order be?]
\label{pqc:rr:q:order}
% --- source 11, lines 1385-1394 ---
The commutator construction gives five frequencies
$0,\pm2\theta,\pm4\theta$. Is there a fixed-source hard family generated
by an order-three recurrence, or by one rational matrix power applied to
a fixed vector, while retaining polynomial-time gate membership?
The order-five bound is not claimed sharp. A promising route is to
analyze whether a different recursively presented two-generator seed
can encode the required membership test with fewer alternating power
factors. Any proposed reduction must preserve both directions; an
arbitrary simplification of the commutator may destroy independence of
the defining relations.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Quantitative exact control and group geometry; exact-versus-approximate comparisons]
\label{pqc:rr:q:geometry}\label{pqc:dr:q:comparisons}
\emph{Source 11 (``Quantitative exact control and group geometry'').}
% --- source 11, lines 1398-1406 ---
The proof establishes nonrecursive worst-case precision, but does not
identify a precise comparison between minimal transfer denominator,
minimal conjugator length in $M(Q)$, and a geometric filling function for
$Q$. Gillis's quantitative study of Miller conjugators provides a useful
starting point \cite{b62s11-Gillis}. The arithmetic step is subtle: different
long products can have small endpoint denominators even though full
transfer matrices cannot be uniformly bounded. Sharp comparisons would
clarify exactly which group-geometric complexity is visible in the
rational control problem.
\emph{Source 16 (``Sharpen exact-versus-approximate quantitative comparisons'').}
% --- source 16, lines 1491-1498 ---
The computable net bound $B(k)$ is deliberately inefficient. A next
project could construct a practical approximation algorithm for the
specific compiler output, while tracking the relators on which its
constants depend. On the exact side, compare the depth function $E(h)$
with filling functions or subgroup distortion for the source presentation.
The present proof establishes its halting degree and lack of computable
majorants, but not an exact asymptotic correspondence with a chosen
geometric group invariant.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Effective approximation versus effective separation]
\label{pqc:rr:q:approx}
% --- source 11, lines 1410-1418 ---
The finite-net algorithm proves computability of $B(\eps)$, not an
attractive rate or practical synthesis method. One can study efficient
approximation using the explicit dense two-generator left subsystem.
A separate question is which additional promises make exact
nonreachability decidable: a supplied separation margin, restrictions on
the admissible target language, or bounded gate denominators could change
the problem substantially. Noise models must be specified precisely;
positive-tolerance reachability in the present system is always true,
whereas repeated adversarial perturbations define a different semantics.
\wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:promise}, which source~16 partly answers.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Other denominator primes and residue automata]
\label{pqc:rr:q:primes}\label{pqc:dr:q:residue}
\emph{Source 11 (``Other denominator primes and local decoders'').}
% --- source 11, lines 1422-1428 ---
The modulo-five proof turns a valuation into a syntactic length
certificate. Which pairs of rational unit quaternions admit comparable
single-prime decoders? One could seek a classification in terms of the
image and kernel lines of numerator matrices over $\F_p$, together with
an exact cancellation criterion over higher powers of $p$. A successful
generalization would yield new arithmetic compiler families rather than
merely another invocation of abstract free-subgroup existence.
\emph{Source 16 (``Develop other residue automata'').}
% --- source 16, lines 1482-1488 ---
For which rational unit-quaternion generating sets does reduction modulo
a prime give rank-one matrices whose zero pairings correspond exactly to
inverse letters? Such a criterion could generate families of exact
denominator encodings and permit optimization over primes and
Pythagorean data. One should distinguish freeness, exact denominator
growth, and deterministic first-letter recovery: none is automatically
equivalent to the others for a different generator family.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[A modular Lean development]
\label{pqc:rr:q:lean}
% --- source 11, lines 1432-1448 ---
A manageable formalization can be divided into four dependency layers.
First, formalize rational quaternion arithmetic, the modulo-five matrix
isomorphism, denominator rigidity, and soundness and completeness of the
decoder. Second, formalize fiber-product generation and the
orbit--conjugacy identity at the group level, keeping these proofs
independent of analytic density. Third, verify the signed trace compiler
and the quartic zero-set equivalence, including length zero, duplicate
gate labels, common-denominator normalization, and natural signed
witnesses. Fourth, connect the exact evaluator's semidecider to
\code{Diophantine.mrdp}.

The existence of a finite presentation with complete word problem and
the density argument can be tracked as separate dependencies until their
own formalizations are available. This avoids contaminating the elementary
arithmetic checker with unproved global claims. The most useful early
milestone would be a kernel-checked theorem that every emitted finite
certificate is equivalent to the actual rational execution relation.
\wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:dr:q:decoder}, Section~\ref{pqc:dr:sec:lean} and
Question~\ref{pqc:q:kernel}.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Instantiate a compact complete source presentation]
\label{pqc:dr:q:instantiate}
% --- source 16, lines 1463-1470 ---
The most valuable completion is a concrete, independently checked finite
presentation $G_0$, fixed words giving a many-one reduction from a chosen
halting language, and the resulting numerical gate matrices. This would
replace the existential specialization by a fully enumerated universal
alphabet. The optimization objectives should be recorded separately:
number of generators, number and total length of relators, expanded
$a,b$ lengths, denominator exponent $K$, and total bit size of the gates.
Reducing one does not necessarily reduce the others.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Verify the denominator decoder first]
\label{pqc:dr:q:decoder}
% --- source 16, lines 1473-1479 ---
The modulo-$5$ proof is finite enough to be an attractive Lean entry
point. A useful deliverable is not merely injectivity but a verified
executable decoder with a bit-complexity analysis. The integer peeling
step uses multiplication by a fixed numerator and division by $25$;
a careful implementation should avoid repeated general rational
normalization. This would yield an efficient certified ambient word
representation for later constructions.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Classify length-dependent precision specifications]
\label{pqc:dr:q:precision}
% --- source 16, lines 1501-1507 ---
The threshold $(qD^n)^{-1}$ forces equality. What can be proved for larger
thresholds $\tau(q,n)$? The right formulation must specify the norm,
the actual output length, padding rules, and whether $q$ is canonical.
Since padding changes $n$ without changing the matrix, such choices can
alter the search problem. A classification of specifications between
fixed tolerance and exact forcing would be more informative than a
single undecidability example.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Remove unrestricted inverse access]
\label{pqc:dr:q:inverse}
% --- source 16, lines 1518-1523 ---
The compiler currently supplies every inverse as an available gate. For
an application with only a one-sided semigroup, an encoding would need
to simulate inverse use or modify the source computation. Compactness
makes inverse approximation easy, but inverse approximation is not an
exact inverse word. That distinction is precisely the kind of gap the
current article exposes and should not be hidden in a semigroup variant.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Build a fixed-arity arithmetic compiler with trace semantics]
\label{pqc:dr:q:fixedarity}
% --- source 16, lines 1526-1532 ---
The bounded quartic family is transparent but has horizon-dependent
arity. A direct fixed-arity compiler should retain a formally proved
relationship between arithmetic witnesses and encoded gate traces,
with explicit bounds on degree, variables, and coefficient complexity.
The repository's bounded-quantifier and trace infrastructure may be a
useful starting point, but importing MRDP as a black box does not
supply these quantitative guarantees.
\wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:qm:q:frontier}.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Investigate finite-foldness with the missing hypotheses visible]
\label{pqc:dr:q:finitefold}
% --- source 16, lines 1535-1541 ---
A controlled arithmetic representation of a canonical successful
execution would be significant. The critical issue is auxiliary
multiplicity, not merely uniqueness of the abstract execution code.
A serious attempt should identify exactly which trace-coding,
bounded-minimality, or computable-reduction graph needs a finite-fold
representation. The parsimonious bounded theorem is a test case, not a
solution to the general unbounded problem.
\wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:counting} and the restricted-class question
of the sibling report \code{canonical-diophantine-certificates}.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Study robust operational questions rather than ideal equality]
\label{pqc:dr:q:robust}
% --- source 16, lines 1544-1550 ---
Because exact yes- and no-instances are both dense, a finite-precision
experiment cannot decide arbitrary exact membership uniformly. More
operational questions might promise a known separation margin, bound
gate length, restrict denominators, or ask for a certified residual.
The separation theorem immediately gives sound certificates under
some such promises. A useful next step is to classify which promises
restore decidability without making the model trivial.
\wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:promise}.
\end{question}

\part{Exact observation in continuous-state dynamics: strict contractions and neural precision (sources 14, 12 and 15)}
\label{pqc:part:b62-VII}

\section{\wtag\ Conventions of Part VII}
\label{pqc:conv:b62-VII}

Part~VII prints three manuscripts of batch~62 in full. Source~14,
\emph{Strict Contractions with Diophantine-Complete Transients} (batch-62
manuscript~11), builds a fixed rational continuous piecewise-linear
$1/2$-contraction of $\R^4$ whose exact half-space reachability is
$\sigone$-complete while point-to-point reachability is decidable. Source~12,
\emph{Exact Diophantine Computation in Contracting $2$-adic Dynamics}
(batch-62 manuscript~08), builds a $1/2$-contraction of $\Ztwo$ whose exact
extinction is $\sigone$-complete while every finite-quotient observation is
decidable. Source~15, \emph{Precision Is Memory} (batch-62 manuscript~12), gives
unique-witness certificates for exact rational saturated-linear networks and
shows that rational synthesis for a class of such networks is equivalent to
Hilbert's tenth problem over~$\Q$. All three carry Part~III's contrast between
exact and robust observation into regimes that Part~III does not treat: global
contractions, a non-Archimedean state space, and exact rational precision.
Sources~14 and~15 were written from the pin \code{526c2557f}, the parent of the
commit that completed Parts~I--IV, and source~12 from \code{b6bf6406a}; none
cites Parts~I--IV.

Sources~14 and~12 reach one phenomenon by independent routes, and both are
printed in full; their comparison, term by term, is
Section~\ref{pqc:contr:sec:overlap}. Source~14's Corollary~\ref{pqc:sc:cor:gap}
re-derives, for its own map, Part~III's Theorem~\ref{pqc:cb:thm:no-gap}; it is
cited there. Source~14's explicit ReLU gate count
(Proposition~\ref{pqc:sc:prop:gates}) and source~15's trace quadratic
(Theorem~\ref{pqc:pm:thm:trace}) bear on Part~III's
Question~\ref{pqc:cb:q:neural} without answering it: neither extracts the
network of Corollary~\ref{pqc:cb:cor:relu}.

\subsection{Letters used differently}
\label{pqc:conv:b62-VII:letters}
One table covers the three sources and Part~III, since sources~14 and~12 are
compared symbol by symbol in Section~\ref{pqc:contr:sec:overlap}.

The tempting false readings are these. Part~III's $\mathsf{Hit}$ and
$\mathsf{Safe}$ are \emph{noisy} reachability and robust avoidance; source~14's
half-space predicates are \emph{exact} and are written $\HitEx$ and $\SafeEx$
here. A zero of source~14's peak function $\Peak$ and a zero of Part~III's
radius $\rho$ are different events: the first is exact non-arrival at an open
half-space, the second is noise-fragility. Source~12's $H$ is a time or a set of
$2$-adic integers, never a target box. Source~15's $H$ is a height and its
$\sigma$ is the clip, not a ReLU.

\subsection{Renamed symbols and macros}
\begin{itemize}
\item Source~14 defines its ReLU macro as $\rho$ and writes $\rho(a)=\max(a,0)$.
Since $\rho$ is Part~III's critical radius, the ReLU is printed $\ReLU(a)$
throughout source~14. Its exact half-space predicates are printed $\HitEx$ and
$\SafeEx$ (source: $\mathsf{Hit}$, $\mathsf{Safe}$).
\item Source~12's set $\{0,1\}$ and indicator macros are replaced by this
report's, with identical output. Its equation~\eqref{pqc:ad:eq:Req} is printed
with $R_{\mathrm{eq}}$: the source lost a backslash there and typeset
$R_{meq}$ (its later use has $R_{\mathrm{eq}}$).
\item Source~15's network macro $\mathcal N$ is renamed internally; its
unused norm macro is dropped. Nothing printed changes.
\item File names printed inside the sources' text are their delivered names;
the shipped names carry the prefixes \code{14-strict-contractions-},
\code{12-twoadic-contraction-} and \code{15-neural-precision-}, mapped in the
README.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Abstracts and status statements of the sources}
\paragraph{Abstract of source 14.}
% --- source 14, lines 55-80 ---
An effectively known attracting fixed point does not make exact finite-time
observations decidable. We give a complete compiler from deterministic
two-counter programs to rational, continuous, positively homogeneous
piecewise-linear maps $F:\R^4\to\R^4$ satisfying
$\norm{F(x)-F(y)}\le\frac12\norm{x-y}$. Every orbit converges to zero,
yet for one fixed compiled map, reaching one fixed rational open half-space
from a rational initial point is computably enumerable complete. In contrast,
point-to-point reachability for every map produced by the compiler is decidable.

The construction yields a uniformly computable Lipschitz peak-value function
that maps every rational point of a compact rational polytope to a rational
number. Its zero test on rational points is nevertheless undecidable.
Every strictly positive rational threshold is decidable, and the function is
locally piecewise affine on its positive locus. The distinction is therefore
not between computable and noncomputable real values, but between effective
approximation and exact zero recognition.

We also compile the integer-scaled dynamics into a zero-bias integer ReLU
circuit. A horizon-$T$ first-hit trace has a unique natural-number certificate
for one polynomial of degree at most four, with explicitly counted variables.
For a three-state example, the supplied implementation exports an actual
2,105-term quartic with 400 witnesses. Unbounded reachability is connected to
the ProveIt MRDP interface, with the fixed-horizon uniqueness claim kept
separate from any unbounded finite-fold assertion. All new mathematical claims
are proved in the text; exact-arithmetic tests and a reproducible compiler are
included. Historical priority for the combined results is not asserted.
Source~14's status statement is its Section~\ref{pqc:sc:sec:intro},
subsection ``Status and relationship to prior work''.
\paragraph{Abstract of source 12.}
% --- source 12, lines 68-94 ---
We construct, from every deterministic binary Turing machine, a computable map
$F\colon\Ztwo\to\Ztwo$ that contracts all distances by at least a factor of
$1/2$, has the unique fixed point $0$, and simulates the machine through the
odd part of each nonzero iterate. For a fixed universal machine, exact
finite-time extinction on natural-number inputs is recursively enumerable
complete, although every orbit enters the ball $2^k\Ztwo$ within an explicit
linear bound in $k$.

The construction is realized by a finite synchronous binary transducer,
not merely an infinite-state Lipschitz machine. More generally, its radial
clock may be replaced by any computable $h(t)\ge t+K$ without changing the
extinction set or extinction times. Within this family, finite-state
realizability is equivalent to eventual periodicity of $h(t)-t$. Arbitrarily
fast prescribed convergence and infinite-order asymptotic flatness at zero
are compatible with the same undecidable exact predicate.

A complementary rigidity theorem proves that a scalar $p$-adic contraction
analytic near its fixed point has a uniform finite extinction horizon. For
rational polynomials we give an explicit horizon and a finite bound on the
extinction basin. Finally, we connect the construction to ProveIt's MRDP
interface and give an executable, clock-independent bounded-run compiler:
its sum-of-squares quartic has a unique natural witness, with explicit linear
counts of variables and equations. The accompanying implementation passes
