121,822 deterministic finite checks. The unbounded representation is an
MRDP consequence; the bounded unique-witness construction does not establish
a fixed-arity single-fold MRDP theorem. The results below have mathematical
proofs, but have not been Lean-verified or independently priority-verified.
\paragraph{Repository basis of source 12.}
% --- source 12, lines 99-104 ---
\textbf{Repository basis.} ProveIt, inspected at revision
\code{b6bf6406a4c49017fedc6fba068b36c634987150}.
The repository's MRDP theorem is inherited; the dynamical construction,
clock classification, rigidity arguments, and bounded compiler are developed
here. This is a research draft for mathematical review, not a claim of a
settled literature-priority breakthrough.
\paragraph{Abstract of source 15.}
% --- source 15, lines 71-90 ---
A bounded real state space can support universal computation when exact rational
precision is an unbounded resource. We develop explicit Diophantine interfaces
for this phenomenon in saturated-linear neural networks. A single natural-number
quadratic equation represents a prescribed $T$-step run of an $n$-neuron rational
network with exactly $4nT$ witnesses, all uniquely determined, including at the
saturation thresholds. A projective variant represents bounded-time reachability
from rational polyhedral input regions; real feasibility and rational feasibility
coincide, with an explicit denominator bound.

The corresponding rational parameter-synthesis problem behaves differently.
We prove that synthesis for a specified class of four-layer clipped networks,
with bounded rational tied weights and one strictly positive output, is
computably equivalent to Hilbert's tenth problem over $\Q$. An explicit
natural-number quartic certificate realizes that equivalence. In contrast,
wholly strict output requirements give a decidable rational synthesis problem.
Finally, we prove
prime-support-sensitive bounds relating first acceptance time to denominator
height, and show that a universal fixed rational network has no computable
precision ceiling valid for all accepting inputs. Complete proofs, exact
arithmetic implementations, examples, and a further research agenda are included.
\paragraph{Status statement of source 15.}
% --- source 15, lines 94-98 ---
\textbf{Status.} This is a research draft with proofs and executable checks, not a
refereed or Lean-certified result. Priority for the specific refinements has not
been established. Neural universality and complementarity representations are
credited to earlier work. The synthesis equivalence does not decide
$\mathrm{H10}(\Q)$.

% --- source 14, lines 88-1277 ---
\section{The result and the question it answers}\label{pqc:sc:sec:intro}
\srcmark{14}

A common reason to expect a dynamical system to be tractable is that it is a
strict contraction. There is a unique fixed point, convergence is effective,
and initial errors do not amplify. These facts do indeed solve many
approximation problems. They do not, by themselves, decide whether an orbit
crosses a particular boundary at some finite time.

The distinction can be expressed as a precise question:
\begin{quote}
Does a rational, globally contractive, finite piecewise-linear description,
together with an explicit exponential convergence rate, suffice to decide
exact half-space reachability from rational initial data?
\end{quote}
The answer is negative. Moreover, the same examples have a positive answer
for exact point-to-point reachability. The observation being requested is
as important as the rate of convergence.

\begin{theorem}[Combined result]\label{pqc:sc:thm:main}
There exist a fixed rational continuous piecewise-linear map
$F:\R^4\to\R^4$, an integer $B\ge8$, a compact rational polytope
\[
\Cone=\{(z_0,z_1,z_2,r):0\le z_i\le r\le1\},
\]
and an integer linear functional $\ell$ with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $F$ is positively homogeneous and globally $1/2$-Lipschitz in the
sup norm. It fixes zero and maps $\Cone$ into itself. On the unbounded cone
$\Cinf=\{0\le z_i\le r\}$, the last coordinate is divided by $B$ at every step.
\item On rational initial points, the question
$\exists t\in\N\,\ell(F^t(y))>0$ is $\Sigma^0_1$-complete.
The same statement holds for the closed half-space $\ell\ge0$.
\item Given arbitrary $y,z\in\Q^4$, whether $F^t(y)=z$ for some
$t\in\N$ is decidable.
\item The function
\[
\Peak(y)=\sup_{t\ge0}\max\{0,\ell(F^t(y))\},\qquad y\in\Cone,
\]
is uniformly computable and Lipschitz, and
$\Peak(\Cone\cap\Q^4)\subseteq\Q$. Its rational-input zero set is
$\Pi^0_1$-complete. Nevertheless, comparison with any strictly positive
rational threshold, using either $>$ or $\ge$, is decidable on rational inputs.
\item The restricted dynamical system $F|_{\Cone}$ has zero topological
entropy and exactly one invariant Borel probability measure, namely the
point mass at zero.
\item Bounded first-hit trajectories have canonical natural-number
quartic certificates. Unbounded half-space reachability has a fixed-arity
Diophantine representation, and hence one of degree at most four after
introducing arithmetic-circuit variables.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

The proofs are constructive at the level of a supplied counter program.
The fixed universal instance uses the classical existence of a universal
halting semidecider expressed as a two-counter program. We do not print a
numerically optimized universal instruction table, nor the coefficients of
the unbounded MRDP polynomial. We do print every formula needed to compile
any instruction table, and supply an executable bounded polynomial compiler.
These are different levels of explicitness.

\subsection{What is substantive here}

The useful strengthening is the conjunction of restrictions: four ambient
coordinates; one globally continuous rational piecewise-linear map; a strict
global Lipschitz bound; one attracting fixed point with an exact radial clock;
a single linear observation; decidable exact point reachability; and
Diophantine-complete region reachability. The peak-function theorem adds an
exact-arithmetic consequence that is not merely the statement that halting
can be translated into a polynomial.

The proof does not require chaotic dynamics, an undecidable limit, an
uncomputable coefficient, an oracle, a discontinuous state update, or an
infinite instruction table. It does require unbounded precision in exact
observations and initial encodings. Computation survives in coordinate
ratios while every absolute coordinate contracts.

\subsection{Status and relationship to prior work}

Moore established foundational examples of computation and undecidability in
dynamical systems~\cite{b62-moore1990}. Koiran, Cosnard, and Garzon developed
low-dimensional dynamical computation~\cite{b62s14-kcg}. Those results make it
inappropriate to present a generic piecewise-affine simulation of a counter
machine as a new discovery. The present report instead supplies the
contractive lift, the point/region separation, and the peak-value and
certificate consequences as a single explicit development.

The distinction between point and region queries is also important when
comparing with Varonka and Watanabe's work on Bellman operators. Their
reachability question asks whether an orbit reaches an exact rational target
point; they give positive results, including the two-dimensional Bellman
case~\cite{b62s14-bellman}. Our map is not claimed to be a Bellman operator of a
Markov decision process, and our undecidability result concerns a half-space,
not a point. Thus these conclusions do not conflict.

Zero entropy alone is not a novelty claim either. Bruera, Cardona, Miranda,
Peralta-Salas, and Salo explicitly construct universal Turing machines with
zero topological entropy, while proving positive-entropy criteria under
additional hypotheses~\cite{b62s14-entropy}. Our zero-entropy proof is elementary
because the ambient map is a contraction. Our decoding uses $z/r$ and does
not extend continuously to the cone apex; it is not a compact conjugacy to a
full symbolic universal machine.

This report proves its construction without relying on informal research
manuscripts in ProveIt. Its external mathematical inputs are classical
counter-machine universality and MRDP. The repository connection is the
actual finite-polynomial MRDP interface inspected at the pinned revision
specified below. The new development has not been checked by Lean or Rocq.
The finite Python checks are reproducibility evidence, not substitutes for
the proofs or for the two external theorems.

\section{Conventions and the repository boundary}\label{pqc:sc:sec:boundary}
\srcmark{14}

All natural numbers include zero. Integer polynomials are evaluated over
$\Z$, but their existential witnesses range over $\N$. A rational
piecewise-affine map is described by finitely many rational polyhedral pieces
and rational affine formulas agreeing on overlaps. The adjective
\emph{continuous} is essential. A piecewise-linear map in this report has
linear, zero-constant formulas on conic pieces. Norms and Lipschitz constants
are in the sup norm unless another norm is displayed.

A rational vector is supplied by finite integer numerator/positive-denominator
codes. Such codes can be canonicalized effectively. Completeness means
computable many-one completeness of the corresponding sets of codes. No
polynomial-time reduction is claimed. Iterates include $F^0=\mathrm{id}$, so
an initially accepting configuration has first-hit time zero.

\subsection{The precise MRDP interface used}

At repository revision
\begin{center}
\small\code{526c2557f2c6173054794f873a9624ebef616510},
\end{center}
\code{Diophantine.mrdp} states that for every computably enumerable
$S\subseteq\N$, there are $k\in\N$ and
$P\in\Z[X,W_0,\ldots,W_{k-1}]$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:mrdp}
 e\in S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists w\in\N^k\;P(e,w)=0.
\end{equation}
The source also exposes \code{Diophantine.mrdp_iff} and
\code{Diophantine.mrdp_dioph_iff}. The guide explicitly distinguishes this
existence theorem from a practical polynomial-generating algorithm or a
numerical degree/witness bound~\cite{b62s14-proveit-mrdp,b62s14-proveit-guide}.

This is exactly the interface needed for the unbounded result. The
fixed-horizon compiler below is independent of MRDP and actually exports its
polynomial. Accordingly, a successful bounded certificate run must not be
reported as a computation of the repository's unbounded universal polynomial.
Likewise, the repository's documented formal status is not a claim that its
entire development was rebuilt in the environment used for this report.

\subsection{A source machine with exactly the needed instructions}

A deterministic two-counter program has states $0,\ldots,n$, with $n\ge1$.
State $n$ is the unique halt state, made absorbing. Each other state has one
of the following instructions:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\operatorname{Inc}(i,k): & c_i\leftarrow c_i+1,\quad j\leftarrow k;\\
\operatorname{Dec}(i,k_0,k_+): &
\begin{cases}
 j\leftarrow k_0,&c_i=0,\\
 c_i\leftarrow c_i-1,\ j\leftarrow k_+,&c_i>0;
\end{cases}\\
\operatorname{Jump}(k):&j\leftarrow k.
\end{array}
\]
Here $i\in\{1,2\}$. The optional jump instruction only simplifies example
programs; universality does not depend on it.

Minsky's Theorem Ia uses exactly increment and conditional decrement
instructions and represents a partial recursive function with initial
counter values $(2^e,0)$~\cite[Theorem Ia, p.~449]{b62s14-minsky}.
Apply it to the partial function that returns zero exactly on a fixed
computably enumerable complete set $\mathcal K$. After relabelling states
and making the halt state absorbing, we obtain one fixed program $U$ with
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:universal}
 e\in\mathcal K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 U\text{ started at }(0,2^e,0)\text{ reaches its halt state}.
\end{equation}
This precise input convention avoids assuming that an arbitrary two-counter
program directly reads an ordinary binary Turing-machine tape.

\section{A general contractive lift}\label{pqc:sc:sec:general-lift}
\srcmark{14}

We first isolate the geometric mechanism from counter-machine syntax.
For $d\ge1$, write
\[
\Cinf^{(d)}=\{(z,r)\in\R^d\times\R: r\ge0,\ 0\le z_i\le r\},
\qquad
\Cone^{(d)}=\Cinf^{(d)}\cap\{r\le1\}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Homogeneous contractive lift]\label{pqc:sc:thm:lift}
Let $f:[0,1]^d\to[0,1]^d$ be a rational continuous piecewise-affine map.
One can effectively construct an integer $B\ge2$ and a rational continuous
piecewise-linear map $F:\R^{d+1}\to\R^{d+1}$ that is positively homogeneous,
globally $1/2$-Lipschitz, and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:general-simulation}
 F^t(rx,r)=rB^{-t}\bigl(f^t(x),1\bigr)
 \quad(x\in[0,1]^d,\ r\ge0,\ t\in\N).
\end{equation}
On rational inputs, point-to-point reachability for this $F$ is decidable.
Every rational polyhedral observation of $f^t(x)$ is transferred to a
homogeneous rational polyhedral observation of $F^t(x,1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Define on the cone
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:perspective}
 H(z,r)=\begin{cases}(r f(z/r),r),&r>0,\\0,&r=0.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
The value at $r=0$ is forced, since the cone then contains only the origin.
If $f(x)=A_a x+b_a$ on a rational polyhedron, its homogeneous lift has the
linear formula $(A_a z+b_a r,r)$ on the corresponding rational polyhedral
cone. These formulas agree on overlaps. Since $0\le r f(z/r)_i\le r$,
continuity at the apex follows too.

For each piece, form the $(d+1)$-dimensional linear matrix of this formula.
Let $M\ge1$ be the largest absolute row sum among all these matrices.
It is a computable rational bound. A line segment in the convex cone can be
subdivided into finitely many segments on which a single linear formula
applies. Summing the bounds on the subsegments gives
$\norm{H(u)-H(v)}\le M\norm{u-v}$. Agreement on boundaries handles
segments that lie in more than one piece.

Put $\ReLU(a)=\max(a,0)$ and define the retraction
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:retract}
 R(z,r)=\bigl(\min(\ReLU(z_1),\ReLU(r)),\ldots,
                 \min(\ReLU(z_d),\ReLU(r)),\ReLU(r)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Both minimum and maximum are nonexpansive in the sup norm on their input
pairs. Thus $R$ is $1$-Lipschitz, positively homogeneous, and the identity on
$\Cinf^{(d)}$. Choose an integer $B\ge2M$ and set
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:Fgeneral}F=B^{-1}H\circ R.\end{equation}
All asserted algebraic and metric properties follow. On the cone the last
coordinate becomes $r/B$, and positive homogeneity proves
\eqref{pqc:sc:eq:general-simulation} by induction.

For a rational inequality $a\cdot x\mathrel{\triangleleft}b$, where
$\triangleleft$ is any of $<,\le,=,\ge,>$, use
$a\cdot z\mathrel{\triangleleft}br$. For $r>0$ this preserves truth,
and finite Boolean combinations are preserved too. The point-reachability
algorithm is proved in \cref{pqc:sc:thm:point}, using only the radial identity just
established, so it applies to this general construction.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the lift preserves]
The lift preserves one-step dynamics in projective coordinates, not absolute
state coordinates. In particular, $x\mapsto(x,1)$ is not a conjugacy onto an
invariant slice: its image immediately moves to a smaller radial slice.
The projection $(z,r)\mapsto z/r$ is defined only for $r>0$ and is singular
at the common limit. This is why the construction is compatible with
strict contraction and with zero ambient topological entropy.
\end{remark}

The theorem is useful beyond the counter encoding below. Any explicitly
verified continuous piecewise-affine simulator on a cube can be used as its
input. The extra radial coordinate supplies both a shrinking scale and a
clock that makes exact target-point queries unusually simple.

\section{An explicit four-coordinate counter compiler}\label{pqc:sc:sec:compiler}
\srcmark{14}

Let $M$ have $m=n+1$ states. We now give all formulas directly, rather than
requiring a polyhedral decomposition to be generated first.

\subsection{Encoding, control hats, and local instruction maps}

For a configuration $q=(j,c_1,c_2)$, set
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:encoding}
 E(q)=\left(\frac{j}{n},2^{-c_1},2^{-c_2}\right),\qquad
 \Enc(q)=(E(q),1).
\end{equation}
A zero counter is represented by $1$, while every positive counter is
represented by a number at most $1/2$. There is therefore room to interpolate
continuously between the zero and nonzero tests.

For $(s,x_1,x_2)\in[0,1]^3$, define
\[
 g_j(s)=\ReLU(1-|ns-j|),\qquad 0\le j\le n.
\]
At a represented control state $s=j/n$, exactly one hat has value $1$ and
every other hat has value $0$.

To every instruction at state $j$, assign a local map
$\phi_j:[0,1]^3\to[0,1]^3$. For an increment of counter $i$ with destination
$k$, its control component is $k/n$, counter $i$ becomes $x_i/2$, and the
other counter is unchanged. For a jump to $k$, only the control component
changes. At the halt state, put $\phi_n=(1,x_1,x_2)$.

For a zero/decrement instruction on counter $i$, put
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:dec-cube}
 b_i=\ReLU(2x_i-1),\quad
 (\phi_j)_0=\frac{k_++(k_0-k_+)b_i}{n},\quad
 (\phi_j)_i=\min(2x_i,1),
\end{equation}
and leave the other counter coordinate unchanged. The control component is
between $k_+/n$ and $k_0/n$ because $0\le b_i\le1$.

Define the global cube map componentwise by
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:cubemap}
 f_a(s,x_1,x_2)=\max_{0\le j\le n}
               \min\bigl(g_j(s),(\phi_j)_a(s,x_1,x_2)\bigr),
 \qquad a=0,1,2.
\end{equation}
Using a maximum here, rather than a sum, keeps every component in $[0,1]$
even between encoded control slices.

\begin{lemma}[Exact cube simulation]\label[lemma]{pqc:sc:lem:cube}
The map $f$ is rational continuous piecewise affine, takes the cube to
itself, and satisfies $f(E(q))=E(Mq)$ for every configuration $q$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The formulas use only affine rational operations, absolute value, minimum,
and maximum, so they have the asserted regularity. All arguments of the
outer minima are nonnegative and at most one, proving cube invariance.
At $s=j/n$, the $j$th term of \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:cubemap} equals $\phi_j$ and all
other terms vanish. The increment rule is
$2^{-c_i}/2=2^{-(c_i+1)}$. If $c_i=0$, then $x_i=1$, $b_i=1$, and the
zero branch is taken while the counter remains $1$. If $c_i>0$, then
$x_i\le1/2$, $b_i=0$, and $2x_i=2^{-(c_i-1)}$. The jump and halt cases
are immediate. This checks every instruction and both decrement branches.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Division-free homogeneous formulas}

Write $Y=(z_0,z_1,z_2,r)\in\Cinf$. The homogeneous hats are
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:hats}
 \theta_j(Y)=\ReLU\bigl(r-|nz_0-jr|\bigr).
\end{equation}
Replace each cube local map by its homogeneous counterpart $V_j(Y)$.
The increment rule has $V_{j,0}=kr/n$, $V_{j,i}=z_i/2$, and the other
counter unchanged. A jump has control $kr/n$ and unchanged counters.
The halt rule is $V_n=(r,z_1,z_2)$.

For a decrement instruction, define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:dec-cone}
 b_i(Y)=\ReLU(2z_i-r),\qquad
 V_{j,0}=\frac{k_+r+(k_0-k_+)b_i(Y)}{n},\qquad
 V_{j,i}=\min(2z_i,r),
\end{equation}
again leaving the other counter unchanged. Set
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:H-explicit}
 H_a(Y)=\max_j\min(\theta_j(Y),V_{j,a}(Y))\quad(a=0,1,2),
 \qquad H_3(Y)=r.
\end{equation}
These formulas contain no division by the radial variable. On $r>0$ they
are precisely the homogeneous lift of \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:cubemap}; at $r=0$ they
vanish. On the cone, every first component lies between zero and $r$.

\begin{lemma}[An explicit global bound on the cone]\label[lemma]{pqc:sc:lem:L}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:constants}
 L=\max(2n+1,4),\qquad B=2L.
\end{equation}
Then $H$ is $L$-Lipschitz on $\Cinf$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For the scalar expression $nz_0-jr$, the absolute coefficient sum is $n+j$.
Absolute value and ReLU preserve a scalar Lipschitz bound. Adding the
outside $r$ in \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:hats} gives
$\Lip(\theta_j)\le n+j+1\le2n+1$.

Increment, jump, unchanged-counter, and halt components have bounds at most
one. For a decrement instruction, $\Lip(b_i)\le3$ and
\[
 \Lip(V_{j,0})\le\frac{k_+}{n}
      +3\frac{|k_0-k_+|}{n}\le4.
\]
The decremented counter has bound at most two, because
$\min(2z_i,r)$ is the minimum of two scalar functions with bounds two and
one. Finally, the minimum or maximum of finitely many scalar functions
with a common Lipschitz constant has that same bound. Apply this first to
the inner minima, then to the maxima in \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:H-explicit}. The radial
component has bound one.
\end{proof}

Use the retraction \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:retract} in dimension three and define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:explicit-F}
 F_M(Y)=\frac1B H(R(Y)).
\end{equation}
This is a finite rational continuous piecewise-linear formula on all of
$\R^4$, not merely on a set of legal encodings.

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative counter simulation]\label{pqc:sc:thm:counter}
The map $F_M$ is globally $1/2$-Lipschitz, positively homogeneous, and
satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:exact-simulation}
 F_M^t\bigl(r\Enc(q)\bigr)=rB^{-t}\Enc(M^tq)
 \qquad(r\ge0,\ t\in\N).
\end{equation}
It preserves $\Cinf$ and $\Cone$. On $\Cinf$, a point of radius $r$ has
norm $r$, and its image has radius and norm $r/B$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The retraction is $1$-Lipschitz and \cref{pqc:sc:lem:L} gives the required bound
$L/B=1/2$. Positive homogeneity follows from the zero-bias min/max/ReLU
formulas. On a legal encoding the retraction does nothing, so
\cref{pqc:sc:lem:cube} proves the one-step identity. Induction and homogeneity
prove \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:exact-simulation}. The inequalities $0\le H_a(Y)\le r$
and $H_3(Y)=r$ give the invariance and radial claims.
\end{proof}

\section{Undecidable regions and decidable points}\label{pqc:sc:sec:observations}
\srcmark{14}

Define the fixed integer linear observation
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:ell}
 \ell_M(z_0,z_1,z_2,r)=2nz_0-(2n-1)r,
 \qquad A_M=\{Y:\ell_M(Y)>0\}.
\end{equation}
On a legal configuration at positive radius,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:signal}
 \ell_M\bigl(r\Enc(j,c_1,c_2)\bigr)
       =\bigl(2j-(2n-1)\bigr)r.
\end{equation}
It equals $r$ at the halt state and is at most $-r$ at every other state.
There is no ambiguity on the boundary for legal finite-time configurations.

\begin{theorem}[Half-space reachability is complete]\label{pqc:sc:thm:halfspace}
For the fixed program $U$ in \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:universal}, the map $F=F_U$ and
half-space $A=A_U$ have $\Sigma^0_1$-complete rational-input reachability.
A specific computable family of rational inputs witnessing hardness is
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:hard-inputs}
 Y_e=\Enc(0,2^e,0)=\bigl(0,2^{-2^e},1,1\bigr).
\end{equation}
The analogous finite-time reachability question for $\ell_U\ge0$ is also
$\Sigma^0_1$-complete.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{pqc:sc:thm:counter} and \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:signal},
\[
 e\in\mathcal K
 \iff\exists t\;U^t(0,2^e,0)\text{ is halting}
 \iff\exists t\;\ell_U(F^t(Y_e))>0.
\]
The rational tuple \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:hard-inputs} is computable from $e$, which proves
hardness. Rational evaluation of a rational CPWL expression is effective.
Iterating and testing the strict rational inequality semidecides reaching
$A$ from any rational initial point. This gives the upper bound.

Along the hard input family, the radius is always positive at finite time
and \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:signal} never vanishes. Thus $\ell\ge0$ has the same answers
on this family. Its upper bound follows from exact rational non-strict
comparison. The fact that the closed half-space contains the limiting fixed
point does not mean it is reached in finite time.
\end{proof}

The denominator in \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:hard-inputs} has exponentially many bits in
$e$ itself. This is acceptable for computable many-one completeness but
precludes reading the proof as an efficient binary-input simulation theorem.
A different source encoding might improve this overhead; none is assumed.

\begin{theorem}[Point-to-point reachability]\label{pqc:sc:thm:point}
For every map obtained by \cref{pqc:sc:thm:lift}, and in particular for every
$F_M$, the relation
\[
 \{(y,z)\in\Q^{d+1}\times\Q^{d+1}:\exists t\in\N\ F^t(y)=z\}
\]
is decidable. From a nonzero cone point, a specified nonzero target point
can occur at most once.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Check $y=z$ first to handle time zero. Evaluate $y_1=F(y)$. Every point
from time one onward lies in the cone, so a target outside the cone can now
be rejected. If $y_1=0$, the only subsequent point is zero.

Otherwise let $r>0$ be the radial coordinate of $y_1$. The radius after
another $t$ steps is $rB^{-t}$. A target of radius zero cannot be reached.
For a target of radius $s>0$, success requires $s=rB^{-t}$. If $s>r$ reject.
Otherwise repeatedly divide the rational $r$ by $B$ until it is at most $s$.
This loop terminates because $s>0$. Strict inequality rules out success;
equality determines a unique candidate time. Evaluate that many iterates
exactly and compare the resulting rational vector with the target.

All exceptional cases were decidable, and all loops terminate. Strict
radial decrease also proves the uniqueness assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Targets separated from the apex]\label[proposition]{pqc:sc:prop:away}
Suppose $D$ has decidable rational membership and a supplied rational
$\delta>0$ such that $\norm{z}\ge\delta$ for every $z\in D$.
Reachability of $D$ from a rational point under a compiled map is decidable.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The global contraction bound gives
$\norm{F^t(y)}\le2^{-t}\norm{y}$. Choose $T$ effectively so that the
right side is less than $\delta$ for $t\ge T$, and test the finitely many
earlier points. On the cone one may replace $2^{-t}$ by $B^{-t}$.
\end{proof}

The undecidable half-space reaches all the way to the apex. There is no
positive separation constant to feed into \cref{pqc:sc:prop:away}.

\subsection{Asymptotic dynamics really are trivial}

\begin{proposition}\label[proposition]{pqc:sc:prop:trivial}
For a compiled map, zero is the only fixed point and the only periodic
point. On $\Cone$, topological entropy is zero and the only invariant Borel
probability measure is $\delta_0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Since $F(0)=0$, contraction gives $\norm{F^t(y)}\le2^{-t}\norm{y}$.
A fixed or periodic point must therefore be zero. For the entropy claim,
let $d_T(x,y)=\max_{0\le t<T}\norm{F^t(x)-F^t(y)}$ be the Bowen metric.
Contraction and the presence of $t=0$ give $d_T(x,y)=\norm{x-y}$.
Thus the maximum size of an $\varepsilon$-separated subset of the compact
polytope is bounded independently of $T$, and its exponential growth rate
is zero.

If $\mu$ is invariant and $h$ is continuous on $\Cone$, invariance yields
$\int h\,d\mu=\int h\circ F^t\,d\mu$. Uniform convergence of $F^t$ to zero
on $\Cone$ makes the right side tend to $h(0)$. Therefore integration
against $\mu$ agrees with integration against $\delta_0$ for every
continuous function, which identifies the measures.
\end{proof}

\section{A rational-valued computable function with an undecidable zero test}
\label{pqc:sc:sec:peak}
\srcmark{14}

Set $g(Y)=\ReLU(\ell_M(Y))$ and, on $\Cone$, define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:peak}
 \Peak(Y)=\sup_{t\ge0}g(F_M^t(Y)),\qquad
 \Peak_T(Y)=\max_{0\le t<T}g(F_M^t(Y))\quad(T\ge1).
\end{equation}
On the cone, $0\le g(Y)\le r$. This upper bound uses
$\ell_M(Y)\le2nr-(2n-1)r=r$, not the larger generic Lipschitz bound.

\begin{theorem}[Effective approximation and regularity]\label{pqc:sc:thm:peakregular}
For $Y\in\Cone$ of radius $r$ and every $T\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:peakerror}
 \Peak_T(Y)\le\Peak(Y)\le
       \max\{\Peak_T(Y),rB^{-T}\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $0\le\Peak-\Peak_T\le B^{-T}$ uniformly on $\Cone$.
The function $\Peak$ is uniformly computable, is $(4n-1)$-Lipschitz,
and takes rational values at every rational point of $\Cone$.
On its positive locus it is locally rational piecewise affine.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $t\ge T$, radial decay bounds $g(F^t(Y))$ by $rB^{-t}\le rB^{-T}$.
Taking the supremum proves \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:peakerror}. Each $\Peak_T$ is a finite
rational continuous piecewise-affine expression, so it is computable; the
explicit uniform error bound supplies a computable approximation algorithm
for $\Peak$ on computable real inputs.

The absolute coefficient sum of $\ell_M$ is $4n-1$. Consequently
$g\circ F^t$ has Lipschitz constant at most $(4n-1)2^{-t}$, and all these
functions have the common bound $4n-1$. Taking a supremum preserves this
bound: apply the individual inequality to every $t$ and then interchange
$x$ and $y$.

Now let $Y$ be rational. If the peak is zero, it is rational. If it is
positive, some rational iterate has a rational value $a=g(F^s(Y))>0$.
Choose $T>s$ such that $rB^{-T}<a$. Then the tail cannot exceed the finite
prefix maximum, and $\Peak(Y)=\Peak_T(Y)\in\Q$.

Finally let $\Peak(Y)>0$, without assuming $Y$ rational. Choose $T$ so that
$B^{-T}<\Peak(Y)/3$. The error bound gives
$\Peak_T(Y)>2\Peak(Y)/3$. By continuity, on a relative neighborhood of
$Y$ in $\Cone$, $\Peak_T$ remains greater than $B^{-T}$.
There the tail is smaller than the prefix and $\Peak=\Peak_T$.
This proves local rational piecewise affinity on the positive locus.
\end{proof}

The rationality proof is existential in its zero branch. It does not give a
total algorithm that recognizes when the peak is zero. On positive rational
inputs it does give a terminating exact algorithm: search for one positive
iterate, use it to bound the remaining tail, and take a finite maximum.

\begin{theorem}[A computable peak with undecidable exact recognition]
\label{pqc:sc:thm:peak-hard}
For $F_U$ and the inputs $Y_e$ in \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:hard-inputs}, let $\tau(e)$ be
the first halting time when it exists. Then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:haltingpeak}
 \Peak(Y_e)=\begin{cases}B^{-\tau(e)},&e\in\mathcal K,\\0,&e\notin\mathcal K.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
On rational points of $\Cone$, positivity of $\Peak$ is
$\Sigma^0_1$-complete and its zero test is $\Pi^0_1$-complete.
No total algorithm returns an exact rational numerator/denominator pair for
$\Peak(Y)$ for every rational $Y\in\Cone$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Before the first halt, \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:signal} is negative, so $g=0$.
At the halt and at every later time it equals the radius $B^{-t}$, because
the halt state is absorbing in the simulated configuration. The largest
positive value is therefore $B^{-\tau(e)}$. If no halt occurs all values
are zero. This proves \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:haltingpeak} and hardness.

For a rational point, a positive iterate semidecides positivity. Its
complement is exactly the zero set because $\Peak\ge0$, proving the upper
bounds as well. A hypothetical total exact-rational output algorithm could
be run on $Y_e$ and its numerator compared with zero, deciding
$\mathcal K$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Every positive rational threshold is decidable]
\label[proposition]{pqc:sc:prop:threshold}
Given rational $Y\in\Cone$ and rational $\varepsilon>0$, each of
$\Peak(Y)>\varepsilon$ and $\Peak(Y)\ge\varepsilon$ is decidable.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Choose $T\ge1$ such that $rB^{-T}<\varepsilon$. Every tail value is then
strictly below the threshold. Both questions reduce to the corresponding
comparison with the rational number $\Peak_T(Y)$. Equality at the threshold
is therefore handled exactly, not by an approximation convention.
\end{proof}

The restriction to rational initial data in this proposition matters.
Exact comparison of a finite piecewise-affine expression at an arbitrary
computable real input can itself require a nontrivial zero test.

\begin{corollary}[No computable positive separation bound]\label[corollary]{pqc:sc:cor:gap}
There is no total computable function $d:\N\to\Q_{>0}$ such that
$e\in\mathcal K$ implies $\Peak(Y_e)\ge d(e)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Such a function, followed by \cref{pqc:sc:prop:threshold} with
$\varepsilon=d(e)$, would decide $\mathcal K$.
\end{proof}
\wtag\ Cf.\ Theorem~\ref{pqc:cb:thm:no-gap} of Part~III, the same absence of a computable positive gap for the critical noise radius of Part~III's map, where infinitely many violations are also proved.

More precisely, there is no total computable function $h:\N\to\N$ such that
every positive peak in the hard family is at least
$2^{-h(\operatorname{length}(\mathrm{code}(Y_e)))}$.
Otherwise that expression would give the function forbidden by
\cref{pqc:sc:cor:gap}. In the formula $B^{-\tau}$, halting time has become signal
amplitude rather than distance from the fixed point.

\subsection{A value equation and its boundary condition}

\begin{proposition}\label[proposition]{pqc:sc:prop:value}
The peak is the unique continuous function $h:\Cone\to\R$ with $h(0)=0$
satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:value}
 h(Y)=\max\{g(Y),h(F(Y))\}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Splitting the supremum at time zero verifies the equation for $\Peak$.
Conversely, iterating \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:value} gives
\[
 h(Y)=\max\{\Peak_T(Y),h(F^T(Y))\}.
\]
Since $F^T(Y)\to0$ and $h$ is continuous with value zero there, the second
term tends to zero. The first tends to $\Peak(Y)\ge0$, so $h=\Peak$.
\end{proof}

Thus even a uniquely specified continuous value function with an effective
geometric approximation scheme can have an undecidable zero test on rational
arguments. The state transition is contractive; the max operator in
\eqref{pqc:sc:eq:value} is not being asserted to be a strict contraction in the
supremum norm on functions.

\section{An integer ReLU compiler for the shrinking dynamics}
\label{pqc:sc:sec:integer}
\srcmark{14}

The real orbit contracts, but its integer certificate need not become
smaller. We exploit a deterministic denominator convention to avoid
introducing arbitrary representations of rational numbers at every step.

Put
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:KD}
 K=2n,\qquad D=BK,\qquad S(Y)=K H(Y)\quad(Y\in\Cinf).
\end{equation}
On the cone, $S=D F_M$. We will express $S$ as a finite integer-coefficient
zero-bias ReLU circuit. A circuit here permits integer linear expressions in
the four inputs and earlier ReLU outputs, followed by ReLU gates; the final
outputs are integer linear expressions. No sign restriction is imposed on
weights, but ReLU outputs are nonnegative.

\subsection{Explicit integer formulas}

First compute $\theta_j$ from \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:hats} using integer linear forms and
ReLU. Its scaled version is $\widehat\theta_j=K\theta_j$.
For an increment instruction,
\[
 \widehat V_{j,0}=2kr,\qquad
 \widehat V_{j,i}=nz_i,\qquad
 \widehat V_{j,a}=Kz_a\quad(a\ne0,i).
\]
For a jump, use control $2kr$ and unchanged scaled counters.
For the halt, use $(Kr,Kz_1,Kz_2)$.
For a decrement instruction,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:int-dec}
 \widehat V_{j,0}=2k_+r+2(k_0-k_+)\ReLU(2z_i-r),\qquad
 \widehat V_{j,i}=K\min(2z_i,r),
\end{equation}
with the other scaled counter unchanged. Every coefficient is an integer.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:int-S}
 S_a(Y)=\max_j\min(\widehat\theta_j(Y),\widehat V_{j,a}(Y)),
 \qquad S_3(Y)=Kr.
\end{equation}
The equalities use positive homogeneity of minimum and maximum under
multiplication by the positive integer $K$.

The elementary identities
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:relu-identities}
 |a|=\ReLU(a)+\ReLU(-a),\quad
 \min(a,b)=a-\ReLU(a-b),\quad
 \max(a,b)=b+\ReLU(a-b)
\end{equation}
turn these formulas into the required integer ReLU circuit.

\begin{proposition}[Gate count]\label[proposition]{pqc:sc:prop:gates}
Let $d_M$ be the number of decrement instructions. The direct compiler in
\code{verify_contraction.py} uses exactly
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:gatecount}
 G=9m+2d_M-3\le11m-5
\end{equation}
ReLU gates for $S$. Its linear forms have bounded support and coefficients
with $O(\log m)$ bits.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For each of the $m$ control states, an absolute value uses two ReLU gates
and the outside positive part of the hat uses one, giving $3m$ gates.
Clipping each of three local components by its scaled hat uses $3m$ more.
Taking the componentwise maximum of the $m$ clipped vectors uses
$3(m-1)$ gates. A decrement instruction additionally uses one gate for its
zero-test bump and one for $\min(2z_i,r)$. This totals
$9m+2d_M-3$. There is one halt state, so $d_M\le m-1$.

The stated construction retains previous ReLU outputs as wires rather than
substituting their formulas recursively. Each local expression has bounded
support. In the running maximum, writing the new result as
$b+\ReLU(a-b)$ keeps the linear output support bounded as well. Coefficients
are bounded by a polynomial in $m$, which proves the bit bound.
\end{proof}

This is a circuit-size statement, not a claim that a full polyhedral
partition into all activation regions has only linearly many cells. The
partition can be much larger; the compiler does not enumerate it.

\wtag\ This is an explicit gate count for this source's contraction, not for Part~III's map~$F$: the extraction of the rational ReLU network of Corollary~\ref{pqc:cb:cor:relu} (Question~\ref{pqc:cb:q:neural}) is not answered by it.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical integer scaling]\label{pqc:sc:thm:scaling}
Let $Y_0=W_0/d_0\in\Cinf\cap\Q^4$ with $W_0\in\N^4$ and $d_0>0$.
Define the integer sequence $W_{t+1}=S(W_t)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:integer-orbit}
 F_M^t(Y_0)=\frac{W_t}{d_0D^t},\qquad
 (W_t)_3=K^t(W_0)_3.
\end{equation}
Every $W_t$ is a nonnegative integer cone point, and
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:integer-observation}
 \ell_M(F_M^t(Y_0))>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\ell_M(W_t)>0.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
All integer circuit operations preserve integrality. Since $S=K H$ and
$H$ preserves the cone, every output remains a nonnegative cone point.
The radial formula follows from $S_3=Kr$. If
$F^t(Y_0)=W_t/(d_0D^t)$, positive homogeneity gives
\[
 F^{t+1}(Y_0)=\frac{F(W_t)}{d_0D^t}
            =\frac{S(W_t)}{d_0D^{t+1}},
\]
which proves the orbit identity by induction. Finally, $\ell_M$ is linear
and the denominator is strictly positive, so it does not affect the sign.
\end{proof}

The denominator convention is intentionally not reduction to lowest terms
at every step. It is one fixed deterministic representation of the orbit.
Its benefit is that the certificate only needs integer circuit transitions;
no exponential Diophantine formula for $D^t$ is needed at a fixed horizon.

\section{Canonical quartic first-hit certificates}\label{pqc:sc:sec:quartics}
\srcmark{14}

The central local device is complementarity with natural variables.

\begin{lemma}[A unique ReLU witness]\label[lemma]{pqc:sc:lem:relucert}
For every $v\in\Z$, the equations
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:relu-certificate}
 y-z=v,\qquad yz=0,\qquad y,z\in\N
\end{equation}
have exactly one solution:
$(y,z)=(\ReLU(v),\ReLU(-v))$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $v>0$, the equation $y-z=v$ implies $y>0$, so $yz=0$ forces $z=0$ and
$y=v$. If $v<0$, the symmetric argument gives $y=0,z=-v$. If $v=0$,
then $y=z$ and $y^2=0$, so both are zero. Each displayed solution satisfies
the equations.
\end{proof}

The nonnegative domain is indispensable. Over unrestricted integers,
$y-z=v$ and $yz=0$ also permit the wrong-sign branch. A real-field certificate
would require explicit nonnegativity inequalities. Here it is built into
Diophantine witness quantification.

\subsection{The complete polynomial schema}

Number the ReLU gates of $S$ in topological order. At gate $a$ of step $t$,
let $v_{t,a}$ be its integer linear preactivation in $W_t$ and previous
positive gate outputs of the same step. Introduce natural variables
$y_{t,a},z_{t,a}$ and impose
\[
 E_{t,a}=y_{t,a}-z_{t,a}-v_{t,a}=0,
 \qquad J_{t,a}=y_{t,a}z_{t,a}=0.
\]
For each of the four outputs, impose the linear equation equating
$W_{t+1,i}$ to its circuit output expression; denote this residual by
$O_{t,i}$. These equations include the exact radial recurrence.

For a prescribed horizon $T\ge0$, add natural slacks $a,b_0,\ldots,b_{T-1}$
with
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:firsthit-slacks}
 \ell_M(W_T)-1-a=0,\qquad
 \ell_M(W_t)+b_t=0\quad(0\le t<T).
\end{equation}
They assert acceptance at time $T$ and nonacceptance at every earlier time.
The strict inequality at the final time is an integer inequality, hence
$\ell_M(W_T)>0$ is equivalent to $\ell_M(W_T)\ge1$.

Define the following one integer polynomial, presented as a finite sum of
squares rather than as a large expanded expression:
\begin{align}
 Q_{M,T}={}&\sum_{t<T}\sum_{a<G}
       \bigl(E_{t,a}^{\,2}+J_{t,a}^{\,2}\bigr)
       +\sum_{t<T}\sum_{i=0}^3 O_{t,i}^{\,2} \notag\\
 &+\bigl(\ell_M(W_T)-1-a\bigr)^2
       +\sum_{t<T}\bigl(\ell_M(W_t)+b_t\bigr)^2.
 \label{pqc:sc:eq:quartic}
\end{align}
Here $W_0$ is the free input tuple. The later $W_t$, the gate pairs, and the
slacks form the witness tuple. All linear preactivations remain linear in
these variables: gate formulas are not recursively substituted into them.

\begin{theorem}[Unique-witness bounded representation]\label{pqc:sc:thm:quartic}
Fix $M,T$ and an integer cone input $W_0$. The polynomial
$Q_{M,T}$ has degree at most four and has a natural witness exactly when
the orbit of $W_0$ under $S$ first satisfies $\ell_M>0$ at time $T$.
When a witness exists, it is unique. Its number of coordinates, and the
number of equations squared in \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:quartic}, are both
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:witnesscount}
 N_T=(2G+4)T+(T+1)=(2G+5)T+1.
\end{equation}
The sum-of-squares arithmetic description has $O(mT)$ size and
$O(mT\log m)$ coefficient-description length.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every $E_{t,a}$ and $O_{t,i}$ is linear and every $J_{t,a}$ is quadratic.
The slack equations are linear. Their squared sum therefore has degree at
most four. Since it is evaluated over integers, it vanishes if and only if
each squared residual is zero.

Given $W_t$, apply \cref{pqc:sc:lem:relucert} in topological order to each gate.
Every positive gate output and negative-part witness is forced uniquely.
The output equations then force exactly $W_{t+1}=S(W_t)$. Induction on $t$
forces the entire trace. The last equations force
$a=\ell_M(W_T)-1$ and $b_t=-\ell_M(W_t)$; these are natural exactly for
the stated first-hit condition. Thus soundness and uniqueness hold.
Conversely, an actual first-hit trace supplies all these forced natural
values and makes every residual zero, proving completeness.

There are $4T$ later-state variables, $2GT$ gate variables, and $T+1$
slacks. The equation count is the same: $4T$ output equations, $2GT$ gate
equations, and $T+1$ slack equations. The circuit bound in
\cref{pqc:sc:prop:gates}, with bounded-support linear forms, gives the size bounds.
When $T=0$, the schema reduces to one accepting slack and one squared
linear residual, so the edge case is included.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Other bounded specifications]
Omitting the earlier nonacceptance slacks represents acceptance at exactly
time $T$, with a unique witness. Prescribing an output tuple instead of
acceptance represents a bounded endpoint graph. For legal machine
encodings, absorbing halting makes acceptance by time $T$ equivalent to
acceptance at time $T$. That equivalence is not asserted for arbitrary
interpolated cone points.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Why this does not prove an unbounded single-fold theorem}

Although the first-hit time is unique when it exists, the number of
variables in \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:quartic} grows with $T$. One cannot replace the
family by a single fixed polynomial merely by writing ``$\exists T$''
in front of it: the displayed formula would then have variable arity.
Encoding a variable-length trace and eliminating its computational
predicates requires an additional representation theorem.

MRDP supplies that representation, but its auxiliary witnesses need not be
unique even when the simulated computation is deterministic. Our conclusion
is therefore a canonical finite-horizon quartic, together with a separate
fixed-arity unbounded representation. It is not a resolution of the
single-fold or finite-fold Diophantine representation problem.

\section{The unbounded Diophantine consequences}\label{pqc:sc:sec:unbounded}
\srcmark{14}

Fix an effective natural-number coding of rational cone points. Invalid
codes can be rejected decidably; this convention does not affect any
hardness assertion. For a fixed compiled program $M$, define
\[
 \HitEx_M(e)\iff\text{$e$ codes $Y\in\Cone\cap\Q^4$ and }
                     \exists t\;\ell_M(F_M^t(Y))>0.
\]

\begin{theorem}[The MRDP connection]\label{pqc:sc:thm:dioph}
For each fixed $M$, there are $k$ and an integer polynomial $P_M$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:hitmrdp}
 \HitEx_M(e)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists w\in\N^k\;P_M(e,w)=0.
\end{equation}
One may choose a representation of degree at most four after adding
finitely many natural witnesses. For $U$, the represented set is
$\Sigma^0_1$-complete. On the hard input family, the never-hit property
has no existential Diophantine representation over $\N$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Exact rational evaluation and enumeration of times semidecide $\HitEx_M$.
Apply \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:mrdp}, using the repository's finite-polynomial interface.
Completeness for $U$ was proved in \cref{pqc:sc:thm:halfspace}.

For the quartic degree reduction, write $P_M=P_+-P_-$, where $P_+$ and
$P_-$ have nonnegative integer coefficients. Compute the two polynomials
by finite addition/multiplication circuits on natural inputs, introducing
one natural variable for each intermediate result. Addition equations are
linear, multiplication equations quadratic, and the final equality is
linear. The sum of their squares has degree at most four. This familiar
circuit reduction adds unique intermediate values for each assignment of
the original MRDP witnesses; it does not make those original witnesses
unique.

If never hitting on the hard family had an existential integer-polynomial
representation with natural witnesses, enumeration of witness tuples and
exact polynomial evaluation would semidecide $\N\setminus\mathcal K$.
Together with the existing semidecider for $\mathcal K$, dovetailing would
decide $\mathcal K$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

The fixed quartic in this theorem is an existence result. The supplied
2,105-term polynomial is instead the explicit bounded example from
\cref{pqc:sc:sec:example}; the two polynomials must not be confused.

\subsection{Exact values, positive values, and approximation graphs}

The positive-value graph of $\Peak$ on rational cone points is computably
enumerable: enumerate until one positive iterate is found, bound the
remaining tail, and compute the exact rational maximum. Canonical rational
output coding then gives a semidecider for the positive graph, so MRDP
represents it as well.

The full exact-value graph, including output zero, is not computably
enumerable for $U$. If it were, restricting the output code to the rational
number zero would semidecide the complete co-enumerable zero set. This
contrasts with the graph of any fixed finite-precision approximation
algorithm, which is decidable on its integer codes and therefore
Diophantine. Effective real approximation, exact rational output, and exact
positivity are three different specifications even though every rational
input has a rational peak value.

\begin{corollary}[No complete enumerable safety-certificate system]
\label[corollary]{pqc:sc:cor:safety}
For $F_U$, there is no sound, complete, computably checkable system of finite
certificates establishing never hitting $A_U$ for all rational initial
points in the hard family.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Enumerating finite certificates and checking them would enumerate every
safe hard input, contradicting the non-enumerability of
$\N\setminus\mathcal K$.
\end{proof}

This is not a criticism of proof assistants or invariant methods. They can
verify particular safety arguments and be complete on restricted classes.
It is a limit on any claimed complete automatic method for this whole
family, even though convergence and the unique attractor are already known.

\section{Regularity, precision, and the limits of the construction}
\label{pqc:sc:sec:limits}
\srcmark{14}

\subsection{Smoothness at the apex is a real restriction}

\begin{proposition}[Homogeneous differentiability rigidity]\label[proposition]{pqc:sc:prop:rigid}
If $G:\R^d\to\R^d$ is positively homogeneous of degree one and Frechet
differentiable at zero, then $G$ is linear. If a polynomial map on all of
$\R^d$ is globally Lipschitz, it is affine; if it also fixes zero, it is
linear.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Positive homogeneity gives $G(0)=0$ and $G(tx)=tG(x)$ for every $t>0$.
Differentiability at zero implies
\[
 DG(0)x=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{G(tx)-G(0)}{t}=G(x),
\]
so $G$ agrees with a linear map everywhere.

For a globally Lipschitz polynomial map, every partial derivative is a
bounded polynomial: its absolute value is bounded by the global Lipschitz
constant using difference quotients along coordinate directions. A
nonconstant polynomial is unbounded on some line, as seen from a nonzero
highest-degree homogeneous part. Therefore every partial derivative is
constant, and the map is affine. Its constant term vanishes when it fixes
zero.
\end{proof}

This proposition explains why one cannot simply demand that our homogeneous
construction become $C^1$ at the origin while retaining its nonlinear
projective simulator. It does not classify all smooth contractions on a
compact set. Nor does it settle all half-space questions for linear maps;
those are distinct problems about signs of linear recurrence sequences.

\subsection{Absolute precision and relative information}

At a halting encoded state of radius $r=B^{-t}$, the signal is $\ell=r$.
The distance in the ambient sup norm to the observation hyperplane is
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:sc:eq:margin}
 \operatorname{dist}_{\infty}(F^t(Y_e),\{\ell=0\})
      =\frac{B^{-t}}{4n-1}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the dual norm of the coefficient vector of $\ell$ is its
$\ell^1$ norm $4n-1$, giving this exact distance to a hyperplane.
Thus an absolute observation error of fixed positive size cannot guarantee
correct classification of arbitrarily late halts. The margin is positive
at every individual encoded step, but it has no uniform positive lower
bound over all possible halting times.

For comparison, if errors of norm at most $\eta$ are added to state updates,
the global $1/2$ contraction gives the standard estimate
\[
 \norm{\widetilde Y_t-Y_t}
 \le 2^{-t}\norm{\widetilde Y_0-Y_0}+2\eta(1-2^{-t}).
\]
This controls absolute trajectory error. It does not ensure a correct
sign readout when the relevant margin shrinks as in \eqref{pqc:sc:eq:margin}.
Consequently the theorem is about exact computation in a finitely described
mathematical substrate, not a proposal for reliable unbounded computation
in finite-precision hardware.

\subsection{What remains unresolved}

The construction neither gives a minimal dimension nor an optimized
universal instruction table. It does not convert the exact reduction into
a polynomial-time reduction on ordinary binary inputs. It does not
establish robustness to persistent noise, a smooth global universal
contraction, or a fixed-arity unique-witness representation of unbounded
halting. None of those conclusions is needed for \cref{pqc:sc:thm:main}.

\section{A worked example and executable verification}\label{pqc:sc:sec:example}
\srcmark{14}

Consider the three-state program
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cl}
\toprule
State & Instruction \\\midrule
$0$ & Decrement counter 1 if positive and go to 1; if zero go to 2.\\
$1$ & Increment counter 2 and go to 0.\\
$2$ & Halt.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
It transfers the entire first counter into the second. Starting from
$(j,c_1,c_2)=(0,3,1)$, it first halts at time $7$ with counters $(0,4)$.
Here
\[
 m=3,\quad n=2,\quad d_M=1,\quad L=5,\quad B=10,\quad K=4,\quad D=40.
\]
The initial rational point and its canonical integer presentation are
\[
 Y_0=(0,1/8,1/2,1)=\frac{(0,1,4,8)}8.
\]
The trajectory is most legible when its common radial factor is displayed
separately:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ccccc}
\toprule
$t$ & $j_t$ & $c_{1,t}$ & $c_{2,t}$ & $\ell(F^t(Y_0))$ \\\midrule
0&0&3&1&$-3$\\
1&1&2&1&$-10^{-1}$\\
2&0&2&2&$-3\cdot10^{-2}$\\
3&1&1&2&$-10^{-3}$\\
4&0&1&3&$-3\cdot10^{-4}$\\
5&1&0&3&$-10^{-5}$\\
6&0&0&4&$-3\cdot10^{-6}$\\
7&2&0&4&$10^{-7}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
At each row,
$F^t(Y_0)=10^{-t}(j_t/2,2^{-c_{1,t}},2^{-c_{2,t}},1)$.
Therefore $\Peak(Y_0)=10^{-7}$, while the orbit still converges to zero.

The integer circuit uses $G=9\cdot3+2-3=26$ ReLU gates. At $T=7$,
\eqref{pqc:sc:eq:witnesscount} gives
\[
 N_7=(2\cdot26+5)\cdot7+1=400.
\]
The exporter retains four free input variables and these 400 natural
witnesses. It generates 400 residual equations and expands their squared
sum into a polynomial with exactly \textbf{2,105 nonzero monomials}, of total
degree four. Both the factored equation system and the expanded polynomial
are included, together with the exact satisfying assignment. This is an
actual polynomial artifact, not merely pseudocode claiming to generate one.

\subsection{What was run}

The standard-library Python program was executed with
\begin{lstlisting}
python verify_contraction.py --self-test --out verification
\end{lstlisting}
All arithmetic uses integers or \code{fractions.Fraction}; random test
inputs are rational and the seed is fixed. The completed checks are:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.69\linewidth}r}
\toprule
Check & Cases \\\midrule
All increment/decrement/jump destinations for program sizes 2--4,
legal tested counters 0--4; compare both real-formula and integer-circuit updates & 5,000\\
Random rational global Lipschitz, homogeneity, and cone-scaling checks & 1,000\\
Exhaustive ReLU-complementarity solutions for preactivations $-10,\ldots,10$ & 21\\
Exact example trajectory and target-point checks & 15\\
Increase each example witness coordinate by one; reject the mutated certificate & 400\\
Reject wrong first-hit horizons in $0,\ldots,9$ & 9\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The expanded polynomial was checked at the canonical assignment and on a
selection of mutated assignments. A second program, \code{check_export.py},
independently read the exported JSON, reconstructed the entire symbolic
sum of squares, and confirmed exact equality with the exported quartic.
It also checked the natural assignment and all 400 single-coordinate
mutations. Zero-time and integer-input edge cases were checked separately.
The machine-readable results are in
\code{verification/test_report.json} and
\code{verification/independent_checker_report.json}.

These tests exercise every instruction type and the sensitive zero/positive
counter distinction. They do not exhaust all rational points, all programs,
or all witnesses; \cref{pqc:sc:lem:L,pqc:sc:thm:counter,pqc:sc:thm:quartic} provide the corresponding
universal proofs. In particular, the finite test set cannot certify
universality of a source program. The worked program is deliberately small
and is not universal.

\subsection{Artifact format and reuse}

\code{integer_circuit.json} records each gate's sparse integer linear
preactivation, with input wires first and earlier positive ReLU wires after
them. \code{certificate_system.json} records the quadratic residuals.
\code{expanded_quartic.json} records the sum-of-squares polynomial as pairs
\code{[coefficient, variable_index_list]}. A repeated variable index is a
power; an empty index list denotes the constant monomial.
\code{certificate_assignment.json} gives the natural values of all
variables, with the four free inputs first. The example trace is stored
separately as exact rational strings.

A user-supplied instruction table can be compiled by passing its JSON path,
initial counters, and claimed first-hit time. Invalid instructions and
incorrect first-hit claims are rejected. The code uses no computer-algebra
package, SMT solver, floating-point solver, or network service.

\wtag\ In this report the two programs are shipped as
\code{code/14-strict-contractions-verify_contraction.py} and
\code{code/14-strict-contractions-check_export.py}, the Makefile as
\code{code/14-strict-contractions-Makefile}, and the files of
\code{verification/} as \code{data/14-strict-contractions-*}. The commands above
are the source's, for its delivered layout; the README gives the rerun recipe
on a copy.

\section{A concrete ProveIt formalization plan}\label{pqc:sc:sec:formal}
\srcmark{14}

The best integration boundary is a proved compiler theorem, not an axiom
asserting that the new map is universal. A small sequence of independent
modules would make the work auditable.

\paragraph{Counter semantics and encoding.}
Define the finite instruction type, deterministic configuration step, and
absorbing halt convention. Prove the two numerical identities for encoded
increment and decrement, including the $c=0$ versus $c>0$ split. The desired
endpoint is the one-step theorem of \cref{pqc:sc:lem:cube}.

\paragraph{Cone geometry and metric bound.}
Define $R,H,F_M$ over $\R^4$. Prove cone preservation, nonexpansiveness of
$R$, the explicit bound $L$, and homogeneity. Derive the iterate formula by
induction. These proofs use ordered-field inequalities and elementary
Lipschitz calculus, independently of computability theory.

\paragraph{Circuit semantics and reflection.}
Use an acyclic integer linear/ReLU circuit datatype. Prove that the compiler
computes $S=K H$ on the integer cone. Prove the natural complementarity
lemma once, then a generic unique-witness theorem for all circuits.
A sparse-polynomial checker can validate the exported example, but the
exporter itself need not become trusted code if its output is checked.

\paragraph{Computability and MRDP.}
Formalize exact rational circuit evaluation and the halting semidecider.
This proves the appropriate \code{REPred} fact. Only then apply
\code{Diophantine.mrdp}. The source-level theorem already supplies ordinary
integer polynomials and finite natural witnesses; no new arithmetic
representation axiom is needed~\cite{b62s14-proveit-mrdp}.

\paragraph{Peak values and negative results.}
Prove the uniform error bound for the finite maxima, followed by the
Lipschitz and rationality statements. A separate computability argument
then turns source-machine completeness into the exact-zero impossibility
result. This separation prevents a numerical convergence proof from being
mistaken for a decision procedure for zero.

The package contains no new Lean file advertised as compiling. The proposed
module decomposition is a development plan, while the mathematical proofs
and Python artifacts are the present deliverables.

% --- source 12, lines 111-1337 ---
\section{The problem, the contribution, and its limits}\label{pqc:ad:sec:intro}
\srcmark{12}

\subsection{Why another computational substrate is not enough}
The assertion that an effectively presented machine's halting set is
Diophantine follows from MRDP once recursive enumerability has been proved.
Replacing a Turing machine by an unusual machine does not, by itself, add
much mathematics. A useful extension should control additional structure:
regularity, finite-state implementation, quantitative convergence, witness
complexity, or the difference between exact and finite-resolution
observation.

This article studies all five in one construction. Its central phenomenon is
\[
\boxed{\text{uniformly predictable convergence does not imply decidable exact extinction.}}
\]
The phrase \emph{exact extinction} always means reaching the point $0$ in
finitely many iterations, not merely approaching it. The target $\{0\}$ is
closed but not open in $\Ztwo$. That topological distinction is essential,
not a technicality to be removed later.

The specific questions answered here are these. Can a scalar strict
contraction with a finite-state digit implementation encode universal
halting? Yes, for exact extinction. Which radial changes of clock retain
finite-state realizability? Exactly those with eventually periodic added
delay. Does arbitrarily fast convergence prevent this phenomenon? No. Does
scalar analyticity near the attracting fixed point prevent it? Yes, by a
uniform finite-horizon theorem. These are precise structural questions posed
and resolved within this article; we do not assert that they were previously
recognized open problems under these exact formulations.

\subsection{Relation to ProveIt and to existing literature}
The inspected ProveIt source exposes
\texttt{Diophantine.mrdp}, which represents every recursively enumerable
subset of $\N$ by one integer polynomial with a fixed finite number of
natural-number witnesses. Its converse and its treatment of input zero are
also explicit. The guide correctly distinguishes this existence interface
from a practical polynomial-generation algorithm or a numerical witness
bound \cite{b62s12-proveit-mrdp,b62s12-proveit-source}. We use that interface only after
proving recursive enumerability of our extinction predicate. We have
inspected the relevant source and documentation, but have not rerun the
repository's Lean build or transitive axiom audit.

Dynamical simulation of computation is classical; Moore's work is an early
landmark \cite{b62-moore1990}. The established correspondence between $p$-adic digit
transducers and Lipschitz maps is developed by Anashin, who also gives a
separate finiteness criterion \cite{b62s12-anashin}. In particular, being
$1$-Lipschitz must not be confused with being realizable by a \emph{finite}
transducer. We prove finiteness directly by constructing a bounded buffer.

There is also an important existing obstruction. Delvenne, K\r{u}rka, and
Blondel study effective symbolic systems with clopen observations; their
Corollary~20 makes equicontinuous systems decidable in that framework
\cite{b62s12-delvenne}. Our map is equicontinuous and is \emph{not} universal in
that robust observation sense. We prove an elementary finite-quotient
version of the obstruction and locate all the hardness in exact singleton
observation. For the formalization context, Carneiro's paper formalizes the
Diophantineness of exponentiation, the Matiyasevich component of MRDP, rather
than being cited here as a formalization of every part of MRDP
\cite{b62s12-carneiro}.

\subsection{Status of the claims}
The construction and theorems in Sections~\ref{pqc:ad:sec:machine}--\ref{pqc:ad:sec:bounded}
are proved below. Finite checks of an implementation supplement those
proofs but do not replace them. A concrete nonuniversal demonstration
machine is exported in the archive. The universal existence theorem uses
any fixed ordinary binary universal machine as the input to the proved
compiler; the archive does not claim to contain a minimized or independently
verified universal transition table.

The following distinctions will remain in force throughout:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{0.28\textwidth}X@{}}
\toprule
Claim & Status and qualification\\
\midrule
Strictly contracting universal exact extinction & Proved by a uniform
compiler from a binary Turing machine.\\
Finite-state clock classification & Proved for the entire radial-clock
family constructed here.\\
Scalar analytic finite horizon & Proved; an effective coefficient formula
is given for rational polynomials.\\
Fixed-arity unbounded polynomial & Inherited from MRDP and ordinary
quadratization; not numerically expanded here.\\
Bounded unique-witness quartic & Explicit construction, implementation,
and exact finite checks. Its arity grows with the bounds.\\
Lean certification and literature priority & Not established in this
article. Proposed formalization tasks are separated from completed work.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\section{Binary tapes inside the odd \texorpdfstring{$2$}{2}-adic integers}\label{pqc:ad:sec:machine}
\srcmark{12}

\subsection{Conventions}
Write $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. For $x\in\Ztwo$, let $\nuu(x)$ be its
$2$-adic valuation, with $\nuu(0)=+\infty$, and write
$|x|_2=2^{-\nuu(x)}$. Digits are always read \emph{least significant first}.
A natural number is viewed as a binary stream with an eventually zero tail.

Fix a deterministic binary Turing machine $M$ with states
$Q=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$, $m\ge2$, an initial state $q_0$, and one halting state
$q_h$. For each $q\ne q_h$ and $b\in\Bit$, its total transition table gives
\[
\delta(q,b)=(q',w,D),\qquad w\in\Bit,\quad
D\in\{\moveL,\moveR,\blank\}.
\]
Here $\blank$ means that the head stays in place; the blank tape symbol is
$0$. Allowing stay moves is inessential. Put
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:rK}
r=\max\{1,\ceil{\log_2m}\},\qquad K=r+3.
\end{equation}
We do not seek the smallest possible $K$.

A configuration is a triple $(q,L,R)$. The low bit of $L$ is the cell
immediately left of the head; subsequent bits extend leftward. The low bit
of $R$ is the scanned cell; subsequent bits extend rightward. Thus natural
$L,R$ describe a finite-support tape. Allowing arbitrary $L,R\in\Ztwo$
extends the same rules to infinite binary tapes and makes the eventual
map globally defined on a compact space.

\subsection{The exact one-step formulas}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:split}
a=L\bmod2,\quad b=R\bmod2,\quad
A=(L-a)/2,\quad B=(R-b)/2.
\end{equation}
The quantities $A,B$ belong to $\Ztwo$. For the selected rule
$(q',w,D)=\delta(q,b)$, the next tapes are
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:tape}
(L',R')=
\begin{cases}
(2L+w,\ B),&D=\moveR,\\
(A,\ a+2w+4B),&D=\moveL,\\
(L,\ w+2B),&D=\blank.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
For example, a left move makes the previous left-neighbor bit $a$ the new
scanned bit. The written bit $w$ is then immediately to its right, followed
by the old right tail $B$. This gives $R'=a+2w+4B$, including both factors
that can easily be lost in an informal encoding.

When discussing a \emph{padded machine trace}, we define the step at $q_h$
to be the identity. The dynamical map below instead sends a halting
configuration to zero. Keeping those two conventions distinct accounts for
the one-step offset in all extinction statements.

\subsection{Interleaving and the unit encoding}
For $L=\sum_{i\ge0}\ell_i2^i$ and $R=\sum_{i\ge0}\rho_i2^i$, define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:interleave}
J(L,R)=\sum_{i\ge0}\ell_i2^{2i}
       +\sum_{i\ge0}\rho_i2^{2i+1}.
\end{equation}
This is a bijection $\Ztwo^2\to\Ztwo$ with an explicit digitwise inverse.
Its restriction is a bijection $\N^2\to\N$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:encoding}
E(q,L,R)=1+2q+2^{r+1}J(L,R),\qquad 0\le q<2^r.
\end{equation}
Every odd $2$-adic integer has a unique such encoding: digit $0$ is the
unit marker, digits $1,\ldots,r$ encode the state, and the remaining digits
alternate the two tapes. State labels $m,\ldots,2^r-1$, when present, are
invalid labels, not additional computational states.

\begin{definition}[Unit computation map]\label[definition]{pqc:ad:def:G}
For an odd unit $u=E(q,L,R)$, put
\[
G(u)=
\begin{cases}
0,&q=q_h\text{ or }q\ge m,\\
E(q',L',R'),&q<m,\ q\ne q_h,
\end{cases}
\]
where the second line uses \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:tape}. Consequently, every nonzero
value of $G$ is odd.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Bounded loss of precision]\label[lemma]{pqc:ad:lem:unitlip}
For odd $u,v\in\Ztwo$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:unitlip}
\nuu(G(u)-G(v))\ge \nuu(u-v)-(r+2).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, $G$ is $2^{r+2}$-Lipschitz on the unit group.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The case $u=v$ is immediate. Put $n=\nuu(u-v)$. If $n\le r+2$, the
right-hand side is nonpositive, while the difference of two $2$-adic
integers has nonnegative valuation.

Suppose $n\ge r+3$. The state headers and both low tape bits agree. In
particular, the two inputs choose the same transition; if they choose the
halting or invalid branch, both outputs are zero. Otherwise, their output
state headers agree. Write $c_j$ for the interleaved input tape digit of
index $j$. Away from the first two tape digits, a right move sends even
output tape index $j$ to input index $j-2$, and odd output index $j$ to
input index $j+2$. A left move reverses these offsets; a stay move has
offset zero. The few written boundary digits are fixed by the common rule
and the common low bits. Thus every output tape digit at global position
less than $n-2$ is determined by common input digits at positions less than
$n$. The outputs agree modulo $2^{n-2}$. Since $r\ge1$, this is at least
the precision claimed in \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:unitlip}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The deliberately generous precision loss makes the proof uniform across
headers, invalid labels, and all three head directions. It is not a claim
of an optimal Lipschitz constant for a particular machine.
\end{remark}

\section{The radial contraction compiler}\label{pqc:ad:sec:radial}
\srcmark{12}

\subsection{A general lemma}
\begin{theorem}[Radial contraction]\label{pqc:ad:thm:radial}
Let $G\colon\Ztwo^\times\to\Ztwo$ satisfy
$\nuu(G(u)-G(v))\ge\nuu(u-v)-\lambda$ for some integer $\lambda\ge0$.
Let $h\colon\N\to\N$ satisfy $h(t)\ge t+\lambda+1$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:F}
F_h(0)=0,\qquad
F_h(2^t u)=2^{h(t)}G(u)\quad(u\text{ odd}).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:strict}
|F_h(x)-F_h(y)|_2\le\tfrac12|x-y|_2
\qquad(x,y\in\Ztwo).
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\nuu(F_h(x))\ge\nuu(x)+\lambda+1$ for nonzero $x$, with the
usual convention when $F_h(x)=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For inputs $x=2^tu$, $y=2^tv$ in the same shell,
\begin{align*}
\nuu(F_h(x)-F_h(y))
&=h(t)+\nuu(G(u)-G(v))\\
&\ge h(t)+\nuu(u-v)-\lambda\\
&\ge\nuu(x-y)+1.
\end{align*}
For distinct shells, say $\nuu(x)=t<s=\nuu(y)$, one has
$\nuu(x-y)=t$. Both output valuations are at least $t+\lambda+1$,
because $h(t)\ge t+\lambda+1$ and $h(s)\ge s+\lambda+1$.
Their difference therefore has valuation at least $t+1$. The comparison
with zero follows from the same bound on the valuation of a single output.
This proves all cases without requiring that $h$ be monotone.
\end{proof}

Apply the theorem with the map in Definition~\ref{pqc:ad:def:G},
$\lambda=r+2$, and any \emph{admissible clock}
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:admissible}
h(t)\ge t+K.
\end{equation}
All the maps below are therefore strict contractions. If $F_h(x)=x$,
\eqref{pqc:ad:eq:strict} applied to $x,0$ forces $x=0$. Also
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:globaldrift}
\nuu(F_h^j(x))\ge\nuu(x)+jK,
\end{equation}
so every orbit converges to zero uniformly in $x\in\Ztwo$.

\subsection{Effectivity on an infinite digit stream}
A formula involving $\nuu(x)$ can conceal an uncomputable zero test on an
arbitrary $2$-adic name. This construction does not require such a test.

\begin{proposition}[Finite-precision evaluation]\label[proposition]{pqc:ad:prop:effective}
If $h$ is total computable, then $F_h$ is a computable map of $\Ztwo$.
Its residue modulo $2^k$ is computable from the input residue modulo $2^k$.
It also restricts to a total computable map $\N\to\N$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If the input residue is zero, \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:globaldrift} shows that the output
residue is zero. Otherwise its valuation $t<k$ is known. Compute $h(t)$.
If $h(t)\ge k$, output zero again. In the remaining case, the required
precision of $G(u)$ is $k-h(t)$. Lemma~\ref{pqc:ad:lem:unitlip} requires at most
\[
k-h(t)+(r+2)\le k-t-1
\]
unit digits, already available from the input residue. Higher input digits
can be filled with zero without changing the answer. On a natural-number
input all tapes have finite support, the unit update produces a natural
number, and the shift by $h(t)$ is an ordinary finite integer operation.
\end{proof}

A rapidly growing clock can make full integer evaluation expensive because
its output has many bits. This proposition is an effectivity statement,
not a polynomial-time bound for arbitrary clocks.

\subsection{Simulation and exact extinction}
\begin{theorem}[Clock-independent simulation]\label{pqc:ad:thm:simulation}
Let $c_j=(q_j,L_j,R_j)$ be the run of $M$ from a valid configuration $c_0$,
and let $H$ be its first halting time, possibly infinite. Start from
$x_0=2^{t_0}E(c_0)$ and define $t_{j+1}=h(t_j)$. For every $j\le H$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:simulation}
F_h^j(x_0)=2^{t_j}E(c_j).
\end{equation}
If $H<\infty$, the first zero iterate occurs at time $H+1$. If $H=\infty$,
no iterate is zero. These extinction times are independent of the choice
of admissible clock.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At time zero the formula is the definition of the input. If the current
state is nonhalting, the unit update is precisely one machine step and is
odd. Hence its prefactor $2^{h(t_j)}$ is its exact power of two, proving the
inductive step. At the first halting configuration, the next unit update
is zero. No preceding update can be zero. If there is no halting
configuration, all unit updates remain odd forever. The case $H=0$ gives
extinction at time one, as stated.
\end{proof}

For $n=0$ extinction is already true at time zero. For a nonzero input
with an invalid state label, extinction occurs at time one. Thus the
entire set
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:extset}
\Ext_M=\{n\in\N:\exists j\ge0\ F_h^j(n)=0\}
\end{equation}
is independent of $h$, including malformed natural-number inputs.

\begin{corollary}[Complete exact extinction]\label[corollary]{pqc:ad:cor:complete}
There is a fixed finite-state binary-machine table $U$ such that, for every
total computable admissible clock, $\Ext_U$ is $\Sigma^0_1$-complete under
computable many-one reductions. Its complement is $\Pi^0_1$-complete.
The completeness already holds on computably encoded odd initial
configurations with a blank left tape.
\end{corollary}
\wtag\ As Section~\ref{pqc:ad:sec:intro} states, the map is \emph{not} universal in the robust clopen-observation sense of Delvenne, K\r{u}rka and Blondel; Corollary~\ref{pqc:ad:cor:clopen} below locates all the hardness in exact singleton observation.
\begin{proof}
Choose a fixed binary universal Turing machine $U$. A program and its input
can be translated effectively to a finite binary input tape $R_e$ for $U$.
Map that instance to $E(q_0,0,R_e)$. By Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:simulation}, this
natural number becomes zero exactly when the simulated program halts.
Conversely, iterating the total computable natural-number function $F_h$
and stopping upon zero semidecides extinction. This gives completeness
and, by complementation, the stated classification of nonextinction.
\end{proof}

The word ``finite-state'' in the corollary describes $U$'s finite control.
The stronger assertion that the \emph{entire digit map} $F_h$ can be a
finite transducer is proved next, for the clocks that permit it.

\section{A finite transducer and an exact clock classification}\label{pqc:ad:sec:finite}
\srcmark{12}

\subsection{The constant-drift realization}
A synchronous binary Mealy transducer has finitely many internal states.
At each step it reads one input bit, emits one output bit, and changes its
state. Its infinite-stream interpretation is a map $\Ztwo\to\Ztwo$.

\begin{theorem}[Finite-state implementation]\label{pqc:ad:thm:mealy}
For the clock $h(t)=t+K$, the map $F_h$ is realized by a finite synchronous
binary Mealy transducer. A direct construction uses at most
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:statebound}
2^{2r+8}+6\cdot2^{r+5}+2
\end{equation}
states before minimization. Its table can be generated effectively from
the finite transition table of $M$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
An initial \emph{leading-zero state} emits zero on every zero input and
stays in that state. It therefore handles an arbitrarily large shell
valuation without storing its value. On the first input one, the unit
part begins. Index that digit by relative position zero. The required
output, from this point onward, is $2^K G(u)$.

There is a finite bootstrap of length
\[
I=K+r+5=2r+8.
\]
It stores the input prefix. At relative position $i<K$ it emits zero. At
position $i\ge K$ it emits digit $i-K$ of $G(u)$, computed by completing
the stored prefix with zeros. This is correct by
Lemma~\ref{pqc:ad:lem:unitlip}: the $i+1$ known unit digits determine at least
$i+1-(r+2)$ output digits of $G$, while the requested digit requires only
$i-K+1=i-r-2$ digits. If the decoded state is halting or invalid, the
transducer enters a permanent zero-output state.

For a nonhalting branch, the bootstrap determines the selected head
movement. After processing relative position $I-1$, it keeps only that
movement, a parity bit, and the last $K+2$ input bits. It discards the
remaining prefix. For the next and all subsequent positions $i\ge I$,
the output tape index is
\[
j=i-K-r-1\ge4.
\]
There are no boundary writes at these indices. The source interleaved
tape index is $j+\Delta$, where
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}c cc@{}}
\toprule
Movement & $j$ even & $j$ odd\\
\midrule
$\moveR$ & $\Delta=-2$ & $\Delta=2$\\
$\moveL$ & $\Delta=2$ & $\Delta=-2$\\
$\blank$ & $\Delta=0$ & $\Delta=0$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Consequently, the source unit bit is at position $i-K+\Delta$.
Append the current bit to the $K+2$ stored previous bits. If the oldest
bit in this block is indexed zero, the desired source is at block position
$2+\Delta$, one of $0,2,4$. Emit it, discard the oldest bit, and toggle the
parity. This is a finite transition rule.

There are fewer than $2^I$ bootstrap states: the initial unit bit is one,
so there are at most $2^{i-1}$ prefixes of length $i$ at a bootstrap stage.
There are at most $3\cdot2\cdot2^{K+2}$ steady states and two special
states. Substituting $I=2r+8$ and $K=r+3$ gives \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:statebound}.
Breadth-first enumeration of reachable states yields an explicit table.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Where the unbounded memory resides]
The machine does not acquire an unbounded internal state. Computation
uses repeated application of a fixed finite transducer to words whose
stored lengths may grow. After each iteration the transducer starts again
in its designated initial state. This is not a claim that a one-pass
finite automaton recognizes arbitrary recursively enumerable languages.
The unbounded tape is in the external digit stream.
\end{remark}

On natural inputs, one constant-drift iteration changes binary length by
at most a constant depending on $M$. The head moves at most one cell, and
interleaving shifts tape positions by at most two. Thus a direct streaming
implementation takes linear time in the current word length; repeated
iteration still allows unbounded computation.

\subsection{Exactly which clocks are finite-state?}
\begin{definition}
A sequence $d\colon\N\to\N$ is \emph{eventually periodic} if some
$A\ge0$ and $P\ge1$ satisfy $d(t+P)=d(t)$ for every $t\ge A$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Clock classification]\label{pqc:ad:thm:clockclass}
Fix the unit computation map $G$ of a machine with at least one nonhalting
state. For any admissible clock $h$, the map $F_h$ is realizable by a
finite synchronous binary transducer if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:delay}
d(t)=h(t)-t
\end{equation}
is eventually periodic. No computability assumption on $h$ is needed for
this equivalence; eventual periodicity supplies computability on the
finite-state side.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Necessity.} Choose one fixed natural odd unit $u_*$ encoding a valid
nonhalting state. Its image $G(u_*)$ is odd. Suppose a finite transducer
realizes $F_h$, and let $s_t$ be its state after reading $t$ zeros from its
initial state. The sequence $s_t$ is eventually periodic because it is
