obtained by repeatedly applying one function to a finite set.

On the input $2^t u_*$, the first $t$ input bits are zero. The emitted
prefix is also zero: the first nonzero output bit is at position $h(t)$,
which is greater than $t$. After this prefix the remaining input is the
same fixed stream of digits of $u_*$ for every $t$. Therefore, if
$s_t=s_{t+P}$, the two remaining output streams are identical. Their first
one occurs, relative to the suffix start, at positions $h(t)-t$ and
$h(t+P)-(t+P)$. Both are finite because $G(u_*)$ is odd. Hence
$d(t)=d(t+P)$ for all sufficiently large $t$.

\emph{Sufficiency.} An eventually periodic $d$ has a finite range. While
reading the initial zeros, a finite controller records $t$ up to its
preperiod and then records its residue modulo a period. It outputs zeros.
At the first one, it knows which of the finitely many values $D=d(t)$ to
use. Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:mealy} gives the unit-output stream $2^K G(u)$ with a
finite implementation. Since $D\ge K$, prepend $D-K$ additional zero
output digits using a fixed finite delay buffer. This realizes
$2^D G(u)$ on the unit suffix. Combining the finitely many delay choices
with the leading-zero controller is a finite transducer and produces
$2^{t+D}G(u)=F_h(2^tu)$. On the all-zero input it produces zero forever.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label[corollary]{pqc:ad:cor:nonfinite}
Unbounded added delay excludes finite-state realizability. In particular,
the quadratic clock $h(t)=(t+1)^2+K$ is not finite-state, although it defines
a computable strict contraction with exactly the same extinction set as
the finite-state constant-drift map.
\end{corollary}

Bounded added delay is not sufficient: a bounded computable but
noneventually-periodic delay also fails the classification. Thus the
boundary is periodic finite control, not merely a bound on buffer size.
The theorem is specific to this radial family, not a classification of all
contracting transducers.

\section{Finite observation is easy; exact extinction is hard}\label{pqc:ad:sec:observation}
\srcmark{12}

\subsection{Finite quotients}
A $1$-Lipschitz map $f\colon\Ztwo\to\Ztwo$ induces a well-defined map
$f_k$ on $\Z/2^k\Z$: congruent inputs give congruent outputs. For a
computable $f$, the finite table of $f_k$ is computable. Therefore,
reachability of any specified residue subset can be decided by exploring a
finite directed graph. This elementary fact already prevents interpreting
our hardness theorem as finite-resolution universality.

Our contractions give a much stronger bound.
\begin{proposition}[Uniform nilpotence of every finite quotient]\label[proposition]{pqc:ad:prop:nilpotent}
For an admissible clock and any $k\ge1$, put $N_k=\ceil{k/K}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:nilpotent}
F_h^{N_k}(x)\equiv0\pmod{2^k}
\qquad\text{for every }x\in\Ztwo.
\end{equation}
The quotient map modulo $2^k$ is nilpotent with exponent at most $N_k$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every $x\in\Ztwo$ has nonnegative valuation, and each nonzero iterate gains
at least $K$ by \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:globaldrift}. After $N_k$ steps its valuation is
at least $k$. Zero iterates cause no exception.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A bounded clopen reachability test]\label[corollary]{pqc:ad:cor:clopen}
Let $C$ be any clopen subset of $\Ztwo$, given as a union of residue classes
modulo $2^k$. For a computably given input, deciding whether some iterate
lies in $C$ requires only the residues at times $0,1,\ldots,N_k$. The same
conclusion holds for existential reachability from a given clopen initial
set after choosing a common residue precision for both sets.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
At and after time $N_k$ the residue is always zero. If the zero class is in
$C$, time $N_k$ already witnesses reachability; if it is not, later times
cannot help. For a clopen initial set, enumerate its finitely many allowed
initial residues and apply the same argument.
\end{proof}

A finite-state observer of a fixed residue precision also sees a constant
symbol from time $N_k$ onward. Its own state sequence thereafter is
ultimately periodic. Reachability, repeated visitation, and the usual
finite-state acceptance conditions reduce to finite computations.
This gives a direct explanation, within the present family, of its
compatibility with the equicontinuity obstruction discussed in
Section~\ref{pqc:ad:sec:intro}.

\subsection{The quantifier distinction}
For every $x\in\Ztwo$, the following statement holds:
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:quantifier1}
\forall k\ \exists j\qquad F_h^j(x)\equiv0\pmod{2^k}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, $j=N_k$ is a uniform witness independent of $x$. Exact extinction
is the different statement
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:quantifier2}
\exists j\ \forall k\qquad F_h^j(x)\equiv0\pmod{2^k}.
\end{equation}
For the universal compiler, \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:quantifier2} is undecidable on natural
inputs. The same iterate must work at every precision. Interchanging those
quantifiers would erase the entire computational content.

On a known natural-number orbit, testing equality to zero is an exact
finite integer operation. On an arbitrary digit-stream name, equality to
zero is not a finite-prefix observation. These are different input and
observation conventions, and the theorems do not conflate them.

\begin{corollary}[No computable bound on positive extinction times]\label[corollary]{pqc:ad:cor:nobound}
For the universal constant-drift map, there is no total computable
$B\colon\N\to\N$ such that every input which eventually becomes zero
already becomes zero by time $B(n)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Such a function would decide extinction by evaluating the orbit up to
$B(n)$, contrary to Corollary~\ref{pqc:ad:cor:complete}. The map fixes zero, so
checking only the last iterate would also suffice.
\end{proof}

Thus even knowing a uniform convergence modulus for \emph{all} inputs
does not furnish an input-dependent computable upper bound for those
inputs that reach the limit exactly.

\section{Arbitrary convergence rates and flatness}\label{pqc:ad:sec:flat}
\srcmark{12}

\subsection{Prescribing a convergence modulus}
\begin{theorem}[Fast clocks with unchanged exact computation]\label{pqc:ad:thm:rates}
Let $b\colon\N\to\N$ be any total computable nondecreasing function. There
is a total computable admissible clock such that, for all $x\in\Ztwo$ and
$j\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:rate}
\nuu(F_h^j(x))\ge b(j).
\end{equation}
The exact extinction set and the first extinction time of every natural
input are unchanged from the constant-drift construction.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose
\[
h(t)=\max\{t+K,\ b(t+1)\}.
\]
Along a nonzero orbit the valuations satisfy $t_{j+1}=h(t_j)$ and
$t_j\ge t_0+jK\ge j$. Hence, for $j\ge1$,
$t_j\ge b(t_{j-1}+1)\ge b(j)$. If an orbit has already become zero, the
inequality holds with infinite valuation. Clock independence is
Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:simulation} together with the immediate treatment of
invalid labels and zero.
\end{proof}

This result controls the number of iterations to achieve a precision, not
the bit complexity of one iteration. The latter can increase substantially
under the clock change. It also does not say that an arbitrary prescribed
clock remains finite-state; Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:clockclass} states exactly when
that is possible.

\subsection{Infinite-order asymptotic flatness}
\begin{proposition}[A flat but computational contraction]\label[proposition]{pqc:ad:prop:flat}
For the clock $h(t)=(t+1)^2+K$, and every integer $d\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:flat}
\lim_{x\to0,\,x\ne0}\frac{F_h(x)}{x^d}=0
\qquad\text{in }\Q_2.
\end{equation}
In particular, $F_h$ is differentiable at zero with derivative zero.
For a universal machine its natural-input extinction set is still
$\Sigma^0_1$-complete.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $x=2^t u$ with $u$ odd and $G(u)\ne0$, the latter is odd, so
\[
\nuu\!\left(\frac{F_h(x)}{x^d}\right)
=h(t)-dt=(t+1)^2+K-dt\longrightarrow+\infty.
\]
If $G(u)=0$, the quotient is zero. The estimate is uniform over units and
proves the limit. The derivative statement is the case $d=1$.
Completeness follows from clock independence.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What flatness does not say]
Equation~\eqref{pqc:ad:eq:flat} is asymptotic, or Peano, flatness at one point. It
is not a proof that the map is globally $C^\infty$, nor that iterated
classical derivatives exist at all nearby points. Digit interleaving on
nonzero shells introduces its own regularity questions. No such stronger
smoothness claim is used below.
\end{remark}

\subsection{An exact differentiability classification}
The clock also gives a simple necessary and sufficient condition for the
ordinary $2$-adic derivative at the attracting fixed point.

\begin{theorem}[Differentiability versus finite control]\label{pqc:ad:thm:derivative}
For the machine compiler, let $d(t)=h(t)-t$. Then $F_h$ is differentiable
at zero if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:diffclock}
d(t)\longrightarrow+\infty\qquad(t\longrightarrow\infty).
\end{equation}
When this holds, its derivative is zero. Consequently, none of the
finite-state maps in Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:clockclass} is differentiable at zero.
More generally, for each integer $a\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:orderclock}
F_h(x)=o(x^a)\text{ as }x\to0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
h(t)-at\longrightarrow+\infty.
\end{equation}
In particular, flatness of every positive integral order is equivalent to
$h(t)/t\to+\infty$ as $t\to\infty$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Along the ray $x=2^t u_h$ for a fixed halting unit $u_h$, the difference
quotient $F_h(x)/x$ is identically zero. Thus, if a derivative exists, it
must be zero. Along a fixed nonhalting unit $u_n$, one has
\[
\nuu\!\left(\frac{F_h(2^tu_n)}{2^tu_n}\right)=h(t)-t=d(t).
\]
Convergence of this quotient to zero forces \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:diffclock}.
Conversely, for every unit $u$, the quotient is either zero or has exactly
that valuation, independently of $u$. Condition \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:diffclock}
therefore gives convergence uniformly over all units and proves the
existence of the derivative. Eventually periodic $d$ is bounded, proving
the assertion about finite-state maps.

The identical argument with $x^a$ in the denominator proves
\eqref{pqc:ad:eq:orderclock}. If $h(t)/t\to\infty$, then $h(t)-at\to\infty$
for each fixed $a$. Conversely, applying \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:orderclock} at every
integer $a$ shows that $h(t)/t$ eventually exceeds every fixed real bound:
choose an integer $a$ larger than that bound and divide $h(t)-at$ by $t$.
\end{proof}

For example, constant or eventually periodic added delay gives finite
control but no derivative at zero. The clock $h(t)=2t+K$ gives derivative
zero but fails $o(x^2)$, since $h(t)-2t=K$. The quadratic clock is flat at
every order. All three cases preserve exactly the same machine computation
and natural-input extinction predicate. These classifications concern the
present radial family; they do not rule out different finite-state or
smooth encodings with other properties.

\section{Scalar analytic rigidity and explicit finite horizons}\label{pqc:ad:sec:analytic}
\srcmark{12}

The preceding examples are continuous contractions and may be arbitrarily
flat at zero, yet they are not analytic there. This is a genuine boundary
for scalar maps.

\begin{theorem}[Analytic extinction horizon]\label{pqc:ad:thm:analytic}
Let $p$ be prime and let $f\colon\Zp\to\Zp$ satisfy $f(0)=0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:pcontract}
|f(x)-f(y)|_p\le p^{-\kappa}|x-y|_p
\quad(x,y\in\Zp)
\end{equation}
for an integer $\kappa\ge1$. Suppose $f$ is analytic on a neighborhood of
zero. Then there is a finite integer $N$ such that, for all $x\in\Zp$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:horizon}
(\exists j\ge0\ f^j(x)=0)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^N(x)=0.
\end{equation}
More precisely, either $f$ vanishes identically on a neighborhood of zero
and every point becomes zero in uniformly bounded time, or a sufficiently
small neighborhood contains no nonzero root of $f$ and no orbit can first
reach zero after its uniform entry time into that neighborhood.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose a ball on which $f$ is represented by a convergent power series.
If that series is zero, there is $B\ge0$ such that $f$ vanishes on
$p^B\Zp$. From \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:pcontract},
$\nu_p(f^j(x))\ge j\kappa$ for every $x\in\Zp$. Thus all points enter
$p^B\Zp$ by time $N_0=\ceil{B/\kappa}$ and become zero by time $N_0+1$.

Otherwise, because $f(0)=0$, its series has a first nonzero term of degree
$m\ge1$. On a sufficiently small ball, factor it as
\[
f(z)=z^m\bigl(a_m+zH(z)\bigr),\qquad a_m\ne0,
\]
where $H$ is analytic and bounded on a smaller closed ball. Shrink that
ball to $p^B\Zp$ so that $|zH(z)|_p<|a_m|_p$ throughout it. The strong
triangle inequality gives
$|a_m+zH(z)|_p=|a_m|_p\ne0$. Consequently, $f(z)=0$ on this ball only when
$z=0$.

All orbits enter the ball by $N=\ceil{B/\kappa}$, and it is forward
invariant by contraction. If $f^N(x)\ne0$, then the no-nonzero-root property
shows inductively that every later iterate is also nonzero. Conversely,
if an earlier iterate was zero, all subsequent iterates, including the
$N$th, are zero. This proves \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:horizon}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An effective polynomial version}
Analytic existence of a small ball is not automatically an algorithm for
finding it from an arbitrary coefficient oracle. A finite polynomial
presentation removes that issue.

\begin{corollary}[A coefficient-computable cutoff]\label[corollary]{pqc:ad:cor:poly}
Suppose a nonzero polynomial
\[
f(z)=\sum_{j=m}^{d}a_jz^j\in\Q[z],\qquad a_m\ne0,\quad m\ge1,
\]
maps $\Zp$ to itself and satisfies \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:pcontract}. Set
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:Bpoly}
B=1+\max\left(\{0\}\cup
 \left\{\floor{\frac{\nu_p(a_m)-\nu_p(a_j)}{j-m}}:
             j>m,\ a_j\ne0\right\}\right),
\qquad N=\ceil{B/\kappa}.
\end{equation}
Then \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:horizon} holds. Exact extinction for rational inputs in
$\Zp$, and hence for natural-number inputs, is decidable by $N$ exact
iterations. The extinction basin in $\Zp$ has at most $d^N$ elements.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $z\ne0$ with $\nu_p(z)\ge B$ and every $j>m$ with $a_j\ne0$,
\[
\nu_p(a_jz^j)-\nu_p(a_mz^m)
=\nu_p(a_j)-\nu_p(a_m)+(j-m)\nu_p(z)>0.
\]
The lowest-degree nonzero term therefore has strictly smaller valuation
than every other term and cannot cancel. There is no nonzero root in
$p^B\Zp$, so the second case of Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:analytic} applies.
Rational arithmetic and a zero test are effective. Finally, the basin is
the zero set of the nonzero polynomial $f^N$ (composition, not pointwise
power), whose degree is $d^N$. A nonzero polynomial over $\Qp$ has at most
its degree many roots.
\end{proof}

The zero polynomial has horizon one. Formula~\eqref{pqc:ad:eq:Bpoly} is a safe
bound, not generally the least one. It assumes that the self-map and
contraction hypotheses have been established; it is not itself a general
algorithm for verifying those hypotheses.

For example, for $p=2$ the polynomial
\[
f(z)=2z(z-1)
\]
is a $1/2$-contraction on $\Ztwo$, since
$f(x)-f(y)=2(x-y)(x+y-1)$. The formula gives $B=N=1$.
Indeed, the only points whose orbits ever become zero are $0$ and $1$.
After one step every orbit is even; the even ball contains no nonzero root
of $f$. This example exhibits a nontrivial extinction basin and an exact
finite horizon without any computability pathology.

\subsection{Why the constructed maps cannot be analytic}
\begin{proposition}\label[proposition]{pqc:ad:prop:notanalytic}
For every admissible clock, the map $F_h$ associated to a machine with a
halting state and a nonhalting state is not analytic near zero.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Choose odd natural units $u_h$ and $u_n$ encoding a halting and a
nonhalting state, respectively. For all $t\ge0$,
\[
F_h(2^tu_h)=0,\qquad F_h(2^tu_n)\ne0.
\]
Both input sequences approach zero. A nonzero analytic germ has an
isolated zero there by the factorization in
Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:analytic}; an identically zero germ vanishes on a whole
neighborhood. The two displayed sequences rule out both possibilities.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Dimension matters]
The proof uses the scalar factorization $f(z)=z^m$ times a local unit.
In several variables an analytic zero fiber need not have an isolated
nonzero-free neighborhood. The theorem is not a multivariate analytic
undecidability obstruction. That extension is a separate research
question, not an omitted case of the proof.
\end{remark}

\section{The Diophantine representation and what MRDP contributes}\label{pqc:ad:sec:mrdp}
\srcmark{12}

\begin{theorem}[Clock-invariant Diophantine extinction]\label{pqc:ad:thm:mrdp}
For a fixed machine $M$, there are an integer $v\ge0$ and an integer
polynomial $P_M(n,w_1,\ldots,w_v)$ such that, for every natural input $n$
and every total computable admissible clock,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:mrdp}
\exists j\ F_h^j(n)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists w\in\N^v\ P_M(n,w)=0.
\end{equation}
The same polynomial can be used for every such clock. It can be chosen of
degree at most four after adding finitely many witnesses. For universal
$M$, the complement of the represented set is not Diophantine over $\N$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the constant-drift map. Its extinction set is recursively enumerable
by exact natural-number iteration. Apply the MRDP theorem in the form
provided by ProveIt \cite{b62s12-proveit-mrdp,b62s12-proveit-source}. The entire set is
clock-independent, so the resulting representation serves every clock.

For the degree reduction, write the resulting integer polynomial as
$P^+-P^-$ with $P^+,P^-$ having nonnegative integer coefficients. Evaluate
both with finite circuits using natural constants, addition, and
multiplication. Introduce one natural variable for every gate. Each gate
is constrained by an equation of degree at most two, and the two final
gate values are constrained to agree. The sum of the squares of all these
residuals is a single polynomial of degree at most four. Its natural zeros
are exactly the original zeros with their circuit evaluations. This adds
only a fixed finite number of variables.

If the universal extinction complement were Diophantine, enumerating its
finite witness tuples would semidecide it. Since extinction itself is
semidecidable, dovetailing the two procedures would decide extinction,
contradicting Corollary~\ref{pqc:ad:cor:complete}.
\end{proof}

The quartic conclusion is standard circuit quadratization, not a newly
improved universal degree bound. The original MRDP witnesses can be
nonunique. Making circuit values unique \emph{conditional on those
witnesses} does not make the entire representation single-fold.

There is also a practical distinction. The proof above identifies the
correct semidecidable predicate and the repository theorem to apply. It
does not print all coefficients of a universal unbounded polynomial or
supply a numerical value for $v$. The explicit compiler in the next
section addresses a different, quantitatively controlled task: a bounded
trace with a unique witness.

\section{A clock-independent unique-witness quartic compiler}\label{pqc:ad:sec:bounded}
\srcmark{12}

\subsection{The bounded input convention}
Fix $M$, a time bound $T\ge0$, and an input-bit bound $S\ge0$. These are
\emph{compiler parameters}. The public polynomial input is one natural
number $n$. A valid initial input has the form
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:initialinput}
n=E(q_0,0,R),\qquad 0\le R<2^S.
\end{equation}
Writing $R=\sum_{i=0}^{S-1}d_i2^i$ with $d_i\in\Bit$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:packedinput}
n=1+2q_0+2^{r+2}\sum_{i=0}^{S-1}d_i4^i.
\end{equation}
The factor $2^{r+2}$, rather than $2^{r+1}$, reflects the odd positions of
the right-tape bits in the interleaving.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit bounded certificate]\label{pqc:ad:thm:bounded}
There is an effectively constructed integer polynomial
$C_{M,T,S}(n,w)$ of degree at most four, with
\begin{align}
V&=(3m+6)T+3S+m+4 \label{pqc:ad:eq:V}\\
R_{\mathrm{eq}}&=(4m+7)T+3S+2m+7 \label{pqc:ad:eq:Req}
%
\end{align}
natural witness variables and quadratic-or-linear squared residuals,
respectively, such that the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item $n$ is a valid input \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:initialinput} and $M$ halts on that
input within $T$ machine steps;
\item there exists $w\in\N^V$ with $C_{M,T,S}(n,w)=0$.
\end{enumerate}
For each fixed $n$, there is at most one such witness. On valid initial
inputs, these conditions are also equivalent to
$F_h^{T+1}(n)=0$ for every admissible clock. The residual coefficients are
bounded in magnitude by a constant depending only on $M$, not on $T,S$.
The sparse description size is $O_M(T+S+1)$, and the accepting witness
coordinates have bit length $O_M(T+S+1)$.
\end{theorem}

We give the full construction and proof rather than treating bounded
trace encoding as a black box.

\subsection{Input bits and bounded-coefficient packing}
Introduce the $S$ bits $d_i$, and two Horner sequences
$x_0,\ldots,x_S$ and $y_0,\ldots,y_S$. Use the residuals
\begin{align}
d_i(d_i-1)&=0 &&(0\le i<S),\label{pqc:ad:eq:bits}\\
x_0=y_0&=0,\nonumber\\
x_{i+1}-2x_i-d_{S-1-i}&=0 &&(0\le i<S),\label{pqc:ad:eq:hornerx}\\
y_{i+1}-4y_i-d_{S-1-i}&=0 &&(0\le i<S),\label{pqc:ad:eq:hornery}\\
n-1-2q_0-2^{r+2}y_S&=0.\label{pqc:ad:eq:packres}
\end{align}
Here $x_S=R$ and $y_S=\sum_i d_i4^i$. Horner evaluation avoids inserting
coefficients such as $4^{S-1}$ directly into the polynomial system. The
only power of two appearing in \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:packres} depends on the fixed
machine.

\subsection{Configurations and one-hot control}
Introduce $L_t,R_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and state bits $s_{t,q}$ for
$0\le t\le T$, $q\in Q$. The constraints are
\begin{align}
L_0&=0,& R_0-x_S&=0,\label{pqc:ad:eq:initialtapes}\\
s_{t,q}(s_{t,q}-1)&=0,& \sum_{q\in Q}s_{t,q}-1&=0,\label{pqc:ad:eq:onehot}\\
s_{0,q}-\indic{q=q_0}&=0.&&\label{pqc:ad:eq:initialstate}
\end{align}
All variables range over $\N$. Thus \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:onehot} says that precisely
one state is selected at each time.

For every $t<T$, introduce $a_t,b_t,A_t,B_t$ and impose
\begin{align}
L_t-2A_t-a_t&=0,&R_t-2B_t-b_t&=0,\label{pqc:ad:eq:division}\\
a_t(a_t-1)&=0,&b_t(b_t-1)&=0.\label{pqc:ad:eq:tapebits}
\end{align}
These enforce the unique quotient and remainder upon division by two.
There is no hidden natural-number truncated subtraction in the equations:
all residuals are ordinary integer polynomials evaluated on natural
variables.

\subsection{Selectors and simultaneous transition equations}
For each $t<T$, $q\in Q$, and $c\in\Bit$, introduce a selector $e_{t,q,c}$
and impose
\begin{align}
e_{t,q,0}-s_{t,q}(1-b_t)&=0,\label{pqc:ad:eq:e0}\\
e_{t,q,1}-s_{t,q}b_t&=0.\label{pqc:ad:eq:e1}
\end{align}
They force exactly one selector to be one and the others to be zero.
Additional Boolean equations for the selectors are unnecessary.

For a nonhalting table entry $(q,c)$, let $\tau_{q,c}$ be its target state,
and let $(U_{q,c},W_{q,c})$ be the affine pair of tape expressions in
\eqref{pqc:ad:eq:tape}, evaluated on the time-$t$ variables. For $q=q_h$ set
\[
\tau_{q_h,c}=q_h,\qquad U_{q_h,c}=L_t,\qquad W_{q_h,c}=R_t.
\]
This is the identity padding of a halting trace. Impose
\begin{align}
s_{t+1,p}-\sum_{\tau_{q,c}=p}e_{t,q,c}&=0 &&(p\in Q),\label{pqc:ad:eq:stateupdate}\\
L_{t+1}-\sum_{q,c}e_{t,q,c}U_{q,c}&=0,\label{pqc:ad:eq:Lupdate}\\
R_{t+1}-\sum_{q,c}e_{t,q,c}W_{q,c}&=0.\label{pqc:ad:eq:Rupdate}
\end{align}
Every expression is of degree at most two. The potentially signed term
$1-b_t$ is used inside an integer polynomial and is zero or one on every
solution. Finally impose
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:finalhalt}
s_{T,q_h}-1=0.
\end{equation}
Let $\mathcal R$ be the ordered list of all the residuals just specified.
The promised polynomial is the literal sum of squares
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:ad:eq:certificate}
C_{M,T,S}(n,w)=\sum_{R\in\mathcal R}R(n,w)^2.
\end{equation}
The use of $R$ as a residual in this display is local; it is not a tape
variable.

\subsection{Soundness, completeness, and uniqueness}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:bounded}: semantic assertions]
A zero of \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:certificate} over natural witnesses makes every
integer residual zero, because a sum of nonnegative integer squares
vanishes only when each square does. The bit and Horner equations force
the input packing \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:packedinput}, with $0\le x_S<2^S$. The initial
tape and state equations therefore specify precisely the claimed initial
configuration.

At each time, the one-hot equations specify one state. Division equations
and Boolean remainders specify the scanned bit and both tape tails.
Equations \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:e0}--\eqref{pqc:ad:eq:e1} select precisely the applicable
transition. Equations \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:stateupdate}--\eqref{pqc:ad:eq:Rupdate} are then
exactly that transition, including identity padding at halt. By induction,
the trace is the deterministic padded run of $M$. Equation
\eqref{pqc:ad:eq:finalhalt} implies that this run has reached its halt state by
$T$. This is soundness.

Conversely, if the machine halts within $T$, fill the variables with the
input digits, the two Horner computations, and the actual padded run.
Use the ordinary quotients and remainders for $A_t,B_t,a_t,b_t$, and the
selected transition indicators for $e_{t,q,c}$. Every residual vanishes.
This proves completeness.

For uniqueness, the public value $n$ fixes $y_S$ by
\eqref{pqc:ad:eq:packres}, and a base-four expansion of fixed length $S$ with
digits in $\Bit$ is unique, including leading zero digits. Thus it fixes
all $d_i$, then all $x_i,y_i$, and then the initial configuration. The
quotient-remainder equations have unique natural solutions. The selectors
are fixed by the current state and scanned bit. The next configuration is
fixed by the update equations. Induction fixes the entire witness tuple.
Identity padding introduces no choice even if the machine halts early.

The equivalence with $F_h^{T+1}(n)=0$ on valid initial inputs follows from
the precise time offset in Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:simulation}. The formulation
includes $T=0$ and $S=0$: an empty input-bit list encodes $R=0$, and a
zero-step trace accepts exactly when the initial state is halting.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact counts and complexity}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
Witness family & Number\\
\midrule
Input bits $d_i$ & $S$\\
Horner accumulators $x_i,y_i$ & $2(S+1)$\\
Tape values $L_t,R_t$ & $2(T+1)$\\
One-hot states $s_{t,q}$ & $m(T+1)$\\
Tape splits $a_t,b_t,A_t,B_t$ & $4T$\\
Transition selectors $e_{t,q,c}$ & $2mT$\\
\midrule
Total & $(3m+6)T+3S+m+4$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
Residual family & Number\\
\midrule
Input Boolean, Horner, packing, initial tapes & $3S+5$\\
All state Boolean and one-hot equations & $(m+1)(T+1)$\\
Initial state equations & $m$\\
Tape divisions and remainder Boolean equations & $4T$\\
Selectors & $2mT$\\
State and tape updates & $(m+2)T$\\
Final halt & $1$\\
\midrule
Total & $(4m+7)T+3S+2m+7$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Each residual has a number of terms bounded in terms of $m$ alone. Its
coefficients are bounded in terms of $r,m$ and the fixed machine table.
Squaring and summing gives degree at most four and
$O_M(T+S+1)$ sparse terms before collection, hence no more after collection.
The theorem claims bounded coefficients for the residual representation;
it does not need an additional bound on collected coefficients of an
arbitrarily chosen expanded presentation.

During $T$ steps, each tape's binary length increases by at most $T$ from
its initial maximum, up to a fixed additive constant. Tape and quotient
values therefore have $O(S+T+1)$ bits. The base-four Horner values have at
most $2S$ bits, and control variables are Boolean. This proves the stated
coordinate bit bound. Since there are $O_M(T+S+1)$ coordinates, a full
witness has $O_M((T+S+1)^2)$ bits under a straightforward explicit encoding.
Linear coordinate count must not be misreported as linear total bit size.

\subsection{Why this is not a single-fold MRDP solution}
For each \emph{fixed pair} $T,S$, the polynomial has at most one accepting
witness. But increasing either bound changes the number of variables and
the polynomial itself. The theorem is a family of bounded representations,
not one fixed-arity representation of unbounded halting. Replacing the
bounds by free variables would require a new compression argument, whose
auxiliary witnesses might cease to be unique. No such argument is assumed
or proved here.

The clock independence is nevertheless useful: even an extremely fast
radial clock can create huge dynamical integers while the certificate stores
only the normalized machine trace. The certificate does not need to store
the clock valuations or the full radial factors at every time.

\subsection{The demonstration machine}
The archive contains a three-state \emph{nonuniversal} machine. Its initial
state is $0$, its halt state is $2$, and its nonhalting rules are

\toprule
State & Read & Next state & Write & Move\\
\midrule
$0$ & $0$ & $1$ & $1$ & $\moveL$\\
$0$ & $1$ & $0$ & $0$ & $\moveR$\\
$1$ & $0$ & $2$ & $1$ & $\blank$\\
$1$ & $1$ & $2$ & $0$ & $\moveL$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Here $r=2$, $K=5$. Start with $L=0$, $R=7$, whose three low bits are one.
Then
\[
J(0,7)=2+8+32=42,\qquad E(0,0,7)=1+8\cdot42=337.
\]
The machine erases the run of three ones, moves left after encountering a
blank, and halts in five machine steps. Under the constant-drift map the
exact orbit is
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrr@{}}
\toprule
Iteration $j$ & $F^j(337)$ & $\nuu(F^j(337))$\\
\midrule
$0$ & $337$ & $0$\\
$1$ & $2592$ & $5$\\
$2$ & $17408$ & $10$\\
$3$ & $32768$ & $15$\\

The rapidly increasing ordinary integer sizes are compatible with rapidly
decreasing $2$-adic norms. The last nonzero iterate encodes the halting

Breadth-first generation gives 1,795 reachable states for the demonstration
transducer, below the generic bound $4,866$ from

\[
V=91,\qquad R_{\rm eq}=117.
\]
Its expanded quartic has 818 nonzero monomials. The archive contains both
the residual presentation and the expanded sparse polynomial, together
with the exact accepting witness for $n=337$.

\subsection{The implementation}
The implementation uses only Python's standard library and exact integers.
\path{code/padic_machine.py} defines the tape machine, encoding,
full-value and residue evaluation, and the finite Mealy compiler.
\path{code/quartic_certificate.py} constructs sparse residual
polynomials and the unique deterministic candidate witness.
\path{code/verify.py} runs the tests and regenerates the example files.
The JSON outputs describe exact polynomial expressions and transition
tables; they are not fitted numerical approximations.

From the archive directory, run

\end{lstlisting}
The deterministic seed is \texttt{20260930}. The suite tests thirteen

zero input, residues at several precisions, and time/input bounds beginning

\section{A concrete formalization route for ProveIt}\label{pqc:ad:sec:formalization}
\srcmark{12}

The useful integration target is not a fresh proof of MRDP. It is a
verified chain from a finite machine table to the predicate consumed by
the existing theorem. The following modular route separates finite
arithmetic from $2$-adic analysis.

\paragraph{Binary tape arithmetic.}
Define the finite transition table and the padded natural configuration
step. Prove the three equations \eqref{pqc:ad:eq:tape} against an elementary
list-of-bits tape semantics. Include explicit theorems for halt padding,
finite support, and the one-step extinction offset.

\paragraph{Encoding and residues.}
Define interleaving first on naturals, prove its inverse and the odd-unit
header decomposition, then prove compatibility of the residue maps.
Construct the $2$-adic map from compatible finite quotients, or use the
existing $2$-adic digit API (\wtag\ that is, Mathlib's \code{PadicInt}; ProveIt has no $2$-adic development of its own) after checking its exact conventions. This
avoids introducing a noncomputable global zero test into an executable
component.

\paragraph{Radial clock and simulation.}
Formalize Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:radial} separately from the machine encoding.
Its proof has only the equal-valuation and unequal-valuation cases.
Next prove the simulation invariant with an explicit clock sequence and
the equivalence of extinction predicates for all admissible clocks.

\paragraph{Finite transducer correctness.}
Use an inductive type for leading, bootstrap, steady, and zero-output
states. Prove the streaming invariant for the bounded buffer. The state
bound is a finite counting theorem; it is logically separate from the
streaming correctness theorem. The necessity half of
Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:clockclass} needs only eventual periodicity of an orbit of
a function on a finite set.

\paragraph{The bounded quartic.}
Represent residuals as multivariate integer polynomials. A finite
sum-of-squares lemma reduces zeros to the residual conjunction. Soundness
and completeness can follow the time-index induction already given.
Uniqueness should be a separate theorem on witness tuples, not an
informal consequence of a Boolean simulator test.

\paragraph{The unbounded MRDP endpoint.}
Establish that natural-number extinction is an \texttt{REPred}; the existing
\texttt{Diophantine.mrdp} then yields the fixed finite polynomial.
A clean theorem should quantify the polynomial before the natural input
and before any admissible-clock choice. The clock-independence lemma is
what makes this order possible.

\paragraph{Analytic rigidity.}
The proof needs local power-series factorization, a bound for the tail,
and uniform entry into a small ball. The polynomial corollary can be
formalized earlier using finite valuation comparisons, without waiting
for the general analytic infrastructure. It is a good independently
useful target.

These are proposed modules and proof obligations. No accompanying Lean
file is represented as having been built, and the Python tests do not
certify a Lean theorem. The inspected public MRDP interface is the only
repository theorem invoked as an inherited endpoint.


\section{\wtag\ Two routes to one phenomenon: sources 14 and 12}
\label{pqc:contr:sec:overlap}
Sources~14 and~12 were written independently, from different pins, and neither
cites the other. Each builds a globally strict contraction with an effectively
known attractor and shows that an exact transient observation is
$\sigone$-complete while every observation separated from the attractor is
decidable. Neither is a special case of the other, and they do not contradict
each other. The table compares them term by term.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.17\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
Item & Source 14 (real piecewise-linear) & Source 12 ($2$-adic)\\
\midrule
Space and metric & $\R^4$ with the sup norm; invariant compact polytope $\Cone$ & $\Ztwo$ with the $2$-adic metric\\
Contraction & globally $1/2$-Lipschitz; on the cone the radius is divided by $B\ge8$ & $|F(x)-F(y)|_2\le\frac12|x-y|_2$; valuation drift at least $K=r+3$ per step\\
Attractor & unique fixed point $0$; zero entropy; unique invariant measure $\delta_0$ (Proposition~\ref{pqc:sc:prop:trivial}) & unique fixed point $0$ (no entropy or measure theorem; its Question~\ref{pqc:ad:q:measure} asks about the basin)\\
Source machine & two-counter (Minsky) program, counters as $2^{-c}$ & binary Turing machine, tapes interleaved in the odd unit part\\
Where computation lives & projective ratio $z/r$; the radius $r$ is the clock (Theorem~\ref{pqc:sc:thm:lift}) & odd unit part $u$ of $x=2^tu$; the valuation $t$ is the clock (Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:radial})\\

No computable bound & no computable positive lower bound on peaks (Corollary~\ref{pqc:sc:cor:gap}) & no computable bound on extinction times (Corollary~\ref{pqc:ad:cor:nobound})\\

Clock freedom & one fixed clock (division by $B$) & any admissible $h(t)\ge t+K$; finite-state exactly when $h(t)-t$ is eventually periodic (Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:clockclass})\\
Finite realization & integer zero-bias ReLU circuit with $9m+2d_M-3$ gates (Proposition~\ref{pqc:sc:prop:gates}) & finite synchronous Mealy transducer (Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:mealy})\\
Regularity at the attractor & a positively homogeneous map differentiable at $0$ is linear, so the construction cannot be $C^1$ at the apex (Proposition~\ref{pqc:sc:prop:rigid}) & differentiable at $0$ exactly when $h(t)-t\to\infty$, and can be flat to all orders (Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:derivative}, Proposition~\ref{pqc:ad:prop:flat})\\
Analytic obstruction & a globally Lipschitz polynomial map is affine; linear half-space problems are not settled & a scalar $p$-adic contraction analytic near $0$ has a uniform extinction horizon (Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:analytic})\\
Bounded certificate & traces the integer-scaled dynamics: $(2G+5)T+1$ witnesses and equations (Theorem~\ref{pqc:sc:thm:quartic}) & traces the source machine: $(3m+6)T+3S+m+4$ witnesses (Theorem~\ref{pqc:ad:thm:bounded})\\
Worked example & three-state counter program, $T=7$: 400 witnesses, 2,105 monomials & three-state machine, $T=5$, $S=3$: 91 witnesses, 117 residuals, 818 monomials\\

\paragraph{The apparent opposition.}
In source~12 reaching the fixed point is hard; in source~14 point reachability is
decidable. The two statements do not conflict. Source~12's map collapses whole
halting shells onto $0$, so it is not injective, and extinction is an exact
singleton observation. Source~14's map is positively homogeneous and never
reaches $0$ from a nonzero cone point, so its hardness must sit in an open region;
that region, the half-space $\ell>0$, reaches all the way to the apex. The common
principle is that a hard target must accumulate at the attractor: $\{0\}$ is
closed but not open in $\Ztwo$, and the halting shells' union is open with $0$ in
its closure; source~14's hard half-space touches the apex. Observations separated
from the attractor are decidable in both.

\paragraph{The regularity mirror.}
The regularity results are mirror images. Source~12 attains differentiability,
and even flatness to all orders, at the fixed point, while scalar analyticity
forces a uniform extinction horizon. Source~14 proves that its homogeneous route
cannot be differentiable at the apex at all. Source~12's analytic horizon
theorem is thus the $2$-adic counterpart of source~14's
Question~\ref{pqc:sc:q:smooth} and of Part~III's
Question~\ref{pqc:cb:q:realizers}, which it partly answers in the scalar
$2$-adic case.

\paragraph{Exact versus robust, and Part III.}
Part~III's map is Lipschitz but expanding (its emergency multiplier is three),
and its robust rejection is a positive per-step noise radius. The two contractions
here have no positive margin to exploit: source~14's margin $B^{-t}/(4n-1)$ tends
to zero (equation~\eqref{pqc:sc:eq:margin}), and source~12's finite quotients are
nilpotent in $\lceil k/K\rceil$ steps, so every positive-precision observation is
trivial. Part~III certifies robust rejection by finite cuts; these sources show
that, for exact observation, even a global contraction with an explicit rate does
not help. Source~12 is a data point for the negative direction of Part~III's
Question~\ref{pqc:cb:q:transfer} (a substrate on which exact simulation destroys
every positive margin), although it does not formalize Part~III's noise-radius
semantics on $\Ztwo$. Source~15 is the exact-precision counterpart on Part~III's
own kind of substrate, rational piecewise-affine networks: without a noise
margin, precision is unbounded memory
(Theorems~\ref{pqc:pm:thm:height} and~\ref{pqc:pm:thm:no-ceiling}).

\paragraph{\wtag\ A third route (batch-78 note, 2 October 2026).}
Part~II of the sibling report \code{stochastic-and-thermal-exactness} of this
category (Theorem \code{ste:ec:thm:main}) gives a real, order-preserving
(coordinatewise monotone) piecewise-affine $1/2$-contraction of $[0,1]^N$, the
Bellman operator of a fixed stochastic game, with the known fixed point
$\frac12\mathbf 1$, for which exact attainment of the fixed point from a dyadic
initial vector is c.e.-complete. Its live clock is erased at halting (Lemma
\code{ste:ec:lem:erasure} there), so the whole vector reaches the fixed point.
It is thus the real counterpart of source~12's exact extinction, and it locates
source~14's decidable point reachability (Theorem~\ref{pqc:sc:thm:point}) in
that compiler's radial clock, which is divided by $B$ at every step and never
vanishes, rather than in real contractions as such. Nothing printed in this
section is contradicted, and the table above is unchanged. The elementary
companions recur there: a fixed positive threshold is decidable (Proposition
\code{ste:ec:prop:threshold}, the argument of
Propositions~\ref{pqc:sc:prop:away} and~\ref{pqc:sc:prop:threshold}), and no
total computable function bounds the first attainment time (Corollary
\code{ste:ec:cor:no-cutoff}, the argument of Corollaries~\ref{pqc:sc:cor:gap}
and~\ref{pqc:ad:cor:nobound}).
