\section{What is being resolved, and what is not}
\label{pqc:pm:sec:scope}
\srcmark{15}

A generic appeal to the Matiyasevich--Robinson--Davis--Putnam theorem shows that
any effectively simulable computational substrate has a Diophantine acceptance
relation. That observation is useful, but by itself says little about the shape,
size, or arithmetic meaning of the certificate. For neural computation the more
informative questions are these: can one certify a trajectory without ambiguous
activation bits, avoid degree inflation, preserve exact rational semantics,
and identify what changes when the weights themselves become unknown?

This article answers those questions for the saturated-linear activation
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:sigma}
 \sigma(u)=\max(0,\min(1,u)).
\end{equation}
The main constructions are summarized in \cref{pqc:pm:tab:results}. In each statement,
``quadratic'' means degree at most two; the domain of the witnesses is $\N$,
including zero. A polynomial is not claimed to be nonnegative on all of $\R^m$
when its proof uses nonnegative coordinates.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.27\linewidth}p{0.35\linewidth}p{0.29\linewidth}}
\toprule
Problem & Representation or bound & Essential qualification\\
\midrule
Fixed rational input, $T$ steps & One quadratic; $4nT$ uniquely determined witnesses & Arity grows with $T$\\
First acceptance at $T$ & Same construction, plus $T$ slacks & No absorbing halt state needed\\
Polyhedral real input, fixed rational weights & Projective quadratic; rational witness exists whenever a real one does & Finite time and linear specifications\\
Bounded rational tied-weight synthesis & Four-layer problem equivalent to $\Hten$; explicit quartic lift & One output must be positive\\
Strict-target rational synthesis & Real feasibility equals rational feasibility; decidable & All target conditions strict\\
First acceptance with denominator height $H$ & $T+1=O_S(H^n(1+\log H)^{|S|-1})$ & $S$ contains the denominator primes\\
Universal fixed rational network & No computable accepting-run precision ceiling & Exact arithmetic, not fixed precision\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The main results and the hypotheses that prevent misleading interpretations.}
\label{pqc:pm:tab:results}
\end{table}

\subsection{Relationship to ProveIt}

The repository was inspected at revision
\begin{center}
\texttt{526c2557f2c6173054794f873a9624ebef616510}.
\end{center}
Its Hilbert-tenth-problem documentation gives the public theorem
\texttt{Diophantine.mrdp}: for a recursively enumerable set $S\subseteq\N$ there
are a fixed finite number of natural witnesses and an integer polynomial
representing membership in $S$. It also documents the converse, bounded-trace
interfaces, and separate article-specific representation bounds
\cite{b62s15-proveit,b62s15-proveit-mrdp}. The guide explicitly distinguishes this existence
interface from a practical polynomial generator with numerical size bounds.

Our contribution is a substrate-specific front end. The local certificate
exposes every scaled neuron value and every saturation deficit. The unbounded
acceptance predicate can subsequently be passed to the repository's MRDP
interface. Neither the repository build nor a Lean formalization of the new
front end was executed for this article. The integration plan in
\cref{pqc:pm:sec:integration} keeps these different obligations separate.

\subsection{Earlier work and the scope of novelty}

Rational saturated-linear recurrent networks are a classical universal model:
Siegelmann and Sontag provide an autonomous simulation with a rational initial
encoding and a coordinate indicating termination \cite{b62s15-ss}. Neural
complementarity formulations also predate this article; for example,
Aydinoglu, Fazlyab, Morari, and Posa represent ReLU-controlled dynamics using
complementarity systems \cite{b62s15-complementarity}. We do not claim either
universality or the complementarity idea as new.

Bounded-time piecewise-affine reachability has an established complexity theory
\cite{b62s15-bounded-reachability}, and real-weight neural training has
$\exists\R$-completeness results \cite{b62s15-real-training}. The proposed refinements
here are the kink-safe unique natural witnesses, the two carefully distinguished
scalings, the restricted four-layer rational synthesis reduction with a direct
quartic lift, and the denominator-prime refinement of the precision bound.
These are explicit statements proved below; a comprehensive priority search
and independent proof review remain necessary before making publication-level
novelty claims.

Most importantly, $\Hten$ is not known to be decidable or undecidable. A 2026
survey still identifies this rational-field case as open, despite major progress
for finitely generated rings \cite[Question 6.2]{b62s15-koymans-pagano}. Our synthesis
result is an equivalence and a barrier, not a resolution of that open problem.

\section{A unique quadratic certificate for a saturated scalar}
\label{pqc:pm:sec:scalar}
\srcmark{15}

\begin{definition}
For $D>0$ and $U\in\R$, put
\[
 [U]_D=\max(0,\min(D,U)).
\]
For nonnegative variables $y,z,a,b$, define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:clamp-poly}
 K_D(U;y,z,a,b)
  =(y+z-D)^2+(y-U-a+b)^2+ya+zb.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Canonical clamp certificate]\label[lemma]{pqc:pm:lem:clamp}
For each $D>0$ and $U\in\R$, the zero set of
$K_D(U;\cdot)$ in $\R_{\geq0}^4$ consists of the single point
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:clamp-witness}
 y=[U]_D,\qquad z=D-y,\qquad
 a=\max(-U,0),\qquad b=\max(U-D,0).
\end{equation}
If $D$ and $U$ are integers, all four coordinates are natural numbers.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Every summand of \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:clamp-poly} is nonnegative on the specified domain.
A zero therefore satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:clamp-relations}
 y+z=D,\qquad y-U-a+b=0,\qquad ya=0,\qquad zb=0.
\end{equation}
In particular $0\leq y\leq D$.

If $0<y<D$, both $y$ and $z$ are positive, so $a=b=0$ and $y=U$.
If $y=0$, then $z=D>0$, whence $b=0$ and $U=-a\leq0$.
If $y=D$, then $a=0$ and $U=D+b\geq D$. These three cases force
\eqref{pqc:pm:eq:clamp-witness}, and substitution verifies that point directly.
At $U=0$ and $U=D$, both excess variables are zero. Thus the thresholds create
no extra witnesses. Integrality follows from the displayed formulas.
\end{proof}

The terms $ya$ and $zb$ are complementarity conditions. Squaring them would
raise the degree to four for no reason: the witness domain already makes them
nonnegative. This simple observation is the degree-saving step used throughout
the fixed-weight constructions.

\begin{remark}[No branch selector is needed]
A lower/middle/upper activation label is ambiguous at a threshold if the
corresponding branch intervals are closed. The four numbers in
\eqref{pqc:pm:eq:clamp-witness} are not ambiguous. We use branch itineraries later only
as an existence proof for rational points, never as part of the canonical
fixed-input witness.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Domain dependence]
Over arbitrary signed witnesses, $ya+zb$ can be negative and cancel the squares.
All subsequent single-polynomial equivalences retain the natural-number domain.
Replacing each natural variable by a sum of four integer squares is possible,
but changes the degree and witness count. Those changed bounds are not the
bounds claimed here.
\end{remark}

\section{Prescribed rational trajectories: one quadratic, unique witnesses}
\label{pqc:pm:sec:trace}
\srcmark{15}

\subsection{The network model and its canonical scale}

Fix $n\geq1$, an integer matrix $A\in\Z^{n\times n}$, an integer bias vector
$b\in\Z^n$, and a positive integer $B$. The synchronous autonomous network is
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:network}
 x^{t+1}_i=\sigma\left(\frac{\sum_j A_{ij}x^t_j+b_i}{B}\right),
 \qquad x^t\in[0,1]^n.
\end{equation}
Every rational-weight, rational-bias network of this form admits such a common
$B$, by clearing denominators. The chosen $B$ need not be minimal.

The initial state is fixed rational data
\[
 x^0_i=p_i/D_0,\qquad D_0\geq1,\quad 0\leq p_i\leq D_0,
 \quad p_i\in\Z.
\]
For a prescribed horizon $T\in\N$, let
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:canonical-scales}
 D_t=D_0B^t\quad(0\leq t\leq T).
\end{equation}
All $D_t$ are constants computed by the compiler. In particular,
\eqref{pqc:pm:eq:canonical-scales} does not introduce exponentiation into the
Diophantine language.

\subsection{The explicit polynomial}

Set $X_{0,i}=p_i$ as constants. For every $0\leq t<T$ and $1\leq i\leq n$,
introduce four natural variables
\[
 X_{t+1,i},\quad C_{t+1,i},\quad L_{t,i},\quad H_{t,i},
\]
and put
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:Utrace}
 U_{t,i}=\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}X_{t,j}+b_iD_t.
\end{equation}
The trace polynomial is
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:trace-poly}
 P_{\NNet,p,D_0,T}
 =\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{i=1}^n
 K_{D_{t+1}}(U_{t,i};X_{t+1,i},C_{t+1,i},L_{t,i},H_{t,i}).
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Canonical finite-trace representation]\label{pqc:pm:thm:trace}
The integer polynomial \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:trace-poly} has degree at most two and exactly
$4nT$ designated witness coordinates. It is nonnegative on their natural-number
domain, has exactly one natural zero, and that zero satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:decoded-trace}
 X_{t,i}/D_t=x^t_i\qquad(0\leq t\leq T),
\end{equation}
where $x^t$ is the unique run of \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:network} from $p/D_0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each $U_{t,i}$ is affine in the witness variables, so every summand has degree
at most two. Nonnegativity follows from \cref{pqc:pm:lem:clamp}.

Construct the witness chronologically. The $X_{0,i}$ are fixed. Given all
$X_{t,i}$, equation \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:Utrace} gives an integer $U_{t,i}$, and
\cref{pqc:pm:lem:clamp} gives a unique natural quadruple at each neuron. Its state
coordinate obeys
\[
 \frac{X_{t+1,i}}{D_{t+1}}
 =\sigma\left(\frac{U_{t,i}}{D_{t+1}}\right)
 =\sigma\left(\frac{\sum_j A_{ij}(X_{t,j}/D_t)+b_i}{B}\right).
\]
Induction proves \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:decoded-trace} and constructs a zero of the whole
sum. Conversely, any zero makes every nonnegative block vanish. Starting at
$t=0$, the scalar uniqueness lemma forces each quadruple in turn, so no second
zero exists. When $T=0$, the polynomial is zero on the unique empty tuple;
the statement remains valid.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Acceptance and first acceptance}

Choose a halt coordinate $h$, with acceptance defined by $x_h=1$. Adding
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:accept}
 (X_{T,h}-D_T)^2
\end{equation}
to \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:trace-poly} gives a polynomial with one natural zero precisely
when the network accepts at time $T$, and no natural zeros otherwise.
For first acceptance, also introduce $s_0,\ldots,s_{T-1}\in\N$ and add
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:first-hit}
 \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}(D_t-X_{t,h}-1-s_t)^2.
\end{equation}

\begin{corollary}[First-hit certificate]\label[corollary]{pqc:pm:cor:first-hit}
The polynomial \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:trace-poly} plus \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:accept} and
\eqref{pqc:pm:eq:first-hit} has degree at most two and $4nT+T$ witness coordinates.
It has exactly one natural zero if first acceptance occurs at $T$, and none
otherwise.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The trace part forces the unique trajectory. Because $X_{t,h}$ is an integer
between zero and $D_t$, a natural solution of
$D_t-X_{t,h}-1-s_t=0$ exists exactly when $X_{t,h}<D_t$, and its value is
uniquely $D_t-X_{t,h}-1$. The final square enforces acceptance. No assertion
that acceptance persists at later times is needed.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Witness and coefficient sizes}

\begin{proposition}[Finite-horizon precision bound]\label[proposition]{pqc:pm:prop:witness-bound}
Let
\[
 R_0=\max\left(1,B,\max_i\bigl(|b_i|+\sum_j|A_{ij}|\bigr)\right).
\]
Every coordinate of the canonical zero, including the first-hit slacks when
present, is at most $R_0D_0B^T$. Its binary length is consequently at most
$1+\lceil\log_2(R_0D_0B^T+1)\rceil$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
State and complement coordinates are at most $D_{t+1}\leq D_0B^T$.
The bound $0\leq X_{t,j}\leq D_t$ gives
$|U_{t,i}|\leq R_0D_t$. The two excesses are
$\max(-U_{t,i},0)$ and $\max(U_{t,i}-D_{t+1},0)$, each at most
$R_0D_t$. Finally $0\leq s_t<D_t$ whenever a first-hit witness exists.
\end{proof}

The structured expression contains $2nT$ squared affine residuals and $2nT$
unsquared complementarity products, before acceptance conditions are added.
In a dense implementation, writing the affine residuals takes $O(n^2T)$
coefficient occurrences. Expanding their squares can take $O(n^3T)$ monomial
occurrences; storing the residuals is usually preferable. Coefficient bit
length grows polynomially in $T$ and the binary description of the rational
data. This is a finite-horizon statement: it gives no computable bound on
$T$ for an eventually accepting universal computation.

\begin{example}[A complete first-hit trace]\label[example]{pqc:pm:ex:trace}
Consider
\[
 x^{t+1}=\sigma\bigl((6x^t-1)/4\bigr),\qquad x^0=3/5.
\]
The first value equal to one occurs at $T=4$:
\[
 \frac35,\quad\frac{13}{20},\quad\frac{29}{40},\quad\frac{67}{80},\quad1.
\]
The integer data are shown in \cref{pqc:pm:tab:example}. There are sixteen trace
witnesses and four first-hit slacks, namely $1,6,21,51$. The complete expanded
quadratic and its twenty-coordinate zero are included in
\pathtext{examples/fixed_trace.json}.
\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{rrrrrr}
\toprule
$t$ & $D_t$ & $X_t$ & $U_{t-1}$ & $C_t$ & $H_{t-1}$\\
\midrule
0&5&3&---&---&---\\
1&20&13&13&7&0\\
2&80&58&58&22&0\\
3&320&268&268&52&0\\
4&1280&1280&1288&0&8\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The canonical scale is not reduced at every step. All lower excesses
$L_{t-1}$ are zero.}
\label{pqc:pm:tab:example}
\end{table}
\end{example}

\paragraph{\wtag\ Relation to Part III's neural corollary.}
Theorem~\ref{pqc:pm:thm:trace} certifies the finite runs of \emph{any} concrete
rational clipped network, and $\sigma(u)=\ReLU(u)-\ReLU(u-1)$, so the same
unique-witness quadratic also certifies a concrete rational ReLU network once it
is rewritten with clipped units. It is therefore the certification layer that an
extraction of the network of Corollary~\ref{pqc:cb:cor:relu} would need. It
does not extract that network: Question~\ref{pqc:cb:q:neural} remains open.

\section{Projective quadratic certificates for real-input reachability}
\label{pqc:pm:sec:projective}
\srcmark{15}

The preceding canonical scale starts from a specified rational input. A finite
reachability question may instead ask whether \emph{some real input} in a
rational polyhedron reaches a target. A preselected grid can miss such a
trajectory. The correct replacement is an existential common denominator,
not arbitrary rounding.

\subsection{Specifications and rationalization}

Fix the rational network, the finite horizon $T$, and a finite conjunction of
rational affine equalities, weak inequalities, and strict inequalities in the
coordinates of $x^0,\ldots,x^T$. The variables remain in $[0,1]^n$ at every
time. This includes rational polyhedral input regions and target regions;
it also allows linear conditions at intermediate times.

\begin{lemma}[Rational finite-trajectory witnesses]\label[lemma]{pqc:pm:lem:rationalize}
Such a specification has a real trajectory if and only if it has a rational
trajectory, meaning all coordinates of all $x^t$ are rational.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The reverse implication is immediate. Given a real trajectory, choose a
lower, middle, or upper activation branch for each of its $nT$ evaluations.
The branch equations and inequalities are respectively
\[
 z\leq0,\ y=0;\qquad 0\leq z\leq1,\ y=z;\qquad z\geq1,\ y=1.
\]
Here $z$ is the rational affine preactivation. Intersect these constraints
with the specification and the state cube. The result is a nonempty bounded
set defined by rational affine equalities and weak or strict inequalities.

For completeness, such a set contains a rational point. Replace each strict
condition $\ell_j(x)>0$ by $\ell_j(x)\geq\eta$, add $0\leq\eta\leq1$, and
maximize $\eta$. The given point makes some $\eta>0$ feasible. A maximum is
attained on the resulting compact rational polytope, and an optimal vertex has
rational coordinates. Its $x$-coordinates satisfy the original strict
conditions. If there are no strict conditions, any vertex of the nonempty
compact rational polytope suffices. Rationality of a vertex follows by solving
a full-rank system of active rational linear equations. All chosen activation
relations hold at this rational point, so it is a genuine trajectory.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The projective lift}

Introduce $Q\geq1$ and write $x^t_i=X_{t,i}/Q$. We eliminate a positivity
inequality by setting $Q=1+r$ with $r\in\N$. For every state coordinate,
introduce a complement $C_{t,i}$ and impose
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:proj-bound}
 X_{t,i}+C_{t,i}=Q.
\end{equation}
For each neuron-time pair put
\[
 V_{t,i}=\sum_j A_{ij}X_{t,j}+b_iQ
\]
and impose
\begin{align}
 B X_{t+1,i}-V_{t,i}-L_{t,i}+H_{t,i}&=0,
 \label{pqc:pm:eq:proj-transition}\\
 X_{t+1,i}L_{t,i}=0,\qquad C_{t+1,i}H_{t,i}&=0.
 \label{pqc:pm:eq:proj-complement}
\end{align}
These are the scalar clamp relations with total output scale $BQ$, after
multiplying the state and complement by $B$; since $B>0$, the unsquared
products in \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:proj-complement} are equivalent to those rescaled
complementarity conditions.

Clear denominators in each affine specification. If
$\ell(x)=c_0+\sum c_{t,i}x^t_i$ has integer coefficients, its homogenization is
\[
 \ell^h(X,Q)=c_0Q+\sum c_{t,i}X_{t,i}.
\]
An equality becomes $\ell^h=0$. A weak inequality $\ell\geq0$ becomes
$\ell^h-s=0$, and a strict inequality $\ell>0$ becomes $\ell^h-1-s=0$, with
one new natural slack in each case.

\begin{theorem}[Projective quadratic reachability]\label{pqc:pm:thm:projective}
For fixed rational weights and a finite affine specification, one can
construct an integer polynomial of degree at most two whose natural zero set
is nonempty exactly when a real satisfying trajectory exists. With $k$
specified inequalities, the construction uses
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:proj-count}
 2n+4nT+k+1
\end{equation}
witness coordinates. Its terms are the squares of the linear residuals just
described, plus the unsquared products in \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:proj-complement}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A natural zero forces every nonnegative summand to vanish. Dividing the state
coordinates by $Q=1+r>0$ gives the network equations by the scalar lemma.
The bound equations place all states in the cube. The specification is
recovered by dividing each homogenized relation by $Q$; in particular,
$1+s>0$ gives a strict inequality.

Conversely, \cref{pqc:pm:lem:rationalize} supplies a rational satisfying trajectory.
Choose a common denominator $Q$ for its finitely many state coordinates. Then
$X=Qx$ and $C=Q-X$ are natural. With $V$ as above, choose
\[
 L_{t,i}=\max(-V_{t,i},0),\qquad
 H_{t,i}=\max(V_{t,i}-BQ,0).
\]
These are integers and satisfy all transition and complementarity relations.
A strictly positive homogenized integer is at least one, so all the
specification slacks also exist. The count is $2n(T+1)$ states and
complements, $2nT$ excesses, $k$ inequality slacks, and $r$.
\end{proof}

There is intentionally no uniqueness assertion: multiplying a successful
common denominator produces further representations of the same rational
trajectory. Moreover, different inputs may satisfy the specification.

\subsection{An explicit small-denominator bound}

\begin{theorem}[A determinant bound]\label{pqc:pm:thm:denom-small}
Let $m=n(T+1)$. After choosing an activation itinerary and clearing all linear
constraints, suppose every coefficient and right-hand side has absolute value
at most $M\geq1$. If the resulting specification is feasible and contains no
strict inequalities, it has a trajectory with a common denominator
\[
 Q\leq m!M^m.
\]
With strict inequalities, it has one with
\[
 Q\leq (m+1)!M^{m+1}.
\]
The bound $M$ includes the coefficient $1$ of the auxiliary margin variable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In the closed case, take a vertex of the bounded feasible polytope. There are
$m$ linearly independent active constraints, including equations represented
as pairs of inequalities when necessary. Their integer coefficient matrix
$E$ has nonzero determinant. Cramer's rule expresses every coordinate with
common denominator $|\det E|$. The Leibniz formula bounds this determinant
by $m!M^m$. Lower-dimensional polytopes cause no exception: at a vertex the
active normals still span the full ambient coordinate space.

For strict constraints use the auxiliary $\eta$ construction in the proof
of \cref{pqc:pm:lem:rationalize}, and choose a vertex of the positive optimal face.
This is a vertex of the entire polytope in $m+1$ variables. The same argument
bounds a common denominator for both the trajectory and $\eta$.
\end{proof}

If $T$ is presented in unary, the bit length of this bound is polynomial in
the expanded linear-system description. This recovers the usual short
rational-witness mechanism behind finite piecewise-affine reachability;
we do not claim a new complexity classification \cite{b62s15-bounded-reachability}.
The determinant bound concerns a successful rational trajectory, not a
uniform denominator for every point in an input region.

\begin{example}[A preselected grid can miss the answer]\label[example]{pqc:pm:ex:projective}
For $x'=\sigma(2x-1/2)$ and the target $x'=1/3$, the input must be $x=5/12$.
A grid with denominator two contains no such input. With $Q=1+r$, a suitable
seven-variable projective polynomial is
\begin{align*}
 &(X_0+C_0-Q)^2+(X_1+C_1-Q)^2\\
 &\quad +(2X_1-4X_0+Q-L+H)^2+X_1L+C_1H+(3X_1-Q)^2.
\end{align*}
At $Q=12$ its zero is
\[
 (X_0,C_0,X_1,C_1,L,H,r)=(5,7,4,8,0,0,11).
\]
Every positive multiple of twelve also supplies a scale, with the associated
coordinates scaled accordingly. The file
\pathtext{examples/projective_trace.json} contains the expanded polynomial.
\end{example}

\section{The rational parameter-synthesis frontier}
\label{pqc:pm:sec:synthesis}
\srcmark{15}

The preceding rationalization theorem depends critically on fixed weights.
When an unknown weight multiplies an unknown activation, activation cells
are no longer polyhedra in all unknowns. The obstruction is not merely
numerical conditioning: rational feasibility can now express a major
Diophantine decision problem.

\subsection{The precise synthesis model}

\begin{definition}[Bounded tied-weight synthesis]\label[definition]{pqc:pm:def:synthesis}
An instance consists of a finite feedforward network with four non-input
layers. Every node uses $\sigma$. There is a single fixed input equal to one.
Each edge weight is either a fixed rational number or one of the named unknown
parameters $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k$. The parameters must belong to
$\Q\cap[0,1]$ and may be reused on multiple edges; such reuse is called a
\emph{tie}. Biases are fixed rationals. Two output nodes, denoted $o$ and $p$,
are distinguished. The question is whether there are parameter values with
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:synthesis-output}
 o=0,\qquad p>0.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

The number of nodes is part of the instance. Four is a depth bound, not a
claim of fixed width or a fixed universal architecture. Parameters do not
change during an evaluation, and all uses of the same named parameter must
agree exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Four-layer rational synthesis equivalence]\label{pqc:pm:thm:synthesis}
The decision problem in \cref{pqc:pm:def:synthesis} and $\Hten$ are computably
many-one equivalent. In the reduction from $\Hten$, unknown weights occur
only in the first two layers. All parameters lie in $[0,1]$, all biases and
remaining weights can be integers, and there is only one strictly positive
output condition.

Using arithmetic circuits, both reductions have polynomial description size.
In particular, the lower reduction avoids expansion of high-degree
polynomials after homogenization.
\end{theorem}

We prove the theorem in three steps, giving every transformation explicitly.

\subsection{Step one: a bounded quadratic presentation of a rational zero}

Let $P\in\Z[z_1,\ldots,z_m]$ be the input to $\Hten$. Introduce variables
for the wires of an arithmetic circuit computing $P$. Its constraints can be
chosen from
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:circuit-relations}
 z_k=z_i+z_j,\quad z_k=z_i-z_j,\quad z_k=z_iz_j,\quad z_i=c,
 \qquad z_{\mathrm{out}}=0,
\end{equation}
where $c\in\Z$. A solution of $P=0$ extends to a solution of these constraints
by evaluating the circuit. Conversely, a solution of the constraints gives
$P=0$ by induction through the circuit.

Even when a sparse polynomial uses exponents in binary, repeated squaring
produces a circuit of polynomial size. Thus no unbounded expansion is hidden
in this step.

\begin{lemma}[Compactification with one positive scale]\label[lemma]{pqc:pm:lem:compactification}
A finite circuit system \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:circuit-relations} has a rational solution
if and only if a corresponding finite system of quadratic integer equations
has a solution in parameters
\[
 a_i,v\in\Q\cap[0,1],\qquad v>0.
\]
The transformation is explicit and increases description size only
polynomially.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For every circuit wire put
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:compactify}
 u_i=2a_i-1,\qquad z_i=u_i/v.
\end{equation}
Translate the relations in \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:circuit-relations} into
\begin{align}
 u_k-u_i-u_j&=0 &&\text{for addition},\label{pqc:pm:eq:bounded-add}\\
 u_k-u_i+u_j&=0 &&\text{for subtraction},\label{pqc:pm:eq:bounded-sub}\\
 vu_k-u_iu_j&=0 &&\text{for multiplication},\label{pqc:pm:eq:bounded-mul}\\
 u_i-cv&=0 &&\text{for a constant},\label{pqc:pm:eq:bounded-const}\\
 u_{\mathrm{out}}&=0.\label{pqc:pm:eq:bounded-out}
\end{align}
After substituting $u_i=2a_i-1$, these are integer polynomials of degree at
most two. For example, the multiplication equation is
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:expanded-mul}
 2va_k-v-4a_ia_j+2a_i+2a_j-1=0.
\end{equation}

Given rational values for the original wires, choose a positive rational
$v\leq1$ so small that $|vz_i|\leq1$ for every wire. Such a choice exists
because there are only finitely many wire values. Set $a_i=(1+vz_i)/2$.
All parameters lie in $[0,1]$ and satisfy the new equations. Conversely,
$v>0$ makes \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:compactify} legitimate, and division by $v$ or $v^2$
recovers each original circuit relation. Every transformed equation has
bounded degree and constant-size support relative to its circuit gate.
\end{proof}

The condition $v>0$ is essential. At $v=0$, the affine chart disappears,
and the homogeneous multiplication constraints no longer reconstruct the
original rational wire values. We retain that condition explicitly rather
than silently admitting points at infinity.

\subsection{Step two: realize the quadratic system in four layers}

Let $R_1(\theta),\ldots,R_E(\theta)$ be the quadratic polynomials supplied by
\cref{pqc:pm:lem:compactification}; the parameter list $\theta$ includes all $a_i$
and $v$. Let $k$ be the number of parameters and let $q$ be the number of
distinct degree-two monomials occurring in the $R_\ell$.

\begin{lemma}[Four-layer realization]\label[lemma]{pqc:pm:lem:four-layers}
There is a network of the form in \cref{pqc:pm:def:synthesis} with
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:neuron-count}
 2k+q+2E+3
\end{equation}
non-input neurons whose outputs satisfy
\[
 o=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ R_1(\theta)=\cdots=R_E(\theta)=0,
 \qquad p=v.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The four layers are as follows.

\emph{Layer one.} For each parameter, set
$h_i=\sigma(\theta_i\cdot1)=\theta_i$. This uses $k$ neurons.

\emph{Layer two.} Copy each $h_i$, using weight one, and for each needed
monomial $\theta_i\theta_j$ create the neuron
\[
 h_{ij}=\sigma(\theta_i h_j)=\theta_i\theta_j.
\]
Both factors lie in $[0,1]$, so clipping does not change the product. The use
of $\theta_i$ here is tied to its occurrence in layer one. This layer uses
$k+q$ neurons, including square monomials when $i=j$.

\emph{Layer three.} Every $R_\ell$ is now an integer affine expression in
the second-layer copies and products. Create
\[
 r_\ell^+=\sigma(R_\ell),\qquad r_\ell^-=\sigma(-R_\ell)
\]
for each equation, and one additional copy of $v$. Since $\sigma(s)=0$ if
and only if $s\leq0$, the two detectors are simultaneously zero exactly when
$R_\ell=0$. Saturation at large values introduces no false zeros. There are
$2E+1$ neurons in this layer.

\emph{Layer four.} Define
\[
 o=\sigma\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^E(r_\ell^++r_\ell^-)\right),
 \qquad p=\sigma(v)=v.
\]
Every summand entering $o$ is nonnegative, so $o=0$ precisely when all
detectors vanish. Adding the four layer sizes gives \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:neuron-count}.
\end{proof}

Together, \cref{pqc:pm:lem:compactification,pqc:pm:lem:four-layers} prove the reduction
$\Hten\leq_m$ bounded tied-weight synthesis. The construction uses products
only where parameters serve as weights; no neuron is given a nonstandard
multiplication activation.

\subsection{Step three: reduce rational synthesis back to a polynomial}

\begin{lemma}[Nonnegativity over the rationals]\label[lemma]{pqc:pm:lem:four-squares}
For $r\in\Q$, one has $r\geq0$ if and only if
$r=t_1^2+t_2^2+t_3^2+t_4^2$ for some $t_i\in\Q$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The reverse implication follows from the ordering of $\Q$. For the forward
implication, write $r=a/b$ with $a\in\N$ and $b\geq1$ integral. Lagrange's
four-square theorem gives integers $k_i$ with $ab=\sum k_i^2$. Taking
$t_i=k_i/b$ proves the claim, including $a=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Completion of \cref{pqc:pm:thm:synthesis}]
Introduce rational variables for all parameters, node values, and the scalar
clamp auxiliaries. For each node use the relations
\eqref{pqc:pm:eq:clamp-relations} with $D=1$ and the node's preactivation $U$.
That preactivation is polynomial of degree at most two in the unknowns:
each edge is a fixed rational weight times a state or a named parameter
times a state. Impose nonnegativity of the clamp variables and both
$\theta_i$ and $1-\theta_i$.

The resulting equations and inequalities describe exactly the rational
network graph by \cref{pqc:pm:lem:clamp}. Enforce $o=0$. The graph already makes
$p\geq0$, so the strict condition $p>0$ is equivalent over $\Q$ to the
existence of a rational $s$ with $ps=1$.

Replace every nonnegativity condition by the four-square equation in
\cref{pqc:pm:lem:four-squares}. Clear rational coefficients in each equation, and
combine all equations $F_j=0$ as $\sum_jF_j^2=0$. Over the ordered field
$\Q$, this single integer polynomial vanishes exactly when all equations
hold. The transformations add only polynomially many variables and
coefficient bits. They are effective and yield an instance of $\Hten$.
This proves the other reduction and completes the theorem.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why real feasibility cannot replace rational feasibility}

\begin{example}[An irrational-only parameter fit]\label[example]{pqc:pm:ex:irrational}
Use a tied parameter $\theta\in[0,1]$, form
\[
 h=\sigma(\theta)=\theta,\qquad z=\sigma(\theta h)=\theta^2,
\]
and demand that both $\sigma(2z-1)$ and $\sigma(1-2z)$ be zero. These
requirements are equivalent to $2\theta^2=1$. A real solution exists, but
no rational solution exists: a reduced fraction $a/b$ would give
$2a^2=b^2$, forcing both $a$ and $b$ even. Padding by copying neurons gives
four layers if desired.
\end{example}

Consequently, a real-arithmetic feasibility engine cannot by itself settle
rational synthesis. The established $\exists\R$-completeness results for
real-weight training concern a different coefficient domain and different
architectural restrictions \cite{b62s15-real-training}. The present reduction
must not be read as a theorem about ordinary untied training, nor as an
undecidability proof for it.

\begin{corollary}[Trading strict positivity for an unbounded gain]
The lower reduction can replace $p>0$ by an exact output condition equal to
one if a single additional unknown nonnegative, unbounded rational weight
$\lambda$ is allowed. The other parameters remain in $[0,1]$, and four
layers still suffice.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
After layer one supplies $v$, add a second-layer neuron
$g=\sigma(\lambda v)$ and copy it through the remaining layers. For
$v\in[0,1]$, a rational $\lambda\geq0$ with $g=1$ exists exactly when
$v>0$: choose $\lambda=1/v$ in the forward direction. At $v=0$, the
output is zero for every finite $\lambda$. The rational upper reduction
works with the extra nonnegativity constraint on $\lambda$.
\end{proof}

This corollary does not remove a hypothesis for free. It exchanges an open
output condition for an unbounded parameter. The all-bounded, closed-target
variant is a separate question.

\subsection{An exact-versus-open-target dichotomy}

There is also a useful positive result on the other side of the exact-zero
boundary. It does not require a four-layer depth restriction.

\begin{theorem}[Strict-target rational synthesis is decidable]\label{pqc:pm:thm:strict}
Consider any finite feedforward clipped network with fixed rational constants
and finitely many tied parameters in $\Q\cap[0,1]$. Suppose that every target
condition is a strict polynomial inequality, with rational coefficients, in
the parameters and the output values. Then rational feasibility is equivalent
to real feasibility and is decidable.

In particular, for a fixed rational $\varepsilon>0$, replacing
$o=0,\ p>0$ by $o<\varepsilon,\ p>0$ produces a decidable problem in this
model.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
As a function of its real parameters in the cube, each node value is continuous:
this follows inductively from continuity of addition, multiplication, and
$\sigma$. Every strict target condition therefore pulls back to a relatively
open subset of the parameter cube. Their finite intersection is relatively
open. The rational points of the cube are dense, so any nonempty such
intersection contains a rational parameter point. Evaluation at rational
parameters is rational, proving the equivalence.

The graph of $\sigma$ is a finite union of sets given by polynomial equations
and inequalities. Thus real feasibility for the entire finite network is an
existential sentence over the real field with rational constants. Real
algebraic decision procedures decide its truth \cite{b62s15-tarski}. By the first
part, their answer is also the answer to the rational problem.
\end{proof}

The theorem requires \emph{all} target conditions to be strict; one cannot
retain an unrelated exact equality and invoke density. The only weak
parameter restrictions used in the proof are the full cube bounds.
Arbitrary extra algebraic restrictions on the parameters would destroy the
density argument. Parameter ties are harmless because each distinct name is
already a single independent coordinate of that cube.

This gives a concrete boundary rather than only a warning: in the specified
finite architecture model, open output tolerance permits a decision
procedure, whereas exact zero together with one positive output can encode
all of $\Hten$. Neither statement asserts an efficient practical algorithm.

\section{A direct quartic natural-number certificate for synthesis}
\label{pqc:pm:sec:quartic}
\srcmark{15}

The reverse reduction in \cref{pqc:pm:thm:synthesis} gives a rational polynomial.
For direct use with a natural-number Diophantine library, one can instead
lift the entire parameter network to one common integer scale. The
construction exposes exactly where degree four enters.

\subsection{Homogenizing parameters and activations together}

For clarity, allow an edge weight to be an affine rational function of the
parameters,
\[
 w_e(\theta)=\frac{a_{e,0}+\sum_a a_{e,a}\theta_a}{B},
\]
with all $a_{e,a}\in\Z$ and a common $B\geq1$. Biases have the form $b_v/B$.
This slightly larger class includes every network constructed above.
The fixed input is one. Choose a common scale $Q=1+r$ and write
\[
 \theta_a=\Theta_a/Q,\qquad x_v=X_v/Q.
\]
Introduce complements $\widehat\Theta_a$ and $C_v$, with
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:syn-bounds}
 \Theta_a+\widehat\Theta_a=Q,\qquad X_v+C_v=Q.
\end{equation}
The integer polynomial representing a preactivation numerator is
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:syn-U}
 U_v=\sum_{e:u\to v}
 \left(a_{e,0}Q+\sum_a a_{e,a}\Theta_a\right)X_u+b_vQ^2.
\end{equation}
For the input node, use $X_{\mathrm{input}}=Q$ as an expression rather than
an extra variable. The actual preactivation is $U_v/(BQ^2)$.

For each non-input node introduce $L_v,H_v\in\N$ and impose
\begin{align}
 BQX_v-U_v-L_v+H_v&=0,\label{pqc:pm:eq:syn-gate}\\
 X_vL_v=0,\qquad C_vH_v&=0.\label{pqc:pm:eq:syn-complement}
\end{align}
The output conditions become
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:syn-target}
 X_o=0,\qquad X_p-1-s=0,\quad s\in\N.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit quartic lift]\label{pqc:pm:thm:quartic}
Square and sum all residuals in
\eqref{pqc:pm:eq:syn-bounds}, \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:syn-gate}, and \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:syn-target}, and add
the unsquared products in \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:syn-complement}. After substituting
$Q=1+r$, the resulting integer polynomial has degree at most four, is
nonnegative on the natural-number orthant, and has a natural zero if and
only if the rational synthesis instance has a solution.

For a network with $k$ bounded parameters and $N$ non-input nodes, the
construction uses $2k+4N+2$ natural witness coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The preactivation numerator \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:syn-U} has degree at most two.
The residual \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:syn-gate} therefore has degree at most two, so its
square has degree at most four. Every remaining squared residual is linear
before squaring, and the two complementarity products per node have degree
two. All summands are nonnegative on natural coordinates.

Suppose the polynomial is zero. Then every residual and every
complementarity product vanishes. Since $Q\geq1$ and $B\geq1$, the bounds
and gate conditions give the clamp relations at scale $BQ^2$, with output
$BQX_v$ and complement $BQC_v$. Multiplication by the positive factor $BQ$
does not alter a zero complementarity condition. The scalar lemma implies
\[
 X_v/Q=\sigma\bigl(U_v/(BQ^2)\bigr).
\]
Induction in the feedforward order recovers the evaluation of the rational
parameter network. The output conditions give $o=0$ and $p>0$.

Conversely, take a rational satisfying parameter assignment and evaluate
all nodes exactly. All activations are rational. Choose a common denominator
$Q$ for all parameters and activations, and set $\Theta_a=Q\theta_a$,
$X_v=Qx_v$. The complements are natural. Each $U_v$ is an integer; choose
\[
 L_v=\max(-U_v,0),\qquad H_v=\max(U_v-BQ^2,0).
\]
The clamp identities make all node conditions hold. Because $x_p>0$,
$X_p$ is a positive integer, so $s=X_p-1$ is natural. This constructs a zero.
The count consists of two coordinates for each parameter, four for each
non-input node, $r$, and the positive-output slack.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Where the quadratic/quartic distinction comes from}

In the fixed-weight projective compiler, the transition residual is
\[
 BX'-AX-bQ-L+H,
\]
which is affine in the unknown integers. In parameter synthesis, it is
\[
 BQX'-U(\Theta,X,Q)-L+H,
\]
which is quadratic. Squaring the latter gives degree four. The increase is
not caused by approximation, by activation branch bits, or by an appeal to
the full MRDP theorem. It records the multiplication of an unknown weight
and an unknown signal.

If $Q$ is replaced by $kQ$ in a valid rational lift, parameter and activation
numerators scale by $k$, while $L_v,H_v$ scale by $k^2$. The positive-output
slack changes from $X_p-1$ to $kX_p-1$. These rescalings provide infinitely
many natural zeros for a successful rational assignment; no uniqueness is
claimed for this compiler.

Combining \cref{pqc:pm:thm:synthesis,pqc:pm:thm:quartic} identifies an explicitly generated
family of quartic natural-number feasibility instances equivalent to
$\Hten$. Here the instance includes its generating network or the displayed
structured residual presentation. No claim is made that recognizing such
presentations from an arbitrary expanded polynomial is automatic. Nor does
the equivalence make the family known to be undecidable.

\begin{example}[A reproducible synthesis instance]\label[example]{pqc:pm:ex:synthesis}
Take the circuit with input wires $x,y$, a constant wire $c=2$, a product
wire $m=xy$, and output wire $z=m-c$. It computes $xy-2$. The rational
solution $x=2,y=1$ gives wire values $(2,1,2,2,0)$. Choose $v=1/4$ and
\[
 (a_x,a_y,a_c,a_m,a_z,v)
   =\left(\frac34,\frac58,\frac34,\frac34,\frac12,\frac14\right).
\]
There are four compactified constraints, two distinct quadratic monomials,
and six parameters. Formula \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:neuron-count} gives
$12+2+8+3=25$ non-input neurons. Their outputs are $(o,p)=(0,1/4)$.
A common scale for these parameters and all evaluated nodes is $Q=32$.
The quartic compiler uses $2\cdot6+4\cdot25+2=114$ natural coordinates.
The complete structured and expanded polynomial, together with a zero, is
in \pathtext{examples/rational_synthesis.json}.
\end{example}

\section{Denominator height as computational memory}
\label{pqc:pm:sec:precision}
\srcmark{15}

The state cube is bounded, but the set of rational points in it is infinite.
The resource that prevents this model from being a finite-state machine is
precision, not the magnitude of the neuron values.

\subsection{Reduced common denominators and prime support}

\begin{definition}
For $x\in\Q^n$, define the reduced common denominator
\[
 q(x)=\min\{q\geq1:q x\in\Z^n\}.
\]
This is the least common multiple of the reduced coordinate denominators,
not the largest individual denominator. For a finite run, define
\[
 H_T=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}q(x^t).
\]
An integer is $S$-smooth if all of its prime divisors belong to a finite
prime set $S$; the integer one is $S$-smooth for every $S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Denominator support invariant]\label[lemma]{pqc:pm:lem:denom-support}
For the rational network \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:network} with initial denominator $D_0$,
\[
 q(x^t)\mid D_0B^t.
\]
Consequently all denominator primes belong to the finite set of prime
divisors of $D_0B$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If the coordinates of $x^t$ have a common denominator dividing $D_0B^t$,
then each affine preactivation divided by $B$ has denominator dividing
$D_0B^{t+1}$. Clipping either leaves that rational value unchanged or replaces
it by zero or one. Induction starts at the given initial state.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Distinct states before first acceptance]\label[lemma]{pqc:pm:lem:distinct}
If a deterministic autonomous network first reaches an accepting state at
time $T$, then $x^0,\ldots,x^T$ are pairwise distinct.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $x^i=x^j$ with $0\leq i<j\leq T$. Determinism gives
$x^{i+k}=x^{j+k}$ for every $k\geq0$. Taking $k=T-j$ gives an accepting state
at $T-(j-i)<T$, contradicting first acceptance. The argument uses only that
acceptance is a predicate of the state.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A prime-sensitive time--height inequality}

\begin{theorem}[First-hit height bound]\label{pqc:pm:thm:height}
Suppose first acceptance occurs at time $T$ in an $n$-neuron network. Put
$H=H_T$, and let $S$ contain all denominator primes along the run. Then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:height-count}
 T+1\leq\sum_{\substack{1\leq q\leq H\\q\ \text{$S$-smooth}}}(q+1)^n.
\end{equation}
If $S=\{p_1,\ldots,p_r\}$ is nonempty, then
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:height-smooth}
 T+1\leq
 \frac{2^n}{1-p_1^{-n}}\,H^n
 \prod_{j=2}^r\left(1+\left\lfloor\log_{p_j}H\right\rfloor\right).
\end{equation}
For fixed $n,S$, this is
$O_S(H^n(1+\log H)^{r-1})$. If $S$ is empty, $T+1\leq2^n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For a fixed common denominator $q$, the grid
$\{0,1/q,\ldots,1\}^n$ has $(q+1)^n$ points. Every state in the run belongs
to the grid of its own reduced common denominator, which is at most $H$ and
has prime support in $S$. Counting the union by the sum of its grid sizes
may overcount, but is an upper bound. By \cref{pqc:pm:lem:distinct}, at least $T+1$
different states must be counted, proving \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:height-count}.

For the sharper estimate, use $(q+1)^n\leq2^nq^n$ for $q\geq1$. Write an
$S$-smooth $q$ uniquely as $q=s p_1^k$, where $s$ has prime factors only in
$\{p_2,\ldots,p_r\}$. For a fixed $s\leq H$, let
$K=\lfloor\log_{p_1}(H/s)\rfloor$. The finite geometric series gives
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^K(sp_1^k)^n
 \leq\frac{(sp_1^K)^n}{1-p_1^{-n}}
 \leq\frac{H^n}{1-p_1^{-n}}.
\]
There are at most
$\prod_{j=2}^r(1+\lfloor\log_{p_j}H\rfloor)$ choices for the exponents
forming $s$. This proves \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:height-smooth}, with the empty product
equal to one when $r=1$. If $S$ is empty, only $q=1$ occurs.
\end{proof}

For a single denominator prime, the bound gives the especially direct
necessary condition
\[
 H\geq\left(\frac{1-p_1^{-n}}{2^n}(T+1)\right)^{1/n}.
\]
Thus, up to an additive constant depending on $n,p_1$, at least
$\log_2(T+1)/n$ bits of common-denominator precision must occur somewhere
before first acceptance. For several fixed primes the logarithmic product
in \eqref{pqc:pm:eq:height-smooth} is the additional factor, rather than the full
extra power of $H$ in the cruder count over all denominators.

\begin{corollary}[Integral weights do not create new precision]
If $B=1$, then every state lies in the fixed grid of denominator $D_0$.
Any first acceptance time satisfies $T+1\leq(D_0+1)^n$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{pqc:pm:lem:denom-support}, $q(x^t)\mid D_0$ for every $t$, so all states
belong to that one grid. Apply \cref{pqc:pm:lem:distinct}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An elementary stack illustration}

The classical base-four binary-stack encoding used in rational neural
universality is \cite{b62s15-ss}
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:pm:eq:stack}
 \enc(s_1\cdots s_k)=\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{2s_i+1}{4^i},
 \qquad \enc(\varnothing)=0.
\end{equation}
For these encodings, a nonempty stack with top bit zero lies in $[1/4,1/2)$,
and one with top bit one lies in $[3/4,1)$. Consequently
\begin{align*}
 \mathrm{nonempty}(x)&=\sigma(4x),&
 \mathrm{top}(x)&=\sigma(4x-2),\\
 \mathrm{push}_b(x)&=(x+1+2b)/4,&
 \mathrm{pop}(x)&=\sigma(4x-1-2\sigma(4x-2)).
\end{align*}
The push identity follows by shifting the base-four expansion. For a
nonempty stack, the inner saturation extracts its first bit, after which
$4x-(1+2s_1)$ is exactly the tail encoding; the outer saturation also maps
the empty-stack case to zero. These formulas explain how a bounded rational
state can carry an arbitrarily long finite word. They illustrate the memory
representation, not a replacement for the full finite-control universality
proof.

\subsection{No computable precision ceiling on accepting computations}

\begin{theorem}[Accepting precision has no computable uniform ceiling]
\label{pqc:pm:thm:no-ceiling}
There exist a fixed rational saturated-linear autonomous network and a
computable rational initial-state encoding $e\mapsto x^0(e)$ such that no
total computable function $f(e)$ bounds $H_T$ for every encoded input that
first accepts at some time $T$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose the fixed network and effective encoding supplied by the autonomous
universality theorem of Siegelmann and Sontag \cite[Theorem 2]{b62s15-ss}, applied
to a universal partial computable function. Its halt coordinate first
becomes one precisely for the accepting machine inputs. Rational network
steps and the equality test for that coordinate are effectively computable
by exact arithmetic.

Suppose such a total computable $f$ exists, and replace it by
$\max(1,f)$ if necessary. On input $e$, compute $H=f(e)$ and
\[
 M(H)=\sum_{q=1}^H(q+1)^n.
\]
Simulate the network for $M(H)$ steps, including the initial acceptance
test. If it accepts, answer yes; otherwise answer no.

To justify the no answer, an eventually accepting run would, by the assumed
bound, have reduced common denominators at most $H$ through first
acceptance. There are at most $M(H)$ possible states of that height in the
cube. By \cref{pqc:pm:lem:distinct}, first acceptance would occur at $T<M(H)$,
and would already have been seen. The algorithm would decide universal
halting, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

The hypothetical precision bound was required only on accepting runs; no
bound on nonaccepting runs was assumed. The same argument excludes a total
computable upper bound on the number of precision bits, since exponentiating
such a bit bound would give a computable denominator bound. It also excludes
a computable bound depending only on input length that works for every
accepting input of that length.

There is no conflict with \cref{pqc:pm:prop:witness-bound}. That proposition bounds
precision as a function of a \emph{given horizon}. The theorem above rules
out a bound computable from the encoded input alone that covers every
successful, unbounded-duration computation.

\section{What can and cannot be compressed into the MRDP back end}
\label{pqc:pm:sec:integration}
\srcmark{15}

\subsection{The honest unbounded statement}

Fix a rational network, an effective rational encoding of natural inputs,
and a decidable acceptance predicate on rational states. Exact simulation
semidecides eventual acceptance: inspect the initial state, then enumerate
time steps until an accepting state appears. The accepted input set is
therefore recursively enumerable. The repository's MRDP interface gives
one fixed integer polynomial $F(e,w_1,\ldots,w_m)$ such that
\[
 \text{input $e$ eventually accepts}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists w\in\N^m\;F(e,w)=0
\]
\cite{b62s15-proveit-mrdp}. For the universal network this is a uniform Diophantine
representation of a complete computably enumerable set.

This conclusion does not preserve the specific degree-two normal form,
the $4nT$ count, or uniqueness of the finite trace witnesses. The MRDP
polynomial has fixed arity, whereas the explicit trajectory compiler has
one block for every simulated neuron-time pair. Describing the latter as a
single-fold fixed-arity representation of unbounded halting would be a
mistake. No assertion about the general finite-fold or single-fold
Diophantine representation questions is proved here.

\subsection{An obstruction specific to the complementarity normal form}

\begin{proposition}[Decidability of the finite affine-complementarity form]
\label[proposition]{pqc:pm:prop:normalform}
Natural feasibility is decidable for any given finite system of rational
affine equations and inequalities, together with finitely many constraints
of the form $u_iv_i=0$, where $u_i,v_i$ are natural-coordinate variables.
Equivalently, it is decidable for a polynomial supplied as a sum of squares
of affine residuals and nonnegative coordinate products, with natural
witnesses and explicitly encoded affine slacks.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For every product $u_iv_i=0$, choose one of the two possibilities $u_i=0$
or $v_i=0$. Enumerate all finitely many such choices. After making a choice,
the remaining constraints are linear integer equations and inequalities
in natural variables, a decidable fragment of Presburger arithmetic. The
original system is feasible exactly when one of these finitely many linear
systems is feasible. A product with a positive rational coefficient has
the same zero condition; a zero coefficient can be discarded.
\end{proof}

Hence no total computable translation of arbitrary machine inputs into this
finite normal form can characterize unbounded halting: following the
translation by the proposition's decision procedure would decide halting.
This explains structurally why the finite quadratic front end cannot simply
retain all its local properties after uniform unbounded compression. The
claim concerns the stated normal form, not an unproved general classification
of all quadratic Diophantine equations.

\subsection{A concrete formalization plan for ProveIt}

A sound integration should establish the following modules in dependency
order. These are proposed proof obligations, not declarations claimed to
have been compiled.

\paragraph{Scalar semantics.}
Define the saturated-linear map and prove \cref{pqc:pm:lem:clamp} first over an
ordered field, then derive the integral specialization. In Lean, separate
integer residual evaluation from the coercions of natural witnesses.
The nonnegative-sum-zero argument should explicitly include the unsquared
products.

\paragraph{Canonical finite execution.}
Represent a rational network by the integer data $(A,b,B)$ and prove the
scale invariant. Define the $T$-step witness constructor recursively and
show that decoding is inverse to zero-set recognition. Prove the first-hit
adapter separately, including $T=0$ and an initially accepting state.

\paragraph{Polynomial extraction.}
Build the finite residual family as multivariate integer polynomials and
verify the degree bound. The $4nT$ count should be a theorem about the
chosen finite indexing type, rather than an informal count of displayed
symbols. Test whether array sharing can reduce the stored expression size
without changing the polynomial semantics.

\paragraph{Unbounded acceptance.}
Prove computability of exact rational iteration and recursive enumerability
of the acceptance set. Only then invoke \texttt{Diophantine.mrdp} or the
corresponding library-level Diophantine predicate. Keep this theorem distinct
from a numerical degree/witness theorem for a specific universal polynomial.

\paragraph{Synthesis and rational algebra.}
Formalize arithmetic circuits, the bounded chart $z_i=(2a_i-1)/v$, and the
four-layer realization. The reverse reduction needs a rational
four-square lemma and effective polynomial assembly, not a decision oracle
for $\Hten$. The direct quartic lift is a separate natural-witness theorem.

The existing repository documentation distinguishes its audited endpoints,
trace interfaces, and article-specific results \cite{b62s15-proveit,b62s15-proveit-mrdp}.
Maintaining that distinction will prevent an implementation test or a
semidecidability proof from being misreported as an audited explicit
polynomial construction.

\section{Exact implementation and validation}
\label{pqc:pm:sec:validation}
\srcmark{15}

The accompanying code uses Python's standard library only. Rational values
are represented by \texttt{fractions.Fraction}; sparse polynomials have
integer coefficients and sorted tuples of variable names as monomials.
There are no floating-point comparisons, numerical optimizers, or external
solver calls.

The main module implements the scalar witness, the canonical trajectory
compiler, the projective example, arithmetic-circuit compactification, the
four-layer network construction, and the quartic synthesis compiler. Each
certificate is stored both as its structured residual presentation and,
for the supplied examples, as an expanded sparse polynomial. A proposed
natural witness is evaluated with a domain check before any polynomial
zero test is accepted.

The deterministic test suite completed \textbf{53,472 assertions}. Its
principal checks are summarized in \cref{pqc:pm:tab:tests}. The full log is
\pathtext{verification_report.txt}; the random seed is \texttt{20260930}.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.52\linewidth}r}
\toprule
Check & Count\\
\midrule
Canonical scalar witnesses & 234\\
Scalar uniqueness checks in a declared finite box & 32,997\\
Random rational network trace instances & 240\\
Independent rational transition comparisons & 972\\
Single-coordinate trace mutations rejected & 13,550\\
Binary words checked through length eight & 511\\
Projective scales checked & 72\\
Quartic synthesis-coordinate mutations rejected & 114\\
Prime-support counting inequalities checked & 840\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Selected checks. Counts are not claims of exhaustive verification of
the infinite theorems. Some objects support several assertions.}
\label{pqc:pm:tab:tests}
\end{table}

The scalar enumeration checks both thresholds and the transition from
unsaturated to saturated behavior. The trace tests include $B=1$, zero
steps, negative coefficients, and exact rational saturation. Every
single-coordinate increment, and every valid decrement, of the tested
canonical trace witnesses produces a positive certificate value. The
synthesis example checks the expanded polynomial as well as the structured
residuals, so a residual-list success is not being confused with a correct
polynomial expansion.

These tests verify the implementation on the specified finite samples.
They do not replace the inductive and algebraic proofs, establish global
uniqueness by testing alone, or prove the absence of a rational solution in
the irrational-only example. That absence was proved arithmetically in
\cref{pqc:pm:ex:irrational}. No Lean execution is included in the package.

\section{Source 14 appendix: minimal decision and approximation algorithms}

The point algorithm for a nonzero cone input, after handling the exceptional
cases described in \cref{pqc:sc:thm:point}, is:
\begin{lstlisting}
PointHit(F, B, y, z):
    r := radius(y); s := radius(z)
    if s <= 0 or s > r: return false
    t := 0
    while r > s:
        r := r / B
        t := t + 1
    if r != s: return false
    return iterate_exactly(F, y, t) == z
\end{lstlisting}

\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
The peak approximation algorithm is:
\begin{lstlisting}
PeakInterval(F, B, ell, y, T):
    r := radius(y)
    a := 0
    for t = 0, ..., T-1:
        a := max(a, ell(y))
        y := F(y)
    return [a, max(a, r / B^T)]
\end{lstlisting}
\end{minipage}
The width is at most $rB^{-T}$. When its lower endpoint is positive, a
sufficiently longer finite run will produce a singleton interval and hence
the exact rational peak. When the true peak is zero, this singleton event
need not occur. Adding an unsupported ``eventually it must'' termination
claim would reintroduce the halting problem.

\section{Source 12 appendix: compact algorithms and file formats}\label{pqc:ad:app:algorithms}

\subsection{Natural-number evaluation}
The essential evaluator is the following; the archive adds validation and
an output-size guard.
\begin{lstlisting}
def F(n, clock):
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    t = valuation_2(n)
    u = n >> t
    q, left, right = decode_unit(u)
    if q == halt_state or q >= state_count:
        return 0
    q1, left1, right1 = machine_step(q, left, right)
    return encode_unit(q1, left1, right1) << clock(t)
\end{lstlisting}
For residue evaluation modulo $2^k$, reduce the input first and avoid the
shift if $h(t)\ge k$. A zero residue is answered by zero. This is valid
because the output depends only on that residue, not because an unknown
higher tail is assumed absent.

\subsection{Polynomial representation}
A sparse monomial is stored as an integer coefficient and a list of
variable names, with repeated names representing powers. The empty factor
list represents a constant. A residual is a list of such terms. The
certificate JSON includes the public parameter name \texttt{n}, the full
ordered witness-variable list, the time and input bounds, the machine
table, and the residual list. Its polynomial is exactly the sum of squares
of those residuals. The expanded example uses the same monomial format
without the residual grouping.

The witness file records a natural value for every declared witness and
the public input separately. Evaluation checks that the set of supplied
witness names agrees exactly with the declaration. It then evaluates all
residuals with exact integer arithmetic.

\section{Source 12 appendix: proof audit and scope boundaries}\label{pqc:ad:app:audit}
The following dependency summary is intended to make the most vulnerable
steps easy to inspect.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{0.3\textwidth}X@{}}
\toprule
Result & Essential dependency or boundary\\
\midrule
Unit Lipschitz estimate & Common state and scanned bit at high precision;
interior tape-digit displacement at most two.\\
Global contraction & Separate same-shell and distinct-shell estimates;
no monotonicity assumption on the clock.\\
Computable $2$-adic map & Residue procedure never needs a global zero test.\\
Simulation & Nonzero unit updates are odd; halting-to-zero uses one extra
iteration.\\
Finite realization & Bounded bootstrap and FIFO; not inferred from
Lipschitz continuity alone.\\
Clock necessity & Eventual periodicity of internal states along the all-zero
input and a fixed nonhalting suffix.\\
Clock sufficiency & Finite leading-zero controller and a finite family of
fixed output delays.\\
Analytic horizon & Scalar local factorization and uniform entry into a
small invariant ball; effectivity stated separately.\\
Bounded quartic uniqueness & Unique input digits, unique natural division,
and deterministic identity-padded trace.\\
Unbounded quartic & MRDP followed by standard gate equations; no uniqueness
of original MRDP witnesses.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

Three claims are deliberately absent. We do not claim robust clopen
universality. We do not claim global smoothness from asymptotic flatness.
We do not claim a fixed-arity single-fold representation from a family
whose arity grows with $T$ and $S$. These absences are mathematical scope
boundaries, not missing steps in the theorems that were actually stated.
