\section{Rational polynomial instances and local bounds}\label{pqc:tu:sec:instances}

\subsection{Input data and semantics}
Throughout, $\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. Fix $d\geq1$ and a vector field
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:field}
 F_j(x)=\frac1A\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_j}c_{j\alpha}x^\alpha,
 \qquad A\in\N_{>0},\quad c_{j\alpha}\in\Z,
 \quad x^\alpha=\prod_{r=1}^d x_r^{\alpha_r}.
\end{equation}
The lists $\mathcal A_j$ are finite; zero polynomials are allowed. Put
\begin{equation}
 k=\max\bigl(1,\max_{j,\alpha}|\alpha|\bigr),
 \qquad |\alpha|=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_d,
\end{equation}
where an empty maximum contributes nothing. The initial point is
$x^0_j=p_j/q_j\in\Q$, with $q_j>0$ and $\gcd(|p_j|,q_j)=1$. The target is
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:target}
 U=\{x\in\R^d:a_\ell\cdot x<b_\ell\text{ for }1\leq\ell\leq m\},
 \quad a_\ell\in\Z^d,\quad b_\ell\in\Z.
\end{equation}
Clearing positive denominators puts every rational open polyhedron in this
form. In particular, rational open boxes are included. The case $m=0$ means
$U=\R^d$. A zero row with a nonpositive bound makes $U$ empty, and is not silently
discarded.

Polynomial fields are locally Lipschitz. Let
$x:[0,T_{\max})\to\R^d$ be the unique maximal forward solution of
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:ode}
 x'=F(x),\qquad x(0)=x^0.
\end{equation}
No global existence assumption is made. Define
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:reach}
 \Reach(F,x^0,U)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists t\in[0,T_{\max})\;x(t)\in U.
\end{equation}
Every successful event can be witnessed at a positive rational time: if it
occurs at $t=0$, local existence and openness provide a positive interval; if
it occurs later, continuity provides an open time neighborhood inside the
existence interval.

\subsection{Integral bounds on a box}
For an integer $R\geq1$, let $B_R=[-R,R]^d$ and define
\begin{align}
 M(R)&=\sum_{j,\alpha}|c_{j\alpha}|R^{|\alpha|},\label{pqc:tu:eq:M}\\
 L(R)&=\sum_{\substack{j,\alpha\\|\alpha|>0}}
 |c_{j\alpha}|\,|\alpha|R^{|\alpha|-1}.\label{pqc:tu:eq:L}
\end{align}
Both are nonnegative integers. The deliberate omission of $1/A$ makes the
bounds coarse but keeps their evaluation integral.

\begin{lemma}\label[lemma]{pqc:tu:lem:bounds}
For $u,v\in B_R$,
\begin{equation}
 \norm{F(u)}\leq M(R),\qquad
 \norm{F(u)-F(v)}\leq L(R)\norm{u-v}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion follows by taking absolute values of every monomial in
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:field}, using $A\geq1$ and $R\geq1$. For the second, the sum of the
absolute values of all first partial derivatives of all components on $B_R$
is at most $L(R)$. In particular every Jacobian row sum is at most this number.
The segment from $u$ to $v$ stays in the convex box, so the integral mean-value
formula gives the asserted infinity-norm Lipschitz bound.
\end{proof}
These choices are not numerically optimal. Their advantages are that they
require only addition, multiplication, and nonnegative integer powers, and
that no optimization oracle is hidden in the checker.

\section{The exact integer certificate}\label{pqc:tu:sec:certificate}

\subsection{Mesh, state lattice, and noise units}
Fix positive integers $N,H,D,R$. The physical step is $h=1/H$, the state lattice
has spacing $1/D$, and the terminal time is $T=N/H$. Fix two natural numbers
$E_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $J$. They specify initial uncertainty
$E_{\mathrm{in}}/D$ and forcing amplitude $\eta=J/D$.
The nominal version sets both to zero; the positive-robustness version sets
both to one.

A certificate consists of signed lattice nodes $X_i\in\Z^d$, natural radius
units $E_i\in\N$, and natural remainders $U_{ij},V_i$. Write
\begin{equation}
 v_i=X_i/D,\qquad e_i=E_i/D.
\end{equation}
The initial constraints are
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:initial}
 q_jX_{0j}=p_jD\quad(1\leq j\leq d),\qquad E_0=E_{\mathrm{in}}.
\end{equation}
Thus $D$ must clear the initial denominators whenever a certificate exists.

Define the homogenized polynomial and the positive divisor
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:homogeneous}
 \widetilde F_j(X,D)=\sum_\alpha c_{j\alpha}X^\alpha D^{k-|\alpha|},
 \qquad Q=AH D^{k-1}.
\end{equation}
Then $D h F_j(X/D)=\widetilde F_j(X,D)/Q$.

\subsection{Canonical floor nodes}
For $0\leq i<N$ and $1\leq j\leq d$, require
\begin{align}
 Q(X_{i+1,j}-X_{ij})+U_{ij}&=\widetilde F_j(X_i,D),\label{pqc:tu:eq:floor}\\
 0\leq U_{ij}&<Q.\label{pqc:tu:eq:floorbound}
\end{align}
Euclidean division applies even when the dividend is negative. These conditions
uniquely determine
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:euler}
 X_{i+1,j}=X_{ij}+\floor{\widetilde F_j(X_i,D)/Q}.
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:rounderr}
 \norm{v_{i+1}-v_i-hF(v_i)}<1/D.
\end{equation}
This is directed floor rounding, not round-to-nearest and not truncation toward
zero. The distinction is essential for negative states or vector-field values.

\subsection{Canonical ceiling radii}
In the remaining formulas abbreviate $M=M(R)$, $L=L(R)$ and set
\begin{align}
 B&=H^2,& K&=H(H+L),\label{pqc:tu:eq:BK}\\
 C&=L(DM+J)+H^2+JH,& G&=DRH-DM-J.\label{pqc:tu:eq:CG}
\end{align}
For $0\leq i<N$, require
\begin{align}
 B E_{i+1}&=K E_i+C+V_i,\label{pqc:tu:eq:ceil}\\
 0\leq V_i&<B.\label{pqc:tu:eq:ceilbound}
\end{align}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:canonicalradius}
 E_{i+1}=\ceil{(KE_i+C)/B}.
\end{equation}
The scaled recurrence gives the two useful estimates
\begin{align}
 e_{i+1}&\geq(1+hL)e_i+L(M+\eta)h^2+1/D+h\eta,\label{pqc:tu:eq:radlower}\\
 e_{i+1}&<(1+hL)e_i+L(M+\eta)h^2+2/D+h\eta.\label{pqc:tu:eq:radupper}
\end{align}
The first $1/D$ budgets the floor rounding. The second, appearing only in the
upper estimate, budgets the ceiling rounding. The coefficient of the local
truncation bound is intentionally twice the elementary $1/2$ bound used below.
That harmless slack simplifies the integer expression.

\subsection{Containment and target tests}
At every nonterminal node require the $2d$ strict inequalities
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:guards}
 G-HE_i-HX_{ij}>0,\qquad G-HE_i+HX_{ij}>0.
\end{equation}
They are exactly
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:guardscaled}
 |v_{ij}|+e_i+h(M+\eta)<R.
\end{equation}
Finally require, for every target row,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:terminal}
 Db_\ell-a_\ell\cdot X_N-\|a_\ell\|_1E_N>0.
\end{equation}
Thus the entire closed infinity-norm ball of radius $e_N$ around $v_N$ is
contained in the open target. Write $\Cert_{E_{\mathrm{in}},J}(I;N,H,D,R)$
when all these equations and inequalities hold, where $I=(F,x^0,U)$.
All fields of the certificate are uniquely determined by the instance and its
four positive integer parameters; the checker merely tests whether that
canonical candidate succeeds.

\section{Soundness, including existence and bounded forcing}\label{pqc:tu:sec:soundness}

\begin{theorem}[Robust soundness]\label{pqc:tu:thm:sound}
Suppose $\Cert_{E_{\mathrm{in}},J}(I;N,H,D,R)$ holds. Let
$w:[0,N/H]\to\R^d$ be measurable with $\norm{w(t)}\leq J/D$ almost everywhere,
and let $z^0$ satisfy $\norm{z^0-x^0}\leq E_{\mathrm{in}}/D$.
The solution of
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:forced}
 z'=F(z)+w(t),\qquad z(0)=z^0,
\end{equation}
exists throughout $[0,N/H]$ and obeys
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:nodebound}
 \norm{z(i/H)-v_i}\leq e_i\quad(0\leq i\leq N).
\end{equation}
In particular $z(N/H)\in U$. Solutions of \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:forced} are understood in
the absolutely continuous, almost-everywhere sense.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Local existence and uniqueness for \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:forced} follow from the standard
integral-equation construction: the polynomial term is locally Lipschitz in
$z$, and the bounded measurable forcing is integrable on compact intervals.
We prove existence and \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:nodebound} simultaneously, one mesh interval
at a time. The initial assertion follows from \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:initial}.

Suppose the solution has reached $t_i=i/H$ and satisfies the claimed bound.
While it remains in $B_R$, \cref{pqc:tu:lem:bounds} gives the speed estimate
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:speed}
 \norm{z(t_i+s)-z(t_i)}\leq (M+\eta)s.
\end{equation}
For $0\leq s\leq h$, each component consequently satisfies
\begin{equation}
 |z_j(t_i+s)|\leq |v_{ij}|+e_i+(M+\eta)h<R
\end{equation}
as long as the solution exists in the box. A first exit would contradict this
strict estimate. Moreover the same estimate leaves a positive distance to the
boundary, uniformly over this step. A finite maximal endpoint before $t_i+h$
would have a finite limit, because the derivative is bounded on the box; the
local integral-equation construction could then extend the solution.
Therefore it exists through $t_i+h$ and does not leave the box during the step.
This is the continuation obligation that a bare approximate trajectory would
not establish.

Using \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:speed}, the triangle inequality, and the Lipschitz bound gives
\begin{align}
 &\norm{z(t_i+h)-v_i-hF(v_i)}\notag\\
 &\quad\leq e_i+\int_0^h
   \bigl(L\norm{z(t_i+s)-v_i}+\eta\bigr)\,ds\notag\\
 &\quad\leq e_i+\int_0^h\bigl(L(e_i+(M+\eta)s)+\eta\bigr)\,ds\notag\\
 &\quad=(1+hL)e_i+\tfrac12L(M+\eta)h^2+h\eta.\label{pqc:tu:eq:localerror}
\end{align}
Adding the rounding error \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:rounderr} and applying
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:radlower} proves the next node bound. The induction therefore reaches
$N/H$. Finally, for every target row,
\begin{equation}
 a_\ell\cdot z(N/H)
 \leq a_\ell\cdot v_N+\|a_\ell\|_1e_N<b_\ell
\end{equation}
by \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:terminal}. This proves the theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What robustness means here]
The theorem certifies one finite time and one open target, for every forcing
within an explicit amplitude bound. It does not claim robustness of an infinite
computation, invariance of an exact algebraic encoding under disturbances, or
completeness of the checker for an arbitrarily prescribed large tolerance.
Positive existential tolerances will be addressed in \cref{pqc:tu:thm:equivalence}.
\end{remark}

\section{Completeness and quantitative parameters}\label{pqc:tu:sec:completeness}

\subsection{A bound for all computed radii}
The key point is that precision and mesh size can be increased independently.
Shrinking the time step without increasing $D$ sufficiently would accumulate
rounding error and would not yield completeness.

\begin{lemma}\label[lemma]{pqc:tu:lem:radiusbound}
For $T=N/H$, the canonical radii satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:generalerrorbound}
 e_i\leq \ee^{LT}\left(
 \frac{E_{\mathrm{in}}}{D}
 +\frac{TL(M+J/D)}H+\frac{2TH}D+\frac{TJ}D\right)
 \quad(0\leq i\leq N).
\end{equation}
When $E_{\mathrm{in}}=J=0$, this simplifies to
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:nominalbound}
 e_i\leq\ee^{LT}\left(\frac{TLM}{H}+\frac{2TH}{D}\right).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $a=1+L/H$ and
$b=L(M+J/D)/H^2+2/D+J/(DH)$. By \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:radupper},
$e_{i+1}\leq ae_i+b$. Hence
$e_i\leq a^i e_0+b\sum_{r=0}^{i-1}a^r\leq a^N(e_0+Nb)$.
Use $(1+L/H)^N\leq\ee^{LN/H}$ and substitute $N=TH$.
The argument includes $L=0$ without division by $L$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Complete canonical certificates]\label{pqc:tu:thm:complete}
If $\Reach(F,x^0,U)$ holds, then for every fixed pair
$E_{\mathrm{in}},J\in\N$ there exist positive integers $N,H,D,R$ for which
$\Cert_{E_{\mathrm{in}},J}(I;N,H,D,R)$ holds.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose a positive rational time $T<T_{\max}$ with $x(T)\in U$.
The trajectory on $[0,T]$ is compact. Choose an integer $R\geq1$ with
\begin{equation}
 \sigma=R-\max_{0\leq t\leq T}\norm{x(t)}>0.
\end{equation}
Because $U$ is open, choose $\mu>0$ such that the closed infinity-norm ball of
radius $\mu$ about $x(T)$ lies in $U$, with strict margin in each defining row.
For $m=0$, any positive $\mu$ is suitable. Choose
$0<\varepsilon<\min(\sigma,\mu)/4$.

Let $H$ tend to infinity through multiples of the denominator of $T$, put
$N=TH$, and let $D$ tend to infinity through multiples of all initial
denominators, with $D/H\to\infty$ sufficiently quickly. For example one can
use a suitable fixed positive multiple of $H^3$. The right side of
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:generalerrorbound} tends to zero. Thus, for sufficiently large
parameters,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:completenesschoice}
 e_i\leq\varepsilon\quad(0\leq i\leq N),
 \qquad (M+J/D)/H<\sigma/2.
\end{equation}
Generate the floor nodes and ceiling radii using the exact formulas.

We first prove $\norm{x(i/H)-v_i}\leq e_i$ without assuming that the certificate
guards have already passed. Initially the difference is zero. If the assertion
holds at node $i$, then $v_i\in B_R$, because the true trajectory is at distance
at least $\sigma$ from the boundary and $e_i\leq\varepsilon<\sigma$.
The true trajectory remains in $B_R$ by its choice, independently of the
candidate. Comparing its integral with the Euler step therefore gives
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:localerror} with zero forcing. The candidate radius is at least the
nominal bound needed for this estimate, even when $E_{\mathrm{in}}$ or $J$ is
positive. After adding floor rounding, the next node bound follows. This
induction avoids a circular appeal to unverified containment.

The guards now follow from
\begin{equation}
 |v_{ij}|+e_i+(M+J/D)/H
 \leq\norm{x(i/H)}+2\varepsilon+\sigma/2<R.
\end{equation}
At the terminal node every point in the radius-$e_N$ ball about $v_N$ is within
$2\varepsilon<\mu$ of $x(T)$, so all target tests pass. The initial and division
equations hold by construction. This gives the certificate.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An explicit nominal choice}
For the nominal case, the proof yields concrete sufficient inequalities once a
successful segment and its margins are known. Choose
$0<\varepsilon<\min(\sigma,\mu)/4$ and an integer $r\geq LT$.
Then $C_{\exp}=3^r\geq\ee^{LT}$. Take a positive integer $H$, divisible by the
denominator of $T$, satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:Hchoice}
 H>\max\left(\frac{2M}{\sigma},
             \frac{2C_{\exp}TLM}{\varepsilon}\right).
\end{equation}
Take a positive $D$, divisible by every $q_j$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:Dchoice}
 D>\frac{4C_{\exp}TH}{\varepsilon}.
\end{equation}
Then the two terms in \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:nominalbound} are each smaller than
$\varepsilon/2$, and the proof applies. These are sufficient bounds, not claims
of optimal precision or practical conditioning. In particular the true
trajectory margins are not assumed computable in advance by the certificate
search: exhaustive enumeration does not need to know them.

\begin{theorem}[Reachability, positive robustness, and arithmetic]\label{pqc:tu:thm:equivalence}
For every rational polynomial instance $I$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $\Reach(I)$.
\item There are a rational $T>0$ and $\delta>0$ such that every solution with
$\norm{z^0-x^0}\leq\delta$ and every measurable forcing of norm at most $\delta$
exists through $T$ and lies in $U$ at $T$.
\item A certificate $\Cert_{0,0}(I;N,H,D,R)$ exists.
\item A certificate $\Cert_{1,1}(I;N,H,D,R)$ exists.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Completeness gives (i)$\Rightarrow$(iii) and (i)$\Rightarrow$(iv).
Soundness gives (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i), and gives (iv)$\Rightarrow$(ii) with
$T=N/H$ and $\delta=1/D$. Taking the unperturbed initial point and zero forcing
proves (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i).
\end{proof}
The equivalence is a finite-event statement. It does not replace a universal
quantifier over an arbitrary infinite execution by a finite witness.

\section{An explicit quartic Diophantine normal form}\label{pqc:tu:sec:quartic}

\subsection{Natural variables and canonical signed wires}
To expose the arithmetic geometry, fix the instance $I$, length $N$, and noise
units $E_{\mathrm{in}},J$. The three parameters $R,H,D$ remain free natural
variables. Every signed integer quantity $z$ is represented by two natural
variables $z^+,z^-$ with
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:canonicalsign}
 z=z^+-z^-,\qquad z^+z^-=0.
\end{equation}
For a prescribed integer $z$, this pair is unique:
$(z^+,z^-)=(\max(z,0),\max(-z,0))$.
\wtag\ This canonical signed pair is the signed normal form of the sibling
report \code{canonical-diophantine-certificates} (its Lemma
\code{cdc:pt:lem:signed}, in Section \code{cdc:pt:sec:arithmetic}), and the
split used in the proof of Part~II's Proposition~\ref{pqc:prop:finitequantum};
source~18 uses it without citing either.

An ordinary arithmetic gate producing $z=u+v$ or $z=uv$ introduces the two
variables $z^+,z^-$, its canonical-sign equation, and the evaluation equation
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:gates}
 z^+-z^- - (u+v)=0
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 z^+-z^- -uv=0.
\end{equation}
Here a wire such as $u$ denotes an affine signed expression or an integer
constant. Thus every gate equation has total degree at most two. Subtraction is
addition with a negative integer coefficient. All powers in the definitions of
$M,L,Q,B,K,C,G$, and $\widetilde F$ are evaluated using such gates.

Let $g$ be the number of these signed arithmetic gates. This number excludes
state-node pairs, division remainders, error-radius variables, and the slack
variables described next. Gate outputs are not macro expressions that can
silently increase the final degree: they are actual new variables constrained
by \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:gates}.

\subsection{Quadratic constraints for the whole certificate}
For each initial coordinate allocate its signed pair and impose both
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:canonicalsign} and \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:initial}. At every step and coordinate,
allocate the signed pair for $X_{i+1,j}$, the natural remainder $U_{ij}$, and
one natural complement $S_{ij}$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 U_{ij}+S_{ij}+1=Q.
\end{equation}
Together with \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:floor}, these encode exactly $0\leq U_{ij}<Q$.
For each radius step introduce $E_{i+1},V_i,W_i\in\N$ and impose
\begin{equation}
 BE_{i+1}-KE_i-C-V_i=0,\qquad V_i+W_i+1=B.
\end{equation}
The quantity $E_0$ is the prescribed constant $E_{\mathrm{in}}$, not an additional
witness. The floor equation is quadratic in its circuit wires and state-node
variables; so is the radius equation.

Every strict integer inequality $A_0>0$ is encoded by a new natural slack
$s$ and the equation $A_0=1+s$. Apply this to the $2dN$ containment tests,
the $m$ terminal tests, and to $R,H,D>0$. The expressions in the containment
and terminal tests are at most quadratic in the circuit variables. Products
such as $DRH$ have already been computed by gates into the wire $G$.

\begin{theorem}[Counted quartic compilation]\label{pqc:tu:thm:quartic}
There is an effective construction of an integer polynomial
\begin{equation}
 P_{I,N}^{E_{\mathrm{in}},J}(R,H,D,w)
   =\sum_{r=1}^{s}f_r(R,H,D,w)^2,
 \qquad \deg f_r\leq2,
\end{equation}
with
\begin{align}
 \#w&=2g+(6d+3)N+2d+m+3,\label{pqc:tu:eq:wcount}\\
 s&=2g+(5d+2)N+2d+m+3.\label{pqc:tu:eq:ecount}
\end{align}
The polynomial has total degree at most four, including its free parameters.
For every $(R,H,D)\in\N^3$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:quarticequiv}
 \exists w\in\N^{\#w}\;P_{I,N}^{E_{\mathrm{in}},J}(R,H,D,w)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Cert_{E_{\mathrm{in}},J}(I;N,H,D,R).
\end{equation}
For fixed $I,N,E_{\mathrm{in}},J,R,H,D$, there is at most one such natural witness
$w$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the construction above. Its variable and equation counts are as follows.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Component & Natural variables & Equations\\
\midrule
Signed arithmetic gates & $2g$ & $2g$\\
Initial signed nodes and values & $2d$ & $2d$\\
Floor node, sign condition, remainder, complement & $4dN$ & $3dN$\\
Ceiling radius, remainder, complement & $3N$ & $2N$\\
Strict tube-containment slacks & $2dN$ & $2dN$\\
Strict target slacks & $m$ & $m$\\
Positivity slacks for $R,H,D$ & $3$ & $3$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Summing gives \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:wcount}--\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:ecount}. Each residual is quadratic
or lower. Over the integers, a sum of squares vanishes exactly when every
summand vanishes. Hence the polynomial zero set is precisely the simultaneous
constraint set, proving \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:quarticequiv}.

For uniqueness, order the circuit and trace variables according to their
construction. Parameters determine all global arithmetic wires. Each rational
initial coordinate determines at most one integer node, and the canonical sign
condition determines its pair. Given $X_i$, all $\widetilde F_j(X_i,D)$ wires
are fixed. Since $Q>0$, Euclidean division fixes $X_{i+1,j}$ and $U_{ij}$;
the complement and signed pair are then fixed. Since $B>0$, the ceiling
constraint fixes $E_{i+1}$ and $V_i$, and then its complement. Every slack is
fixed by its equality. Induction therefore fixes every witness coordinate.
If any divisibility, nonnegativity, containment, or target condition fails,
there is no witness rather than a second choice.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Size, semantics, and the meaning of uniqueness}
For a fixed source instance there is a fixed circuit size $g_F$ for one
homogenized vector-field evaluation and a fixed global overhead $g_0$, so the
construction can use $g=g_0+Ng_F$. Its variable and equation counts are linear
in the unrolling length. This is not a bound on the bit size of the witness
integers, which may be very large. Repeated squaring evaluates each prescribed
power with logarithmically many multiplications in its exponent; sparse field
representations can be retained.

The polynomial is nonnegative at every real assignment because it is a sum
of squares. Its \emph{intended witness domain is $\N$}. Replacing that domain
by arbitrary real or integer witnesses without further constraints would
change the statement. In particular, the canonical-sign proof uses
nonnegativity.

The uniqueness claim is also deliberately local: $N,R,H,D$ and the source
instance are fixed. Successful events generally admit many mesh choices.
Moreover $N$ indexes polynomials with different numbers of variables.
Neither this family nor its local uniqueness constitutes a single-fold
Diophantine representation of an arbitrary recursively enumerable set.

\section{From the checker to MRDP, and the exact universality boundary}\label{pqc:tu:sec:mrdp}

\subsection{Uniform recursive enumerability}
\begin{theorem}\label{pqc:tu:thm:re}
Under any standard effective finite encoding of rational polynomial instances,
the set of valid instance codes satisfying $\Reach$ is recursively enumerable.
It therefore has a fixed-dimensional Diophantine representation over $\N$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Validity of a finite instance code is decidable. For a valid instance, enumerate
positive tuples $(N,H,D,R)$, discard those for which $D$ does not clear the
initial denominators, and compute the unique floor-node and ceiling-radius
candidate. Test all of its integer constraints. Each candidate computation
terminates. Soundness prevents false positives and completeness ensures that
every successful instance eventually passes. Invalid instance codes are never
accepted. This is a semidecision procedure. Applying MRDP to its acceptance set
gives the fixed-dimensional representation.
\end{proof}
\wtag\ \emph{Credit.} The qualitative statement of
Theorem~\ref{pqc:tu:thm:re} is Part~IV's paragraph \emph{Robust observations of
computable continuous trajectories} (Section~\ref{pqc:sec:substrates}): reaching
an effectively open target at some finite time is semidecidable for a
continuous trajectory with certified evaluation at rational times, hence
Diophantine by MRDP. That paragraph is not reprinted here. Source~18, which does
not cite it, makes it explicit, complete, counted and robust for rational
polynomial flows: the semidecision procedure is a fixed canonical integer
checker, sound under bounded forcing
(Theorem~\ref{pqc:tu:thm:sound}), complete for every fixed pair of noise units
(Theorem~\ref{pqc:tu:thm:complete}), with a counted unique-witness quartic for
each unrolling length (Theorem~\ref{pqc:tu:thm:quartic}); and it treats the
solution's existence interval, which the paragraph assumes to be supplied.
The implementation uses arbitrary-precision integer operations, finite lists,
integer powers, and Euclidean division. With conventional natural encodings,
these operations and the bounded trace evaluation can be arranged primitively
recursively. The only unbounded search is the outer search for a successful
parameter tuple. ProveIt's documented primitive-recursive and r.e.-to-
Diophantine interfaces are a natural downstream destination \cite{b64s18-repo}.

\begin{corollary}[A fixed quartic exists, without the explicit trace count]\label[corollary]{pqc:tu:cor:fixedquartic}
The set in \cref{pqc:tu:thm:re} also has a representation by one fixed integer
polynomial of degree at most four in a fixed finite number of natural witness
variables.
\end{corollary}
\noindent\wtag\ \emph{Batch-78 note (2 October 2026).} The statement's last
words are reworded; source~18 wrote ``with finitely many natural witnesses''.
The claim is unchanged: a fixed polynomial has a fixed number of variables, and
the proof below fixes them once (the MRDP witnesses and the circuit
intermediates). The old wording could be misread as finitely many witness
\emph{tuples} for each input, which is not claimed: the remark after the proof
leaves the multiplicity of the MRDP witnesses uncontrolled. Part~III of the
sibling report \code{stochastic-and-thermal-exactness} makes this difference
concrete: there finite witness multiplicity is exactly compact resolvent and a
finite thermal trace of the associated diagonal Hamiltonian
(Theorem \code{ste:ta:thm:classification}), and one free padding coordinate
makes the multiplicity of a fixed universal family infinite on every halting
input (Theorem \code{ste:ta:thm:padding}).
\begin{proof}
Let $Q_0(a,z)$ be the polynomial provided by MRDP for the encoded input $a$.
Evaluate $Q_0$ by a fixed integer arithmetic circuit, represent every signed
intermediate by a canonical natural pair, and impose its quadratic gate
constraints and the linear equation saying the output is zero. The sum of the
squares of these residuals is quartic. Projecting out the intermediate variables
recovers exactly $Q_0(a,z)=0$.
\end{proof}
This degree-reduction argument is standard, not a new universality bound.
\wtag\ It is Part~I's Lemma~\ref{pqc:lem:quarticlower}, whose proof is the same
circuit-and-square argument without the canonical sign condition.
The explicit linear-in-$N$ counts in \cref{pqc:tu:thm:quartic} belong to the unrolled
analytic certificate. After MRDP, the number and size of witnesses are not
computed by this article, and possible multiplicity in the original MRDP
witness $z$ remains. Canonical arithmetic gates do not remove it. The repository's
separate universal-polynomial results address different quantitative questions
\cite{b64s18-repo,b64s18-jones}.

\subsection{A contract for a Turing-complete front end}
Published uses of ``computation by ODE'' can mean approximation of a real
function, convergence with an error output, robust discrete simulation, or
recognition of a finite event. Those meanings should not be interchanged
without proof. For the present purpose the needed contract is short.

\begin{definition}[Effective finite-event simulation]\label[definition]{pqc:tu:def:universal}
A finite-event compiler is a total effective map sending a program-input pair
$(e,n)$ to a rational polynomial instance $I_{e,n}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:simulationcontract}
 \text{program }e\text{ halts on input }n
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Reach(I_{e,n}).
\end{equation}
Any promised restrictions on the degree, dimension, coefficients, initial data,
or target shape are part of the contract, not inferred from the word
``universal.''
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-event transfer]\label{pqc:tu:thm:transfer}
For every compiler satisfying \cref{pqc:tu:def:universal}, its halting relation is
represented both by the complete family of explicit quartic certificates from
\cref{pqc:tu:thm:quartic} and by a fixed-dimensional Diophantine equation from
\cref{pqc:tu:thm:re}. Moreover, the kinetic construction in Sections~\ref{pqc:tu:sec:chemical}--\ref{pqc:tu:sec:global} transfers it
to rational mass-action instances whose prescribed trajectories are global.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Substitute $I_{e,n}$ in \cref{pqc:tu:thm:equivalence,pqc:tu:thm:quartic,pqc:tu:thm:re}.
The kinetic part follows from the orbit and reachability equivalence proved in
\cref{pqc:tu:thm:globalchemical} below. All transformations of finite descriptions
are effective.
\end{proof}
This is a conditional compiler theorem with an explicit hypothesis. It is not
an assertion that merely citing an asymptotic real-function universality theorem
has already verified \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:simulationcontract} with rational coefficients
and rational initial states. The published continuous-computation results
\cite{b64s18-bournez,b64s18-fages,b64s18-graca} are relevant front ends, but the exact finite-event
adapter for a selected construction should be audited separately.

\subsection{A conditional limit on uniform certificate bounds}
\begin{proposition}\label[proposition]{pqc:tu:prop:nobound}
For a family with a finite-event compiler satisfying
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:simulationcontract}, there is no total computable function bounding
the bit length of the shortest successful certificate for every successful
compiled instance, as a function of its finite instance description.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Suppose such a function existed. Given a compiled instance, compute the bound
and enumerate the finitely many strings of at most that length. Run the exact
checker on each. A successful certificate implies reachability by soundness;
if none succeeds, the bound and completeness imply nonreachability.
Together with the compiler this would decide halting, a contradiction.
\end{proof}
The proposition does not say that every successful instance is difficult.
It explains why a complete finite verifier cannot be accompanied by a general
computable cutoff that decides all cases in a universal family.
\wtag\ The same argument gives Part~III's Corollary~\ref{pqc:cb:cor:witness-bounds}
(no computable mesh, certificate-length or witness-height bound for positive
critical radius) and Part~II's Corollary~\ref{pqc:qm:cor:nobound} (no
computable bound on the shortest zero word). Unlike those two statements,
Proposition~\ref{pqc:tu:prop:nobound} is conditional: it needs a finite-event
compiler satisfying \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:simulationcontract}, and source~18 does not
instantiate one (Question~\ref{pqc:tu:q:adapters}).

\section{A failure of naive chemical encoding, and its repair}\label{pqc:tu:sec:chemical}

\subsection{Mass-action semantics}
Let $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_s)$ be nonnegative species concentrations. A reaction
\begin{equation}
 \alpha\cdot Y\xrightarrow{c}\beta\cdot Y,
 \qquad \alpha,\beta\in\N^s,\quad c\in\Q_{>0},
\end{equation}
contributes $cY^\alpha(\beta-\alpha)$ to the derivative of $Y$.
Finite sums give rational polynomial fields. This is deterministic continuous
mass-action semantics. It is not the discrete stochastic jump process or Petri
net firing semantics. We do not impose mass conservation, reversibility,
bimolecularity, or an experimentally realizable choice of physical chemicals.
\wtag\ The sibling report \code{canonical-diophantine-certificates} treats the
discrete firing semantics: its Section \code{cdc:cs:sec:substrates} covers
discrete chemical reaction networks with stoichiometric integer updates and
excludes continuous concentrations and rates, and its batch-62 source~11
(\emph{One Shared Fallback}, files \code{11-reaction-fallback-*}) concerns
conservative priority reaction networks, again with discrete firings. Part~VIII
shares no theorem with either.

\begin{lemma}[Direct kinetic realization]\label[lemma]{pqc:tu:lem:kinetic}
A rational polynomial vector field $G(Y)$ is realizable by this reaction scheme
whenever each negative monomial coefficient in component $G_i$ belongs to a
monomial divisible by $Y_i$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Collect monomials componentwise. For a term $cY^\alpha$ in component $i$, if
$c>0$ use the reaction $\alpha\to\alpha+e_i$ at rate $c$. If $c<0$, the
hypothesis gives $\alpha_i\geq1$, so use $\alpha\to\alpha-e_i$ at rate $-c$.
Each reaction changes only the specified coordinate and contributes exactly
the desired term. Sum the finitely many contributions.
\end{proof}
This elementary inverse-kinetic construction and more sophisticated ODE-to-CRN
transformations belong to an established literature; polynomialization and
chemical compilation are not new claims of this article \cite{b64s18-fages,b64s18-hemery}.
We give the lemma's proof to keep the exact sign convention auditable.

\subsection{A bounded projected trajectory with exploding rails}
A tempting dual-rail encoding writes $x=p-n$, expands $F(p-n)=A(p,n)-B(p,n)$
with nonnegative-coefficient polynomials, and sets $p'=A$, $n'=B$.
It has the correct projected derivative while it exists, but that is not
sufficient for a complete reachability reduction.

\begin{proposition}[Naive-rail incompleteness]\label[proposition]{pqc:tu:prop:naive}
For $x'=1-x^2$, $x(0)=0$, the naive split
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:naivesplit}
 p'=1+2pn,\qquad n'=p^2+n^2,\qquad p(0)=n(0)=0
\end{equation}
has finite-time blow-up although the original solution is bounded and global.
It fails to preserve reachability of the rational open interval $(99/100,1)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The difference satisfies
$(p-n)'=1-(p-n)^2$, so $p-n=\tanh t$ for as long as the lift exists.
The sum $u=p+n$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 u'=1+u^2,\qquad u(0)=0,
\end{equation}
whence $u=\tan t$ and blow-up occurs at $t=\pi/2$.
Before that time, $p-n<\tanh(\pi/2)<\tanh 2<99/100$.
For the last inequality, $\ee^4<3^4=81<199$, and
$\tanh 2=(\ee^4-1)/(\ee^4+1)<99/100$.
The original $\tanh t$ tends to $1$ and hence enters $(99/100,1)$ at a finite
time, whereas the naive lift ceases to exist first.
\end{proof}
The example refutes this unregulated split, not published chemical-universality
constructions that may use additional controls or different semantics.
The lesson is that correctness of a projection identity must be supplemented
by a continuation theorem for the auxiliary variables.

\subsection{Hyperbolic rails with conserved products}
Let $F:\R^d\to\R^d$ be rational polynomial. Introduce positive rails
$p_j,n_j$ and write $x_j=p_j-n_j$. Set
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:clockC}
 \mathcal C(p,n)=\prod_{r=1}^d(p_r+n_r),
 \qquad\mathcal C_j(p,n)=\prod_{r\ne j}(p_r+n_r).
\end{equation}
Define a $2d$-component polynomial field $G$ by
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:hyperbolic}
 p_j'=p_j\mathcal C_j F_j(p-n),\qquad
 n_j'=-n_j\mathcal C_j F_j(p-n).
\end{equation}
Use the rational strictly positive initialization
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:railinit}
 p_j^0=1+\max(x_j^0,0),\qquad
 n_j^0=1+\max(-x_j^0,0),\qquad c_j=p_j^0n_j^0>0.
\end{equation}
Then $p_j^0-n_j^0=x_j^0$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact hyperbolic kinetic lift]\label{pqc:tu:thm:hyperbolic}
The field \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:hyperbolic} is rational mass-action realizable. Its prescribed
solution has invariants $p_jn_j=c_j$ and projects to $x'=F(x)$ under the positive
change of time
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:baseclock}
 \frac{d\tau}{dt}=\mathcal C(p(t),n(t)).
\end{equation}
Every finite original trajectory segment has a finite lifted segment, and no
finite original open-target visit is lost through cancellation-induced rail
blow-up. If $\deg F\leq k$, its polynomial degree is at most $k+d$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Each component in \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:hyperbolic} is divisible by the corresponding
rail. Hence every negative monomial contains that rail, and
\cref{pqc:tu:lem:kinetic} applies. Direct differentiation gives
\begin{equation}
 (p_jn_j)'=n_jp_j\mathcal C_jF_j
             -p_jn_j\mathcal C_jF_j=0.
\end{equation}
Strictly positive initial rails remain positive on every finite existence
interval, either by their multiplicative equations or by the invariant and
continuity. Subtracting the two equations gives
\begin{equation}
 (p_j-n_j)'=(p_j+n_j)\mathcal C_jF_j(p-n)
           =\mathcal C F_j(p-n).
\end{equation}
The common clock factor is positive, proving the projection identity.

For completeness of the lift, take any original segment $x(\tau)$,
$0\leq\tau\leq T<T_{\max}$. The unique positive rails with difference $x_j$ and
product $c_j$ are
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:railformula}
 p_j(\tau)=\frac{x_j(\tau)+\sqrt{x_j(\tau)^2+4c_j}}2,
 \qquad
 n_j(\tau)=\frac{-x_j(\tau)+\sqrt{x_j(\tau)^2+4c_j}}2.
\end{equation}
They are positive, bounded, and continuously differentiable on the compact
segment. From $p_j-n_j=x_j$ and $p_jn_j=c_j$ one obtains
\begin{equation}
 \frac{dp_j}{dx_j}=\frac{p_j}{p_j+n_j},\qquad
 \frac{dn_j}{dx_j}=-\frac{n_j}{p_j+n_j}.
\end{equation}
Define
\begin{equation}
 t(\tau)=\int_0^\tau\frac{du}{\mathcal C(p(u),n(u))}.
\end{equation}
This is finite, continuously differentiable, and strictly increasing on the
segment. Reparameterizing \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:railformula} by its inverse yields exactly
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:hyperbolic}, by the derivative identities above. Uniqueness of the
polynomial ODE identifies it with the prescribed lifted solution. Thus every
finite original segment is covered, and bounded original states force bounded
rails on that segment. Finally, the factor $p_j\mathcal C_j$ or
$n_j\mathcal C_j$ has degree $d$, so the total degree is at most $k+d$.
\end{proof}
The square roots in \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:railformula} appear only in the mathematical
proof and inverse orbit description. Neither the emitted polynomial field nor
its prescribed initial data needs an irrational coefficient.

\section{One more species makes the chemical trajectory global}\label{pqc:tu:sec:global}

\subsection{Polynomial damping without changing the orbit}
Write $y=(p,n)\in\R_{>0}^{2d}$ and let $G(y)$ be the field from
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:hyperbolic}. Put
\begin{equation}
 \kappa=k+d,\qquad s=\ceil{\kappa/2},\qquad
 S(y)=\sum_{i=1}^{2d}y_i^2.
\end{equation}
Introduce a single species $q$ and define the rational polynomial field
\begin{align}
 y_i'&=q^sG_i(y)\qquad(1\leq i\leq2d),\label{pqc:tu:eq:dampedrails}\\
 q'&=-2q^{s+2}\sum_{i=1}^{2d}y_iG_i(y).\label{pqc:tu:eq:dampedq}
\end{align}
Initialize $y$ by \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:railinit} and
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:qinit}
 q^0=\frac1{1+S(y^0)}\in\Q_{>0}.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}\label[lemma]{pqc:tu:lem:damping}
Along the prescribed solution,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:qinv}
 q(1+S(y))=1,
\end{equation}
and $p_jn_j=c_j$. Every rail derivative is bounded in absolute value by a
constant depending only on the coefficients of $G$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Multiplication of the original rail field by a common scalar preserves the
product invariants. Let $A_1(y)=\sum_i y_iG_i(y)$ and
$E=q(1+S(y))-1$. Direct differentiation gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:Einvariant}
 E'=-2q^{s+1}A_1(y)E.
\end{equation}
Since $E(0)=0$, uniqueness for this scalar linear equation gives $E=0$ on the
existence interval. In particular $q=(1+S(y))^{-1}\in(0,1]$.

For a monomial $y^\alpha$ of $G_i$ with $|\alpha|\leq\kappa\leq2s$, set
$r=\max_i|y_i|$. If $r\leq1$, then
$|y^\alpha|/(1+S(y))^s\leq1$. If $r\geq1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{|y^\alpha|}{(1+S(y))^s}
 \leq\frac{r^{|\alpha|}}{(1+r^2)^s}\leq1.
\end{equation}
Therefore $|q^sG_i(y)|$ is at most the sum of the absolute values of the
coefficients of $G_i$. This bound is uniform along the prescribed trajectory.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Global rational chemical normal form]\label{pqc:tu:thm:globalchemical}
For every rational polynomial initial-value problem in dimension $d$, of degree
at most $k\geq1$, the construction \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:dampedrails}--\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:qinit}
produces a rational mass-action system with $2d+1$ species and degree at most
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:chemdegree}
 k+d+\ceil{(k+d)/2}+3.
\end{equation}
Its prescribed trajectory exists for all physical times $t\geq0$ and remains
strictly positive. With
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:fullclock}
 \theta'(t)=q(t)^s\mathcal C(p(t),n(t)),\qquad\theta(0)=0,
\end{equation}
its projection satisfies $p(t)-n(t)=x(\theta(t))$. The clock covers every finite
time of the original maximal forward solution. Consequently, for every open
rational polyhedron $U$,
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:chemicalreach}
 \Reach(F,x^0,U)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Reach(\widehat F,(y^0,q^0),\widehat U),
\end{equation}
where $\widehat U=\{(p,n,q):p-n\in U\}$ is again an open rational polyhedron.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every component $q^sG_i$ retains the target-species factor possessed by $G_i$.
Every monomial in the $q$ component contains $q$. Thus negative monomials in
all components satisfy \cref{pqc:tu:lem:kinetic}; the field is mass-action realizable.
The rail degree is at most $\kappa+s$, and the $q$ component has degree at most
$\kappa+s+3$, proving \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:chemdegree}.

All coordinates start positive and their equations are multiplicative in the
corresponding coordinate. Positivity holds on every finite existence interval.
By \cref{pqc:tu:lem:damping}, each rail grows at most linearly in physical time, and
$q\in(0,1]$. If the maximal physical endpoint were finite, the full state would
remain in a bounded set. Polynomial local existence would then extend the
solution, contradicting maximality. Thus the solution is global. On every
finite interval the coefficients in the multiplicative equations are bounded,
so none of the initially positive species reaches zero at a finite time.

Subtracting the damped rail equations gives
$(p-n)'=q^s\mathcal C F(p-n)$, which proves the projection relation under the
strictly increasing clock \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:fullclock}. It remains to prove that the
clock does not omit a finite original segment. Take such a segment and use
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:railformula} to recover its positive bounded rails; put
$q(\tau)=(1+S(y(\tau)))^{-1}$. Define physical time by
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:dampedtime}
 t(\tau)=\int_0^\tau
 \frac{du}{q(u)^s\mathcal C(p(u),n(u))}.
\end{equation}
On the compact original segment the denominator is continuous and strictly
positive, so this integral is finite and strictly increasing. The rail
derivative calculation from \cref{pqc:tu:thm:hyperbolic} verifies
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:dampedrails} after reparameterization. Differentiating
$q=(1+S)^{-1}$ then verifies \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:dampedq}. Uniqueness identifies this with
the globally defined chemical trajectory.

Conversely, every finite physical segment has a finite clock value, because
its state and clock derivative are continuous and bounded there. The projection
is an original solution up to that clock value. Were it to continue the original
solution through a finite maximal original endpoint with bounded state, it
would contradict maximality of the original solution. Hence the projection
covers exactly the original forward orbit, with a possible infinite physical
time needed to approach an original blow-up endpoint. The strict target
inequalities are unchanged by substitution $x=p-n$, proving
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:chemicalreach}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{What the global theorem does and does not say}
The theorem is global for the \emph{prescribed rational initialization}, or more
generally for appropriate initial data on the invariant manifold
$q(1+S)=1$ with positive rails. It does not assert global existence from every
arbitrary concentration vector of the emitted reaction network. In particular,
an independently chosen $q^0$ need not satisfy the damping invariant.

The clock is positive but need not have a globally uniform positive lower
bound. Slowdown near large states is how a finite original blow-up is moved to
infinite physical time. The theorem preserves finite-event existence and the
ordered orbit, not a polynomial-time complexity bound or the original physical
rate. Since finite compact segments have positive clock minima, no finite
successful original event is pushed all the way to infinite physical time.

The hyperbolic invariants need not survive arbitrary perturbations of chemical
concentrations. Nevertheless each nominal finite open event of the emitted
polynomial system has its own positive finite-horizon robustness certificate
by \cref{pqc:tu:thm:equivalence}. That statement is weaker than infinite-horizon fault
tolerance, and does not require an off-manifold perturbation to retain the exact
simulation identity. Physically admissible perturbations are a subset of the
bounded real forcing perturbations in \cref{pqc:tu:thm:sound}.

\subsection{Common-offset compression: fewer species at a degree cost}
There is a second exact encoding with a useful dimension--degree tradeoff.
Instead of assigning two rails to each source coordinate, use one positive
coordinate $u_i$ for each $x_i$ and one common positive offset $z$, with
$x_i=u_i-z$. Write
\begin{equation}
 P(u)=\prod_{i=1}^d u_i,\qquad
 A_F(u,z)=\sum_{i=1}^d(u_i-z)F_i(u-z\mathbf1).
\end{equation}
Define the $(d+1)$-component field
\begin{align}
 u_i'&=zP(u)\bigl(zF_i(u-z\mathbf1)+A_F(u,z)\bigr),\label{pqc:tu:eq:offsetu}\\
 z'&=zP(u)A_F(u,z).\label{pqc:tu:eq:offsetz}
\end{align}
Choose rational initial data
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:offsetinit}
 z^0=1+\sum_i|x_i^0|,\qquad u_i^0=z^0+x_i^0,
 \qquad c=(z^0)^2-\sum_i(x_i^0)^2>0.
\end{equation}
All $u_i^0,z^0$ are strictly positive.

\begin{theorem}[Species--degree tradeoff]\label{pqc:tu:thm:compressed}
Let
\begin{equation}
 \Delta=k+d+\ceil{(k+d)/2}+3.
\end{equation}
Every rational polynomial initial-value problem in dimension $d$, of degree at
most $k\geq1$, has either of the following global rational mass-action normal
forms, both with a linear projection and exact preservation of finite open
polyhedral events:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Construction & Species & Degree upper bound\\
\midrule
Separate hyperbolic rails and damping & $2d+1$ & $\Delta$\\
Common offset and damping & $d+2$ & $\Delta+3$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The common-offset form thus saves $d-1$ species at a cost of three in the degree
upper bound. These are construction bounds, not optimality claims.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first line is \cref{pqc:tu:thm:globalchemical}. For the second, each component
$u_i'$ in \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:offsetu} is divisible by $u_i$, because $P$ contains every
$u_i$. The $z$ component is divisible by $z$. Thus the field is kinetic by
\cref{pqc:tu:lem:kinetic}. Its degree is at most $\kappa_*=k+d+2$.
The projection satisfies
\begin{equation}
 (u_i-z)'=z^2P(u)F_i(u-z\mathbf1).
\end{equation}
A direct derivative calculation gives the conserved quantity
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:offsetinvariant}
 z^2-\sum_i(u_i-z)^2=c.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the derivative of the first term is $2z^2P A_F$, and the derivative
of the sum is the same expression.

For any finite original segment, the unique corresponding positive offset
coordinates are
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:offsetinverse}
 z(\tau)=\sqrt{c+\sum_i x_i(\tau)^2},\qquad
 u_i(\tau)=z(\tau)+x_i(\tau).
\end{equation}
Because $c>0$, $z>|x_i|$ and all $u_i$ are strictly positive. They are bounded
and bounded away from zero on each compact original segment. Differentiation
gives $dz/d\tau=(\sum_i x_iF_i)/z$ and
$du_i/d\tau=F_i+(\sum_i x_iF_i)/z$. Reparameterizing by the positive clock
$d\tau/dt=z^2P(u)$ yields exactly \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:offsetu}--\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:offsetz}.
The reciprocal clock has a finite integral on every finite original segment,
so none is lost through an offset blow-up.

Apply the polynomial damping construction to the base state
$Y=(u_1,\ldots,u_d,z)$, using $s_*=\ceil{\kappa_*/2}$ and one species $q$:
\begin{equation}
 Y'=q^{s_*}G_*(Y),\qquad
 q'=-2q^{s_*+2}\sum_iY_i(G_*)_i(Y),
 \qquad q^0=(1+\|Y^0\|_2^2)^{-1}.
\end{equation}
The proof of \cref{pqc:tu:lem:damping} applies in any finite dimension and gives a
uniform bound on each derivative of $Y$. Positivity and global existence
follow exactly as in \cref{pqc:tu:thm:globalchemical}. The invariant
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:offsetinvariant} survives the common time multiplier. The degree bound
is
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_*+\ceil{\kappa_*/2}+3
 =k+d+\ceil{(k+d)/2}+6=\Delta+3.
\end{equation}
The projected clock is $q^{s_*}z^2P(u)$, positive and bounded away from zero on
each lifted compact source segment. Finally a target row becomes
\begin{equation}
 a_\ell\cdot u-\left(\sum_i a_{\ell i}\right)z<b_\ell,
\end{equation}
with zero coefficient on $q$. Thus the projection remains linear and the
target remains an open rational polyhedron with the same number of rows.
\end{proof}
As with separate rails, the square root is used only in the inverse orbit
proof. The emitted field and the initialization \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:offsetinit} are
rational. For $d=1$ the species counts agree and the separate-rail degree bound
is better; for $d>1$ the common-offset construction gives a genuine species
reduction.

\begin{corollary}[Chemical-to-integer equivalence]\label[corollary]{pqc:tu:cor:composite}
Every rational polynomial instance admits an effective transformation to a
well-initialized global rational mass-action instance, and its reachability is
equivalent to existence of a canonical integer tube for that chemical instance.
For any fixed chemical trace length the latter has the explicit quartic
representation of \cref{pqc:tu:thm:quartic}, with $d$ there replaced by the chosen chemical dimension $2d+1$ or $d+2$ and
the same number $m$ of target inequalities.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Combine \cref{pqc:tu:thm:globalchemical,pqc:tu:thm:compressed,pqc:tu:thm:equivalence,pqc:tu:thm:quartic}. For separate rails, each row
$a_\ell\cdot x<b_\ell$ becomes
$a_\ell\cdot p-a_\ell\cdot n<b_\ell$, with zero coefficient on $q$.
For common offsets use the row substitution in \cref{pqc:tu:thm:compressed}. All coefficients
are integral, and no additional terminal inequalities are needed.
\end{proof}
This corollary gives a direct arithmetic interface to a continuous chemical
computational substrate, with no numerical trajectory accepted on faith and
no auxiliary finite-time explosion hidden in the reduction.

\section{Worked examples and reproducible checks}\label{pqc:tu:sec:examples}

\subsection{A positive-noise certificate for a nonlinear flow}
Consider
\begin{equation}
 x'=1-x^2,\qquad x(0)=0,\qquad U=(7/10,41/50).
\end{equation}
Take $R=1$, $N=H=1000$, $D=10^8$, and $E_{\mathrm{in}}=J=1$.
The integral bounds are $M=2$ and $L=2$. The exact checker returns
\begin{equation}
 X_N=76\,177\,343,\qquad E_N=1\,279\,638.
\end{equation}
Consequently every allowed perturbed solution exists to time $1$ and ends in
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:logisticinterval}
 \left[\frac{74\,897\,705}{10^8},
       \frac{77\,456\,981}{10^8}\right]
 =[0.74897705,\,0.77456981]\subset(0.7,0.82).
\end{equation}
Both tolerances equal $10^{-8}$. The smallest integer tube guard is
$22\,388\,007\,999$, which is positive. The two terminal integer margins,
using rows $-10x<-7$ and $50x<41$, are $48\,977\,050$ and
$227\,150\,950$. No value of $\tanh(1)$ is used in the acceptance test.
The exact elementary solution is useful for intuition, but the arithmetic
certificate proves the event independently of evaluating it.

\subsection{A successful event before an actual blow-up}
For $x'=x^2$, $x(0)=1$, the solution is $x(t)=1/(1-t)$ on $[0,1)$.
The instance with target $(9/5,11/5)$ has a successful certificate at $T=1/2$:
\begin{equation}
 N=5000,\quad H=10000,\quad D=10^{10},\quad R=3,
 \quad E_{\mathrm{in}}=J=0.
\end{equation}
The final node and error units are
\begin{equation}
 X_N=19\,997\,222\,819,\qquad E_N=171\,654\,968.
\end{equation}
The certified terminal interval is
$[1.9825567851,2.0168877787]$, inside the target. This example illustrates why
requiring global existence of the \emph{source} polynomial ODE would be an
unnecessary restriction. The certificate establishes just the finite segment
needed for the event. The chemical transformation separately makes its own
prescribed physical trajectory global.

\subsection{A compact verification inventory}
The package includes eight accepted exact-arithmetic examples:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrl}
\toprule
Example & $N$ & $H$ & $D$ & $R$ & Exact final radius\\
\midrule
Constant flow & 10 & 10 & $10^3$ & 2 & $1/100$\\
Constant, positive noise & 10 & 10 & $10^3$ & 2 & $21/1000$\\
Logistic, positive noise & 1000 & 1000 & $10^8$ & 1 & $639819/50000000$\\
Negative floor division & 3 & 3 & $10^2$ & 2 & $3/100$\\
Negative-state decay & 1000 & 1000 & $10^8$ & 2 & $172977/50000000$\\
Pre-blow-up event & 5000 & 10000 & $10^{10}$ & 3 & $21456871/1250000000$\\
Rational coefficients/data & 1000 & 1000 & $10^8$ & 2 & $517653/100000000$\\
Three-species chemical & 2000 & $2\cdot10^6$ & $3\cdot10^{12}$ & 2 & $39593237/1500000000000$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The negative-state example exercises signed nodes. The negative-floor example
uses $x'=-1$, $N=H=3$, and $D=100$: each increment is
$\floor{-100/3}=-34$, with remainder $2$, rather than truncation to $-33$.
An additional exhaustive finite check covers $4020$ signed Euclidean divisions
and $4020$ ceiling divisions.
The rational-data example uses $x'=(1+x)/3$, $x(0)=1/2$ and target $(1,6/5)$;
it tests a nontrivial common field denominator and initial denominator.

The rejection checks alter, independently, a state node, an error radius, a
floor remainder, a ceiling remainder, the scale, and the initial error units.
All six mutated certificates are rejected. Two additional candidates fail
because of a tube boundary and an unreachable constant trajectory. Rejection
of an individual candidate is not a general proof of nonreachability; these
are tests of the checker, not negative-instance decision results.

Five generic witness-carrying quartic compilations were checked:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
Instance & Signed gates $g$ & Natural witnesses & Equations & Residual degree\\
\midrule
Constant flow, $N=2$ & 19 & 63 & 59 & 2\\
Chemical field, $N=1$ & 65 & 162 & 158 & 2\\
Negative decay, $N=3$ & 21 & 76 & 70 & 2\\
Negative floor, $N=3$ & 20 & 74 & 68 & 2\\
Rational constant field, $N=2$ & 19 & 63 & 59 & 2\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
All residuals evaluate to zero at the exported natural witnesses, and both
count formulas are checked programmatically. The emitted expressions retain
$R,H,D$ as symbolic free parameters; the sample values only instantiate the
accompanying witness. The current implementation's public compiler interface
accepts an already verified certificate and emits its parameterized schema
and witness together. The general source-to-schema construction is specified
mathematically in Section~\ref{pqc:tu:sec:quartic}; a separate witness-free command-line interface is
not supplied.

\subsection{Exact chemical checks}
Symbolic checks were run for the fields
\begin{equation}
 1-x^2,\qquad x^2,\qquad \tfrac13-2x,
 \qquad (z,-x),\qquad (xz-1,x^2-z),\qquad 1.
\end{equation}
For each, the program verifies the rail-product invariants, the projection
identity, the damping identity \eqref{pqc:tu:eq:Einvariant}, the kinetic sign
condition, reconstruction from the emitted reaction list, and the degree bound.
The resulting species counts are $3,3,3,5,5,3$; the reaction counts after
componentwise monomial collection are $14,10,12,8,48,4$.
The actual degrees are $8,8,6,5,9,5$, within the stated bounds.
All six fields were also checked in the common-offset form. In dimension two,
the oscillator uses four species and six reactions, and the nonlinear example
uses four species and fifty-three reactions; their actual degrees are $11$ and
$12$. The latter complete reaction list is also included.

For the logistic example, $p^0=n^0=1$ and $q^0=1/3$ are rational. Before damping,
\begin{align}
 G_p&=p-p^3+2p^2n-pn^2,\\
 G_n&=-n+p^2n-2pn^2+n^3.
\end{align}
With $s=2$ the complete three-species field is
\begin{align}
 p'&=q^2(p-p^3+2p^2n-pn^2),\\
 n'&=q^2(-n+p^2n-2pn^2+n^3),\\
 q'&=-2q^4(pG_p+nG_n).
\end{align}
The package contains all fourteen reactions, not just the field. For example,
the term $-q^2p^3$ is realized by
$3P+2Q\to2P+2Q$ at rate $1$, and $2q^2p^2n$ by
$2P+N+2Q\to3P+N+2Q$ at rate $2$. Each negative term consumes a species already
present in its reactant monomial.

\subsection{An end-to-end chemical certificate}
The constant source flow $x'=1$, $x(0)=0$ produces the three-species damped
chemical field
\begin{equation}\label{pqc:tu:eq:constantchem}
 p'=qp,\qquad n'=-qn,\qquad q'=-2q^3(p^2-n^2),
 \qquad (p^0,n^0,q^0)=(1,1,1/3).
\end{equation}
Its four reactions are included in \code{constant_flow_reactions.json}.
For the projected target $1/2000<p-n<1/1250$, the exact checker accepts
\begin{equation}
 N=2000,\quad H=2\cdot10^6,\quad D=3\cdot10^{12},\quad R=2,
 \quad E_{\mathrm{in}}=J=1.
\end{equation}
Here $M=136$, $L=328$, and the final integer state is
\begin{equation}
 X_N=(3\,001\,000\,165\,502,\ 2\,999\,000\,165\,668,\
       999\,999\,850\,963),
 \qquad E_N=79\,186\,474.
\end{equation}
The projected terminal interval is therefore
\begin{equation}
 \left[\frac{1\,841\,626\,886}{3\cdot10^{12}},
       \frac{2\,158\,372\,782}{3\cdot10^{12}}\right]
 \subset (1/2000,1/1250).
\end{equation}
This is a certificate for the chemical ODE itself, not just a symbolic check
that it simulates a source equation. It permits both initial and forcing
uncertainties of $1/(3\cdot10^{12})$ until physical time $1/1000$.

The exact syntactic gate counter gives $g=42044$ for the corresponding full
unrolling, hence $126099$ natural witnesses and $118099$ quadratic residuals.
That large polynomial was counted but not materialized in this package; its
accepted integer tube is supplied. A one-step certificate for the same chemical
field and the wider projected target $(-1,1)$ was fully compiled, producing
$162$ natural witnesses and $158$ quadratic residuals, all verified to vanish.
Thus the package contains a direct, fully emitted chemical-to-quartic example
as well as the longer, tighter chemical event certificate.

\subsection{What was computationally verified}\label{pqc:tu:sec:verified}
The computations use Python 3.13.5 and SymPy 1.14.0 in the supplied run.
The tube generator and verifier use Python integers and exact fractions, with
no floating-point arithmetic. SymPy is used for the symbolic compiler and
chemical identities. Detailed inputs, certificates, residuals, witnesses,
reaction lists, and results are stored in JSON files.

These checks are finite computations, not a formal proof of the general
analytic theorems and not an independent verification of the Python interpreter
or SymPy. The general soundness, completeness, and continuation arguments are
proved in the text. The exact checks give reproducible evidence against
implementation and transcription errors.

\wtag\ \emph{Shipped names.} Source~18's text keeps its delivered file names. In
this report its six programs are \code{code/18-rational-tubes-tubes.py},
\code{-quartic.py}, \code{-kinetic.py}, \code{-run_checks.py},
\code{-constant_example.py} and \code{-verify_json.py}, with its
\code{Makefile} as \code{code/18-rational-tubes-Makefile}; its nineteen
\code{results/} files and its \code{requirements.txt} are
\code{data/18-rational-tubes-<name>}. The programs import one another by their

\section{Relation to existing methods and limitations}\label{pqc:tu:sec:related}

\subsection{Validated integration and logical reachability}
Validated numerical integration already produces rigorous solution enclosures.
For example, Immler formalized reachability analysis using adaptive
Runge--Kutta methods and affine arithmetic in Isabelle/HOL \cite{b64s18-immler}.
Our first-order Euler construction should not be mistaken for an improvement
in numerical efficiency over those methods. Its role is to make the full
acceptance condition an elementary integer circuit, with a completeness proof
and explicit accounting of every rounding witness.

Gao, Avigad, and Clarke's $\delta$-decision framework addresses bounded
first-order real formulas using controlled numerical relaxation
\cite{Gao2012}. The present acceptance test is exact integer equality and strict
integer inequality, but searches unboundedly over finite certificates. It is
a positive semidecision procedure, not a decision procedure for exact
unbounded reachability. There is therefore no conflict between its exactness
and the limitations of general real decision problems.

\subsection{ODE-to-chemical compilation}
The chemical-compilation literature includes exact generation of functions,
computation by convergence, polynomialization of elementary expressions, and
reductions of reaction complexity \cite{b64s18-fages,b64s18-hemery}. Those are different
specifications from the joint one here: rational initialization, exact forward
orbit projection, explicit finite-event preservation, a fixed species bound,
and no finite physical-time blow-up along the prescribed trajectory. The
common-offset construction additionally exposes a species--degree tradeoff.

Time changes and extra state variables are familiar tools in kinetic modeling.
The present contribution is not the observation that they can be used. It is
the explicit pairing of the conserved products $p_jn_j=c_j$ with the polynomial
damping invariant $q(1+S)=1$, followed by a proof of the complete arithmetic
interface. A more exhaustive comparison of normal forms may reveal earlier
instances of some or all of this construction; no priority conclusion is drawn
from the literature search performed for this manuscript.

\subsection{Open targets are essential to this proof}\label{pqc:tu:sec:open}
The completeness argument uses two positive margins: distance from the compact
trajectory to the containing box boundary, and distance of the terminal point
to the complement of the target. An exact equality target need not have the
second margin. For example $x'=-x$, $x(0)=1$ approaches zero without ever
reaching it, while a constant zero trajectory is always in the equality target.
The enclosure test cannot infer an exact zero merely from arbitrarily small
nonzero intervals.

Accordingly, this article does not solve general exact zero-hitting,
closed-target reachability, asymptotic convergence, universal safety, or
Zeno-sensitive hybrid verification. Some special cases may have additional
algebraic certificates, but they require new hypotheses or methods.
\wtag\ Two of these are treated elsewhere for discrete time. Part~III of this
report certifies robust avoidance of closed rational targets, a universal safety
property, for rational piecewise-affine maps under per-step noise
(Theorem~\ref{pqc:cb:thm:quartic}), and shows the noise-fragile remainder
$\pione$-complete (Theorem~\ref{pqc:cb:thm:classification}). The sibling report
\code{liveness-beyond-halting} classifies recurrence, deadline and
temporal-logic properties of discrete computable systems (its Theorem
\code{lbh:thm:hierarchy}: fixed deadlines $\pione$, bounded gaps $\sigtwo$,
computable deadlines $\Sigma^0_3$, recurrence $\Sigma^1_1$) and proves that none
of them has an ordinary Diophantine representation. Neither treats continuous
time.

\subsection{The chemical normal form is not a physical implementation claim}
The emitted system is an idealized finite deterministic mass-action network.
Species concentrations may become arbitrarily large as physical time tends to
infinity; rate constants are exact rational values; and the construction may
use high-order reactions and source or sink behavior without conservation of
physical mass. None of this proves that a small laboratory reaction network
can run an unbounded Turing computation under realistic stochastic noise.
The theorem concerns the mathematical semantics explicitly stated in Section~\ref{pqc:tu:sec:chemical}.

\section{A concrete route to formalization in ProveIt}\label{pqc:tu:sec:formal}

\subsection{Separate arithmetic from analysis}
The smallest useful trusted interface is a theorem of the form
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{check}(I,c)=\mathrm{true}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \text{every permitted perturbed solution reaches the target at }T(c).
\end{equation}
An integer checker can be made executable before formalizing the analytic
completeness proof. The implementation should use a finite sparse polynomial
syntax over integer coefficients, a positive common denominator, integer
vectors for nodes, and natural vectors for radius and remainder data.
The checker should reject malformed dimensions, zero denominators, invalid
natural parameters, and inconsistent list lengths before evaluating a field.

The arithmetic correctness layer proves Euclidean floor semantics for signed
dividends, ceiling semantics for natural dividends, the scaled guard identities,
and the exact relationship between $F(X/D)$ and $\widetilde F(X,D)$.
The analytic layer proves the box bounds, local solution comparison,
first-exit argument, and continuation lemma. This separation prevents a
fast numerical implementation from being silently treated as a proof of
ODE semantics.

\subsection{Suggested module boundaries}
A prospective module layout, not files claimed to exist in the repository, is:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{.34\textwidth}p{.57\textwidth}}
\toprule
Proposed module & Main obligation\\
\midrule
\code{PolynomialFlow.Syntax} & Rational sparse fields, rational initial data, open polyhedra\\
\code{PolynomialFlow.Bounds} & Coefficient bounds $M,L$ and infinity-norm estimates\\
\code{PolynomialFlow.TubeCheck} & Exact integer data and executable checker\\
\code{PolynomialFlow.TubeSound} & Perturbation estimates, existence, and terminal inclusion\\
\code{PolynomialFlow.TubeComplete} & Compact margins, mesh refinement, and successful certificate existence\\
\code{PolynomialFlow.Quartic} & Signed gates, slack compilation, counts, and unique fixed-parameter fibers\\
\code{KineticFlow.Hyperbolic} & Positive rails, conserved products, orbit correspondence\\
\code{KineticFlow.GlobalClock} & Damping invariant, derivative bounds, global existence\\
\code{KineticFlow.Offset} & Common-offset invariant and species--degree tradeoff\\
\code{PolynomialFlow.Diophantine} & Encoded checker enumerability and existing MRDP adapter\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The names are design suggestions, not tested Lean code. Exact compatibility with
the repository's pinned toolchain and current Mathlib ODE interfaces remains a
formalization task.
\wtag\ Part~III's plan (Section~\ref{pqc:cb:sec:formalization}) proposes a
\code{RobustReachability} namespace with modules \code{Grid},
\code{CutCertificate} and \code{Diophantine} for its discrete-time cut
certificates. The two proposals share their last layer: an encoded finite
checker proved primitive recursive, enumerated, and passed to
\code{Diophantine.mrdp}. A single namespace, with one shared
checker-to-MRDP adapter and separate modules for the discrete-time cut
certificates and for these continuous-time tubes, would avoid proving that
layer twice. None of the modules of either table exists in ProveIt.

\subsection{Trust and audit obligations}
A useful audit distinguishes the following claims: the arithmetic checker
terminates; its implementation matches the stated integer predicate; an accepted
certificate implies an actual analytic event; every event has a certificate;
the quadratic compiler preserves the checker; and MRDP applies to the encoded
predicate. Each needs its own theorem. A generated JSON certificate is not part
of the trusted boundary until a proved checker accepts it.

For the chemical lift, most identities are polynomial identities suitable for
ring normalization. The genuinely analytic obligations are positivity,
continuation from derivative bounds, and finiteness of the time-reparameterizing
integral on compact source segments. These should not be replaced by numerical
samples of the same identities.

\section{Further research questions and topics}\label{pqc:tu:sec:questions}
The following questions are specific continuations of the proved normal forms.
They are not all claimed to be established open problems in the literature;
several are proposed engineering or optimization problems for this project.

\begin{question}[An end-to-end kernel-checked analytic certificate]\label{pqc:tu:q:kernel}
Formalize robust soundness and completeness, then connect the exact natural
checker to the existing MRDP endpoint. A meaningful first milestone is a
kernel-checked positive-noise certificate for the logistic example, including
existence and containment rather than only arithmetic evaluation.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:kernel} (Part~I's compiler) and Part~III's recommended order after Question~\ref{pqc:cb:q:boundary}: all three put a kernel-checked finite certificate layer first.

\begin{question}[Higher-order canonical tubes]\label{pqc:tu:q:higher}
Replace Euler by rational Taylor or Runge--Kutta schemes while preserving a
unique arithmetic witness at fixed precision parameters. Determine explicit
tradeoffs between gate count per step, order, derivative bounds, and the
number of steps required by a target margin. Canonical interval bounds and
rounding policies must be specified rather than chosen nondeterministically.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Local rather than global conditioning]\label{pqc:tu:q:local}
Use a distinct rational box and Lipschitz bound on each step. Can the witness
normal form retain linear size and unique fibers while replacing the coarse
factor $\ee^{LT}$ by a computably accumulated local growth estimate? This could
substantially reduce the size of witnesses in stiff or strongly dissipative
regions without weakening soundness.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Part~III's Question~\ref{pqc:cb:q:grids}, which asks the same for its dense grids.

\begin{question}[A smaller global kinetic lift]\label{pqc:tu:q:smallerlift}
Can the common-offset construction be made global with only $d+1$ species,
while retaining polynomial mass-action semantics, rational initialization,
a linear projection, and every finite source event? Alternatively, can a
$d+2$-species construction attain the lower degree bound of the separate-rail
form? A lower bound would require a clearly stated class of encodings.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Low-molecularity normal forms with all guarantees retained]\label{pqc:tu:q:molecularity}
Known chemical transformations motivate reducing reaction order. The joint
question here is whether one can obtain a quantitative bimolecular construction
that simultaneously preserves rational preparation, the exact forward orbit,
finite-event completeness, and nonexplosion. Any quadratization must be checked
for auxiliary blow-up and time-change degeneracy, not only for local algebraic
identities.
\end{question}
\wtag\ The discrete reaction networks of the sibling report \code{canonical-diophantine-certificates} (the note in Section~\ref{pqc:tu:sec:chemical}) use discrete firings, not mass-action kinetics; that is a different semantics, and they do not answer it.

\begin{question}[Certified finite-event adapters for published universal flows]\label{pqc:tu:q:adapters}
Select one concrete polynomial or chemical universal construction and verify
\eqref{pqc:tu:eq:simulationcontract} for its actual coefficient field, initial-state
encoding, and terminal detector. This would turn the conditional transfer
statement into a fully instantiated theorem with explicit dimension and
reaction bounds.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Questions~\ref{pqc:q:direct} and~\ref{pqc:cb:q:realizers}: an instantiated adapter would be a polynomial continuous-time front end, but not a realizer of Part~III's trichotomy.

\begin{question}[Off-manifold chemical error budgets]\label{pqc:tu:q:offmanifold}
Study perturbations of $p_jn_j=c_j$ and $q(1+S)=1$. On a prescribed successful
finite segment, derive a projection error estimate from deviations of these
invariants. Such a result would describe how physical disturbances affect the
simulated clock and state, rather than merely certifying a terminal target in
the full chemical state space.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:cb:q:transfer}. Theorem~\ref{pqc:tu:thm:globalchemical} gives an exact orbit lift, explicitly not a noise transfer (Section~\ref{pqc:tu:sec:global}); this question asks for the missing estimate.

\begin{question}[Witness bit complexity and clock slowdown]\label{pqc:tu:q:bitcomplexity}
Relate source trajectory size, target margin, local conditioning, and elapsed
source time to the bit size of integer certificates before and after chemical
lifting. The degree and species bounds alone do not control computational cost.
Seek upper bounds under effective promises and matching lower bounds for
chosen simulator families.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Part~III's Question~\ref{pqc:cb:q:tradeoff} (radius--time tradeoffs).

\begin{question}[Beyond polynomial autonomous fields]\label{pqc:tu:q:beyond}
Polynomial nonautonomous systems can be handled by adjoining a clock variable
$t'=1$ and applying the present theorem. More ambitious extensions include
rational fields with certified nonvanishing denominators and hybrid systems
with explicitly separated switching guards. Exact contact events and Zeno
behavior must remain outside a claimed completeness theorem until separately
addressed.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:continuous}, whose Zeno and explosion clauses this question keeps open.

\begin{question}[Arithmetic optimization and fixed-dimensional compression]\label{pqc:tu:q:optimization}
Optimize the straight-line residual circuit, share repeated powers and
bounds, and compare the resulting explicit operation counts for the same
certificate semantics. Separately investigate fixed-dimensional compression
through the repository's MRDP infrastructure. Do not conflate uniqueness of
arithmetic gate values with uniqueness of the compressed existential witness.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Questions~\ref{pqc:q:smaller} and~\ref{pqc:qm:q:smaller} (smaller explicit quartics for other predicates) and Remark~\ref{pqc:conv:rem:fixedpoly}; Corollary~\ref{pqc:tu:cor:fixedquartic} adds a fourth unexpanded fixed polynomial.

\begin{question}[Boundary events with additional structure]\label{pqc:tu:q:boundary}
Identify classes of equality targets that admit complementary algebraic
certificates, such as a preserved polynomial invariant together with a strict
transversality condition. Determine exactly which hypotheses restore a
finite complete certificate and which merely prove one-sided sufficient tests.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:cb:q:critical}, the discrete-time question of exact critical-level reachability.

\section{Conclusion}\label{pqc:tu:sec:conclusion}
Finite open events of rational polynomial dynamics admit more than an abstract
appeal to recursive enumerability. They admit a complete integer error-tube
language whose existence and noise obligations are proved, whose fixed-length
acceptance relation is a counted quartic sum of squares, and whose fixed-mesh
witness is canonical. The construction supplies a precise analytic front end
to the Diophantine interfaces already developed in ProveIt.

For continuous chemical computation, an exact projection identity by itself is
not enough: the encoding must also survive until the simulated event. Conserved
hyperbolic rail products eliminate one source of auxiliary blow-up, and a single
polynomial damping species makes the prescribed chemical trajectory global.
The separate-rail normal form uses $2d+1$ species. Common-offset compression
saves $d-1$ species at a cost of three in the degree upper bound. Both preserve
every finite original open event without introducing irrational data.

The strongest unconditional claims of this article are these certificate and
embedding theorems. Their combination gives a concrete, reproducible research
result and a formalization target. It is not presented as a solution of a
classical single-fold conjecture, as a new discovery of chemical universality,
or as an exact decision procedure for arbitrary continuous dynamics.

\section{Source 18 appendix: a fully written quartic family for a constant flow}\label{pqc:tu:app:explicit}
This appendix removes every arithmetic-circuit abbreviation in a simple case.
Consider $x'=1$, $x(0)=0$, $U=(9/10,11/10)$ and the nominal certificate.
Here $M=1$, $L=0$, $Q=H$, and the canonical error radius is exactly $E_i=i$.
The floor nodes are nonnegative, so no signed pairs are needed in this
specialized example.

Fix $N\geq1$. In addition to the free natural parameters $R,H,D$, use natural
witness variables
\begin{equation}
 A_*,G_*,r_*,h_*,d_*,t_-,t_+,
 \quad X_1,\ldots,X_N,
 \quad U_i,S_i,L_i^-,L_i^+\quad(0\leq i<N),
\end{equation}
and put $X_0=0$. Define $\mathcal P_N$ to be the sum of the squares of these
$4N+7$ residuals:
\begin{align}
 &A_*-DH,\qquad G_*-RA_*+D,\label{pqc:tu:eq:specialglobal}\\
 &R-1-r_*,\qquad H-1-h_*,\qquad D-1-d_*,\label{pqc:tu:eq:specialpositive}\\
 &H(X_{i+1}-X_i)+U_i-D &&(0\leq i<N),\label{pqc:tu:eq:specialfloor}\\
 &U_i+S_i+1-H &&(0\leq i<N),\label{pqc:tu:eq:specialrem}\\
 &G_*-Hi-HX_i-1-L_i^- &&(0\leq i<N),\label{pqc:tu:eq:specialguardminus}\\
 &G_*-Hi+HX_i-1-L_i^+ &&(0\leq i<N),\label{pqc:tu:eq:specialguardplus}\\
 &10X_N-9D-10N-1-t_-,\label{pqc:tu:eq:speciallower}\\
 &11D-10X_N-10N-1-t_+.\label{pqc:tu:eq:specialupper}
\end{align}
Each displayed residual has degree at most two. The family has $5N+7$ natural
witness variables, and $\deg\mathcal P_N\leq4$. It is the specialization of the
certificate equations after eliminating deterministic arithmetic identities;
its smaller counts are not the counts of the generic compiler.

For $N=2$, $R=H=2$, $D=100$, a complete witness is
\begin{align*}
 A_*&=200,&G_*&=300,&r_*&=1,&h_*&=1,&d_*&=99,\\
 X_1&=50,&X_2&=100,&U_0&=0,&U_1&=0,\\
 S_0&=1,&S_1&=1,&L_0^-&=299,&L_0^+&=299,\\
 L_1^-&=197,&L_1^+&=397,&t_-&=79,&t_+&=79.
\end{align*}
Thus a single explicitly specified quartic equation with seventeen natural
witnesses certifies a genuine continuous-time reachability event. The file
\code{specialized_constant_quartic.json} contains all fifteen residuals and
all witness values, while \code{specialized_constant_expanded.txt} contains
the expanded ordinary polynomial. Its degree is checked to be exactly four.

\section{\wtag\ Conventions of Part IX}
\label{pqc:iq:conv}

Part~IX prints one manuscript of batch~76 in full: source~19,
\emph{Infinite Quantum Runs, Finite Diophantine Certificates: canonical group
inverses, all stopping-time moments, and geometric clocks with undecidable
supports} (batch-76 manuscript~04, dated 2 October 2026, pin \code{c58206ca1}).
For a rational, finite-dimensional, time-homogeneous quantum loop it
characterizes the group inverse $G=(I-T)^\#$ and the Ces\`aro projection $P$ by
four quadratic matrix identities with a unique solution
(Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:group}); derives from them the exit probabilities,
stopped output states and every finite-path factorial moment
(Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:moments}) and a finite recurrence for all of them
