unique natural witness through seven-coordinate canonical rational wires
(Lemma~\ref{pqc:iq:lem:wire}, Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:quartic}); gives a
convergent Laurent law for a weak killing clock (Theorems~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:regulator}
and~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:mixture}); wraps the Eisert--M\"uller--Gogolin instruments
in a geometric clock that fixes the whole runtime law while keeping the existence
of a forbidden completed record undecidable (Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:geometric});
and refutes the unrestricted reading of a generalized-inverse rationality
conjecture (Proposition~\ref{pqc:iq:prop:counterexample}). Everything in

except the passages marked \wtag.

``Canonical rational quartic compilation'' and extends that integer compiler to
rational wires (the note after it). Theorems~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:moments}
and~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:allmoments} extend the Part~V remark above from absorption
probabilities of finite Markov chains to stopped operators and all finite-path
moments of quantum loops, with a unique-witness certificate.

\paragraph{A question of source 19 that Part~II answers.} Source~19's
Question~\ref{pqc:iq:q:clocks} asks for the same exact geometric law with fewer
outcomes or a smaller Hilbert dimension. Source~19 deliberately did not use
Part~II's four-dimensional theorem. Composing its clock with
Theorem~\ref{pqc:qm:thm:47} (source~07) gives dimension four with seven
continuation outcomes and one halting outcome
(Corollary~\ref{pqc:iq:cor:dimfour}, written here, conditional on Part~II);
the question is re-scoped in a dated note after it.

\paragraph{Questions of Parts I--VIII.} Source~19 answers none. It bears, by
analogy, on Question~\ref{pqc:q:operator} (canonical characteristic-polynomial
data instead of spectral bases) and on Question~\ref{pqc:q:histories} (exact
infinite histories); dated notes after both say what it does and does not do.
Its Question~\ref{pqc:iq:q:smaller} is of the kind of
Questions~\ref{pqc:q:smaller} and~\ref{pqc:qm:q:smaller}, and its
Question~\ref{pqc:iq:q:formal} of the kind of Question~\ref{pqc:q:kernel}. It
does not touch Question~\ref{pqc:q:instruments}: its own construction keeps
dimension fifteen. The sibling reports \code{canonical-diophantine-certificates}
and \code{liveness-beyond-halting} share no theorem with it.

The tempting false readings are these. ``Dimension four'' in Part~II is a

\subsection{Abstract and status statement of source 19}
\paragraph{Abstract of source 19.}
% --- source 19, lines 86-110 ---
An execution can have unbounded duration without requiring an unbounded
arithmetic certificate for its aggregate stopping statistics. For a rational,
finite-dimensional, time-homogeneous quantum loop, we characterize the group
inverse $G=(I-T)^\#$ and fixed-point projection $P$ by four quadratic matrix
identities. The pair is unique, including on singular and nonterminating
instances. It gives exact exit probabilities, stopped output states, every
finite-path factorial moment, and a finite recurrence determining all of them.
We compile these identities into a single quartic polynomial over natural
numbers with a unique witness for each correct rational answer. The elementary
rational-wire construction uses seven natural coordinates; a dense inverse
certificate has exactly $88D^3+9D^2+14$ natural witnesses for matrix dimension
$D$, independently of execution duration.

A second result sharply separates runtime from support. Applying an independent
rational geometric clock to the published quantum measurement-occurrence
construction yields almost-surely terminating devices with exactly the same
geometric runtime distribution, yet undecidable existence of a forbidden
completed measurement record. A weak-clock analysis gives a convergent Laurent
expansion whose residue is the nontermination probability, whose regular
coefficients are finite-path binomial moments, and whose inverse has an
all-orders rational expansion. Finally, we give a counterexample to the
unrestricted reading of a published generalized-inverse rationality conjecture
and prove its canonical, rank-stratified replacement. Four quantum examples,
four exported quartic certificates, and 33,708 exact assertions accompany the
proofs.

\wtag\ ``A dense inverse certificate'' means the supplied unsimplified dense
schedule of Section~\ref{pqc:iq:sec:compiler}, for which the count is exact; it
is not a lower bound for dense certificates in general, as source~19 itself says
there.

\paragraph{Status statement of source 19.}
% --- source 19, lines 74-80 ---
This manuscript provides self-contained proofs for an
explicit certificate construction and several consequences, together with exact
arithmetic software and independently checked certificate files. It is
AI-assisted and unrefereed; no Lean formalization is claimed. Classical
spectral, quantum-runtime, and undecidability results are identified separately
from the synthesis developed here. Historical priority for the assembled
construction is not established.

\wtag\ Source~19's claims and inherited ingredients are listed in
Section~\ref{pqc:iq:sec:scope}; its limitations there (exact rational inputs,

Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:allmoments} (a recurrence, not a graph in a variable

single-fold MRDP theorem''), after Corollary~\ref{pqc:iq:cor:tail}, in
Sections~\ref{pqc:iq:sec:geometric}--\ref{pqc:iq:sec:scheduled} (no physical

\section{The research target and what is actually claimed}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:scope}
The question motivating this work is not merely whether quantum computation can
be represented by polynomial equations. For an effectively specified finite
witness relation, the Matiyasevich--Robinson--Davis--Putnam theorem already gives
an existential Diophantine representation. The inspected \reponame{} interface
states precisely a finite integer polynomial with finitely many natural
witnesses, chosen before the input, and includes input zero
\cite{b76s19-RepoMRDP}. What that theorem alone does not provide is a small,
transparent, unique certificate for an \emph{infinite sum of execution
probabilities}.

The repository's existing coherent-computation report already addresses finite
circuits, interference, exact rational and cyclotomic arithmetic, and canonical
witnesses \cite{b76s19-RepoCoherent}. Its larger quantum/probabilistic collection also
contains measurement mortality, continuous dynamics, and normalization reports
[\wtag\ this report: Parts~I--III, and Parts~V--VIII]. This manuscript therefore changes the mathematical object:
the principal certificate concerns the entire stopping law of a finite-state
quantum loop, not a selected bounded execution.

\wtag\ The ``coherent-computation report'' is source~10, Part~VI of this report
(Sections~\ref{pqc:cc:sec:wires}--\ref{pqc:cc:sec:unbounded}); its audit is
shipped here as \code{10-coherent-circuits-SOURCE_AUDIT.md}. The
``quantum/probabilistic collection'' is this report, whose README source~19 read.

There are two very different meanings of ``unbounded'' here. A loop can repeat
arbitrarily many times while its unnormalized density matrix evolves in one
fixed finite-dimensional vector space. Alternatively, an existential question
can range over arbitrary outcome words; this retains information that is lost
when all outcomes are summed into one continuation operator. The first admits
our finite rational summary. The second can remain undecidable even after an
independent clock makes the length distribution completely elementary.

\subsection{Main contributions and inherited ingredients}
The principal constructive theorem is the combination of
Theorems~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:group}, \ref{pqc:iq:thm:allmoments}, and
\ref{pqc:iq:thm:quartic}: a rank-independent rational certificate, an all-orders
recurrence, and an explicit unique-witness quartic compiler. Their joint
purpose is to make infinite-run statistics checkable using ordinary integer
arithmetic, with exact accounting and no time horizon.

The geometric-clock theorem, Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:geometric}, is an explicit
preservation result built on Eisert--M\"uller--Gogolin's published
undecidability theorem \cite{emg}. The regulator theorem gives the associated
all-orders singular expansion and a distributional scaling limit. The
rationality counterexample in Section~\ref{pqc:iq:sec:conjecture} is elementary but
addresses an actual sentence in the literature: arbitrary generalized-inverse
selection need not preserve rational dependence on parameters.

We do \emph{not} claim that the following underlying facts originate here:
generalized inverses in Markov-chain hitting-time theory, resolvent generating
functions, finite-dimensional quantum expected-runtime methods,
Cayley--Hamilton recurrences, or MRDP. In particular, Lardizabal already uses
generalized inverses and generating functions for quantum hitting times
\cite{b76s19-Lardizabal}; Liu--Zhou--Barthe--Ying prove finite-dimensional quantum
almost-sure/finite-expected-runtime equivalences and develop symbolic methods
\cite{b76s19-LZBY}. The contribution is the exact canonical certificate architecture,
its accounting, and the particular consequences proved below, not a claim that
infinite quantum paths had never previously been handled.

\subsection{Boundaries that matter}
Our arithmetic input consists of \emph{exact rational coordinates}, not black-box
approximations to real numbers. The loop is finite-dimensional and
\emph{time-homogeneous}; arbitrary unbounded classical memory is not secretly
included. Physical validity is a promise on the input maps. The quartic itself
certifies the algebraic equations, not a general quantum-synthesis problem.

For each fixed dimension and requested finite interface there is one finite
polynomial. A separate all-moments interface encodes an infinite sequence by a
finite recurrence. Neither construction produces one unique-witness polynomial
for the halting behavior of every Turing machine. In particular, it does not
resolve the general single-fold or finite-fold Diophantine representation
problems. No comparison with the repository's optimized universal-operation
bounds is intended.

\section{An exact model of a stopping quantum loop}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:model}
Let $\mathcal H=\C^d$. A continuation map
$\cT:M_d(\C)\to M_d(\C)$ is completely positive and trace nonincreasing. Let
$\cE_1,\ldots,\cE_r$ be completely positive exit maps into finite-dimensional
matrix spaces, satisfying, for every $X\geq0$,
\begin{equation}
 \tr\cT(X)+\sum_{j=1}^r\tr\cE_j(X)=\tr X.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:conservation}
\end{equation}
At each test the experiment either exits with label $j$ and output
$\cE_j(X)$, or continues with unnormalized state $\cT(X)$. Normalizing after
individual outcomes gives the usual conditional states, but the unnormalized
formalism already includes their probabilities and avoids divisions along
execution paths.

The initial state $\rho$ is positive semidefinite with trace one. We assume
that $\rho$ and every map have rational coordinates in the real vector space
of Hermitian matrices. Use the basis
\begin{equation}
 E_{ii},\qquad E_{ij}+E_{ji},\qquad iE_{ij}-iE_{ji}\quad (i<j),
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:basis}
\end{equation}
with diagonals first. Its dimension is $D=d^2$. Write $T\in\Q^{D\times D}$
for the continuation matrix, $x\in\Q^D$ for $\rho$, and $\ell$ for the trace
row. Thus $\ell$ has $d$ ones followed by zeros. The scalar exit rows are
$e_j=\tr\circ\cE_j$, in coordinates, and
\begin{equation}
 e_\Sigma:=\sum_j e_j=\ell(I-T).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:exitrow}
\end{equation}
Rational real or complex-rational Kraus matrices are sufficient for these
assumptions. Rational superoperators are the actual input class; they need not
come with a rational Kraus decomposition.

Let $N$ denote the number of continuations before an exit, so $N=0$ means
immediate exit. Let $L=N+1$ count tests including the terminal test, and put
$N=L=\infty$ on a divergent execution. Then
\begin{align}
 a_{j,n}&:=\Pr(N=n,\text{exit }j)=e_jT^nx,\\
 s_n&:=\Pr(L>n)=\ell T^nx,\\
 s_n-s_{n+1}&=\sum_j a_{j,n}.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:survival}
\end{align}
The numbers $s_n$ decrease from $s_0=1$, so they have a limit $w$, the
probability of nontermination.

\begin{definition}
For $k\geq0$, the \emph{normalized defective factorial moment} is
\begin{equation}
 b_{j,k}=\sum_{n\geq0}\binom nk a_{j,n}.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:binomialmoment}
\end{equation}
It is a moment of the finite-exit subprobability measure. Divergent paths are
excluded from this sum. In particular, $b_{j,0}$ is the exit probability, not
necessarily one.
\end{definition}
When $b_{j,0}>0$, the corresponding conditional factorial moment of $N$ is
$k!b_{j,k}/b_{j,0}$. Ordinary moments follow from
$n^m=\sum_{k=0}^m S(m,k)\fall nk$, with $S(m,k)$ the Stirling numbers of the
second kind. This convention separates finite-path statistics from the
unconditional expectation, which is infinite as soon as $w>0$.

Finite classical control can be included by replacing $M_d(\C)$ with a finite
direct sum of matrix algebras. Then $D$ is the sum of the squares of the local
Hilbert dimensions. The same proofs apply. An unbounded tape or counter,
however, does not fit in such a fixed direct sum.

\section{The canonical rational inverse certificate}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:group}
\begin{lemma}[Power boundedness]
\label[lemma]{pqc:iq:lem:bounded}
For every Hermitian $X$ and $n\geq0$,
$\|\cT^n(X)\|_1\leq\|X\|_1$. Consequently $T$ is power bounded, every
eigenvalue has modulus at most one, and every eigenvalue of modulus one is
semisimple.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $X=X_+-X_-$ with $X_\pm\geq0$ and
$\|X\|_1=\tr X_++\tr X_-$. Positivity and trace nonincrease give
\[
 \|\cT^n(X)\|_1\leq\tr\cT^n(X_+)+\tr\cT^n(X_-)
 \leq\tr X_++\tr X_-.
\]
Complexifying the Hermitian space changes a norm bound by at most a fixed
factor, so the powers are uniformly bounded on the full complex vector space.
An eigenvalue of modulus greater than one would produce exponential growth.
A nontrivial Jordan block at modulus one would produce polynomial growth.
Both contradict that bound.
\end{proof}

Put $A=I-T$. Zero is therefore a semisimple eigenvalue of $A$ whenever it
occurs, and
\begin{equation}
 \Q^D=\ker A\oplus\im A.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:splitting}
\end{equation}
The two subspaces have rational bases. On the first summand define $G=0$; on
the second define $G$ to be the inverse of the restriction of $A$. Let $P$
be identity on $\ker A$ and zero on $\im A$. This is the group inverse
$G=A^\#$ and its associated projection.

\begin{theorem}[Four equations, with no rank choice]
\label{pqc:iq:thm:group}
For the continuation matrix $T$, there is exactly one rational pair
$(G,P)\in\Q^{D\times D}\times\Q^{D\times D}$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{AG+P=I,\qquad GA+P=I,\qquad AP=0,\qquad GP=0.}
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:four}
\end{equation}
In fact the pair is unique over $\C$. It satisfies
$P^2=P$, $PG=GP=0$, $TP=PT=P$, and $TG=GT$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 P=\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac1m\sum_{n=0}^{m-1}T^n.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:cesaro}
\end{equation}
The same equations characterize a unique pair for any rational $A$ whose
zero eigenvalue is semisimple, whether or not $A$ arises from a physical map.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
In a basis adapted to \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:splitting}, write
$A=\diag(0,B)$ with $B$ invertible. The prescribed matrices
$G=\diag(0,B^{-1})$ and $P=\diag(I,0)$ satisfy all four equations and are
rational when the basis is rational.

Conversely, the first two equations imply $AG=GA$ and $P=I-AG$.
Multiplying $GA+P=I$ on the left by $A$ yields $AGA=A$, because $AP=0$.
Multiplying $AG+P=I$ on the left by $G$ yields $GAG=G$, because $GP=0$.
Commutation with $A$ forces the off-diagonal blocks of $G$ to vanish in the
adapted basis. The bottom block is $B^{-1}$, and $GAG=G$ forces its top block
to be zero. Thus $G$ and then $P$ are uniquely determined. The additional
identities follow immediately in that basis.

For \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:cesaro}, the Ces\`aro means are identity on the eigenspace of
$T$ at one. On any other peripheral eigenspace their scalar factors are
$m^{-1}(1-\lambda^m)/(1-\lambda)$ and tend to zero. On the generalized
stable eigenspaces they also tend to zero. This proves the limit.
\end{proof}

The point of \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:four} is its \emph{fixed syntax}. The certifier never
needs to guess the rank, a nonzero minor, a spectral decomposition, a Jordan
form, or a limiting time. Such objects may be used by a generator, but they
are not part of the certificate's interface. Every displayed matrix identity
is quadratic in its entries.

\begin{corollary}[Exact nontermination]
\label[corollary]{pqc:iq:cor:nontermination}
The map represented by $P$ is completely positive and trace nonincreasing.
For a density coordinate vector $x$,
\begin{equation}
 w=\ell Px,\qquad \Pr(L<\infty)=1-\ell Px.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:w}
\end{equation}
Almost-sure termination on this state is equivalent to $Px=0$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The Ces\`aro maps in \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:cesaro} are completely positive and trace
nonincreasing. These properties are closed under finite-dimensional limits;
for complete positivity this also follows by taking limits of their positive
semidefinite Choi matrices. Hence $P\rho\geq0$. The Ces\`aro means of the
convergent scalar sequence $s_n$ have the same limit $w$, and their limit is
$\ell Px$. A positive semidefinite matrix has trace zero exactly when it is
zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The projection $P$ is a \emph{superoperator} projection. It is not generally
an orthogonal Hilbert-space projection. The limit $T^n$ itself need not exist;
only its Ces\`aro average is used. Confusing these two limits would exclude
legitimate trapped unitary dynamics, including our qutrit example.
\end{remark}

\section{Stopped kernels and every finite-path moment}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:moments}
A singular $I-T$ does not prevent convergence of an exit distribution. What
matters is the interaction between the exit map and the peripheral spectrum.

\begin{lemma}[Exit maps annihilate the entire peripheral subspace]
\label[lemma]{pqc:iq:lem:peripheral}
For every exit map $\cE_j$ and every eigenvector $v$ of the complexified $T$
with $|\lambda|=1$, one has $\cE_j(v)=0$. Consequently there exist $C>0$
and $0<\theta<1$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \|\cE_jT^n\|\leq C\theta^n\qquad(n\geq0).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:exitdecay}
\end{equation}
The constants may depend on the maps; no uniform gap is asserted.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $X\geq0$, telescoping \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:conservation} gives
\[
 \sum_{n\geq0}\|\cE_j\cT^n(X)\|_1
 =\sum_{n\geq0}\tr\cE_j\cT^n(X)\leq\tr X.
\]
Decompose each member of a finite Hermitian basis into its positive and
negative parts. By the triangle inequality, the same series of norms is
finite on each basis vector, and therefore on every vector after
complexification. If $Tv=\lambda v$ and $|\lambda|=1$, its summands are
$\|\lambda^n\cE_j(v)\|$, which can be summable only when $\cE_j(v)=0$.

All peripheral eigenvalues are semisimple by Lemma~\ref{pqc:iq:lem:bounded}.
Therefore the remaining terms in $\cE_jT^n$ come from finitely many Jordan
blocks at eigenvalues of modulus less than one. They are polynomial factors
in $n$ times exponentially decaying terms; enlarging the exponential rate to
any number strictly between the largest surviving modulus and one absorbs
these polynomial factors. Nilpotent blocks contribute only a finite initial
segment. This proves \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:exitdecay}.
\end{proof}

Define the stopped output generating function
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal F_j(z)=\sum_{n\geq0}z^n\cE_j\cT^n(\rho).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:operatorpgf}
\end{equation}
For $|z|<1$ this equals $\cE_j(I-zT)^{-1}x$ in coordinates. Although the
resolvent alone may be singular at $z=1$ or other points of the unit circle,
Lemma~\ref{pqc:iq:lem:peripheral} cancels every such singularity after applying the
exit map.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical stopped moments]
\label{pqc:iq:thm:moments}
Each $\mathcal F_j$ is a rational matrix-valued function that is analytic in
some disk $|z|<R_j$ with $R_j>1$. For every integer $k\geq0$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\mathcal F_j^{(k)}(1)}{k!}
 =\sum_{n\geq0}\binom nk\cE_j\cT^n(\rho)
 =\cE_jG(TG)^kx.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:operatormoments}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{b_{j,k}=e_jG(TG)^kx.}
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:momentformula}
\end{equation}
All finite-path moments are finite and rational. The map
$\cE_jG(TG)^k$ is completely positive, even though $G$ itself need not be a
positive map.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The exponential bound \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:exitdecay} permits termwise differentiation
in a disk of radius greater than one. Rationality follows from the adjugate
formula for $(I-zT)^{-1}$ and cancellation of removable singularities.

On a stable generalized eigenspace, $G=(I-T)^{-1}$. Differentiating the
resolvent gives
\[
 \frac1{k!}\frac{d^k}{dz^k}(I-zT)^{-1}
 =(I-zT)^{-1}\bigl(T(I-zT)^{-1}\bigr)^k.
\]
At $z=1$ this is $G(TG)^k$. On the entire peripheral space both sides become
zero after applying $\cE_j$, by Lemma~\ref{pqc:iq:lem:peripheral}. This proves
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:operatormoments} without requiring $T^n$ to converge. Taking traces
proves \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:momentformula}.

Finally, each partial sum of
$\sum_n\binom nk\cE_jT^n$ is completely positive, and the series converges
in operator norm. Its limit is completely positive. Rationality follows from
Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:group} and finite rational matrix operations.
\end{proof}

The zeroth operator moment is the full unnormalized exit state. Dividing it by
$b_{j,0}>0$ gives the density matrix conditioned on exit $j$. Thus the same
construction certifies not only numbers but complete stopped output states.
If an exit has probability zero, no conditional state is defined; the
unnormalized operator remains exactly zero.

\begin{proposition}[A finite part with a direct probabilistic meaning]
\label[proposition]{pqc:iq:prop:finitepart}
For $m\geq0$, set
\begin{equation}
 a_m^*=\ell G(TG)^m x.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:astar}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 a_m^*=\E\left[\binom L{m+1};\ L<\infty\right]\geq0.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:tailmoments}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \ell Gx=\sum_{n\geq0}(s_n-w)=\E[L;L<\infty].
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:finitefirst}
\end{equation}
If $w=0$, this is the ordinary expected number of tests. If $w>0$, it is
not the unconditional expectation, which is infinite.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $H=TG$. Since $AG=I-P$, we have $G=I-P+H$ and $I+H=G+P$.
The total exit row is $e_\Sigma=\ell A$, so $e_\Sigma G=\ell(I-P)$.
Pascal's identity and Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:moments} give
\begin{align*}
 \E\left[\binom L{m+1};L<\infty\right]
 &=e_\Sigma G(H^{m+1}+H^m)x\\
 &=\ell(I-P)H^m(G+P)x=\ell GH^mx.
\end{align*}
Here $PG=GP=0$ and $PH=HP=0$; the formula also holds at $m=0$.
Alternatively, the elementary tail identity
$\sum_{n=0}^{L-1}\binom nm=\binom L{m+1}$ gives
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:tailmoments} by summing $s_n-w$ with binomial weights. All sums are
finite or absolutely convergent by the preceding theorem.
\end{proof}

This proposition is useful when manipulating $G$: individual entries can have
signs with no direct probability interpretation, while these complete exit
maps and trace functionals are positive. Dropping the fixed-point contribution
without identifying the appropriate finite-path quantity would give an
incorrect interpretation of the answer.

\section{One finite recurrence certifies all orders}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:allorders}
Unrolling the recurrence
\begin{equation}
 v_0=Gx,\qquad v_{k+1}=GTv_k,\qquad b_{j,k}=e_jv_k
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:vectorrecurrence}
\end{equation}
requires $O(D^3+K D^2+rKD)$ rational arithmetic gates through order $K$,
including the inverse constraints. But even the moment order can be eliminated
from the interface by certifying one rational generating function.

\begin{theorem}[Finite all-moments certificate]
\label{pqc:iq:thm:allmoments}
Let $H=TG$ and write
\begin{equation}
 q(u)=\det(I-uH)=1+c_1u+\cdots+c_Du^D.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:q}
\end{equation}
For each exit $j$, the first $D$ moments $b_{j,0},\ldots,b_{j,D-1}$ and the
$D$ coefficients $c_1,\ldots,c_D$ determine every subsequent moment by
\begin{equation}
 b_{j,n}+c_1b_{j,n-1}+\cdots+c_Db_{j,n-D}=0\qquad(n\geq D).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:momentrecurrence}
\end{equation}
More precisely, with $c_0=1$ and
\begin{equation}
 p_j(u)=\sum_{n=0}^{D-1}\left(\sum_{i=0}^nc_i b_{j,n-i}\right)u^n,
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:p}
\end{equation}
we have, as rational functions and as power series near zero,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\sum_{k\geq0}b_{j,k}u^k
 =e_jG(I-uH)^{-1}x=\frac{p_j(u)}{q(u)}=F_j(1+u),}
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:allpgf}
\end{equation}
where $F_j=\tr\mathcal F_j$. A rational arithmetic circuit of size
$O(D^4+rD^2)$ certifies this entire finite description, independently of any
execution horizon or moment order.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Cayley--Hamilton gives
$H^D+c_1H^{D-1}+\cdots+c_DI=0$. Multiply by $e_jGH^{n-D}$ and $x$ to get
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:momentrecurrence}. Multiplying the generating series by $q(u)$
then leaves precisely \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:p}. Since $q(0)=1$, these coefficients define
a unique formal power series; no minimality of $q$ is required.

The matrix geometric series gives the first equality in
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:allpgf}. The last follows from the Taylor expansion at one in
Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:moments}. Thus the finite data determine not just a list of
moments but the complete rational stopping generating function and hence its
probabilities at every finite time.

For the claimed circuit, compute $H$, the first $D$ moment vectors, and the
coefficients of \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:q} by the following fixed recursion:
\begin{align}
 B_0&=I,\qquad M_k=HB_{k-1},\\
 c_k&=-\frac1k\tr M_k,\qquad B_k=M_k+c_kI
 \quad(1\leq k\leq D).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:fl}
\end{align}
This is the Faddeev--LeVerrier recursion, whose verification is included in
Section~\ref{pqc:iq:app:fl}. The only divisions are by the fixed positive integers
$1,\ldots,D$; equivalently they are multiplications by pinned rational
constants. Dense matrix products cost $O(D^4)$ for all $D$ stages. Computing
the first $D$ moment vectors costs $O(D^3+rD^2)$. The same circuit works on
every admissible rank stratum.
\end{proof}

The all-orders interface certifies a finite recurrence and its initial data.
It does not claim a fixed single-fold polynomial graph with an arbitrary
moment index $k$ supplied as an additional input.

The denominator may contain factors canceled by $p_j$, for example factors
arising from a trapped rotating sector. This is harmless. Keeping the
nonminimal characteristic denominator avoids choices among observable
subspaces, degrees, and factorization patterns, thereby preserving a simple
canonical certificate.

\begin{remark}[Whole laws versus individual words]
The function $F_j$ sums all continuation outcomes at each time. It does not
record which individual word produced that outcome. Therefore a certificate
for every coefficient of $F_j$ does not automatically certify the zero/nonzero
status of every word probability. Section~\ref{pqc:iq:sec:geometric} makes this
information loss decisive.
\end{remark}

\section{A unique-witness quartic over natural numbers}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:compiler}
All variables in this section are natural numbers including zero unless
specified otherwise. The construction uses no existential real variables,
integer inequalities, hidden exponentiation, or nonunique four-square
representations. Its output is an ordinary integer polynomial displayed
succinctly as a sum of squares of quadratic residuals.

\subsection{Seven coordinates for one rational number}
Represent a rational wire by the tuple
\begin{equation}
 (p,m,h,u,v_+,v_-,s)\in\N^7,
 \qquad n=p-m,\quad d=h+1,\quad v=v_+-v_-.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:wire}
\end{equation}
Impose four equations:
\begin{equation}
 pm=0,\qquad v_+v_-=0,\qquad nu-dv=1,\qquad u+s=h.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:wireconstraints}
\end{equation}
The represented rational number is $n/d$.

\begin{lemma}[Canonical rational wire]
\label[lemma]{pqc:iq:lem:wire}
Every rational number has exactly one representation satisfying
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:wireconstraints}. All four residuals have degree at most two.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The sign constraints uniquely encode the signed integers $n$ and $v$ by their
positive and negative parts. The denominator is positive. The B\'ezout equation
forces $\gcd(n,d)=1$, and the last equation forces $0\leq u\leq d-1$.
For a fixed reduced fraction with $d>1$, multiplication by $n$ permutes
residue classes modulo $d$, so there is a unique $u$ in this interval with
$nu\equiv1\pmod d$. It uniquely fixes $v=(nu-1)/d$ and $s=d-1-u$.
For $d=1$, the unique values are $u=s=0$ and $v=-1$. This also handles the
rational number zero: $n=0,d=1$. Conversely these choices satisfy all four
constraints. The reduced signed numerator and positive denominator are
uniquely determined by their rational value.
\end{proof}

The bounded B\'ezout coefficient is essential. An unbounded B\'ezout pair
would introduce infinitely many witnesses for the same rational number.
Likewise the complementary slack $s$ turns the bound into a unique natural
coordinate rather than a separate inequality.

To pin a wire to a given rational $a/b$, with $b>0$, add
\begin{equation}
 bn-ad=0.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:pin}
\end{equation}
For a polynomial uniform in the input, encode the signed input numerator by
two natural parameters and write $b=b_0+1$. Equation~\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:pin} remains
quadratic jointly in input parameters and witnesses. The input fraction need
not itself be reduced: the internal wire still has a unique canonical value.

\subsection{Quadratic arithmetic gates}
A signed integer auxiliary $r$ is encoded by two natural rails $r_+,r_-$,
with $r=r_+-r_-$ and $r_+r_-=0$. Whenever $r$ is prescribed by a quadratic
expression, this uses two variables and two quadratic residuals, including
the equation defining $r$.

Suppose wires $a,b,c$ have canonical numerators and denominators
$n_a,d_a,n_b,d_b,n_c,d_c$. For an addition or subtraction $c=a\pm b$,
introduce signed auxiliaries $r,t$ and a natural auxiliary $k$:
\begin{align}
 r&=n_a d_b,& t&=n_b d_a,& k&=d_a d_b,\\
 (r\pm t)d_c&=n_c k.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:addgate}
\end{align}
Together with the two sign constraints, these are six quadratic residuals in
five new natural variables, in addition to the seven coordinates of the
output wire. All denominators are positive, so they are equivalent to the
required rational equality. The auxiliary values are unique.

For a multiplication $c=ab$, introduce signed $r$ and natural $k$:
\begin{equation}
 r=n_an_b,\qquad k=d_ad_b,\qquad rd_c=n_ck,
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:mulgate}
\end{equation}
plus the sign constraint for $r$. This uses three new natural variables and
four quadratic residuals. Equality of two already-encoded rational wires is
just
\begin{equation}
 n_a d_b-n_b d_a=0.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:equalgate}
\end{equation}
No denominators are allowed to vanish, and no gate relies on canceling an
unknown expression that could be zero.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical rational quartic compilation]
\label{pqc:iq:thm:quartic}
Consider a rational arithmetic system consisting of $W$ wire vertices, $a$
addition or subtraction gates, $m$ multiplication gates, and $e$ additional
pins or equalities. Suppose its rational wire assignment is unique for each
correct input/output instance. Then an explicit polynomial
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr Q(\text{input},\text{output},\boldsymbol z)=\sum_{i=1}^{R}r_i^2
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:quartic}
\end{equation}
in integer coefficients has degree at most four, and
\begin{align}
 V&=7W+5a+3m,\label{pqc:iq:eq:V}\\
 R&=4W+6a+4m+e.\label{pqc:iq:eq:R}
\end{align}
For fixed rational input/output parameters, $\mathscr Q=0$ has exactly one
natural witness if the instance is correct, and none if it is incorrect.

Applied to \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:four} and either moment interface above, this gives
unique-witness quartic certificates for the finite-dimensional quantum-loop
statistics. Their size depends on dimension and the chosen finite interface,
not on how long any execution runs.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Allocate the seven-coordinate block and its four residuals for each wire.
Allocate the gate auxiliaries and residuals just described, and add all pins
and rational equalities. The formulas \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:V}--\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:R} are direct
counts. Every residual is quadratic, including pins when the raw rational
input and answer are treated as free integer parameters. A sum of integer
squares vanishes exactly when all residuals vanish.

For soundness, every zero determines genuine reduced rational values, and
the positive denominators make every gate equality valid in $\Q$. Thus it
satisfies the original rational system. For completeness, take its correct
rational solution, use the unique wire encodings, and insert the uniquely
specified signed products and positive denominator products. Every residual
then vanishes. Uniqueness follows first for the rational solution, then for
each canonical wire, then for each auxiliary.

For the application, Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:group} gives uniqueness of the only
non-acyclic algebraic component $(G,P)$. Every later arithmetic wire is the
output of an acyclic rational circuit and is therefore uniquely determined.
Theorems~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:moments} and \ref{pqc:iq:thm:allmoments} identify the resulting
values with the claimed statistics.
\end{proof}

\wtag\ Source~19 titled this theorem ``Canonical quartic compilation'', the
title of Part~VI's Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:wires} (source~10), which source~19
does not cite; the word ``rational'' was added to tell them apart. It extends
that theorem from integers to rationals. Source~10's canonical signed wire is a
pair $(z^+,z^-)$ with $z^+z^-=0$ (Lemma~\ref{pqc:cc:lem:canonical}), and an
integer evaluation network with $N$ wires needs $2N$ variables and $2N$
residuals. Source~19's wire keeps that pair as $(p,m)$ for the numerator and
adds a positive denominator $h+1$, a B\'ezout pair bounded by the slack $s$, and
the sign pair $(v_+,v_-)$, so that a rational number has exactly one natural
encoding (Lemma~\ref{pqc:iq:lem:wire}); an integer $n$ is the wire
$(p,m,0,0,0,1,0)$. Both theorems keep a unique witness; source~19 pays seven
coordinates and four residuals per wire for division-free rational arithmetic.
Part~I's Lemma~\ref{pqc:lem:quarticlower} lowers degree without uniqueness and is
not used here.

\subsection{Exact dense inverse counts}
The supplied generator intentionally uses an unsimplified dense matrix
schedule. It allocates $D^2$ input entries of $T$, $2D^2$ unknown entries of
$G,P$, and the two constant wires zero and one. It computes $A=I-T$, the
four products $AG,GA,AP,GP$, and the two sums $AG+P,GA+P$.

This schedule has
\begin{align}
 m&=4D^3,& a&=4D^3-D^2,\\
 W&=8D^3+2D^2+2,& e&=5D^2+2.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:coreledger}
\end{align}
The pins are $D^2$ input entries and two constants; the other $4D^2$
equalities are the four matrix constraints. Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{V_{\rm core}=88D^3+9D^2+14,\qquad
 R_{\rm core}=72D^3+7D^2+10.}
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:corecounts}
\end{equation}
These are exact counts for this schedule, not lower bounds or optimization
claims. For $D=1$, they are $111$ variables and $89$ residuals; for a qubit,
$D=4$, they are $5790$ and $4730$. The degree is four, and the domain is
$\N$, not all of $\Z$.

Our complete qubit certificate through normalized factorial order three,
including the initial density, trace and exit rows, moment answers, and
nontermination probability, has $8686$ natural variables and $7089$
quadratic residuals. The all-moments qubit version has $14258$ variables and
$11657$ residuals. Sparse or observable-subspace compilers could be much
smaller; retaining the dense form makes the ledger independent of accidental
zeros and exposes every constraint to inspection.

\subsection{Why this is not a single-fold MRDP theorem}
The system has a unique witness because a \emph{finite rational linear-algebra
object} is already unique and can be described with bounded algebraic syntax.
There is no hidden arbitrary computation history in the inverse equations.
In the undecidable word-existence problem considered later, the word length is
unbounded and cannot be replaced by this aggregate-state certificate.
Applying MRDP to that separate existential problem supplies a finite
Diophantine representation, but does not supply the uniqueness proved here.

\section{Rank strata, witness heights, and computable tails}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:heights}
The canonical inverse has more structure than mere rational existence. Its
entries have explicit rational formulas on each semisimple-zero rank stratum,
and those formulas control their arithmetic height.

\begin{proposition}[Coefficient formula without a pivot choice]
\label[proposition]{pqc:iq:prop:rank}
Let $A$ be a $D\times D$ matrix with semisimple zero and nullity $r\geq1$.
Write
\begin{align}
 \det(A+tI)&=t^r(h_0+h_1t+\cdots),\qquad h_0\ne0,\\
 \adj(A+tI)&=t^{r-1}(B_0+B_1t+\cdots).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:coeffexp}
\end{align}
Then
\begin{equation}
 P=\frac{B_0}{h_0},\qquad
 G=\frac{B_1h_0-B_0h_1}{h_0^2}.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:rankformula}
\end{equation}
For $r=0$, the formulas are simply $P=0$ and $G=A^{-1}$.
Thus, for a matrix family rational in parameters, the canonical $G$ and $P$
are rational functions on every fixed-nullity semisimple-zero stratum.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In the splitting $A=\diag(0,B)$,
\[
 (A+tI)^{-1}=t^{-1}P+G-tG^2+t^2G^3-\cdots
\]
near $t=0$. Multiplication by $\det(A+tI)$ gives the adjugate, first for
$t\ne0$ and then as a polynomial identity. Its coefficients at degrees
$r-1$ and $r$ are respectively $h_0P$ and $h_0G+h_1P$. Solving gives
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:rankformula}. Every coefficient in \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:coeffexp} is a
polynomial in the entries of $A$; rational dependence on the external
parameters follows wherever $h_0\ne0$.
\end{proof}

A single rational expression need not extend regularly through a rank change.
The inverse of $[p]$ already diverges as $p\to0$, while its group inverse at
$p=0$ is zero. The fixed syntax of \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:four} is rank independent even
though the values are not continuous across all rank changes.

\begin{proposition}[Explicit height control]
\label[proposition]{pqc:iq:prop:height}
Suppose $A=C/Q$, where $C$ is integral, $Q\geq1$ is integral, and
$|C_{ij}|\leq \Lambda$ with integral $\Lambda\geq1$. Set
\begin{equation}
 M=D!(1+\Lambda)^D.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:heightM}
\end{equation}
If zero is semisimple, each reduced entry of $G=A^\#$ has numerator of
absolute value at most $2QM^2$ and positive denominator at most $M^2$.
The entries of $P$ have numerator and denominator bounded by $M$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every coefficient of $\det(C+tI)$ has absolute value at most
$D!(1+\Lambda)^D$ by expanding the determinant and bounding all coefficient sums.
Every adjugate coefficient has the smaller analogous bound
$(D-1)!(1+\Lambda)^{D-1}$ and hence is also bounded by $M$.
Apply \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:rankformula} to $C$. A nonzero integral $h_0$ has
$|h_0|\geq1$. The numerator of its inverse formula is bounded by $2M^2$
and the denominator by $M^2$; the projection formula has both bounded by $M$.
Finally $(C/Q)^\#=Q C^\#$, while $P$ is unchanged. Reduction of a fraction
cannot enlarge these bounds. In the invertible case the adjugate/determinant
formula gives even smaller bounds, still within the stated estimates.
\end{proof}

Thus the bit lengths of the canonical core witness are polynomial in the
matrix dimension and rational input bit length. For a fixed reduced wire
$n/d$, its B\'ezout witness satisfies $u<d$ and $|v|\leq|n|+1$, so the
canonicalization itself does not introduce a hidden large search. Repeated
matrix-vector multiplication through order $K$ gives polynomial bit growth
in $K$, dimension, and input size: common-denominator matrix powers give a
direct bound linear in the power on logarithmic height. The characteristic
recursion uses only $D$ matrix stages and fixed reciprocals $1/k$.

These statements are about the displayed finite-dimensional arithmetic
circuits. They are not bounds on witnesses produced by an arbitrary MRDP
representation of an undecidable word problem.

\subsection{Uniform almost-sure termination}
\begin{proposition}[Uniform termination criterion]
\label[proposition]{pqc:iq:prop:uniform}
For a finite-dimensional completely positive trace-nonincreasing continuation
map, the following are equivalent:
\begin{equation}
 \text{AST on every density},\qquad P=0,\qquad
 \det(I-T)\ne0,\qquad \rho(T)<1.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:uniform}
\end{equation}
Here $\rho(T)$ denotes spectral radius, not an initial state.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first condition is equivalent to $P=0$ because positive matrices span the
Hermitian space and Corollary~\ref{pqc:iq:cor:nontermination} applies to every density.
The splitting in Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:group} makes $P=0$ equivalent to the absence
of eigenvalue one, or to invertibility of $I-T$.

If $P=0$, then $\tr T^nX\to0$ for every $X\geq0$. Its trace is its trace
norm, so $T^nX\to0$. Positive matrices span; hence $T^n\to0$ on the whole
finite-dimensional space. There are therefore no eigenvalues of modulus one,
and Lemma~\ref{pqc:iq:lem:bounded} gives $\rho(T)<1$. The converse follows from
exponential decay of matrix powers.
\end{proof}

The equivalence between almost-sure termination and finite expected time in
finite-dimensional quantum programming is established in earlier work
\cite{b76s19-LZBY}. The following elementary quantitative version is useful for an
exact arithmetic interface.

\begin{corollary}[An input-height tail bound]
\label[corollary]{pqc:iq:cor:tail}
Assume uniform AST and $I-T=C/Q$ with $C,Q,\Lambda$ as above. For the basis
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:basis}, put
\begin{equation}
 B=dD Q(D-1)!\Lambda^{D-1}.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:B}
\end{equation}
Then $\E L\leq B$ for every initial density, and
\begin{equation}
 \Pr(L>2Bk)\leq2^{-k}\qquad(k\geq0).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:geotail}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Since $C$ is nonsingular integral, $|\det C|\geq1$. Each cofactor is bounded
by $(D-1)!\Lambda^{D-1}$, so every entry of
$G=(I-T)^{-1}=QC^{-1}$ is bounded in absolute value by
$Q(D-1)!\Lambda^{D-1}$. Coordinates of a density in \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:basis} have absolute
value at most one. Since $\ell$ has $d$ nonzero entries,
$\E L=\ell Gx\leq B$.

Markov's inequality gives $\Pr(L>2B)\leq1/2$. Condition on survival to
$2B$: the normalized surviving matrix is again a density, and the same bound
applies to it because the estimate is uniform over all densities. Repeating
this argument proves \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:geotail}. If a conditioning event has
probability zero, the subsequent bound is automatic.
\end{proof}

The bound is deliberately crude. It is sufficient to show that a computable
exponential tail can be extracted without a numerical spectral-gap oracle.
It does not decide whether a particular outcome word has exactly zero
probability, nor whether some such word exists.

\section{Weak killing: a Laurent law, scaling limit, and inverse}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:regulator}
At each test, first terminate independently with probability
$\epsilon\in(0,1)$; otherwise perform the original test. The new continuation
matrix is
\begin{equation}
 T_\epsilon=(1-\epsilon)T.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:regulatedT}
\end{equation}
One realization uses a new exit superoperator $X\mapsto\epsilon X$ and
rescales every old map by $1-\epsilon$. For rational $\epsilon$ these are
rational superoperators, irrespective of whether a particular Kraus
square root is rational.

Let $L_\epsilon$ count tests of the modified loop. Equivalently, take an
independent geometric random variable $R_\epsilon$ on
$\{1,2,\ldots\}$ with success probability $\epsilon$ and put
$L_\epsilon=\min(L,R_\epsilon)$. Hence
\begin{equation}
 \Pr(L_\epsilon>n)=(1-\epsilon)^ns_n.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:regulatedsurvival}
\end{equation}
This construction turns every loop into an almost-surely terminating one.

\begin{theorem}[Exact resolvent and all-orders weak-clock law]
\label{pqc:iq:thm:regulator}
For $\epsilon\in(0,1)$,
\begin{align}
 [I-(1-\epsilon)T]^{-1}
 &=\epsilon^{-1}P+G[I+\epsilon TG]^{-1},
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:regresolvent}\\
 M(\epsilon):=\E L_\epsilon
 &=\frac{w}{\epsilon}
 +\sum_{m\geq0}(-\epsilon)^m a_m^*,
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:laurent}
\end{align}
where $a_m^*=\E[\binom L{m+1};L<\infty]$. The series converges in a
neighborhood of zero after its displayed pole is removed. It is therefore a
convergent Laurent expansion, not merely a formal asymptotic series. Every
coefficient is rational and has the canonical certificates above.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
On $\ker A$, the left side of \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:regresolvent} is
$\epsilon^{-1}I$, and the second term on the right is zero. On $\im A$,
$A$ is invertible and commutes with $T$; therefore
\[
 (A+\epsilon T)^{-1}=G(I+\epsilon TG)^{-1}.
\]
This also shows that $I+\epsilon TG$ is invertible for real
$0<\epsilon<1$: $I-(1-\epsilon)T$ is invertible because the spectral
radius of $(1-\epsilon)T$ is less than one. Thus
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:regresolvent} holds on both summands.

Summing the survival probabilities \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:regulatedsurvival} gives
$M(\epsilon)=\ell[I-(1-\epsilon)T]^{-1}x$. A Neumann expansion of
$(I+\epsilon TG)^{-1}$ for sufficiently small $|\epsilon|$ proves
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:laurent}; Proposition~\ref{pqc:iq:prop:finitepart} identifies its
coefficients. For example, $|\epsilon|\|TG\|<1$ in any submultiplicative
norm is a sufficient convergence condition.
\end{proof}

The residue is precisely the mass of genuinely infinite executions. The
regular coefficients describe only finite executions. In particular,
\begin{equation}
 M(\epsilon)=\frac{w}{\epsilon}
 +\E[L;L<\infty]
 -\epsilon\E\!\left[\binom L2;L<\infty\right]+O(\epsilon^2).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:firstlaurent}
\end{equation}
A rare independent stopping event reveals both aspects in one observable.

\begin{theorem}[Mixture limit and convergence of moments]
\label{pqc:iq:thm:mixture}
As $\epsilon\downarrow0$,
\begin{equation}
 \epsilon L_\epsilon\ \Longrightarrow\
 (1-w)\delta_0+w\operatorname{Exp}(1).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:mixture}
\end{equation}
For every integer $k\geq1$,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\E[(\epsilon L_\epsilon)^k]=wk!.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:scaledmoments}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $y>0$, let $n=\lfloor y/\epsilon\rfloor$. Equation
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:regulatedsurvival} gives
\[
 \Pr(\epsilon L_\epsilon>y)
 =(1-\epsilon)^n s_n\longrightarrow e^{-y}w.
\]
This determines the claimed distribution at all its continuity points,
including the possibility of an atom at zero. The coupling
$L_\epsilon\leq R_\epsilon$ provides a uniform exponential tail for
$\epsilon L_\epsilon$: for $0<\epsilon\leq1/2$,
$(1-\epsilon)^{\lfloor y/\epsilon\rfloor}\leq e^{1/2}e^{-y}$.
The tail integral formula for moments and dominated convergence then give
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:scaledmoments}.
\end{proof}

There is also an exact factorial identity, useful independently of the limit:
\begin{equation}
 \E[\fall{L_\epsilon}{k}]
 =k!\,\ell T_\epsilon^{k-1}(I-T_\epsilon)^{-k}x
 \qquad(k\geq1).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:regulatedfactorials}
\end{equation}
Indeed, $\binom Lk=\sum_{n=0}^{L-1}\binom n{k-1}$, and
$\sum_{n\geq0}\binom n{k-1}T_\epsilon^n
=T_\epsilon^{k-1}(I-T_\epsilon)^{-k}$. On the fixed-point summand its
leading contribution is
$k!w(1-\epsilon)^{k-1}\epsilon^{-k}$; the complementary contribution is
analytic at zero.

\subsection{Inverse calibration}
Suppose $w>0$ and choose a desired large mean duration $y$. Since
$M(\epsilon)$ is strictly decreasing, there is a unique small positive
$\epsilon$ with $M(\epsilon)=y$. Put $r=1/y$ and
$A_0(t)=\sum_{m\geq0}(-t)^m a_m^*$. The inverse equation is
\begin{equation}
 \epsilon=r\bigl(w+\epsilon A_0(\epsilon)\bigr).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:inversefunctional}
\end{equation}
At $(r,\epsilon)=(0,0)$ the derivative of the left side minus the right
side with respect to $\epsilon$ is one. The analytic implicit-function
theorem gives a convergent inverse power series. Comparing coefficients
recursively gives
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\epsilon(y)=\frac{w}{y}
 +\frac{wa_0^*}{y^2}
 +\frac{w(a_0^*)^2-w^2a_1^*}{y^3}+O(y^{-4}).}
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:inverseexpansion}
\end{equation}
Every subsequent coefficient is a rational polynomial expression in $w$ and
finitely many $a_m^*$. Equation~\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:inversefunctional} is also an
all-orders coefficient algorithm: the coefficient of $r^n$ on the right
only involves previously determined coefficients of $\epsilon$. This is a
concrete inversion problem connecting the present certificate construction
to the repository's broader interest in asymptotic series and their inverses.
The case $w=0$ has no diverging $1/\epsilon$ scale and is not covered by this
large-$y$ inversion.

\section{A geometric runtime with undecidable forbidden records}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:geometric}
The next construction is where the unconventional computational substrate
enters essentially. Its source of undecidability is not a divergent mean or
an unknown convergence rate, but destructive interference inside products
indexed by arbitrarily long words.

We use the following published theorem as an external input, not as a new
result of this manuscript.

\begin{theorem}[Eisert--M\"uller--Gogolin, 2012]
\label{pqc:iq:thm:EMG}
For devices specified by nine rational real Kraus matrices
$A_1,\ldots,A_9\in\Q^{15\times15}$ satisfying
$\sum_i A_i^\dagger A_i=I$, it is undecidable whether some nonempty finite
word $v=i_1\cdots i_n$ has
$A_v=A_{i_n}\cdots A_{i_1}=0$.
Equivalently, from any full-rank density, it is undecidable whether there
exists a finite measurement record of probability zero.
\end{theorem}
This is Theorem~1 of \cite{emg}; its matrix-mortality reduction and rational
normalization are part of that source. We retain its published dimensions
rather than depend on unrefereed dimension improvements in the repository.

\wtag\ Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:EMG} is the benchmark already quoted in Part~II
(Section~\ref{pqc:qm:sec:scope} and the table after
Theorem~\ref{pqc:qm:thm:47}); it is printed here because source~19 states it,
and it adds nothing to Part~II. The ``unrefereed dimension improvements'' are
Part~II's Theorem~\ref{pqc:qm:thm:47} and Corollary~\ref{pqc:qm:cor:57}; what
they give in place of Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:EMG} is
Corollary~\ref{pqc:iq:cor:dimfour} below.

\begin{theorem}[Geometric-clock preservation]
\label{pqc:iq:thm:geometric}
There is an undecidable forbidden-completed-record problem for rational
quantum instruments on a fixed $15$-dimensional Hilbert space with nine
continuation outcomes and one terminating outcome, under all of the following
promises:
\begin{equation}
 \Pr(N=n)=\frac{16}{25}\left(\frac9{25}\right)^n
 \quad(n\geq0),\qquad \E L=\frac{25}{16}.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:fixedgeo}
\end{equation}
Every instrument is almost surely terminating; its complete length
distribution and all length moments are identical to those of every other
instrument in the family. The forbidden records under consideration are
exactly the syntactically legal words $v\,\mathsf H$, with $v$ a string of
continuation outcomes and $\mathsf H$ the single final halt symbol.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take an instance $A_1,\ldots,A_9$ of Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:EMG}, fix the
rational full-rank initial density $\rho=I_{15}/15$, and define
\begin{equation}
 C_i=\frac35 A_i\quad(1\leq i\leq9),\qquad
 H^{\mathrm{halt}}=\frac45 I.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:clockkraus}
\end{equation}
All matrices remain rational and
$\sum_i C_i^\dagger C_i+(H^{\mathrm{halt}})^\dagger H^{\mathrm{halt}}=I$.
Interpret the $H^{\mathrm{halt}}$ outcome as termination, not as another outcome after which
the device continues.

The summed continuation map is
$\cT(X)=\frac9{25}\sum_i A_iXA_i^\dagger$, so
$\tr\cT(X)=\frac9{25}\tr X$ for every $X\geq0$.
Thus $s_n=(9/25)^n$ independently of the initial density and of all details
of the $A_i$. The halt probability at the next test is $16/25$, proving
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:fixedgeo} and almost-sure termination.

For a particular continuation word $v$ of length $n$, followed by halt, its
probability from a full-rank density $\rho$ is
\begin{equation}
 \Pr(v\mathsf H)
 =\frac{16}{25}\left(\frac9{25}\right)^n
    \tr(A_v\rho A_v^\dagger).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:wordpreserve}
\end{equation}
The scalar factor is strictly positive. Since $\rho$ is positive definite,
$\tr(A_v\rho A_v^\dagger)=\|A_v\rho^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm F}^2$ vanishes
exactly when $A_v=0$. A decision procedure for existence of a forbidden
completed record in the new family would therefore decide the published
undecidable problem. The empty continuation word has positive halt
probability and introduces no spurious zero.
\end{proof}

The restriction to legal records is indispensable: a string containing an
outcome \emph{after} a halt is syntactically impossible and would make an
unrestricted question trivial. Equation~\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:wordpreserve} preserves the
meaningful zero set, not this grammatical artifact.

\begin{corollary}[No computable shortest-forbidden-record bound]
\label[corollary]{pqc:iq:cor:nobound}
There is no total computable function of the finite device description
length that bounds the shortest forbidden legal record whenever one exists
in the family of Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:geometric}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}[\wtag\ Pointer to the proof]
This is the argument of Part~II's Corollary~\ref{pqc:qm:cor:nobound}, with
Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:geometric} in place of Theorem~\ref{pqc:qm:thm:47}: a
computable bound would turn the exact evaluation of the finitely many legal
words up to that length into a decision procedure. Source~19's proof is this
bounded search and is not reprinted.
\end{proof}

\wtag\ Source~19 next observes that the existence of a forbidden record is
computably enumerable, so that an MRDP polynomial represents it uniformly over
an effective coding of the rational devices \cite{b76s19-RepoMRDP}, and that
malformed descriptions can be rejected and rational normalization checked
before the enumeration. That is the semidecider and
Theorem~\ref{pqc:qm:thm:mrdp} of Section~\ref{pqc:qm:sec:mrdp}, stated there for
$\QMort_{4,7}$, and the paragraph is not reprinted. Its non-claim is kept:
``No explicit fixed-arity polynomial or single-fold property for this separate
problem is claimed here.''

\begin{corollary}[\wtag\ The same clock in dimension four, given Part~II]
\label[corollary]{pqc:iq:cor:dimfour}
Assume Theorem~\ref{pqc:qm:thm:47} of Part~II. Then the forbidden-legal-record
problem is undecidable for rational quantum instruments on a fixed
$4$-dimensional Hilbert space ($d=4$, $D=16$) with seven continuation outcomes
and one terminating outcome, under the same promises \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:fixedgeo}:
every instrument terminates almost surely, and all of them have the same length
law $\Pr(N=n)=\frac{16}{25}(\frac9{25})^n$. No total computable function of the
description length bounds the shortest forbidden legal record. Assuming instead
Corollary~\ref{pqc:qm:cor:57} (Lagrange in place of Meyer), the same holds in
dimension five with seven continuation outcomes and one terminating outcome.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take an instance $A_0,\ldots,A_6\in\Q^{4\times4}$ of Theorem~\ref{pqc:qm:thm:47},
so that $\sum_jA_j^{\mathsf T}A_j=I_4$, put $\rho=I_4/4$, and define
$C_j=\frac35A_j$ ($0\leq j\leq6$) and $H^{\mathrm{halt}}=\frac45I_4$, as in
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:clockkraus}. The proof of Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:geometric}
applies word for word: the summed continuation map multiplies traces by $9/25$,
which gives the law, and \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:wordpreserve} together with
Lemma~\ref{pqc:qm:lem:fullrank} shows that the record $v\mathsf H$ with $v$
nonempty has probability zero exactly when $A_v=0$, while the empty $v$ has
probability $16/25$. A decision procedure would therefore decide whether some
nonempty word of the instrument of Theorem~\ref{pqc:qm:thm:47} has probability
zero. The no-bound statement follows as Corollary~\ref{pqc:iq:cor:nobound}. For
dimension five, use the instruments of Corollary~\ref{pqc:qm:cor:57}.
\end{proof}

This corollary is only as strong as Part~II's Theorem~\ref{pqc:qm:thm:47},
which rests on Neary's published six-generator theorem, Meyer's theorem and
source~07's unrefereed Gram-packing theorem; source~19, which preferred the
published fifteen-dimensional input, proves neither. It answers source~19's
Question~\ref{pqc:iq:q:clocks} for dimension four with seven continuation
outcomes (the note after that question).

\subsection{What carries the computational hardness?}
The result does not say that a fixed-dimensional autonomous mixed state stores
an unbounded classical tape. Rather, an unbounded \emph{word quantifier}
ranges over a noncommutative matrix semigroup. The summed channel discards
that word information. Two instruments can consequently share every runtime
moment while their exact word-support questions have radically different
answers.

In the geometric family, the entire runtime series is simply
\[
 F(z)=\frac{16}{25-9z},\qquad
 \sum_{k\geq0}\E\binom Nk\,u^k=\frac{1}{1-(9/16)u}.
\]
Yet the existence of one zero-probability completed record is undecidable.
This rules out using aggregate moments, a computable tail estimate, or
normalization alone as a decision procedure for exact word support.
It does not imply a limitation on every approximate or restricted support
question, and it does not establish any form of physical hypercomputation.

\section{An actual rationality conjecture: false unrestricted, true canonically}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:conjecture}
In the overview of his generalized-inverse study, Lardizabal observes rational
parameter dependence for certain examples and conjectures the same behavior
for every generalized inverse \cite[Section 3]{b76s19-Lardizabal}. Taken literally,
without specifying how a generalized inverse is selected, this is false.
The distinction is not about difficult quantum dynamics: it already appears
in an ergodic two-state classical chain.

\begin{proposition}[Nonrational generalized-inverse selection]
\label[proposition]{pqc:iq:prop:counterexample}
For $0<p<1$, let
\begin{equation}
 T(p)=\begin{pmatrix}1-p&p\\p&1-p\end{pmatrix},\quad
 A(p)=I-T(p)=p\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:counterT}
\end{equation}
This is an irreducible aperiodic classical Markov chain. Its canonical pair is
\begin{equation}
 P=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 G(p)=\frac1{4p}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:counterG}
\end{equation}
For every scalar function $f:(0,1)\to\R$,
\begin{equation}
 J_f(p)=G(p)+f(p)P
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:Jf}
\end{equation}
is a generalized inverse in the sense
$A(p)J_f(p)A(p)=A(p)$. With $f(p)=e^p$, its entries are not rational
functions of $p$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
All transition probabilities are strictly positive, so the chain is
irreducible and aperiodic. Direct multiplication gives
$AP=PA=0$ and $AGA=A$. Hence $A(G+fP)A=A$ for every $f$.

If an entry of $J_{e^p}$ were a rational function, subtracting its rational
$G$ entry and multiplying by two would make $e^p$ rational on $(0,1)$.
This is impossible. Indeed, for a nonzero rational function $R=U/V$, the
identity $R'=R$ would imply the polynomial identity
$U'V-UV'=UV$. The degree of the left side is smaller than that of the
nonzero right side. Thus no such rational function exists.
\end{proof}

The proposition addresses the unrestricted quantifier over generalized
inverses. It does \emph{not} refute a theorem about a specified canonical
inverse, nor a rational algorithm for choosing one, nor the validity of the
hitting-time identities in \cite{b76s19-Lardizabal}. Those distinctions are essential:
nullspace freedom can import an arbitrary external function into an otherwise
rational family.

The appropriate corrected statement for our purposes is
Proposition~\ref{pqc:iq:prop:rank}: the unique group inverse and its projection are
rational functions on each fixed-nullity semisimple-zero stratum. The four
equations in Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:group} eliminate exactly the arbitrary freedom
that makes \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:Jf} possible. This also explains why canonical choice is
not a cosmetic preference in a Diophantine compiler: without it, witness
uniqueness is lost before any integer encoding is attempted.

Our literature search verifies the original statement and supplies the
counterexample and corrected theorem. It does not establish that this
interpretational issue had never been noticed, or that any stronger
well-specified conjecture remains open as of the date of this manuscript.

\wtag\ \emph{The quoted sentence, checked (2 October 2026).} In
arXiv:1907.01313v2 (dated 9 July 2019) the sentence is not in a Section~3 of
the paper: it is item~3, ``Computing concrete examples'', of the overview in the
Introduction (Section~1), and source~19's \code{19-quantum-runs-SOURCE_AUDIT.md}
repeats the inaccurate location. There Lardizabal writes, of his Example~8.2 (a
nonunital quantum Markov chain on two vertices depending on $0<p<1$), that the
entries of certain generalized inverses are rational functions of $p$, and adds
in parentheses that he conjectures this for every generalized inverse. His
Section~6 defines a generalized inverse as any $A^-$ with $AA^-A=A$, the
definition of Proposition~\ref{pqc:iq:prop:counterexample}. That proposition's
chain is classical, not his Example~8.2; but its construction needs only a
projection $P\ne0$ with $AP=PA=0$ and some generalized inverse $G$, and every
trace-preserving $T$ has such a $P$ (the Ces\`aro projection of
Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:group}, nonzero because $\ell P=\ell$). So
$G+f(p)P$ is also a generalized inverse in his example, with entries that are
not rational functions of $p$ when $f(p)=e^p$, as soon as $P$ has an entry that
is a nonzero rational function of $p$. Source~19's hedges stand: this concerns
only the unrestricted reading of the conjecture, not his fundamental matrix or
his hitting-time theorems.

\section{A sharp boundary: computable time dependence already breaks the graph}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:scheduled}
Finite dimension alone is not sufficient for the main theorem. Even a
one-dimensional quantum system can inherit unbounded computational information
from a computably specified external schedule.

\begin{proposition}[No uniform Diophantine graph for scheduled exact probabilities]
\label[proposition]{pqc:iq:prop:scheduled}
There is a computable family of time-dependent one-dimensional rational
quantum loops, each using only the two Kraus pairs
\begin{equation}
 (K_n,H^{\mathrm{halt}}_n)=(1,0)\quad\text{or}\quad(3/5,4/5),
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:schedulealphabet}
\end{equation}
whose eventual exit probabilities belong to $\{0,1\}$, but whose exact exit
probability graph has no uniform existential Diophantine representation.
There is not even an algorithm that, from an arbitrary schedule index in this
family, produces a finite polynomial representing its exact probability
relation, with unrestricted degree and witness count.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Given a Turing-machine index $e$, at test $n$ simulate that machine for $n$
steps. Choose $(1,0)$ if it has not halted in that time, and $(3/5,4/5)$ if
it has. This defines a total computable schedule of rational normalized Kraus
pairs. If the machine never halts, the loop never exits and its exit
probability is zero. If the machine halts, then from a finite time onward the
continuation probability at each step is $9/25$, so its eventual exit
probability is one.

\wtag\ The rest of source~19's proof is the probability-zero endpoint of
Parts~I and~V, not reprinted. There, $p=0$ is $\pione$ (the end of
Section~\ref{pqc:sec:hierarchy}) and $\pione$-complete (Part~V's endpoint table
in Section~\ref{pqc:ql:sec:normalforms}), and an existential Diophantine graph
makes the probability-zero instances c.e.\ (search for witnesses with the answer
fixed to zero). Here the probability-zero indices are exactly the complement of
the halting set. Source~19 adds that the same search also works when an
algorithm builds a separate polynomial for each $e$, because its coefficients
and witness arity are then computable from $e$.
\end{proof}

The external schedule supplies the unbounded computation; the quantum system
itself has only one dimension and no coherent degrees of freedom. Thus this is
a representation boundary, not a claim of quantum advantage. It explains why
one cannot take a finite-horizon simulator, let its horizon ``go to infinity,''
and assume the resulting exact probability graph remains Diophantine.

Together, the results now give three distinct outcomes. Time-homogeneous
finite-dimensional aggregate laws have canonical finite certificates.
Time-homogeneous word-support existence can be undecidable but computably
enumerable. Computably scheduled exact probability graphs need not even be
computably enumerable. The observable and its quantifiers are as important as
the substrate.

\wtag\ Part~VI draws a parallel boundary for algebraic quantum controllers with
unbounded classical memory (``Three interfaces that must not be conflated'' in
Section~\ref{pqc:cc:sec:unbounded}): exact finite circuits have canonical
quartic witnesses, positive halting is c.e.\ (Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:positivehalting}),
and almost-sure halting is $\pitwo$-complete (Theorem~\ref{pqc:cc:thm:ast}).
Source~19's first and second outcomes are the finite-dimensional,
time-homogeneous counterparts of its first two; its third outcome uses an
external schedule instead of an unbounded controller.

\section{Four exact examples}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:examples}
All numbers in this section were computed as exact rationals and checked by
substitution. The software also compares the group-inverse moment formula
with direct derivatives of the rational generating function.

\subsection{A scalar geometric loop}
Take $T=[9/25]$, $x=[1]$, and exit row $e=[16/25]$. Then
\[
 G=[25/16],\quad P=0,\quad F(z)=\frac{16}{25-9z},\quad
 b_k=\left(\frac9{16}\right)^k.
\]
The mean number of tests is $25/16$. Adding the weak clock gives
\[
 M(\epsilon)=\frac{25}{16+9\epsilon},
\]
which has no pole because the original loop is already almost surely
terminating. The exported certificate through moment order three has $262$
natural variables and $213$ residuals.

For a concrete view of canonical arithmetic, the reduced rational $25/16$ is
encoded by
\[
 (p,m,h,u,v_+,v_-,s)=(25,0,15,9,14,0,6).
\]
The key B\'ezout residual is $25\cdot9-16\cdot14-1=0$. Both sign residuals
and the complementary-slack residual also vanish. No alternative natural
encoding of the same reduced rational satisfies all four equations.

\subsection{A partially terminating qubit}
Let
\[
 K=\diag(1,3/5),\qquad H^{\mathrm{halt}}=\diag(0,4/5),\qquad \rho=I_2/2.
\]
Then $K^\dagger K+(H^{\mathrm{halt}})^\dagger H^{\mathrm{halt}}=I$. In the chosen Hermitian basis,
\[
 T=\diag(1,9/25,3/5,3/5),\quad
 G=\diag(0,25/16,5/2,5/2),\quad P=\diag(1,0,0,0).
\]
The nontermination probability is $1/2$, while
\[
 F(z)=\frac8{25-9z},\qquad
 (b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3)
 =\left(\frac12,\frac9{32},\frac{81}{512},\frac{729}{8192}\right).
\]
The unconditional mean is infinite. Its finite-path first moment is
$\ell Gx=25/32$, and
\[
 M(\epsilon)=\frac1{2\epsilon}+\frac{25}{2(16+9\epsilon)}.
\]
The first term is the trapped half of the state waiting for the artificial
clock; the second is the contribution from the decaying half. This simple
example catches the common mistake of labeling $\ell Gx$ an unconditional
mean on a partially terminating instance.

\subsection{A coherent qubit with nontrivial moment recurrence}
Let
\begin{equation}
 U=\begin{pmatrix}3/5&-4/5\\4/5&3/5\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 K=\diag(1,3/5)U,\qquad H^{\mathrm{halt}}=\diag(0,4/5)U,
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:coherentexample}
\end{equation}
and take $\rho=\frac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Again $K^\dagger K+(H^{\mathrm{halt}})^\dagger H^{\mathrm{halt}}=I$. This time $I-T$ is invertible and
\begin{equation}
 F(z)=\frac{1960-512z+600z^2}{3125-1005z+603z^2-675z^3}.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:coherentpgf}
\end{equation}
Its first normalized factorial moments are
\begin{equation}
 (b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3)
 =\left(1,\frac{157}{128},\frac{17037}{8192},
                \frac{1590417}{524288}\right),
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:coherentmoments}
\end{equation}
so $\E L=285/128$. The full four-dimensional matrix certificate gives
\begin{align}
 q(u)&=1-\frac{153}{64}u+\frac{657}{1024}u^2
          +\frac{729}{1024}u^3+\frac{2025}{4096}u^4\nonumber\\
 &=\frac{(3u-2)^2(225u^2+624u+1024)}{4096}.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:coherentq}
\end{align}
Equations~\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:coherentmoments} and \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:momentrecurrence} with
this $q$ determine every higher moment. One factor is redundant after
canceling against the numerator of the scalar generating function; the
certificate deliberately retains it. This is an explicit all-orders result,
not a numerical extrapolation from the displayed first four values.

\subsection{A rotating dark sector: matrix powers do not converge}
On a qutrit, use the same $U$ and set
\[
 K=\diag(U,3/5),\qquad H^{\mathrm{halt}}=\diag(0,0,4/5),\qquad
 \rho=\psi\psi^\dagger,\quad \psi=\frac13(1,2,2)^T.
\]
The first two coordinates form a trapped unitary sector of mass $5/9$; the
third has mass $4/9$ and decays geometrically. The trapped two-dimensional
rank-one block is not fixed by conjugation with $U$. Its consecutive-iterate
trace-norm difference is therefore a positive constant, because conjugation
is an isometry. Hence $T^n x$ does not converge. The bright and cross terms
decay and cannot cancel this persistent difference.

Nevertheless,
\begin{align}
 w&=\frac59,&
 s_n&=\frac59+\frac49\left(\frac9{25}\right)^n,\\
 F(z)&=\frac{64}{225-81z},&
 b_k&=\frac49\left(\frac9{16}\right)^k.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:qutritvalues}
\end{align}
The weak-clock expansion is particularly transparent:
\begin{equation}
 M(\epsilon)=\frac5{9\epsilon}
 +\frac{100}{9(16+9\epsilon)}
 =\frac5{9\epsilon}+\frac{25}{36}
     \sum_{m\geq0}\left(-\frac{9\epsilon}{16}\right)^m.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:qutritlaurent}
\end{equation}
Thus $a_0^*=25/36$, $a_1^*=25/64$, and inverse calibration begins
\begin{equation}
 \epsilon(y)=\frac5{9y}+\frac{125}{324y^2}
                   +\frac{6875}{46656y^3}+O(y^{-4}).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:qutritinverse}
\end{equation}
The limiting distribution of $\epsilon L_\epsilon$ has atom $4/9$ at zero
and exponential component of mass $5/9$. The example simultaneously tests
partial nontermination, coherent peripheral dynamics, rational aggregate
statistics, and the singular small-clock limit.

\section{Implementation, reproducibility, and proof status}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:verification}
The package contains four Python modules. The exact matrix analyzer uses
SymPy for rational nullspaces, image bases, inverses, and symbolic generating
functions. The certificate generator uses Python's exact integer arithmetic
and reduced \texttt{Fraction} values. The independent checker uses only the
standard library and imports neither the generator nor the analyzer.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.27\textwidth}p{0.65\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
File & Purpose\\\midrule
\texttt{quantum\_loops.py} & Rational Hermitian coordinates, continuation maps,
canonical $(G,P)$, moment and regulator formulas.\\
\texttt{quartic.py} & Seven-coordinate wires, sparse quadratic residuals,
complete natural witnesses, bounded-order and all-moments circuits.\\
\texttt{verify\_certificate.py} & Independent residual evaluation, canonical
fraction checks, decoded inverse equations, moment recurrences, and
characteristic coefficients.\\
\texttt{run\_checks.py} & Exact examples, deterministic randomized gate tests,
certificate export, mutation rejection, and machine-readable reports.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Every exported polynomial is specified as an explicit list of quadratic
residuals with integer coefficients, together with the instruction to sum
their squares. This is a complete exact description of a quartic polynomial;
it is not an appeal to an unspecified MRDP oracle. Avoiding expansion merely
keeps the files small and preserves the equation structure for audit.

\toprule
Certificate & Wires & Natural variables & Residuals & Moment data\\\midrule
Scalar geometric &28&262&213&orders $0$--$3$\\
Partial qubit &817&8686&7089&orders $0$--$3$\\
Coherent qubit &817&8686&7089&orders $0$--$3$\\

The recorded run used Python 3.13.5 and SymPy 1.14.0 and passed
\textbf{33,708 exact assertions}. Of these, \textbf{31,892} increment one
witness coordinate by one and verify rejection by at least one incident
quadratic residual. This is a mutation test of every coordinate in the four
exported assignments, not 31,892 different quantum systems. The remaining
checks include 492 canonical-fraction cases, 492 bounded-B\'ezout uniqueness
checks, 180 rational gate cases, Kraus normalizations, symbolic derivatives,
all-moments rational identities, rank-stratum formulas, and exact
geometric-support preservation on a small test instrument.

The independent checker validates 26,048 residuals across the four files and
also recomputes the decoded matrix identities. Its small geometric test
instrument is \emph{not} the published undecidable 15-dimensional family;
it checks the clock transformation algebra. Undecidability rests on
Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:EMG} and the proof of Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:geometric}, not on
finite experiments.

From the package directory, reproduce the results with
\begin{verbatim}
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python code/run_checks.py
python code/verify_certificate.py \
    examples/coherent_qubit_all_moments_certificate.json
make pdf
\end{verbatim}
The test runner overwrites only its generated example and verification files.
No network access is used by the mathematical code. The tests check exact
identities, not floating-point approximations; there are no empirical
convergence thresholds hidden in the construction.

\subsection{A feasible formalization path}
The first independent formalization target should be the rational core, not a
large quantum semantics development. In a finite-dimensional vector space,
prove the unique solution of \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:four} for semisimple zero, then prove
canonical wire uniqueness and the gate lemmas over $\N$. Those two results
already establish soundness, completeness, and uniqueness of the compiler as
an algebraic theorem.

A second layer would formalize the CP/TNI power bound, Ces\`aro projection,
peripheral annihilation, and stopped moment identity. The finite recurrence
then uses standard polynomial matrix identities. A third layer would connect
the quantum measurement-occurrence reduction to the repository's
computability infrastructure. These layers should remain distinct: a verified
integer checker does not by itself prove the spectral theorem, and the
repository's existing MRDP theorem does not by itself prove this compiler.
No such formalization or transitive axiom audit was executed for this package.
