\section{Further research questions}
\label{pqc:iq:sec:questions}
The following questions are concrete continuations, not claims of unresolved
historical status in every possible formulation. They are chosen to preserve
the distinction between a proved certificate theorem and an optimization or
extension problem.

\begin{question}[Smaller rank-independent certificates]\label{pqc:iq:q:smaller}
Can the dense $O(D^3)$ inverse certificate be replaced by an
$O(D^\omega)$ arithmetic circuit while retaining canonical rational witnesses
and exact, rank-independent syntax? Fast matrix multiplication is one route,
but useful constants, signed products, and the final quartic ledger must all
be counted. A practical first target is a sparse qubit compiler with an
independent checker and a substantially smaller variable count.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Questions~\ref{pqc:q:smaller} and~\ref{pqc:qm:q:smaller}, which ask the same kind of question for Part~I's $F_{N,m}$ and Part~II's $\mathscr Q_{D,K,n}$, and Question~\ref{pqc:tu:q:optimization}.

\begin{question}[Canonical observable quotients]\label{pqc:iq:q:quotients}
The all-moments denominator may contain factors invisible to every exit row.
Can one construct a unique rational certificate for the minimal observable
quotient of $(T,x,e_1,\ldots,e_r)$, without introducing arbitrary basis choices?
A canonical row-echelon policy is computable; the open engineering and
algebraic task is a small certificate whose unique witnesses enforce that
policy across rank changes.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:operator}, which asks whether canonical characteristic-polynomial data can replace spectral bases for Part~II's operator factors.

\begin{question}[Witness-preserving physical-input validation]\label{pqc:iq:q:validation}
Replace the physical promise by a canonical rational certificate of complete
positivity and trace nonincrease. Rational positive semidefinite matrices
admit exact elimination methods, but arbitrary Gram decompositions are
nonunique and may introduce irrational entries. A useful target is a
rank-stratified rational factorization with canonical pivot and sign choices,
compiled without losing the unique-witness property.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Perturbations that are not scalar clocks]\label{pqc:iq:q:perturbations}
For $T_\epsilon=T-\epsilon S$ with positivity preserved for small
$\epsilon>0$, determine precise hypotheses under which the pole structure of
$(I-T_\epsilon)^{-1}$ is governed by an effective operator on $\ker(I-T)$.
Scalar killing gives one simple pole and an exponential mixture. Nonuniform
killing can produce several rates, and singular effective killing can demand
higher-order analysis. The certificate should distinguish proved analytic
expansions from merely formal perturbation calculations.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Sharper clocks preserving undecidable support]\label{pqc:iq:q:clocks}
Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:geometric} adds exactly one halt outcome and preserves the
published dimension. Can one preserve the same exact geometric law with fewer
continuation outcomes or smaller Hilbert dimension under a fully explicit,
published or independently proved mortality reduction? Any improvement should
include its rational normalization and a proof that no new zero products were
introduced.
\end{question}
\par\noindent\wtag\ \emph{Batch-76 note (2 October 2026).} Answered for dimension four with
seven continuation outcomes, by Part~II. Corollary~\ref{pqc:iq:cor:dimfour} composes the clock of
Theorem~\ref{pqc:iq:thm:geometric} with Theorem~\ref{pqc:qm:thm:47} of source~07, which source~19 set
aside as unrefereed, and keeps the exact law \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:fixedgeo}; Corollary~\ref{pqc:qm:cor:57}
gives dimension five with seven continuation outcomes by the elementary route. The answer is as strong
as Part~II's theorem, whose normalization and absence of new zero products are proved there. The
question stays open below dimension four, or with fewer than seven continuation outcomes; any answer
to Part~II's Question~\ref{pqc:q:instruments} (dimension three, or fewer than seven outcomes in
dimension four) would carry over through the same clock.

\begin{question}[Controlled extensions beyond homogeneous finite state]\label{pqc:iq:q:schedules}
Proposition~\ref{pqc:iq:prop:scheduled} rules out arbitrary computable schedules.
Between periodic schedules, which can be folded into finite control, and
arbitrary schedules, which subclasses still have rational or algebraic
stopping laws with finite exact certificates? Candidate restrictions include
finite automaton controllers and explicit algebraic generating functions for
the schedule. The model must specify whether the controller has unbounded
memory.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Question~\ref{pqc:q:histories} (periodic transformations and linear recurrences for Part~I's infinite histories), and the note after it.

\begin{question}[Exact tail bounds using observable rather than full dimension]\label{pqc:iq:q:tails}
The cofactor bound in Corollary~\ref{pqc:iq:cor:tail} ignores cancellation and the
minimal scalar recurrence. Can a checkable rational bound use only the
observable denominator of $F$ and give useful constants near a dark-state
transition? An informative first result would compare coefficient-height,
Lyapunov-functional, and exact root-isolation bounds on the same examples.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Formal proof and certified code generation]\label{pqc:iq:q:formal}
Implement the two-stage theorem ``unique rational system $\Rightarrow$
unique natural quartic'' in Lean, then instantiate it for \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:four}.
The success criterion is an exported polynomial plus a theorem of exact
zero-set equivalence, not merely a verified sample assignment. The supplied
JSON checker and ledger provide a concrete target format.
\end{question}
\wtag\ Compare Questions~\ref{pqc:q:kernel} and~\ref{pqc:tu:q:kernel}: both put a kernel-checked compiler first, for Part~I's and Part~VIII's certificates.


\section{Conclusion}\label{pqc:iq:sec:conclusion}
The useful boundary is not ``classical versus quantum'' or ``finite versus
infinite execution.'' It is whether the requested observable has a finite
canonical algebraic summary. A rational homogeneous finite-dimensional loop
has such a summary: four quadratic matrix identities, a finite moment
recurrence, and an explicit unique natural witness for one quartic equation.
The summary remains valid with partial nontermination and with trapped states
that never converge.

An independent clock exposes the difference between observables. It makes the
whole runtime distribution geometrically simple without deciding the support
of individual completed records. A vanishing clock also produces a rational
Laurent law whose residue is nontermination and whose remaining coefficients
are exact finite-path moments. Arbitrary computable time dependence crosses a
further boundary and destroys a uniform Diophantine graph even in dimension
one. These distinctions supply a concrete extension of the repository's
Diophantine-substrate program, together with an auditable arithmetic artifact
rather than a generic appeal to universality.

\section{Source 19 appendix: Verification of the characteristic recursion}
\label{pqc:iq:app:fl}
For completeness, here is a direct proof of the recursion used in the
all-moments certificate. Let
$q(u)=\det(I-uH)=\sum_{k=0}^D c_ku^k$, $c_0=1$.
The adjugate identity, or differentiation of the determinant term by term,
gives the formal identity
\[
 \frac{q'(u)}{q(u)}=-\tr\bigl(H(I-uH)^{-1}\bigr)
 =-\sum_{i\geq1}\tr(H^i)u^{i-1}.
\]
Comparing coefficients gives Newton's relation
\begin{equation}
 kc_k=-\sum_{i=1}^k c_{k-i}\tr(H^i).
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:newton}
\end{equation}
By induction, the matrices in \eqref{pqc:iq:eq:fl} satisfy
$B_{k-1}=H^{k-1}+c_1H^{k-2}+\cdots+c_{k-1}I$.
Thus $-\tr(HB_{k-1})/k$ is exactly the right side of
\eqref{pqc:iq:eq:newton} divided by $k$. The recursively computed coefficients are
therefore the coefficients of $q$. Cayley--Hamilton then gives $B_D=0$.

This proof uses divisions only by positive integer constants. Consequently
its implementation is an arithmetic circuit with additions and
multiplications after the constants $-1/k$ are pinned. The independent checker
recomputes those coefficients from the decoded rational $H$ and verifies
$B_D=0$; the mathematical proof above establishes why this recursion certifies
the characteristic polynomial for every input, not just the exported example.

\section{Source 19 appendix: A completely displayed canonical rational polynomial}
\label{pqc:iq:app:wirepoly}
For a fixed rational $a/b$ with $b>0$, define
\begin{align}
 \mathscr R_{a,b}(p,m,h,u,v_+,v_-,s)
 &=(pm)^2+(v_+v_-)^2\nonumber\\
 &\quad+\bigl((p-m)u-(h+1)(v_+-v_-)-1\bigr)^2\nonumber\\
 &\quad+(u+s-h)^2+\bigl(b(p-m)-a(h+1)\bigr)^2.
 \label{pqc:iq:eq:wirepolynomial}
\end{align}
This is an ordinary quartic polynomial over $\Z$ in seven natural variables.
It has exactly one natural zero for every fixed rational value $a/b$,
regardless of whether that displayed fraction is reduced. It is the complete
building block from which the exported larger polynomials are assembled.

The positivity of the denominator is encoded by $h+1$. The sign uniqueness
comes from products of nonnegative rails equaling zero. The coprimality and
bounded inverse are encoded by the B\'ezout and slack equations. Each feature
is necessary to justify the precise witness count and uniqueness statement;
none may be omitted merely because a generated example happens to satisfy it.

\subsection{Manuscript 07: algorithmic contracts and reproduction notes}
\label{pqc:qm:app:contracts}
\subsubsection{Rational Gram search}

The search routine uses a common-denominator presentation. At height $h$, it considers denominators $1\leq q\leq h$ and integer column vectors in $[-h,h]^s$. Candidate columns are first filtered by the equations
\[
 \lVert v_j\rVert^2=q^2Q_{jj},
\]
and then by the mutual inner products
$v_i^{\mathsf T}v_j=q^2Q_{ij}$. A successful tuple gives $B=q^{-1}(v_1,\ldots,v_d)$. Every rational matrix has such a representation for some finite $h$, so Proposition~\ref{pqc:qm:prop:d3} proves termination when $s=d+3$ and no height cap is imposed. Repeating earlier candidates is inefficient but harmless.

The implementation checks positive definiteness first. A finite height cap raises a timeout-style exception and is explicitly not interpreted as nonexistence. The same routine may be called with a smaller $s$, but then the general termination guarantee no longer applies.

\subsubsection{Polynomial serialization}

The expanded sample polynomial is stored as a list of integer coefficients and monomials. A monomial is a sorted list of variable names, with a name repeated according to its exponent. Thus
\begin{lstlisting}
{"coefficient": -2, "monomial": ["x", "x", "y"]}
\end{lstlisting}
means $-2x^2y$. The file also lists the free input names and existential witness names. The symbolic checker includes the free $H^+,H^-$ coordinates in the degree computation, which verifies the uniform degree claim rather than only a specialization to constant matrix entries.

\subsubsection{Independent checks worth repeating}

The most failure-sensitive identities are the completeness equation, the order of multiplication in the word evaluator, the fact that a zero source word may need one extra target letter, and the uniqueness of the natural sign split. These are all tested in the package and proved in the text. A useful independent review should also inspect that the inactive right block columns are zero and that no restriction on the allowable target outcome language is silently being imposed.

PDF, the two Python files, and three example JSON files. Here the manuscript
is merged into \code{article.tex}, its PDF is not shipped, and the Python
and JSON files are shipped under the prefixed names of the README. The
source compiled with a standard pdf\LaTeX{} installation, and its test

\section{The exact PWA evaluation recipe}
\label{pqc:cb:app:evaluator}

The reference compiler evaluates the global extension without expanding a
large list of affine matrices.  Locate a point in a rectangular cell with
lower corner $a$, upper corner $b$, and normalized coordinates
$t_i=(x_i-a_i)/(b_i-a_i)$.  Choose a deterministic ordering
$t_{\sigma(1)}\ge t_{\sigma(2)}\ge t_{\sigma(3)}$.
Let $v_0=a$ and form $v_j$ by changing coordinates
$\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(j)$ to their upper endpoints.  Then
\begin{equation}
 F(x)=(1-t_{\sigma(1)})F(v_0)
 +(t_{\sigma(1)}-t_{\sigma(2)})F(v_1)
 +(t_{\sigma(2)}-t_{\sigma(3)})F(v_2)
 +t_{\sigma(3)}F(v_3).
 \label{pqc:cb:eq:barycentric}
\end{equation}
All four coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one.  At ties, the formula
agrees on the common simplex face.  At rectangular boundaries, it agrees with
the adjacent cell formula.  This makes endpoint behavior explicit, including
points exactly on $1/3$, $2/3$, or a terminal slab boundary.

The Python compiler first checks terminal slab membership at a vertex, then
active emergency membership, then active low-coordinate digit membership.
Because the relevant prescribed sets are disjoint, this order is a convenient
implementation convention rather than a mathematical priority rule.  Vertices
outside all prescribed sets get the rejecting sink value.  The cache stores
rational vertex values only.

\section{A finite-certificate pseudocode contract}
\label{pqc:cb:app:checker}

A proposed safety certificate contains a mesh index $n$, an ordering of the
vertices consistent with the public grid convention, and a bit for each
vertex.  An untrusted producer may generate it by any method.  A trusted
checker can use the following contract.

\par\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\begin{lstlisting}
N := D * 2^n
V := all d-dimensional N-grid vertices, plus the exact source if absent
T := grid vertices belonging to a target box
lambda := (L + 1) / N
reject unless every certificate entry is 0 or 1
reject unless the source entry is 1 and every target entry is 0
for each ordered pair (u, v) in V x V:
    if ||v - f(u)||_infinity < lambda:
        reject if bit[u] = 1 and bit[v] = 0
accept, certifying rho >= (L + 1) / (2*N)
\end{lstlisting}
\end{minipage}\par

The inputs $f,H,L,D$ are not arbitrary unchecked text.  The checker assumes a
validated map description, a valid global Lipschitz bound, a target inside
the cube, and a denominator-clearing integer.  These form its specification.
The companion implementation checks several syntactic conditions but cannot
prove an externally supplied Lipschitz bound for an arbitrary Python callable.
For maps produced by the TM compiler, \cref{pqc:cb:lem:extension} supplies the bound.

The accepted certificate guarantees safety for every per-step budget
strictly below the reported radius bound.  This final strictness is not an
implementation detail: critical-value attainment can fail, and the radius
lower bound alone does not settle the equality case.

\section{Source and verification notes}
The repository was inspected at the pinned commit printed in
Section~\ref{pqc:sec:context}. Bibliography entries for repository sources use
that commit rather than a moving branch. The references on weakly computable
reals, probabilistic-program hardness, exact Clifford+$T$ arithmetic, and
max-relative entropy provide the established context; the proofs of the
specific budget and compiler statements appear in full in this manuscript.

No claim is made that the literature search establishes first publication
of every consequence proved here. In particular, general c.e.-to-Diophantine
existence, fair-coin representation of lower semicomputable output laws,
and the entropy formulas are not advertised as new discoveries. The primary
new deliverable of this work is the explicit synthesis of these ideas with
the canonical finite normalization certificate, including its verified
implementation and its carefully separated infinite semantics.

\section{Proof audit, provenance, and non-claims}
\label{pqc:cb:app:audit}

\subsection{Dependencies}

The core construction and quantitative results use elementary finite graph
theory, real infima, rational affine geometry, and the standard existence of a
binary universal Turing machine.  MRDP is used only to pass from an enumerable
finite-certificate predicate to one fixed polynomial.  The recurrent ReLU
corollary additionally uses the cited max--min representation theorem.
Earlier dynamics literature motivates and contextualizes the questions; its
qualitative robustness results are not substituted for the proofs of the
explicit estimates here.

\subsection{Points checked in the mathematical argument}

The real infimum need not be attained.  The source is never inadvertently
rounded.  Target rounding works for closed boxes with aligned endpoints,
including degenerate ones.  The graph is complete, so a bottleneck minimum and
finite cut minima exist.  Strict versus non-strict edge thresholds are kept
separate.  Integer polynomial subtraction is signed.  The quartic family has
varying arity, while the MRDP polynomial has fixed arity.

The Turing update formulas map entire guard boxes into the cube.  Terminal
slabs have genuine neighborhoods, and the extension is continuous across all
faces.  The rejected computation has a finite-prefix error estimate followed
by an invariant rejecting slab.  Emergency timing is indexed so that a first
rejection at $T$ can be bypassed at time $T$, not one step too late.  The
universal map is fixed before the enumerable pair is selected.  The original
machine's halting time is never silently identified with the universal
interpreter's rejection time.

\subsection{Limits of the claim}

No named classical open conjecture is declared solved.  The proposed
three-dimensional joint theorem package is presented with proofs, but without
an exhaustive novelty certification or independent peer review.  No minimal
dimension, optimal Lipschitz constant, optimal polynomial degree, optimized
network size, or finite-fold MRDP result is asserted.  No ordinary polynomial
map, smooth flow, chemical network, or physical device is claimed to implement
the construction without additional work.

The proofs and code were prepared with ChatGPT for this request.  All reported
finite tests were actually run on the included code.  No Lean verification,
repository-wide audit, expanded universal transition table, extracted ReLU
weight list, or expanded fixed MRDP polynomial is included.  The archive
contains the precise ingredients that were produced, rather than placeholders
masquerading as those further artifacts.

Their contributions:
\begin{itemize}
\item Source~10: Part~VI: unique-witness contraction certificates over $\Z[e^{i\pi/4}]$, the $\Q(\sqrt2)$ comparator, exact circuit probabilities with counts and heights, graph-state branches, the $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}$ limit, the Cauchy-name obstruction, positive and almost-sure halting of quantum controllers; twelve projects.
\item Source~11: Part~VI: the shared core's main proofs (denominator rigidity, polynomial-time decoder, matrix membership), the Miller instantiation (polynomial-time membership, c.e.-complete state transfer, order-five recurrence, no recursive precision bound), the state-transfer quartic; seven questions.
\item Source~12: Part~VII: the $2$-adic $1/2$-contraction with c.e.-complete exact extinction, Mealy realization, clock classification, flatness, the analytic horizon theorem, the bounded quartic; twelve questions.
\item Source~13: Part~V: well-conditioned sparse quartics, rounding and topology, the degree-two/degree-three counting frontier, left-c.e.\ realization with uniform constants, quantifier normal forms, finite mean, substrate transfer; ten questions.
\item Source~14: Part~VII: the rational CPWL $1/2$-contraction of $\R^4$, c.e.-complete half-space reachability, decidable point reachability, the peak function, the ReLU compiler and first-hit quartic; ten questions.
\item Source~15: Part~VII: trace quadratics for clipped networks, projective certificates, synthesis equivalent to $\Hten$, strict-target decidability, denominator height as memory; twelve questions.
\item Source~16: Part~VI: the shared core's second routes (finite-field tables, residue decoder, rank-$d$ embedding, Tarski net), the complete instantiation (local completeness, precision gap, depth of degree $\mathbf0'$, dimension obstruction), the matrix-synthesis quartic; ten questions.
\item Source~17: Part~V: reversible chains with a sharp common gap, rationality versus eventual periodicity, one-defect halting, the rational/Liouville dichotomy, Thue--Morse transcendence, prefix quartics; twelve questions.
\end{itemize}
